prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Tell a conviction you once held strongly, how it changed, and what that change shows about the way you grow.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You were sure of something once, in the language you used then. Then you were less sure, or sure of a different thing. The interesting part is rarely the victory lap of being right tonight. It is the texture of the change: what moved you, what was hard to put down, and what the whole shift reveals about how you grow.

The conviction can be small. Strength of the old belief matters more than the topic's prestige. A changed mind about cilantro, about a way of working, about money, about parenting, or about your own temperament counts. A debate about who is correct in the room tonight drops the third beat. This hour has three beats, in order, and the third one is about you.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
People tell stories of changed minds in friendship, in politics, in religion, and in apology. The stories often stop at "I was wrong," which is a confession, or at "I was right to change," which is a press release. Neither one shows the mechanism of the person. Growth, here, means a present-tense description of how change tends to happen in you. Quickly, after one witness. Slowly, by drift. Only after a failure. Only when a respected person goes first. You are letting your partner see the method, not only the result.

The three beats are a design, not a validated reflection protocol. No belief-change research is cited for this chapter, and none should be inferred. Certainty is information. This hour does not grade openness, and it does not treat a mind that has stayed sure as an immature mind. You may also, on another day, describe a conviction you still hold, and how you would recognize a real change if it arrived. That is a variation. The standard piece is a change that already happened.

If the old conviction was about the listening partner, "I used to think you were careless," name that before the story and let them opt into hearing it. This is not a reconciliation procedure. It is an account of how one person revises a belief.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
One card each, and a timer. 5 minutes in private. Write the old sentence in the language you would have used then. "I was sure that..." is a useful start, in your real diction, including the swagger or the fear. Then a plain account of what shifted it: a person, a fact, a failure, or a slow drift. Then one present-tense line about how you tend to change. If you cannot find a noble change, take a smaller one. Nobility is not a requirement. Accuracy is.

If a topic will spike the two of you, pick a different conviction before you start, while the card is still private. Changing horses in the middle of a fight is how the third beat disappears. Speech or writing both work. Use the channel you already converse in. Stay seated. A call is enough. If the room is overloaded, one conviction is the whole session.

A change that outs another person, or that retells harm done to someone else, needs a version that stays with your belief. Their private facts can leave the room. Either of you may pass and choose a lighter conviction. You may also stop.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Decide who goes first by appetite, not by who has the more impressive conversion. Set about 8 minutes. The teller speaks the three beats in order. Old sentence. What shifted it. How they tend to change. The listener does not prosecute the teller's current view, and does not applaud a flattering conversion as if the point were moral improvement. The listener asks one question, and the question is this: "What was the hardest part to let go?"

After the answer, the listener reflects the growth line back in one sentence, so the teller can correct it. "I heard that you change when you see someone treat the thing as ordinary." The teller may say, "Ordinary is right. Survive would have been too large." That correction is the listening. It is a practical check, not a clinical technique. If the reflection is fair, the teller says so in a few words. Then you swap, with equal time and the same single question.

You are done when each of you has told one conviction with all three beats, or has used the short form below, and each growth line has been reflected and either accepted or corrected. Stopping at "I was wrong" is an unfinished turn. Add the present-tense line, even if it is modest. "I change slowly, and I change by watching someone do the thing without a speech."

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
The short version takes about 15 minutes. One conviction total, chosen by the person who wants to go first, told with the three beats. The listener asks what was hardest to let go, and reflects the growth line for correction. Then the other person answers the growth question about a smaller change of their own, in a few minutes, without a full second history. The smaller change still gets a present-tense line. The hour stays mutual. It simply gives the longer story to the person who asked for it.

The standard version takes about 25 minutes. 5 minutes to write in private. About 8 minutes each, plus the one question and the reflected growth line. One conviction per person.

The extended version takes about 45 minutes. After both standard turns, each of you may add a second conviction. This time choose a taste, a habit of judgment, or a belief about relationships. Same three beats. Same question. Same chance to correct the growth line. If the second conviction is about your partner, repeat the opt-in before you speak. A second round about cilantro is complete. A second round that exists only to look profound is the one to skip.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Tell the shift from the point of view of the moment it happened, and mark what you are guessing. "I think the fact landed on a Tuesday. I am guessing about the Tuesday." The listener still asks only what was hardest to let go. They do not interview the absent person who influenced you, and you do not impersonate that person for comic effect unless the comedy can survive a real line underneath it.

On a later day, bring a conviction you still hold. Say how you would know if it changed. The partner reflects that test back in one sentence and lets you edit it. You are mapping the method, including the part that has not moved.

If you want a written trace, put the old sentence and the new sentence on the same card, with the growth line underneath. Read the card once more a week later and note whether the growth line still feels fair. Fair is the standard. Flattering is a different document.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Side by side keeps the hour from feeling like a cross-examination. A walk works if you can still hear the three beats in order and still pause. Long-distance, use a call, and send nothing until both cards are written, so the first reader is not shaping the second draft.

Replay whenever a real change has happened, including a change back. Minds are allowed to revise their revisions. Read the old growth line before you write a new one. The interest is whether the method still describes you.

If writing by hand hurts, dictate the three beats and review them before you share. Extra time is part of the accommodation, not a disruption. One conviction, chosen because it will not spike you, is a full short session on a brittle day.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. Their opinions are props.

Rowan's old sentence, in the language of an earlier year: "I was sure that wanting help was a kind of failure, and that a finished person carried their own boxes." What shifted it was a friend who asked for a ride to a clinic without apologizing, then talked about a film on the way home as if the ask had not soiled the afternoon. The growth line Rowan offers: "I change when I see someone survive the thing I was refusing."

Vale asks, "What was the hardest part to let go?" Rowan says, "The picture of myself as the one who does not need the ride." Vale reflects, "You change when you watch someone survive a need you used to despise." Rowan corrects it. "Survive is too dramatic. Despise is harsher than I was. I change when the ordinary version looks allowed." Vale repeats the corrected line and stops. There is no speech about whether Rowan accepts help often enough now.

Vale's conviction is smaller. Old sentence: "I was sure that a clean counter meant a serious life." What shifted it was a month of illness, when the counter was a disaster and the life was still theirs. Growth line: "I change when a rule fails a real week and I let the week win." Rowan reflects that line almost exactly. Vale accepts it. They do not upgrade the story into a theory of domestic virtue.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Read the old sentence and the new sentence once more, and keep the growth line only if the teller accepts it as fair. Leave the partner's commentary out of the shared book unless you both want it kept. The commentary was a tool for correction. The line that survived the correction is the souvenir.

Ask what was hard to let go, and whether the telling tried to become a debate. If it did, you can say so without restarting the debate. If an old conviction about each other still needs a different conversation, schedule that on purpose, with the right to decline. Tonight's card can stay a card about how you change, which was the assignment.

A small change, accurately told, is a complete result. You do not owe the evening a politics.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Note the date, time, place, version, mood if you want one, intention, and initials if you want them. Mark done or paused. Private pages are optional to share. In the short version, one of you may have a full conviction and the other a smaller change. Both still get lines. Revisit when a belief actually moves. Each attempt can sit under the last one.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The old sentence, the new sentence, and the growth line I accept as fair
- The hardest part to let go, in a phrase I am willing to store
partner_b:
- The growth line I reflected, and the correction you made
- The smaller change I would name if the hour had room for only one full conviction between us
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. Stories of changed minds are common in friendship, politics, religion, and apology. The three-beat structure, the single listener question, and the reflected growth line are a design for this book, not a validated protocol.

No belief-change or attitude research is cited. None was used to build the hour. Do not score openness. Do not treat certainty as immaturity. A change of mind about work, money, taste, parenting, or temperament is sufficient material.

Related experiences: 003 The Five Defining Moments, 008 The Secret Biography, and 016 No Armor Tonight.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 25 minutes · Extended 45 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Write a short biography of your own contradictions, motives, vulnerabilities, and less visible qualities, then choose which lines are heard.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Some qualities show up more clearly on a page, before a beloved face can talk you into a smoother version. You will write a short biography of yourself. It has to contain contradictions, motivations, vulnerabilities, and less visible qualities. Then you will decide which sentences another person gets to hear.

"Secret," in this chapter, means less visible. It does not mean the most dangerous fact you know, and it does not mean a vault. A spoken self-summary, a highlight reel, and a biography of your partner all miss the premise. The page is yours. The listening comes after, and only for the lines you choose to release.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Third-person self-portraits are a writing-class exercise. Therapeutic journals sometimes ask for the same material in the first person. Neither tradition tested this hour, and this chapter does not borrow their authority. What the design does is practical. You write before you speak, at a length someone can actually hear, and you include four ingredients that a public résumé leaves out.

This book asks you to put motive and feeling on the page, along with a contradiction and a quality friends underuse. That is writing advice for this biography. It is not a research result, and it is not a ranking of one kind of page against another. A list of favorite things will not meet the four ingredients. A clinical self-diagnosis will not meet them either. The page is a portrait by the person who lives in it.

Write in the third person if you can. "They are both the person who arrives early and the person who dreads the room" is often easier than "I am both," because the pronoun lets two truths sit in one sentence without a punch line rushing in to save you. First person is allowed if third person turns into a joke you cannot exit. Comedy is welcome. A sketch that never risks a real line has not started the biography.

The listening rule you will use, two questions and no edits, is this book's design, so the portrait can be received without being rewritten. It is not a result borrowed from a diary study. The notes state what that research actually reported. They also state that the study did not test writing a biography.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need paper or a private note, something to write with, and a timer. About one page, roughly 250 to 400 words, so it will actually be read. If writing hurts, take extra time. There is no required posture. Dictation counts as writing when you can review it before anyone else hears it. If reading a page is hard, dictate and then listen back alone, and cut what you do not want shared. If hearing a page read aloud is hard, exchange the pages in silence.

Agree on the order before you draft, then be quiet. On a call or across cities, exchange the pages only after both drafts are finished, so nobody writes toward a face that is already reacting. If the room is overloaded, use the four-sentence version and stop.

The author decides which sentences are read. Writing a line does not obligate sharing it. Vulnerabilities that involve ongoing harm, or another person's safety, are outside this game. Confession Without Consequence, later in the book, names a receptive style of listening. It is not immunity for harm, and a biography marked secret is not immunity either. The partner does not psychoanalyze the page, does not edit it, and does not argue with the self-portrait.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Both of you draft a short biography at the same time, in silence, contradictions included. About 20 minutes is the limit on the draft. Include four ingredients, in whatever order serves the prose.

Two traits that pull against each other. A motive that does not match the public story. One vulnerability, stated without a rescue clause. One quality friends underuse. A rescue clause is the sentence that arrives to make the vulnerability charming, impressive, or already solved. You may write that sentence on a scrap if it insists. It does not go in the portrait.

When the timer ends, you may cut. A page so long that it has to be summarized has outgrown the hour. Each author either reads aloud or hands the page over. Skip any sentence you want to keep unread, and do not apologize for the skip. Then the partner asks two questions of clarification. A clarification asks what a word points to. "When you say early, do you mean the appointment or the feeling?" is a clarification. "Here is what I think this means about your childhood" is an edit wearing a question mark. The author may answer, correct the question, or pass.

Swap. The second author gets the same silence, the same right to withhold a sentence, and the same two questions. You are done when each of you has written a portrait that contains the four ingredients, has shared only what you chose, and has heard two clarifications or a pass. If the draft turned into a biography of your partner, set it aside and write four sentences about yourself before the time is gone. Their character is not the assignment.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
The short version takes about 15 minutes. Four sentences, one per ingredient, written in the room and read at the altitude you choose. The partner asks one clarification, not two. Withholding one of the four sentences is allowed. Name the ingredient you are keeping private, or do not name it. Both choices are complete.

The standard version takes about 40 minutes. 20 minutes of simultaneous drafting, then each page read or handed over, with two clarifications and no edits. The 20 minutes overlap. You are not waiting through 40 minutes of writing before anyone speaks.

The extended version takes about 55 minutes. After both portraits have been heard, an author may add a second paragraph on where the contradiction shows up in the relationship. Only with that author's consent, asked in a sentence and answered with a yes that can be no. The partner still does not edit. If the second paragraph would require a disclosure about harm or about someone else's safety, it does not belong in this game. Stop at the first page.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A week later, reread your own page alone and underline only the sentence that still feels true. Bring that sentence back, if you want, and let your partner ask one new clarification. The rest of the page can stay in a private file. Underlining is a way to see which line had stamina.

You may invite a margin note. The partner writes one question, not a correction, in the margin or in a separate note. The author may decline to answer it. An unanswered margin is a finished exchange.

If third person keeps turning into a comedy sketch, switch to first person for the vulnerability sentence only, then return to third person for the rest. The shift in pronoun can mark the line you mean. It can also be a place you decide not to read aloud. Either use is legitimate.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Write by hand if the hand slows you into honesty. Type if the hand cramps or races. Review a dictation with the playback private. Long-distance, finish both drafts before any file is sent, and decide in advance whether the file is destroyed after the call. A biography that remains in someone else's inbox has a longer life than the hour. Say what you want done with the file.

Replay every season, or after a change in work, health, or the household. A new contradiction is allowed to replace an old one. Read the archived sentence you were willing to have remembered, and notice whether you still consent to it. Consent can expire. Cross out a stored line in the shared book when it no longer has your permission, and leave the cross-out visible if you want the record of a change.

If you want a lighter door into the same four ingredients, borrow the manners of a book jacket. Two sentences of flap copy, then the vulnerability without the jacket's usual boast. The ingredients remain. The costume is optional.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. This portrait is an illustration of the four ingredients, not a prompt you must match.

Vale writes in the third person, about 300 words, and then reads all but one sentence. The heard portion includes this passage. "Vale is the person who arrives early and the person who dreads the room once they are inside it. The public story is that Vale likes hosting. The motive underneath is a wish to have a hand on the moment people leave, because an ending Vale did not choose still lands hard. Vale is afraid of being ordinary company. Friends underuse Vale's accuracy about timing. They praise the food."

Vale says, "There is a sentence about a family member I am not reading." Rowan does not ask what it was. Rowan asks two clarifications. "When you say the moment people leave, do you mean the clock or the feeling in the doorway?" and "Which part of the hosting story do you want left as the public story?" Vale answers the first: the feeling in the doorway. Vale says the public story can stay public at parties. Rowan does not offer a better motive, does not suggest a diagnosis, and does not add a paragraph about Rowan's own arrivals. Those can be Rowan's biography, which comes next, with the same rules.

Rowan's page names a contradiction between generosity and a private ledger, a motive about being unmistakable, a vulnerability Rowan reads in one bare sentence, and a quality friends treat as fussiness that Rowan experiences as care. Vale asks what "unmistakable" points to, and whether the ledger is money or attention. Rowan answers. They put the full pages in separate private files. The shared note, later, holds one contradiction each.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Say, if you want to, which line you are willing to have remembered. Say which clarification helped, and which one you would rather not repeat. If a portrait left either of you raw, the next step can be a glass of water and a change of subject. Insight is optional. Accuracy to the page you actually released is enough.

The full biography can stay private. The shared book can hold the contradiction you consent to archive, and nothing else. If you wrote a line and then kept it back, you do not owe it to the journal, even as a hint. "Kept private" is a complete marker for anyone who wants a marker at all.

A week from now you may still like the sentence. You may not. The portrait was true enough for the hour in which you wrote it. It is allowed to age.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Record the date, time, place, version, mood if you want one, intention, and initials if you want them. Mark done or paused. Private pages are optional to share. The full biography belongs in a private file unless the author moves a sentence into the shared page. Repeat the portrait when you want a new draft. Old lines can be crossed out when consent to store them ends.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The contradiction I am willing to have remembered
- A sentence I wrote and chose not to read, noted only as "kept private" if I want a marker at all
partner_b:
- The two clarifications I asked, and what they opened
- A less visible quality I understood, in language you would accept
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. Third-person self-portraits are a writing-class exercise, and some journals ask for similar material in the first person. The four ingredients and the choice to write before speaking are this chapter's design, not a published protocol.

See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. The study did not test writing a biography. A preference for motive and feeling on this page is this book's writing advice, not an L1998 result.

Related experiences: 005 The Things Nobody Thinks to Ask, 011 What I Don’t Show the World, and 013 Confession Without Consequence.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 40 minutes · Extended 55 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Say something that is actually hard to admit, then let it sit for 3 minutes without a repair.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
One admission, then a pause before anyone repairs it. 020, The Listening Experiment, is the other shape: about 6 minutes of talk, a reflection, and a minute to correct it. Tonight is the admission. The helpful sentence is already in your mouth. You can feel it forming while the other person is still hunting for a verb. A suggestion, a brighter angle, a story of your own that proves you understand: any of those can be love on an ordinary night. In the first minute, they also move the furniture. The Uncomfortable Truth asks you to receive something that is hard to admit, and to wait before you repair it.

This is for two adults who already like each other and can share a quiet room. The admission is willing, and the speaker decides what counts as hard. A vanity counts. A fear of being ordinary counts. A kindness you withheld counts. The plot can be small. The difficulty has to be real to the person speaking.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
You know the sound of this person shrinking a feeling, and you reach for the line that will put them back together. Sometimes they want that line. Sometimes the speed of it tells them the feeling was too awkward to leave on the table. Tonight the material is one chosen admission. The pause is what keeps the repair in your pocket.

In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. See L1998 in the notes. That work did not define responsiveness as silence, and it did not test a ban on advice. The hold in this chapter is a design, so the first response can be reception.

R1988 is the framework that work drew on: disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood. It is a framework, not a script, and it is not a verdict on your relationship. Bring an admission that costs something to say. If you want advice in the same breath, say so and have that conversation on purpose. It is a good conversation. It is a different one.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can see a timer, or set one where a call will not bury it. Phones go face down. You need two seats, or two ends of a couch, and a pause phrase you will both honor. "Pause" is enough. "Smaller" is enough. Either of you can use it to stop, to choose an easier truth, or to leave the chapter.

Agree the window before anyone speaks the hard part. During the telling, and for 3 minutes after the teller stops, the listener sets aside problem-solving, bright sides, cross-examination, and a bigger confession of their own. One sentence is allowed: "I'm taking this in." Say it when you need the other person to know you are still in the room. Stillness that feels like contempt is a miss. The sentence is the railing.

Speech is the usual path. If speaking is hard, write the truth on a card. The listener reads it once, says the sentence, and sits with it. On a call, both of you put other tasks down for the window. If sound is too much, use the card and a shorter telling. Stay seated, shift, or stand. No printed text is required if you are talking. No eye contact is required at all.

Pick something you are willing to say tonight. A pass is a finished session. A smaller admission is a finished turn. If you are about to build a case against the other person, give them a conversation where they can answer. That case does not belong in a repair ban. If the truth you are holding reveals ongoing harm, abuse, or a safety problem, stop this frame. Ordinary responsibility resumes. You do not park a safety problem inside an exercise.

For this window, judgment includes scoffing, eye-rolling, and courtroom questions, along with harsh words. Surprise is allowed. A moment to breathe is allowed. The one sentence is allowed. A plan can wait until it is asked for.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
1. Say the pause phrase out loud. Decide who speaks first by preference. The second turn gets the same clock, even if the first truth was short.

2. The speaker takes a quiet minute to choose. A useful private test: would a polished anecdote be easier? If yes, you are near the right material. Keep it to one admission. If the item is an old disappointment that still has weight, 014, The Part of Me That Still Hurts, can hold that on another night. If you want curious questions about a harmless embarrassment, 013, Confession Without Consequence, is built for that menu. Tonight, one difficult admission, and a delay before repair.

3. The speaker says it in ordinary sentences. A handful is enough. You do not owe a full history and a moral. The listener listens. If they speak, the line is "I'm taking this in." "Have you tried" can wait outside the window, however gently it wants to enter.

4. When the speaker stops, the listener starts 3 minutes. Those minutes are the exercise. Comfort that smuggles a solution still counts as a solution. A matching confession, even a loving one, waits its turn. If the quiet starts to feel like a wall, the listener may repeat the permitted sentence and stop there.

5. When the 3 minutes end, the speaker chooses. They may ask for a response and name the kind: what you heard, one question, or an idea. They may also end the turn. Ending the turn means the truth was received. It does not mean anyone failed.

6. If a response was requested, keep it inside the kind they named, and keep it short. Then swap. The second speaker gets a full telling and a full 3 minutes. The listener does not grade the two truths against each other. Difficulty is the speaker's to name.

7. Say whether you are done. One truth each, received under the rule, completes the standard session.

A laugh can happen because people are ridiculous and dear. Let it be brief and kind. A joke that shrinks the admission belongs outside the window. Either person can call the pause phrase, trade for an easier truth, or save the rest.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 10 minutes.** One truth in the room. The listener keeps the rule for the telling and the 3 minutes. After that, schedule the second person's turn, or let them offer a smaller admission if they want a turn now. A scheduled turn is a real session. It is not an IOU pinned to someone's courage.

**Standard, about 30 minutes.** One truth each, with the telling, the quiet minutes, and either a requested response or a clean stop. Use this when you have half an hour and the thing you might say does not need a crisis plan.

**Extended, about 50 minutes.** Finish the standard round. Only if both of you still want more, take a second round. The second truth can be smaller. Stop when appetite stops. If one of you is done, the extended path closes, and the chapter is still complete.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
After both turns, a speaker may ask for one response they did not want inside the window: a reflection of what it meant, a single question, or practical help. One kind. The listener does that, then stops.

On another night you can return to the same truth and notice only the reception. You are allowed to keep the content the same. You can also name a category you are leaving closed, "a vanity," "a withheld kindness," and let that sentence be your whole contribution. A pass with a shape is still a pass.

When you want a style rule on a modest topic, 016, No Armor Tonight, asks you to set jokes-as-cover, defensiveness, and impressive answers down for a few minutes. When you want a longer stretch of uninterrupted speech and a reflection, 020, The Listening Experiment, is the room for that. Play those when you want them. This chapter stays with one hard admission and a short ban on fixing it.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
On a walk, keep the same rule and a phone timer in a pocket. On a call, name the window at the start so a lag in the audio does not get stuffed with advice. If one of you thinks more clearly on paper, the card is the session.

Replay when the truths change, or when the same truth gets a steadier reception. Some pairs need the permitted sentence twice, so the quiet has a handle. Some pairs need the listener's hands on a mug. Keep whichever railing helps, and retire it when it starts to feel like a performance.

A low-energy version is the short path, under a blanket, card optional. Skip any demand to gaze. If the day has already been a lot, choose a small hard truth on purpose. Small and difficult is the design, not a warmup you must outgrow.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
A fictional pair, Rowan and Vale. They are not you.

Rowan says, "I still check who responded to the thing I made public, and I hate that I care. I want you to think I am above being ranked."

Vale feels a speech about self-worth lining up. They leave it where it is. "I'm taking this in."

The mug is warm. The 3 minutes are clumsy, then merely quiet. Rowan says, "Tell me what you heard. No ideas yet."

Vale says, "You care about being ranked, and you don't want that caring to lower you in my eyes."

Rowan says, "Yes. The advice can stay in your pocket."

Vale starts, "Have you tried leaving the phone in another room," and stops. Rowan says, "Leave it." The advice stays declined for the rest of the night. They do not reopen it over the dishes.

They do not swap into a second confession. Vale says, "I'm not telling one tonight." Rowan nods. The decline stays. There is no smaller substitute, and Rowan does not spend the 3 minutes waiting Vale into a speech.

The rule gets lost if Vale finishes the phone advice, or if Rowan treats the pass as too small to count. It also gets lost if Rowan uses the turn to prosecute something Vale did last week. That prosecution needs a conversation with answers in it.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay a few minutes. You might ask:

- Did the 3 minutes feel like company?
- Which sentence were you glad you held?
- Did either of you perform a freeze and call it respect?
- Do you want a response later, and if so, what kind?

You may feel tender, foolish, or strangely ordinary. The chapter is complete if a difficult thing was said and received under the rule, or if you passed on purpose. Nothing here has to arrive as a revelation.

If the truth opened a practical problem you do need to solve, set a different time for the solving. The delay was the point of the window. Help is still allowed in the rest of your life.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Private pages are optional to share. Keep the wording of the truth off this page if you want it to stay spoken. A note about being received is a full record.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Whether you felt received, in a few words, without rewriting the truth
- What you wanted after the window: silence, a reflection, or a stop
partner_b:
- What it was like to have only one permitted sentence
- A response you held back, named by type (advice, cheer, a question), not by retelling what you heard
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. A willing admission, plus a time-limited hold on judgment and repair, is a designed exercise. The advice to hold off fixing is common in peer support and in couples education. It is not a validated protocol, and this chapter has not been tested as a couple intervention.

See L1998. In diary studies, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. Withholding advice is not what that work measured.

See R1988. Reis and Shaver describe intimacy as an interpersonal process: disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood. The model is a framework. It does not script these 3 minutes.

Neighbors, when you want them: 013 Confession Without Consequence, 014 The Part of Me That Still Hurts, 016 No Armor Tonight, and 020 The Listening Experiment.

experiences.title: The Fear Beneath the Fear

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Start from a fear you can already name, then walk down two more steps to a need, an experience, or a belief.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Start from a fear you can already say. The party. The waiting room. The quiet worry that you will be the less interesting person at the table. Any of those can be true and still be standing on something else: a need, an old experience, a belief about what counts. The Fear Beneath the Fear is a short ladder. Three lines. Then you stop, while the fear is still a size you chose.

You start with a fear you can already say. Your partner does not get to announce the "real" one. The lower line is yours, and it is not certified truer by being lower.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A named fear is often a doorway with a label already on it. Ask what sits under it, and a second thing becomes speakable: the need to be accompanied, the memory of being left in a hallway, the belief that a quiet life will be scored as small. The value is in hearing the lower line in the speaker's words. The value is not in winning a deeper diagnosis.

In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. See L1998. That work did not test layered questions, and it did not show that a lower layer is truer than the surface fear. The listener's rule in this chapter is separate from that finding: say back what you heard, then wait to be corrected.

"And what is under that?" is a familiar move in coaching and in therapy, sometimes stretched into a long drill. This chapter is a consent-bound ladder for two adults, three lines and no more. It is not those methods, and it is not a protocol anyone has validated on your behalf.

097, The Emotional Archaeologists, begins somewhere else. It starts from a powerful reaction and holds off interpreting it. This chapter starts from a fear you can already name, then looks for a need, an experience, or a belief underneath. The bottom line is a sentence you are willing to own tonight. It is not a verdict. Keep both chapters. Use this one when the fear has a name you can say for about 10 minutes. Use 097 when a reaction is already hot and you want to slow the naming. They ask different questions, and neither one retires the other.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need a pencil, a timer, and a card with three stacked lines labeled Surface, Under it, and Under that. Spoken sentences work if writing is painful or if you would rather not see the words on paper. Pointing at the next line can replace the spoken question if hearing is hard. On a call, each person can use a private note and read the three lines when it is time.

Pick a fear you can talk about without a crisis plan. Useful scale: a party, a medical wait that is already being handled, the chance of being the less interesting one in a group. Leave aside a phobia, a panic, or a fear you have never said and do not want to say. If a layer arrives as "I don't know," that line is complete. You are not instructed to dig until anyone cries. There is no darkened room, no breath-holding, and no cue to stay inside the fear for endurance.

If the fear is that your partner is hurting you, this ladder is the wrong tool. Say that plainly and choose a different conversation, one with room for limits and help. Either of you may stop the descent at any line. The bottom line is not a lever for later arguments.

Agree a pause word before you start. Changing the fear for a smaller one is an ordinary move.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
1. Each person privately picks one fear at the agreed scale. Write the surface line, or hold it in mind. One sentence. "I am afraid of the reunion" is a full surface. A speech is optional and usually in the way.

2. The speaker reads the surface fear. The partner asks only, "What might sit under that?" They do not offer a candidate. The speaker writes the next line themselves. If the honest line is "I don't know," they write that.

3. Repeat once. The partner asks the same question. The speaker writes the third line. Stop at three, even if a fourth feels tempting. The method can feel powerful. Power is a reason to keep the limit.

4. The last line has to name a need, an experience, or a belief, in the speaker's words. "I need company in rooms where I might be invisible." "I still feel the year nobody saved me a seat." "I believe a life has to be narratable or it does not count." If the third line is still "I don't know," add a short tail that makes the kind clear: "I don't know the need yet, and I believe I am supposed to." That tail is enough. You are not required to produce a cleaner insight.

5. The partner reads the three lines back, slowly, and asks, "What did I scramble?" The speaker corrects the wording. A scramble is any place the listener improved, deepened, or translated the line into their own theory. The correction stands. The listener does not argue for their version.

6. Swap. Equal time. The second ladder gets the same three lines, the same single question, and the same chance to fix a scramble.

7. Stop. Thank each other for the wording, not for how far you went. Going far is not the score.

The listener's job is to keep the question clean and the read-back faithful. Supplying the deeper fear, even as a loving guess, takes the pencil out of the speaker's hand.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 12 minutes.** Two layers each. Surface, then one line under it. The second line still names a need, an experience, or a belief if you can reach one. If you cannot, "I don't know" closes the short ladder. Use this when attention is thin, the room is loud, or you want a practice run of the form.

**Standard, about 25 minutes.** Three lines each, a read-back, and a correction. This is the chapter as designed. The timer is there so the third line does not become an hour.

**Extended, about 40 minutes.** Finish both standard turns. Then each person says what help would fit the bottom line. The other person listens and does not commit tonight. "Company at the door of the party" can be heard without becoming a promise. If either of you is spent after the ladders, skip the help sentence and call the session done.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A week later, you may look at the bottom line and ask whether any small, decline-able request belongs beside it. The request is a separate sentence. The ladder does not force it. "I might ask you to walk in with me" can be answered yes, no, or not that night.

You can also replay the form on a lighter fear, just to feel the three-line limit when the stakes are mild. Practice is allowed to be easy. A fourth line is still off the card.

087, The Question Behind the Question, follows an ordinary answer with successive questions. It is a different staircase, aimed at meaning in everyday replies. This chapter is three lines and a fear you already chose. Both can live in a month. Use 015, When I Feel Small, when the lower line is about inadequacy or being overlooked and you want to know which reassurances actually help.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Writing is optional. Three spoken sentences, repeated back, are a full ladder. Vision needs no card if the lines are spoken. Long-distance works at a quiet table on each end, cameras optional. If sensory load is high, use the short version and a long pause between turns.

Replay with a new fear, or with the same surface and a new willingness to let "I don't know" stay on line two. The interesting change is often in the scramble: what your partner hears the second time, and what you still have to correct. Do not treat a repeated bottom line as a personality. It is a sentence from a night.

If you want the card to survive, date it and keep it in private pages. Many people will want only the bottom line stored, not the whole descent. That choice belongs to the speaker.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
A fictional pair, Rowan and Vale. They are not you.

Rowan's card:

Surface: "I am afraid of the reunion."

Under it: "I don't know."

Under that: "I need my life to be tellable, and I believe a quiet one gets scored as small."

Vale reads the three lines and scrambles the middle into "You don't care about the reunion." Rowan says, "That's the scramble. I care. I don't know what the caring is made of yet. The third line is the belief, and I don't want it upgraded into 'Rowan thinks Rowan is boring.'"

Vale repeats the third line as written. They do not offer a better fear.

Vale's ladder, spoken because Vale dislikes the pencil:

Surface: "I am afraid of the test results, even though the plan is already in place."

Under it: "I am afraid of the afternoon in the waiting room with nothing to do but imagine."

Under that: "I need a pointless task in my hands, and I have a history of white rooms where nobody told me the next step."

Rowan reads it back cleanly. Vale says, "You didn't scramble it. Leave it."

They do not add a fourth line about childhood, though both can feel one hovering. The card ends at three.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
You might ask:

- Which line was easiest to say, and which one did you almost edit into something more impressive?
- Did your partner put a theory in your mouth, and did the correction land?
- Does the bottom line want company, a practical help, or privacy?
- Are you willing to let the surface fear remain true, even after you saw under it?

The surface fear does not expire because a belief showed up beneath it. You can still be afraid of the party. The lower line gives that fear a floor. It does not have to abolish it.

If the descent stirred more than you wanted, stop and do something ordinary. Tea, a window, a stupid show. You are not required to keep the lamp on the lowest layer.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Private pages are optional to share. The speaker chooses whether the card is copied here. Many will keep only the need, the experience, or the belief, and leave the rest of the ladder in the room where it was said.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The bottom line you are willing to keep, if any: a need, an experience, or a belief
- Whether three lines were enough, or whether you stopped earlier
partner_b:
- What you were glad the other person did not invent for you
- What help would fit your bottom line, with no promise attached
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. A short, consent-bound ladder is a design. No therapy manual and no five-whys study was opened for this chapter. Do not treat the third line as the true fear. Do not cite this exercise as a test of anything clinical.

See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. Layered questioning was not the method, and a deeper sentence was not shown to be truer. The read-back is this chapter's listener rule. It is not a definition taken from L1998.

097, The Emotional Archaeologists, remains its own chapter: a powerful reaction, interpretation delayed. This one remains a named fear and three lines. Play either, or both, when the starting point matches.

Also nearby: 015 When I Feel Small, and 087 The Question Behind the Question.

experiences.title: What I Don’t Show the World

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Name a specific part you keep offstage, and the conditions that would make showing it less costly.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Most people keep a second coat on the hook. The one in public is competent, funny, a little above needing anything. Under it there is a tenderness, an ambition, a shame, a taste you have decided the room cannot hold. What I Don’t Show the World asks for both halves of that fact: one specific hidden part, and the conditions that would make showing it less costly.

Hiding can be skill. Privacy is not a flaw this chapter is here to cure. A reveal with no conditions is a dare. A list of conditions with nothing hidden is a memo. You need the pair.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
The world in the title is flexible. It may include your partner, and it may mean everyone except your partner. You get to say which. Sometimes the useful news is not the secret. It is the rule that has been protecting it: who may be in the room, what happens to the information, which joke is retired, how fast advice is allowed to arrive.

In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. See L1998. Those diaries did not map hiding, and they did not test a conversation about safety conditions. Perceived safety in this chapter is the speaker's report. It is not a measured state, and writing a condition down does not create it.

R1988 is only a framework: disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood. The choice of what stays covered remains yours. The design here is the pair of prompts, a hidden part plus conditions a person could actually offer.

If the part is already known between you, the live half is often somewhere else: where it is still hidden from other people, and what your partner does that helps that privacy or complicates it. 002, The Life You’ve Never Told Me, is for an episode they have never heard in detail. 008, The Secret Biography, is a written portrait of contradictions. This chapter is narrower. One part, and the terms.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need a page with two columns, Hide and What would help, plus a pen and a timer. Typing or dictation into a private note is the same draft. Trade paper or talk if vision or hearing makes one of them easier. Stay seated. Take extra draft time if pain asks for it. On a call, draft offline, then read. If the day is already loud, one item is the whole session. No audience, no group, and no recording unless you both ask for it.

Agree that either of you may leave an item in the unread column. A pass is a finished contribution. Changing a prompt to something smaller is ordinary. Agree a pause word before you write.

Each item in Hide should be specific. A tenderness, an ambition, a shame, a taste. "The real me" is too large to use, and it turns the page into a performance of mystery. Beside each item, write two conditions another person could actually offer. At least one of them should be a behavior you could see: who is in the room, what they do with the information afterward, what they do not joke about, how soon they give advice.

A part that involves harm, illegal risk, or another person's safety is not a reveal-for-intimacy item. Leave it off the page. This exercise does not ask for the thing you are most afraid to say.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
1. Write in private. The page is a hidden part you might actually say, and the conditions that would make saying it less costly. About 8 minutes is the limit on the draft. Two items in Hide, so one can stay unread. Two conditions beside each. Keep the conditions observable. "Be trustworthy" is a wish. "Ask me once, then wait a week before you mention it again" is a condition.

2. Mark, for the item you might read, whether it is hidden from everyone or only outside this relationship. That sentence can be spoken even if you leave the content vague.

3. Each person chooses one pair to read. The other item can stay unread. Say so if you are leaving it: "One stays in the unread column." You do not owe its name.

4. Read the pair. The partner's only reply is a restatement of the conditions, plus whether they can offer each one, cannot, or are unsure. They do not negotiate the conditions down. They do not answer "You are safe with me" as a blanket. They do not turn the condition into a plan to fix the feeling.

5. The speaker corrects the restatement if a condition got softened. The corrected version stands.

6. Swap, with equal time. The second person is not required to match the size or the category of the first reveal.

7. Stop. You have finished when each person who wanted a turn has been heard under that reply rule, or has passed.

If your partner already knows the part, use the turn for the outer world. Where is it still hidden, and what does your partner do, in actual behavior, that protects that or makes it harder? "You announce it at dinner" is a complication with a shape. "You love me" is not yet a condition.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 15 minutes.** One pair each. Drafting can be a few quiet minutes, or a single spoken pair if writing is the hard part. The reply rule stays the same: restate, then can, cannot, or unsure.

**Standard, about 30 minutes.** About 8 minutes of private drafting, two items each, then one pair read aloud by each person. The second item remains on the page, unread, unless you both move to the extended path.

**Extended, about 45 minutes.** After the standard round, each person may read the second written item. It is still optional. Unread is a complete ending. If you read it, the same reply rule applies, and you still do not promise a blanket of safety.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
You can take one condition and make it so concrete that a stranger could see it on a video. "Don't make it weird" becomes "If I tell you I still write songs, you do not sing them back at the table." The partner says again whether that behavior is one they can offer.

On another night, look only at a part that is hidden from other people and already known between you. The question is what the partner's habits do to that privacy. Helps, complicates, or both. This is information, not a trial of their character.

012, The Permission Slip, is a neighbor when the hidden part is less a secret than a way of being you have not allowed yourself. You can do that chapter with the condition still in mind. You do not have to open the hidden content in order to sign a permission.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Low energy: one item, spoken, conditions included, then stop. Outdoors works if you can write on a phone note and no one is close enough to overhear. Budget is a pen. Mobility stays in the chair you already have.

Replay when the conditions change, or when you want to test one condition for a week and report only whether you used it. Do not collect hidden parts as a series you must complete. A month later, the interesting line is often the condition you still want remembered, not a new confession.

If you both like written portraits, 008 can come later, and you may still leave this chapter's unread column unread. Different pages, different jobs.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
A fictional pair, Rowan and Vale. They are not you.

Rowan's page has two items. They read one.

"I want to apply for the night program, and I have not told friends. Hidden from everyone outside this room. Conditions: you do not mention it to anyone this month, and if you ask, you ask one question and then leave it. No jokes about the odds."

Vale says, "You want silence outside this room for a month, one question from me, and no odds joke. I can keep it quiet. I can skip the joke. I am unsure about asking only once, because I get curious. I will not promise a feeling of safety. I can promise the quiet and the skipped joke."

Rowan says, "Keep those two. Leave the question unless I open it."

Vale does not improve the ambition, does not offer a study plan, and does not say that Rowan is safe in general.

Vale's turn is a taste, not a matching ambition. "I still get teary at a particular cartoon, and I hide it from colleagues. At home you already know. Conditions: if your sister is here, you do not bring it up as a bit. If we are alone, you can sit down and not narrate it."

Rowan restates both conditions and says they can do both. Vale leaves the second written item, a shame, in the unread column, and says only that. Rowan does not guess.

The instructions fail if Vale says, "What if the quiet only lasts a week, that is more realistic," or if Rowan treats the cartoon as too small to need conditions. They also fail if either person presses for a larger secret than the one offered.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
You might ask:

- Which condition was the one you actually needed, and which was decoration?
- Did "can," "cannot," or "unsure" feel more usable than a promise?
- Is this part hidden from everyone, or only past the door of this relationship?
- What, if anything, do you want tried this week, as a behavior?

You may feel more known, or you may feel that the coat stays on, and that is the right call. Both are finishes. Naming a condition is not the same as being safe, and it is not a repair for the feeling underneath the hidden part.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Private pages are optional to share. The condition you want remembered is the line this page is for. The hidden content can stay off it.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The condition you want remembered, without the hidden content unless you choose to write it
- Whether this part is hidden from everyone or only outside the two of you, if you want that noted
partner_b:
- A condition you can offer, cannot offer, or are unsure about
- Anything left unread, recorded only as "left unread" if you want a mark at all
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. Talk of masks and private selves is everyday language. The paired prompt, a hidden part plus conditions, is a design. It has not been tested as a couple intervention. Naming a condition does not create safety.

See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. The diaries did not map hiding, and they did not test a safety-conditions conversation. Perceived safety here is the speaker's report, not a measured state.

See R1988. The framework is disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood.

Neighbors: 002 The Life You’ve Never Told Me, 008 The Secret Biography, and 012 The Permission Slip.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 30 minutes · Extended 45 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Sign your own permission to be unfinished in one specific way, and let your partner hear it without granting it.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
A permission slip is a school object with one serious trick. It lets someone leave the room they are supposed to stay in. In this chapter you are the person who signs it. Your partner may witness the sentence. They do not become the office that approves your personality.

The menu is a pile of examples, not six assignments: imperfect, playful, uncertain, ambitious, needy, emotionally open. One true permission is the whole exercise. Six tidy adjectives, cranked out so the list is covered, miss the point.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A lot of self-management is a private hall pass you never write down. You may speak once the answer is polished. You may be silly once the kitchen is finished. You may want something once you have proved you do not need it. The slip makes one of those rules visible, and it puts the signature on your side of the table.

No empirical study is claimed for this activity. Permission slips are a familiar prop from school and, later, from self-help writing prompts. Used here, the prop does one job: one adult authorizes a specific way of being, and another adult hears the sentence without taking it over. That is a design. It is not a treatment, and it is not a complete model of a healthy personality. The six words in the premise are examples of doors you might open. They are not a chart of the self.

Witnessing is optional. You may write the slip and put it in a book, unread. If you do read it, the witness says what they heard and stops. Improvements to your wording wait until you ask for them. A joke that dissolves the sentence before it has been heard sends you back to the hallway.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Each of you needs a small card and a pen, and a surface that can be a table or a lap. Large print or a phone note works. If writing hurts, dictate, and still choose the final words yourself. If one of you cannot see the card, the witness reads it back and then stops. If hearing is hard, exchange the cards in silence and read them with your eyes. On a call, draft first, then read, or send the sentence after both drafts exist. If the room is overloaded, one sentence and a break. No candles, no audience, no ceremony.

The sentence has three parts when you are playing the standard version: the permission, the situation where it is hard, and one thing you will stop requiring of yourself this week. Keep it specific enough that you could notice it happening on a Tuesday.

A slip that is really a rule for the other person has to be rewritten. "I give myself permission to need a reply within 5 minutes" puts their phone on the card. Permission to be needy, or emotionally open, does not license you to ignore their limits. If the want would land on their body, their time, or their money, the slip stays a self-permission until you make a separate request, and that request can be declined.

Either of you can pass, write and pocket the card, or change the adjective. One honest permission outranks a complete set.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
1. Read the menu once, aloud or silently: imperfect, playful, uncertain, ambitious, needy, emotionally open. Circle nothing. Let one word tug, or ignore the menu and write the permission that is actually yours.

2. Draft in silence. Shape, if you want a shape: "I give myself permission to be [one way] when [a real situation], and I will stop requiring [a specific self-demand] of myself this week." The weekly clause is for the standard and extended versions. It is a practice, not a vow to become a new person by Sunday.

3. Read the sentence to yourself. Ask whether you signed it, or whether you wrote your partner a job. If their body, time, or money is the object of the sentence, split the card. The permission stays. The request, if you still want to make it, waits for a separate, decline-able sentence after the exercise, or on another day.

4. Read aloud only if you want to. The witness says what they heard, in a sentence or two, then stops. They do not upgrade the wording. They do not add a virtue you left out. They do not grant the permission with "You have my blessing" or "I allow it." You already signed.

5. If you want a wording change, ask. Otherwise the card stands as written, including a clumsy phrase you meant.

6. Swap. Equal time, including the right to keep a card unread.

7. Optional: put the card in a wallet, a book, or the private journal. Date it. The witness's reaction stays off the card unless you invite it on.

You are done when each person who wanted a slip has either signed one or chosen not to show it. There is no second signature required.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 10 minutes.** One sentence each. Permission and situation. No weekly clause. Read it or pocket it. If you read it, the witness reflects and stops.

**Standard, about 25 minutes.** Silent drafting, the full sentence with the weekly clause, optional reading, a witness reflection, then the swap. This is the version that fits a kitchen table after dinner.

**Extended, about 40 minutes.** After the first slips, write a second card for a different example from the menu, only if you want a second door. Add one note about how a witness can avoid trampling the permission. "Do not finish the sentence for me." "Do not clap." "Do not turn it into a plan." The witness hears that note and does not negotiate it into something easier for them.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Take the weekly clause into the actual week, then add one dated line later: used, unused, or used and awkward. Awkward counts. The slip is not a streak.

If the permission was "needy" or "emotionally open," write the separate request on a different card, in a form the other person can refuse. "I may ask you to sit with me for 10 minutes tonight. No is a complete answer." Keep the permission and the request from collapsing into one instruction.

016, No Armor Tonight, is useful when the permission is about plain speech and the joke usually gets there first. 011, What I Don’t Show the World, is useful when the permission depends on a condition about who hears it. 028, Instructions for Loving Me, is a wider manual. This slip is one line, signed by the author.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Write a slip for a role that is usually polished: the host, the competent one, the person who does not make a fuss. Or write one for a private hour, with no witness at all. Both are the chapter.

Replay on a different adjective, or on the same one in a new situation. Money, a party, a creative project, a sick day. Retire a slip that has become a slogan you no longer mean. The interesting revisit is whether you stopped requiring the old thing of yourself, even once.

Low energy: the short sentence, in bed, dictated into a phone. Long-distance: draft apart, read on a call, hang up before either of you edits the other. If you want a keepsake, the card is the keepsake. Date it and keep it with the private pages or in the book.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
A fictional pair, Rowan and Vale. They are not you.

Rowan writes, "I give myself permission to be ambitious about the workshop I want to teach, even when the plan is half finished, and I will stop requiring a full syllabus before I let the idea be heard."

Vale says, "I heard permission to be ambitious while the plan is unfinished, and a stop to waiting for a full syllabus before you speak." Vale does not add, "You should also be confident," and does not offer a schedule.

Vale's card: "I give myself permission to be playful on a weeknight while the dishes are still in the sink, and I will stop requiring a finished kitchen before I am allowed to be silly."

Rowan reflects the sentence and stops. Nobody improves "silly."

A slip they do not use, shown here so the failure has a shape: "I give myself permission to need you to answer within 5 minutes." That sentence is a rule for the other person. The repair, if they want one, is a self-permission ("I give myself permission to be needy and say so") and, separately, a request the partner can decline.

They keep the real cards. Vale does not sign Rowan's ambition. Rowan does not sign Vale's silliness. The ink is already dry on the author's side.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
You might ask:

- Which self-demand did you actually name, and which one did you almost hide inside a nobler sentence?
- Did the witness stop, or did a better version try to climb onto the card?
- Is there a request sitting next to this permission that still needs its own yes or no?
- Do you want the card in a pocket, or was saying it enough?

The week will not grade you. One use of the permission is a use. Forgetting it is information, not a broken streak. You can write the slip again when the old requirement sneaks back.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Private pages are optional to share. The permission sentence can live here, dated, with a later line for whether you used it. The witness's reaction stays off the card unless you invite it.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Your permission sentence, if you want it written here
- One place this week where you might use it
partner_b:
- Your permission sentence, in your own wording, if you want it kept
- How you want a witness to avoid trampling it
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: reimagined. A school object and a self-help writing prompt, used so the author signs and the partner may witness. No empirical citation is claimed. No self-compassion trial was opened or cited. The six adjectives are a menu of examples, not a model of personality, and this slip has not been tested as a couple intervention.

A want that would land on a partner's body, time, or money remains a self-permission until a separate request is made. That request can be declined.

Neighbors: 011 What I Don’t Show the World, 016 No Armor Tonight, and 028 Instructions for Loving Me.
