experiences.title: Two Truths and a Beautiful Lie

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Three short stories, one of them a generous fiction, and a second look at the two that really happened.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Three peer stories, then a guess. Two of them happened. One is a beautiful fiction, artful, comic, or generous, and its own scene, not a symbol tucked into a real day. You will each tell them at about the same size. Then you uncover, and you spend the last minute of the round on the stories that are true.

107, The Memory Smuggler, is one true story with one symbolic seam, three guesses, and then the real version. This chapter does not hide a stitch. The guess is play. It is a grin across the table, a reason offered for the sport of it. It is a poor instrument for deciding whether someone really knows you. The truths are the part you keep.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Three stories of about the same size, two that happened and one made, give you something a fact cannot. You get the pace, the embarrassment, the detail they bother to include.

The beautiful lie has a job too. It lets the teller be inventive without spending a real secret. A flattering adventure that never occurred, a comic mishap in a city they have never visited, a tiny honor nobody awarded: these are fictions that can sit beside the truth without kicking it. When the fiction is uncovered in a single sentence, the two true stories get restated as things worth remembering. The evening ends on a life, not on a successful fraud.

Another chapter in this book, The Memory Smuggler, hides one invented detail inside an otherwise true memory. That detail stands for a wish, a fear, or a possibility that has not happened, and the listener tries to find it. Two Truths and a Beautiful Lie uses three separate stories. Two are wholly true. One is wholly made. The made story is its own scene, not a symbol tucked into a real day. Both games can live in the same season. They ask for different kinds of attention.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can hear each other, or open a note you can both read. You need a timer and a way to make three stories look alike. Paper, index cards, or three text messages all work. Speech and print are equal methods. If one of you would rather not perform aloud, read the cards in turn, or exchange them in a long-distance chat labeled only Story 1, Story 2, and Story 3.

Give yourselves a way to pass. The teller may throw out a story before it is told. The listener may pass on the guess. A pass is a finished move. You still uncover the round if the teller wants the truths heard, or you set the cards aside and take the other person's turn.

Leave sex, health, and other people's private lives off the cards. Leave out any story that would hurt if it were true, or hurt if it were false. A beautiful lie is a terrible place to hide a real betrayal. If a scene would matter in your actual life, it is the wrong scene. Replace it with a generous invention before the round starts.

Agree the length out loud: about 1 minute each, roughly 120 to 160 spoken words, or eight to 12 lines on a card. Similar length is the fairness. If one story runs long, the teller cuts it before anyone guesses, so duration is not a clue.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Play at least two rounds, one telling from each of you. A round belongs to one teller.

**Prepare, privately, for about 8 minutes.** The teller builds three stories from their own life and invention. The listener can make tea, or start drafting their own set for the next round, without peeking.

Each true story is a scene, not a trivia chip. "I once ate oysters" is too thin to stand beside a minute of narrative. Give the truth a place, a small trouble, and a detail you can picture: the borrowed coat, the bus that waited, the class where the clay refused to center. You are allowed to tell a story the other person has never heard. You are also allowed to tell one they know, if you tell it as a scene and not as a quiz.

The fiction is a whole story, invented from the first sentence to the last. It should be able to stand next to the truths without mocking them. Use one of these shapes if you want a pattern:

- A flattering adventure that did not happen. You were briefly mistaken for someone useful, you played along kindly, and the thanks were slightly absurd.
- A comic mishap in a city you have never visited. Name the city to yourself so you remember it is fiction. Keep the mishap small and survivable: a parade, a wrong train, a pastry bigger than the plan.
- A tiny honor that was never awarded. A prize for patience, a ceremonial spoon, a ribbon for returning a lost glove with unusual style. The honor should make the teller look human, not saintly, and it should not mock a real person in the room.

Apply this test before you speak. If the story mocks your partner or anyone else, replace it. If the "fiction" is actually a real undisclosed wound wearing a costume, replace it. If you would be ashamed for the story to be false, it is not beautiful yet. Cruelty does not qualify, however well it is told.

Label nothing. Mix the three so the fiction is not always in the middle. Number them only as Story 1, Story 2, and Story 3.

**Tell.** Read or speak the three stories in order, with a short breath between them. The listener listens. No cross-examination in the middle. If you are playing by text, send them as three separate messages of similar length.

**Guess.** The listener names which story they think is the fiction, and gives one reason. The reason can be structural ("that city arrived with too much scenery") or affectionate ("you would have told me about the spoon"). The listener may pass. If they pass, say so, and move to the uncovering. A confident guess is not a verdict on intimacy. A miss is not a hole in the relationship. You have lived a great many days, and some of them have not been reported.

**Uncover.** The teller does this in a set order, so the truths get the last word.

1. Name the fiction in one sentence. "The parade was the invention. I have never been to that city."
2. Restate the first truth as something you want remembered. One or two sentences, in your ordinary voice.
3. Restate the second truth the same way.

The listener does not grade the performance. They may say which detail they are keeping. If a story landed badly, the teller may retire it on the spot: "Leave that one here. Remember the other." Retired means retired. It does not become a topic for the rest of the night unless the teller opens it.

Then you switch. The second teller uses a fresh set of three. Do not reuse the first round's fiction as a template so obvious that the guess is automatic, unless you both think that is funny and you say so.

**If the round snags.** Stories of wildly different lengths: stop and trim before the guess. The listener spots the lie in the first sentence: laugh, and still do the uncovering. The teller realizes, mid-story, that the lie has a sharp edge: stop, say "I am replacing that one," and tell a kinder fiction of the same length, or end the round with the two truths only. Tired: one round each is a complete game.

**What you might print.** Three cards per person, blank on the face, with a small 1, 2, or 3 on the back if you want to keep order without labeling the lie. A shared slip titled "Keep" with two lines, one for each truth you restated. Large type if you are reading. No board and no score column. Matches are a pleasure. They are not a tally of who knows whom.

**Ending.** The game ends when both of you have uncovered a set and each of you has named at least one truth you want kept. Close by reading those kept lines once, slowly, without voting on the fictions again.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 15 minutes.** One round each. Keep every story near 30 seconds, four to six sentences, still a scene. Guess in a phrase. Uncover in three sentences total. This is the version for a weeknight or for fatigue. You still each tell, and you still restate the truths.

**Standard, 40 minutes.** About 8 minutes of private drafting, then a full minute for each story, a guess with a reason, and a proper uncovering. Two rounds, one apiece. Leave a few minutes at the end to say which true detail you are glad entered the room.

**Extended, 70 minutes.** Play the standard game, take a break, then each tell a second set. The second fiction should change shape: if the first was a fake honor, the next might be a comic mishap. After the second uncovering, choose one true story from the night and retell it in two sentences you would be willing to see in a letter later. The letter is optional. The two sentences are the souvenir.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Stay with stories, and raise the care, not the stakes. In a deeper round, each true story comes from a different decade or a different city, so the listener meets more than the current year. The fiction stays light. Depth in this chapter means a truer scene, a more specific sensory detail, a truth you had filed as too ordinary to tell. It does not mean a confession you have been avoiding, and it does not mean a fiction that confesses by disguise.

After the second set, you may each ask one question about a truth, not about the lie. "What did you do with the clay afterward?" is a fine question. "How did you keep a straight face?" is a question about craft, and it can wait. If a truth opens a door you would like to walk through on another night, name the door and leave it shut for now. Entry 083, The Secret Nobody Would Guess, is a place for a volunteered surprise. Entry 047, Truth, Dare, or Discover, is a place for a game with more than one kind of turn. This chapter's deeper round still ends by restating what was true.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Replay whenever you have new scenes. A good interval is long enough that the last fiction is not still famous between you.

**Postcard round.** Each story must fit on a postcard, about 80 words. Read them cold. The constraint makes the lie work harder and keeps the truths from wandering into speeches.

**Decade tags.** Write the years on the cards after the uncovering, not before. Seeing that a truth came from age 19, or from last April, often does more than the guess did.

**Swap reader.** One of you can read the other's cards aloud if a voice is tired, while the author remains the teller who uncovers. The guess is about the story, not about vocal performance.

**Long-distance.** Three messages, a reply with the guess and the reason, a reply with the uncovering. You can do the two rounds on different evenings if the time zones are rude.

On a later attempt, notice which kinds of truth you reach for: travel, work, childhood, the last month. If every truth is a highlight, try one story whose scale is a single room. If every fiction is a hero tale, try a fiction in which you are slightly foolish and well treated.

The Memory Smuggler remains its own game when you want to plant one impossible detail inside a real memory and let your partner try to detect it. This chapter is here when you want three whole stories and a clean line between what happened and what you made.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you. The stories below are illustrations, shortened a little for the page. At a real table, each one would run about 1 minute.

Rowan tells three stories.

Story 1. "In a pottery class I took on a dare from myself, the instructor said to keep my elbows soft. I kept them soft. The clay still fled the wheel, twice, and hit the apron of a stranger who bowed as if we had planned it. I never centered a bowl. I did bring home a lump that I dried on the radiator and still use as a doorstop."

Story 2. "The year the upstairs neighbor worked nights, their radio leaked a trumpet solo through the floor every evening at 9. I learned the chorus by accident. One Tuesday I met them on the stair and hummed it before I said hello. They looked relieved, as if the song had been a question. We never became close. The humming was the whole friendship."

Story 3. "In Lisbon, which I was visiting alone, a trumpet player missed a parade and asked me, in three languages, which way the drums had gone. I guessed, correctly, because a child was selling paper flags on the corner. The player put a doughnut the size of a hat in my hands and disappeared after the bass drum. I ate it on the steps of a closed museum."

Vale guesses Story 3. "You described the doughnut more carefully than the person. Also, you save real cities for stories with worse luck."

Rowan uncovers. "The parade was the fiction. I have never been to Lisbon. Please remember the pottery, because I still cannot center the clay, and the radio, because I still know that chorus."

Vale's set, same fictional evening, shows the other shape of a beautiful lie. The truths: a bus driver who waited while Vale ran, badly, from a pharmacy; and a song Vale can only remember as the bridge, never the verse. The fiction: Vale once won a county prize for polite queuing, and the trophy was a single perfect spoon. Vale names the spoon as the invention in one sentence, then asks Rowan to remember the bus and the bridge. Rowan had guessed the song, and was wrong, and both of them liked the miss.

Two more fictions, also fictional, if you want the tone without the full scene. A beautiful lie can be: you were mistaken for the person who had reserved the last sunny table, and you invited the real party to sit down with you anyway. A beautiful lie can be: in a city you have never seen, you returned a stranger's glove and they insisted on walking you to the corner as if you were the one who was lost. Neither story needs a victim.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay with the kept lines for a few minutes. You might tell your partner which truth surprised you, and which one you want repeated someday at greater length. You might admit which fiction you admired as craft. Admiration of the craft is not a request to be deceived about anything that matters.

If a story stirred an actual tender spot, say so before you leave the table. "I do not want the bus story used as a joke later" is a complete request. So is "I liked being the person who hummed." If you would rather close the book and talk about dinner, that is a complete ending too.

A guess, correct or wild, changes nothing about consent, trust, or what you owe each other tonight. You played a storytelling game. You told the truth twice on purpose. That is enough to write down.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write what you want kept. Skip any line. The two private halves are for each of you. Sharing a private page is optional. Either of you can leave yours unread.

If you wrote on cards, date the two "keep" lines and tuck them here. They are a memento of the truths, not of the score you did not keep.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Which true story of mine do I want remembered, and what detail makes it mine?
- When I listened, which guess did I make, and which truth from my partner's round do I most want to keep straight?
partner_b:
- Which fiction did I enjoy inventing, and which of my own truths almost felt too ordinary to tell?
- What did I hear in my partner's true stories that I do not want filed under a joke?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Two truths and a lie is a parlor game, common at parties and in classrooms. This chapter is a paired retelling with a kinder fiction and a second look at the truths. No research finding is claimed for it. Knowing which anecdote was invented is not, in this book, a measure of honesty, compatibility, or love. The fictional examples use Rowan and Vale and were written for these pages.

experiences.title: Would You Rather: Unhinged Edition

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A forced choice between two invented options, a one-sentence reason, and a third door if the question is a cage.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Some choices are too silly to be advice and too pointed to be small talk. You take them anyway. One of you reads two invented options. Both of you choose in secret, reveal at the same moment, and give a single sentence about why. Unhinged, here, means surprising. It means a goose with opinions, a year of only instrumental music, a last good peach with a guest in the doorway. It means you get to be strange on purpose.

It does not mean cruel. It does not mean a sexual dare, a jab at a body, or a question aimed at a real wound. The answer is hypothetical. You may not cash it later as consent, as a promise, or as a confession.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A forced choice is a toy. The reason sentence is where a person actually stands. "The unicycle, because the float would make me responsible for waving" tells you something a biography rarely bothers to include: how they handle dignity, inconvenience, and an audience.

Four tones keep the evening from collapsing into one joke. Ludicrous logistics let you laugh before anyone is brave. A revealing pair asks for self-knowledge at a safe altitude. A moral pair offers a value collision with no tragic victim and no real plan for harm. A romantic pair spends comfort or time in imagination, and stays in imagination unless you deliberately make a plan another day.

The third door is part of the mechanism. Either of you may reject the frame. A clever question can still be a bad frame, and saying so is a legal move, not a failed sense of play.

This is a game of paired hypotheticals, including silly ones. Entry 082, The Moral Gray Area, is a conversation about competing values with no obvious right answer. Entry 085, What Would You Do If…?, considers unexpected dilemmas in a life. Play those when you want the ethics at full size. Play this when you also want the goose.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need a way to choose privately. A coin under a hand works. Heads means the first option, the one before "or." Tails means the second. If coins feel fiddly, write L or R on a scrap, place it face down, and turn both scraps over together. On a call, type the letter into a note and send on a count of three.

Decide who speaks the reason first. A fair rule: the person seated on the left speaks first on odd cards, and the other person speaks first on even cards. On a call, alternate by card. Speaking first keeps the second reason from becoming an echo.

Agree on a small limit before you start. Standard play is eight cards, two from each suit. You may stop earlier. Discarding a card is allowed before the coins go down. A discarded card is not a forfeit, and it does not hand the turn to the other person's preference. Passing after you reveal is also allowed: say "pass" instead of a reason. The choice you showed can be forgotten. It is not evidence.

If the night is loud, tired, or raw, stay in the ludicrous suit. Hearing and reading are equal. Pass the options in text if one of you wants them in print. Large type helps. No one has to stand, travel, or touch.

A hypothetical yes is not consent to do the thing, spend the money, change a habit, or be touched. Romantic options stay imaginary unless, later and separately, you both make a plan in ordinary language.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Shuffle each suit, or have one person read the numbers while the other says "stop." Draw so you do not always play the first card printed in the book.

**A turn.**

1. Read the pair aloud, slowly enough that both options arrive intact. Point to which one is heads or Left, and which one is tails or Right.
2. Sit with it in silence for up to 30 seconds. Choose privately.
3. Count "three" and reveal.
4. Each of you gives one sentence of reason, in the order you agreed. One sentence is the rule. A second sentence is a luxury you may skip. You are not building a case.
5. If you want the third door, say "Third door" before your reason. Then reject the frame in one sentence, or offer a third option. You still listen to your partner's choice. Their choice does not stick to you.
6. Optional, if you matched: the person who spoke second may add a condition, still one sentence. "Only if the goose pays rent." Conditions are jokes or clarifications. They are not negotiations you have agreed to live by.

Then draw the next card. Do not stack questions until someone is too tired to pass. The stop is part of the design. When the planned number is done, stop even if the deck is still funny.

**What a third door sounds like.** "Third door: both options assume we want a performance." "Third door: I already live a version of the first, and the question is tired." "Third door: I want the walk and the evening, and I refuse the scarcity." All three are complete moves.

**What you might print.** 24 cards, about four by six inches, one pair on each face. Suit name at the top. The two options labeled Left and Right. Footer on every card: "Third door is open. A choice is hypothetical." Backs show only the suit, so you can draw blind. 14-point type or larger. Four piles on the table. No score sheet. A match is interesting. It is not a compatibility result, and it does not reveal character. Do not total the matches. If you are curious how often you landed together, you may say the number once, as a remark, and then leave it.

**Ending.** After the last card, each of you names one choice that should stay imaginary. That sentence seals the game. If a card made you want a real plan, say "I might want to talk about this later," and write the topic on a slip. Do not have the real conversation inside the game. The slip can wait for another night, or it can be thrown away.

### Ludicrous logistics

These six pairs are original to this book. They are the absurd suit, and they are ready to play.

1. Would you rather live in a house where every door is a curtain, or a house where every curtain is a locked door?
2. Would you rather commute by unicycle with a dignified basket, or on a parade float that travels only at walking speed?
3. Would you rather carry a phone that speaks only in weather forecasts, or own a kettle that sings a full opera when it boils?
4. Would you rather share the home with a well-mannered goose who has opinions, or with a houseplant that must be read to every night?
5. Would you rather eat breakfast as soup, using a tiny fork, or eat dinner as a sandwich the size of a hardcover book?
6. Would you rather wake each Sunday to find the furniture politely rearranged by an unseen helper, or discover each Monday that your two shoes are different sizes?

### Revealing, and still safe

Self-knowledge at a humane volume. Either of you may discard any of these.

7. Would you rather have a year of only instrumental music, or a year of only live conversation at dinner?
8. Would you rather be known for your competence and rarely asked how you feel, or be known for your feelings and rarely asked to fix anything?
9. Would you rather keep one hobby entirely unseen, or share every hobby and lose the private one?
10. Would you rather spend a week saying every small appreciation out loud, or spend a week receiving appreciation without deflecting it?
11. Would you rather wake with the sun and miss the morning's noise, or stay up late and own the quiet after midnight?
12. Would you rather be the person who remembers everyone's drink order, or the person who remembers the sentence someone did not finish?

### Morally complicated

Value collisions. No tragic victim. No real plan to harm anyone. If a card brushes an actual dilemma you are living, discard it and say "too close."

13. Would you rather tell a friend their new haircut is "brave" when you dislike it, or stay warmly quiet and let them enjoy the mirror?
14. Would you rather spend the last good peach on a guest, or save it for the person who bought it and serve the guest something else?
15. Would you rather admit you broke the ugly mug everyone pretends to treasure, or buy a quiet replacement and let the mystery stand?
16. Would you rather give up the better seat on a long ride, or keep it because you are the one who gets queasy?
17. Would you rather correct a small public mistake that is making someone look clever, or let the cleverness stand because the correction would embarrass them?
18. Would you rather do a promised favor you dread on the only free afternoon, or ask to move it and offer a better hour?

### Romantic, and still imaginary

These cost comfort or time inside the fiction. They do not assume a script, a wedding, or a shared address. If you live apart, "home" means wherever you each start the evening.

19. Would you rather keep a standing walk on Tuesdays in any weather, or protect one carefully planned evening a month?
20. Would you rather learn a dance badly together for six weeks, or learn one favorite album well enough to talk about it for an hour?
21. Would you rather trade one hour of solo screen time for a shared puzzle on most nights, or keep the hour and guard one unhurried morning each weekend?
22. Would you rather leave a three-line note on ordinary Tuesdays, or cook one meal a week for pleasure rather than for logistics?
23. Would you rather take the long way from where you usually part, twice a week, or stay in and keep a 20-minute ritual that uses no screen?
24. Would you rather let your partner plan a surprise afternoon inside a budget you both already set, or plan it together and give up the surprise?

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 15 minutes.** Four cards, all from the ludicrous suit. Reasons stay one sentence. Skip the romantic and moral suits. This is the right cut for sensory overload, a short evening, or a mood that wants nonsense and nothing else.

**Standard, 35 minutes.** Two cards from each suit, eight in all. Read, choose, reveal, one sentence each. Use the third door whenever the frame fails. End with the sealing line: one choice that stays imaginary.

**Extended, 70 minutes.** Play 12 cards, three from each suit. After the eighth, pause and each rewrite one card you disliked into a fairer pair. Play the two rewrites with the same reveal rules. Rewriting is part of the fun. It is also how you teach the deck your actual boundaries. Close by naming the imaginary choice, and, if you wrote a "later" slip, decide whether it lives in a pocket or in the recycling.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A deeper round uses the revealing and romantic suits only, and it lengthens the reason from one sentence to three. The first sentence is the choice. The second is the cost you noticed. The third is whether the cost is interesting or merely annoying. You still reveal together, so nobody's longer speech becomes a lecture the other must survive.

You may ask one follow-up: "What would make the option you refused into a yes?" The answer stays hypothetical. If it starts to sound like a scheduled promise, move it to the later slip.

Do not deepen this game by pressing on a wound, by adding sexual stakes, or by treating a match as proof that you are the same kind of person. Sameness is not the prize. A clearly loved difference is often the better story. If you want dilemmas with no game clock, use The Moral Gray Area or What Would You Do If…? on a night when absurdity would get in the way.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Single suit night.** All eight cards from one suit. A ludicrous night and a romantic night are different parties. Keep the third door in both.

**Silent reasons.** Write the one-sentence reason, then read them aloud together. Useful when one of you thinks better on paper, and useful at a distance.

**House rule card.** Once per night, either of you may replace a printed pair with one you invent on the spot, using the same tone as the suit you are in. Read it, then give the other person a veto before any coin goes down. A veto discards the house pair with no replacement penalty.

**Replay.** The deck has 24 pairs so a second night can avoid the greatest hits. When a pair goes stale, retire it. Add a new one in the same tone if you want the pile to stay full. Retire any pair that starts to humiliate a body, an identity, or a real argument you are actually having.

If the moral suit stops feeling like play, you have learned something useful. Leave that suit in the box for a while. The ludicrous suit will still be there, wearing its ridiculous hat.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you.

They draw card 4. Rowan covers heads. Vale covers tails. On three, Rowan has chosen the goose. Vale has chosen the houseplant.

Rowan, one sentence: "The goose can be negotiated with, and I respect a creature who states its opinions at the door."

Vale, one sentence: "I will read to a plant, because a plant does not follow me into the bathroom to continue the argument."

They do not total the split. They move on.

Later they draw card 7, the year of instrumental music or the year of live dinner conversation. Both coins show heads. Vale speaks second and adds a condition: "Only if percussion counts, and only if breakfast is allowed to be quiet." Rowan says, "Third door on the condition. I want some dinners with talking and some without a law." The third door closes the card. Nobody has agreed to a year of anything.

On card 19, Vale says "Third door" immediately. "I want the Tuesday walk and the planned evening. The question pretends we only get one kind of time." Rowan had chosen the walk, explains in one sentence that weather makes a plan feel real, and then writes nothing on a later slip. The walk remains imaginary. They get up to find out whether the actual kettle sings. It does not. This disappoints neither of them very much.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
If you are still quoting the goose at the sink, the game worked. If a card left a real wish sitting on the table, you already have a way to carry it: the later slip, in plain language, outside the rules. Wishes can wait. They do not have to be paid tonight.

Tell each other which suit you would play again, and which suit you would shelve. Shelving is information, not a disappointment. A night that stayed in the ludicrous suit is a complete night.

Nothing you chose under a coin is permission for the morning. If you want the puzzle, the note, or the long way, ask for it in a new conversation, where a yes can be about the real week and a no can be about the real week too.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
The private lines are for each of you. Sharing them is optional. A pocket full of later slips can be taped here, dated, and marked "imaginary" or "maybe a real plan." Either marking is allowed. Neither marking is a promise by itself.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Which suit was the most fun to choose in, and which suit made me reach for the third door?
- What did my partner's reason sentence show that the coin by itself could not?
partner_b:
- Where did my own choice surprise me once I heard the reason out loud?
- Which of my partner's answers should stay play, and which, if any, do I want to discuss later as a separate plan?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: "Would you rather" is common speech and an old parlor habit. Commercial decks exist. This chapter does not use their prompts and is not affiliated with any branded set. The 24 pairs above were written for this book. No research finding is claimed. Choosing between absurd alternatives is not a moral assessment, a character test, or a clinical values protocol. Rowan and Vale are fictional.

experiences.title: The Newlywed Game, Without the Wedding

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Write what you think is true of each other, then see which guess describes the person in the room and which describes an older year.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You can know the drink, the joke, and the way someone drops their keys, and still be describing a person they were three years ago. This is a trivia game about that gap. You each write, privately, what you believe is true of the other. You reveal one item at a time. You compare knowledge, assumptions, and surprises. The title is a joke you are allowed to enjoy: you do not need to be newly wed, or wed at all. You need to be two adults willing to update the file.

Nobody gets a podium. A match is a pleasure. A miss is information about an assumption, not an offense, and not a lack of love.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Everyone who loves someone carries a working model of them. Some of the model is current. Some of it is a season you liked and kept. Some of it was borrowed from their family, from an old story, or from your own habits, then quietly applied to the person across from you. The model is useful. It is also capable of lag.

Writing the guess down, before you hear the correction, makes the lag visible. Speech is slippery. A sentence on paper is easier to sort. When you reveal in pairs, you get three kinds of result, and all three are worth having. Knowledge: you were close, and the closeness is specific. Assumption: you answered for an older version, or for someone who is not in the room. Surprise: they have a stress, a comfort, or a wish you had not been told, and the blank is an invitation rather than a verdict.

Entry 101, The Borrowed Brain Experiment, asks you to answer a scenario as you think your partner would, then compare the reasoning, not only the final decision. This chapter compares trivia about habits, tastes, and knowledge, and it lingers on the surprises. One studies how a decision gets made. The other studies what you think you already know. They are neighbors, not the same room.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Print or copy two answer sheets. Each sheet has a line for every question you plan to use, and three empty marks you will fill only at the reveal: Now, Older, Borrowed. You each write about the other person. You do not write about yourself until the reveal, and only if you want to correct the record.

Sit so you cannot read each other's pages. On a call, use two notes and share a screen only when that number is up. Large type is welcome. A screen reader is a fine way to hear your own guesses before you read them aloud. Speech is optional at the reveal. You may trade papers and read in silence, then talk.

Skip any item. Write "pass" on the line. A pass is read as a pass. Your partner does not fill the blank as a penalty, and does not owe you the answer. Leave sex, family secrets, money, and any third person's story off the sheet. If a question would require a fact you have never been told, the interesting result is "I have not said that," which you may follow with the fact if you want it known. An unknown fact is a gap in the conversation. It is not proof of neglect.

Optional: a small pile of paper stars, buttons, or torn slips. If a prediction matches, the person who was described may drop one star on the table. Stars stay scattered. You will not add them up. If a podium begins to form, sweep the stars into a pile and call them confetti. Confetti has no ranking.

Agree the set before you write. Short uses four questions. Standard uses eight. Extended uses 12. The questions below are original to this book.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Write, privately, for 8 to 12 minutes.** Answer in a phrase or a sentence. Specific beats clever. "Tea, too hot, in the blue mug" will teach you more than "a drink." If you do not know, write your best current guess and add a question mark. The question mark is honest, and it still counts as a guess you are willing to check.

**Reveal, one question at a time.**

1. One of you reads the question. Trade this job so nobody becomes a permanent host.
2. Both of you read your prediction. If speaking is tiring, exchange the lines in print.
3. The person being described speaks first, if they want to. They give the current answer in one sentence. They may add "that matches," "that is close," or "that surprises me."
4. They mark the guess, out loud or on the sheet: Now, Older, or Borrowed. Now means it fits the person in the room this month. Older means it fit a previous season and has gone stale. Borrowed means it seems to come from someone else, or from the guesser's own life.
5. If it matches and you are using stars, drop one. Do not applaud a miss into shame, and do not applaud a match into a trophy.
6. If the described person wants to update the record, they do it in one sentence. "The annoyance this month is the flickering bulb, not the dishes." That sentence is the new knowledge. It retires the old guess.

Go to the next question. Either person may skip a reveal even after the words are written. Fold the line over and say "leaving this one." Folded lines stay folded.

**The debrief, which is the point.** After the last question, each of you answers this once: "Which guess described an older version of me, or an assumption you borrowed from someone else?" Give the guesser a chance to say where the assumption came from, if they know. "I borrowed it from your sister's story about college" is a useful origin. "I borrowed it from my last relationship" is also useful, and it does not need a trial. Thank the correction. Do not defend the outdated file as if it were loyalty.

**Questions.** Each line is something you write about your partner.

1. In the first 10 minutes after getting home, my partner usually...
2. The small household sound my partner notices before I do is...
3. My partner's current low-grade stress, the one that is not a crisis, is...
4. When the day has been long, the taste my partner wants is... (salt, sweet, sour, bitter, hot, or name another)
5. The ordinary object that is currently my partner's comfort is...
6. A petty annoyance my partner has mentioned more than once this month is...
7. A wish my partner has for the coming month, small enough to actually happen, is...
8. The joke or phrase my partner uses when stalling is...
9. The time of day my partner is most like themselves is...
10. What my partner rereads, rewatches, or replays when they want the world familiar is...
11. My partner prefers good news delivered... (immediately, in person, after the bag is down, or another way)
12. A skill my partner is quietly proud of, which rarely comes up, is...

If you do not share a home, read "getting home" as "arriving wherever they land at the end of the day," and read "household sound" as "a sound in the place they are today." The questions should still make sense.

**What you might print.** Two identical sheets, 14-point type, with the question, a long blank, and three small circles labeled Now, Older, and Borrowed. A cover sheet so the pages can travel to a call unopened. No buzzer, no host's podium, no score box. If you want a header, use the chapter title and the date.

**Ending.** The game ends when the debrief question has been answered by both of you, or gently declined. Close by each updating one fact in a sentence, if you want the record current. "This month, the comfort object is the gray sweater, not the radio." Then stop. Do not add a lightning round. Lightning rounds are how a friendly miss turns into an exam.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 20 minutes.** Use questions 1, 4, 5, and 7: a habit, a taste, a comfort, and a wish. Write for about 6 minutes. Reveal with the marks. Ask the debrief question once each. This cut still includes a surprise and a possible older version. It drops the annoyance question on purpose, so a short night does not have to include a complaint.

**Standard, 40 minutes.** Use questions 1 through 8. Write for about 10 minutes. Reveal in pairs with the three marks. Use stars if they stay a joke. Debrief. One updated fact each, if you want it.

**Extended, 65 minutes.** Use all 12. After the debrief, each of you writes one new question the deck missed, still about a habit, a taste, a stress, a comfort, or a wish. Both of you answer that new question about the other, privately, then reveal it with the same marks. The new question has to be one the person being asked could know from ordinary life. If it depends on a secret they never offered, scrap it and enjoy the 12 you have.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Depth here is currency. Play the standard set, then ask, for two items only: "When did this become true?" A comfort object that arrived last winter is a different story from one that has survived three apartments. You are not digging for pain. You are dating the model.

A second deeper question, once each: "What do you wish I would stop assuming?" The answer can be as small as "that I want company the moment I get home." If the answer is larger than the evening, thank them and pick it up in a conversation that is not a game. Entry 083, The Secret Nobody Would Guess, is a better door for a volunteered surprise than a trivia sheet is.

Do not deepen the night by adding sexual-embarrassment questions, traps about fidelity, bodies, or ex-partners, or a final score. A high number of stars would still not mean you will stay together. A low number would not mean you have failed at love. You would have learned where the file is out of date. That is the whole prize.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Month stamp.** Play on the first evening of a season. Date the sheets. When you play again, read one old sheet aloud before you write the new guesses. The comedy is watching last year's petty annoyance lose its job.

**One-theme night.** All of the questions you use must be about comfort, or all about the coming month. Narrowing the theme keeps the game from feeling like a census.

**Sealed notes.** Write in advance and open on a call. Useful across distance. Agree that either person may leave a seal unbroken.

**No stars.** Some pairs will have more fun without tokens. The marks Now, Older, and Borrowed are the real score, and even they are labels, not points.

On replay, notice whether your guesses have moved closer to the present. If they have, you have been listening. If a borrowed assumption keeps returning, that assumption has a source worth naming once, kindly, so it can retire.

The Borrowed Brain Experiment is waiting when you want to compare how a decision gets made. Would You Rather: Unhinged Edition is waiting when you want hypothetical choices instead of facts. This chapter is for the ordinary, current, slightly messy record of a person you already like.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you. They play the short set at a kitchen table.

Vale's guess for question 1: "Checks the mail, even when it is Sunday, then stands at the sink."
Rowan's correction: "That matches the first apartment. Now I put the bag down, wash my hands, and see whether the sourdough has done anything dramatic."
Mark: Older.

Rowan's guess for question 5: "The chipped blue mug."
Vale's correction: "The mug is yours. My comfort this month is the window I open six inches, even in bad weather. I have never made a speech about it."
Mark: Borrowed, and also a surprise. Vale drops no star. Vale looks pleased anyway. "You borrowed the mug from the way I use yours when I am cold."

Rowan's guess for question 7: "A weekday with no plans after 8."
Vale: "That matches. That is the wish."
A paper star goes onto the table. They do not make a second star compete with it.

In the debrief, Rowan says the mail-checking guess came from a story Vale's brother tells. Vale asks that the brother edition be retired. Rowan agrees in one sentence. The fictional evening ends there, with the window open six inches because Vale got up and did it, not because the game required a ceremony.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Read one updated fact back, so the new version has been heard. If you want, thank your partner for a guess that was exact, and for a miss they corrected without a speech. Exactness is sweet. A clean correction is also sweet.

If you feel tender about an older version of yourself that your partner still loves, you can say that. "I like that you remember the mug era" and "please use the window era" can both be true. Neither sentence has to win.

Leave the stars on the table until you are done laughing at them. Then throw them away, or keep one with the date. A kept star means "we played," not "we scored."

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
These pages can hold the guesses you want to remember and the corrections you want on record. The private halves do not have to be shown. Sharing them is optional.

If you keep an answer sheet, date it and note which version you played. An old sheet is a fine then-versus-now document. It is not a report card.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Which of my guesses described my partner now, and which described an older version?
- What assumption did I borrow from someone else, from a past season, or from my own habits?
partner_b:
- Which description of me was surprisingly exact, and which one missed the person I am this month?
- Where did I feel known, and what one-sentence update did I want entered into the record?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Predicting a partner for the pleasure of the comparison is an old party custom. A long-running television contest made a prize version of that custom famous. This chapter is a private game for any adult pair. It uses none of that show's questions, host, set, or branding, and the show has no role in these pages. No research finding is claimed. A wrong guess is an assumption you can see. It is not a score that predicts a future. Rowan and Vale are fictional.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 20 minutes · Standard 40 minutes · Extended 65 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Play each other, lightly and too much, then let the person who was played sort the joke.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You already do a small impression of each other when you tell a story at dinner. The hands change. A phrase gets quoted with extra varnish. This chapter turns that varnish up until it squeaks, for 2 minutes, inside a scene you both agreed to. Then it hands the floor to the person who was played.

They sort what you did into three piles: accurate, flattering fiction, and that stung. The sort is half the game. Without it, you have a roast, and a roast is a different, worse party.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
An affectionate impression says you have been paying attention to your style. Style is how you thank a server, how long you look at a menu, the gesture you make when you are stalling. Being recognized in those details can feel different from being praised. Praise says you are wonderful. Recognition says you are particular.

Exaggeration is the ridiculous part, and it needs a fence. You magnify a joke you already share. You do not invent a new sore spot for the sake of the scene. You do not borrow identity, a body, a disability, a family, or a distressed mood and call it comedy. The person portrayed gets the last sort, including the right to say that something stung. What stung is named before anyone explains that it was only a joke. The discussion is not a debate the impersonator wins.

Entry 018, The Silent Conversation, is communication by expression and gesture, with the words set down. Entry 101, The Borrowed Brain Experiment, compares reasoning on a scenario. This chapter is style and manner, deliberately enlarged, then corrected by the person who wears that manner on ordinary days.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Agree that either of you can stop a portrayal mid-scene. A raised hand, or the word "stop," ends it. Stopping is a success of the rules. You move straight to the sort, or you drop the scene if the portrayed person would rather. No one owes a laugh.

Each of you writes one veto on a slip and shows it before the timer starts. A veto might be a family phrase, a speech pattern, a body habit, a sore mood, an accent, the way pain makes you move. The portrayal leaves the veto out. If it hits the veto anyway, stop. Do not imitate a stutter, a tic, an accent tied to ethnicity or place, or a mobility pattern. Do not perform your partner's anger, sadness, or desire. Do not use their body, their mental-health history, or their family as the material.

Name the inside joke you are willing to see enlarged. A phrase. A pace. A courtesy that runs slightly too long. If you cannot think of a joke, use manners only: how you order, how you pause, how you thank someone. Manners are enough to be funny.

Choose the scene together from the menu below, or invent a mundane one at the same altitude. Both of you will play the same scene as each other, so you are comparing style inside one situation.

If a voice impression is difficult, unwanted, or just not your instrument, write a short monologue in your partner's cadence, or play a single gesture while seated. Trade written dialogue if hearing makes audio hard. Long-distance works on video or as exchanged scripts. Nobody has to stand.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Scenes.** Pick one.

1. Ordering dinner while hungry and still trying to be polite to the menu.
2. Narrating a weekday morning from the alarm to the door.
3. Telling a harmless party story about a lost umbrella.
4. Choosing a film, and taking slightly too long to do it.
5. Returning a coffee order that is a little wrong, with excessive courtesy.
6. Explaining a simple recipe while the pan is already hot.

**The portrayal, 2 minutes.** The portrayer "is" the other person inside the scene. Seated. One gesture or one phrase, already an inside joke, gets enlarged. The rest can be ordinary. You may talk to an invisible server, an invisible door, or the actual partner as if they were the audience at that party. You may not leave the scene for a confession, a conflict, or a sexual caricature.

The person being portrayed watches without correcting. Laughing is allowed. A straight face is allowed. Notes are allowed if you want them for the sort. Interruptions wait, unless you need to stop the scene.

**The monologue option.** Fill this shape in your partner's voice, on paper, about 120 words, then read it or hand it over:

"When I am in this scene, I tend to ___. The phrase I reach for is ___. What my hands do is ___. The story I think I am in is ___."

Exaggerate one of those four lines. Leave the veto untouched. Reading time still caps at 2 minutes.

**The sort, about 4 minutes, and it is required.** The portrayed person has the floor. They sort lines into the three piles, in this order if anything stung, and in any order if nothing did.

- That stung. Name it in one sentence. "When you stretched my pause into a full minute, it felt like a comment on how slow I am." The portrayer listens. They apologize in one sentence, or they offer a redo of that single beat. They do not explain the joke until they are invited. What stung is information for an apology or a redo. It is not material for a second joke.
- Accurate. "That is me, and I claim it." One or two examples are enough.
- Flattering fiction. "That was kinder than the truth," or "I wish I were that polite to bread."

If nothing stung, the portrayed person still touches the category. They say, "Nothing stung. I checked." Skipping the category because the laugh was loud is how the roast sneaks out the side door. The check is the game.

The portrayer may ask, after the sort, "Is there a line you want retired?" They may not argue a sting into a compliment. If a redo is offered and accepted, it lasts 20 seconds, and then the sort stands.

**Switch.** Same scene, reversed roles. The second portrayal does not "correct" the first. It is a new impression, followed by a new sort of equal length. Both people portray. Both people are sorted. That balance is the chapter.

**If it snags.** The scene slides toward a real annoyance: stop, name the slide, and either return to the umbrella or end. The laugh is huge and the sort is about to be skipped: set a second timer for the sort and let it run. Someone feels too seen: they can retire a line, keep the accurate pile, and decline the redo. Someone cannot find an inside joke: manners, pace, and courtesy are a complete costume.

**What you might print.** Two veto slips. One scene card with the six options. Three small cards labeled Accurate, Flattering fiction, and That stung, to place on the table as a sorting mat. A timer with a gentle end, not an alarm that sounds like a scolding. No score. Recognition is not a point.

**Ending.** The game ends when both sorts are finished, including both sting checks. If you want a last beat, each of you may offer one accurate line you liked hearing, and the other person may accept it or wave it off. Then the coats, metaphorically, go back to their own sleeves.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 15 minutes.** One scene. Each portrayal lasts 60 seconds. Each sort lasts 2 minutes. Veto slips still happen. Both directions still happen. This is a sketch, not a single impersonation of one partner while the other hosts.

**Standard, 30 minutes.** Vetoes, one scene, 2 minutes of portrayal and about 4 minutes of sort, each direction. Leave a minute between directions so the second portrayer is not answering the first sketch like a rival.

**Extended, 55 minutes.** Play the standard game. Take a short break. Choose a second scene from the menu. Before you start it, each of you may keep the same veto or write a new one. Use the monologue for one scene and the spoken impression for the other, if you want both instruments. The sorts stay the same length as the performances, or longer. Extended does not mean a sharper joke. It means a second situation, so a mannerism can turn out to be about menus and not about mornings.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Pick one accurate line from the sort and ask, only with permission, "Where did that habit come from?" The answer might be a job, a parent, a crowded house, a love of precision. Hear it. Do not turn the origin into a new impression on the same night.

You may also ask, "Which flattering fiction would you like me to keep as a private compliment, and which one should I drop?" Some exaggerated kindness is a gift. Some of it is a portrait of a person they are tired of pretending to be.

Leave real conflict in its own chapter. If the sting opens a recurring tenderness, apologize, retire the bit, and stop. You are not in a therapy exercise where partners switch positions inside a live fight. You are two people who borrowed each other's coats and then checked the fit.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Gesture only.** 30 seconds. One seated gesture, enlarged. Then a full sort, which may be longer than the gesture. This is a good variation when voices are tired or when impressions of speech feel risky.

**Script exchange.** Write the monologue in advance. Exchange sealed. Read silently. Sort on a call without performing at all.

**Party-story limit.** Use only scene 3, the lost umbrella, so the content stays harmlessly plotless and the comedy has to live in the telling.

**Replay.** New scene, same vetoes unless you lift one. Notice which accurate lines have become dear. Notice which joke has expired. An expired joke can be thanked and buried. Burying it is a form of attention too.

The Great Debate of Absolutely Nothing, entry 045, is the chapter for formal seriousness about empty subjects. Come to this one when the subject is each other's manner, and the correction belongs to the person portrayed.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you.

They choose scene 1, ordering dinner. Vale's veto slip says "my shoulder when it hurts." Rowan's veto slip says "my mother's way of saying 'well.'" Those slips sit on the table, face up.

Vale portrays Rowan, seated, menu in hand. "Good evening. I will have the soup, provided the soup understands its responsibilities. If the menu disagrees, I am prepared to negotiate with it for a reasonable period. I will also thank the bread for waiting."

Rowan sorts. "Nothing stung. I checked. Accurate: I do interview the menu, and I do thank people a half-second longer than the moment requires. Flattering fiction: I am not that polite to bread. I would like the bread line retired, not because it hurt, because it makes me into a mascot."

Vale says, "Retired." Vale does not explain the joke.

Then Rowan portrays Vale in the same booth. Rowan taps the menu once, orders the first hearty thing, and adds, "And whatever you would eat if you were cold." Rowan almost reaches for a shoulder shrug, remembers the veto, and lets the hands stay on the table.

Vale sorts. "That stung, a little: 'whatever you would eat if you were cold' felt like a portrait of me as someone who cannot choose. Please retire it." Rowan says, "I am sorry. Retired." Only then does Vale continue. "Accurate: I decide fast when I am hungry. Flattering fiction: I am not that considerate of the server's imaginary inner life. The fast decision, you can keep."

They do not do a second joke about the sting. They eat, in the fiction of the example, something hearty. The bread is not thanked again.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Say out loud which lines are retired. Retired lines do not become nicknames on the way to the car. If you want, each of you can repeat one accurate line you are happy to claim. Claiming it makes the recognition mutual.

If a sting is still warm, let the apology be the last word on it tonight. You can ask tomorrow whether the apology landed. You do not have to settle it by being funnier.

The game gives nobody permission to touch, to diagnose, or to perform the other person for an audience who was not in the room. If you retell the scene later, retell the sort as well. The sort is the part that makes the ridiculousness kind.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write the retired lines if you want them remembered as retired. The private pages are optional to share. A veto slip can be dated and kept, especially if the same veto should travel into the next time you play.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- When I was portrayed, what was accurate, what was flattering fiction, and what, if anything, stung?
- What did I need after I named a sting, or after I confirmed there was none?
partner_b:
- When I did the portraying, which inside joke did I enlarge, and what did the sort ask me to retire?
- Which gesture or phrase of my partner's felt like recognition I am glad I noticed?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Affectionate impressions are an ordinary comic custom among people who know each other. This chapter is that custom with a required sort. No research finding is claimed. Being imitated is not treated here as empathy training, a look into the unconscious, or a clinical role-play. Rowan and Vale are fictional. Any sample dialogue is an illustration, not a script you must perform.
