experiences.title: The Great Debate of Absolutely Nothing

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Defend an empty proposition with a straight face, then set the opinion down in an ordinary voice.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The moon has been showing off again, and someone must answer for it. You will argue opposite sides of a proposition that cannot matter, with exaggerated seriousness, for about 3 minutes. A coin decides who defends the moon. When the timer ends, you both put the opinion down in your ordinary voice and say that you do not hold it.

The seriousness is a costume. The content is nothing. Soup. Socks. Spoons. Tuesday. If a joke proposition is actually a complaint about your partner, the game has slipped, and the right move is to stop.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Shared absurdity is a cooperative game wearing the clothes of a fight. You practice picking up a position you did not choose, decorating it with fake evidence, and then abandoning it on purpose. Abandoning it is the closing move, and it is the part that keeps the joke from following you into the kitchen as a barb.

There is a particular pleasure in gravity spent on nothing. A definition, a fictional survey of spoons, a grave warning about the future of cereal: these are tools borrowed from real debate and used where they cannot do harm. You get the music of argument without a grievance.

Entry 059, The Gentle Disagreement, is where a manageable real disagreement goes, with warmth and curiosity. This chapter is allowed to sound serious only because the subject is empty. It is not a warm-up that slides into an unresolved fight. Entry 086, The Unpopular Opinion Club, is for actual opinions you hold and rarely air. If you truly care about the topic, it does not belong on these slips.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need six motion slips, a coin, a timer, and a little paper for notes. Sitting is the whole stage. There is no podium. On a call, read the motion aloud or paste it in text. If the room is easily overloaded, skip applause and keep the seriousness quiet. A grave whisper is still grave. Hearing differences are handled by text. One motion is a complete game if you are tired.

Either of you may throw out a proposition that lands on a real wound. Discarding is a success. Stopping a round mid-sentence is a success. You do not have to prove you can take a joke.

The proposition must be empty of real grievance. It cannot be about your partner's habits, body, family, work, or politics, and it cannot be a household chore in a funny hat. It cannot require an example from your actual week. If the best argument you can think of is something that happened on Thursday between the two of you, you are in the wrong sport.

No one is scored for intellect, persuasion, or rank. If you want a token for committed absurdity, use a piece of string as a ribbon. The ribbon is returned at the end. Nobody leaves the room wearing a title.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Draw.** Put the six motions in a bowl, a hat, or a face-down pile. Draw one. Read it aloud. If either of you says "too close," bury it and draw again. If you bury three, stop for the night and play another time. The motions are trying to be nothing. Let them.

**Assign sides with a coin.** One of you flips it. If you both reach for the coin, the person who did not draw the motion flips. Heads: the flipper defends the motion. Tails: the flipper opposes it. The other person takes the remaining side. You can end up sincerely attacking socks. That is the assignment working. You are not stuck defending a real pet peeve, because the motions do not contain one.

**Notes, 30 seconds.** Each of you writes two serious points. Use the footholds printed under the motion if you go blank, then add one of your own. A point may be:

- a definition that favors your side,
- fake evidence, clearly fake ("a survey of spoons," "the minutes of a cloud"),
- a grave warning about what the other side will cause.

Ban anecdotes from your actual week, your families, and the news. If a real proper noun wants to enter, show it the door.

**The debate, about 3 minutes.** Set a timer. The affirmative speaks for 70 seconds. The negative speaks for 70 seconds. If you want rebuttal, add 20 seconds each, and stop when the timer ends even if the warning about cereal is unfinished. Address the motion, not the person. Use your debate voice: formal, committed, slightly too dignified. Volume is optional. Interruptions are out. You may say "the honorable opposition." You may not say "you always."

**Applause, optional.** When the timer ends, you may applaud the more committed absurdity. Commitment means they stayed inside the bit, used a straight face, and did not reach for a real complaint. If you cannot agree, applaud both. If sound is too much, a silent nod counts. This applause is not a ruling that one of you is smarter.

**Abandonment, required.** Both of you, in an ordinary voice, not the debate voice, say this sentence: "I do not hold this position." Say it even if, by some accident, you do think soup is a beverage. Inside this game, the sentence means the bit is over. The costume comes off.

**The glad list, required.** Each of you names one real topic you are glad was not on the card. Name it in a few words. Do not open it. Do not comfort it into a second debate. "I am glad the card was not about the dishes." "I am glad it was not about my family." Then leave those topics where they are. If the game has stirred an actual disagreement, stop playing and decide whether you want The Gentle Disagreement on another day. Do not convert this table into that one.

**If a joke turns into a barb.** Stop. Say, "This has become a real complaint." The other person does not argue you out of that sentence. Tear the motion in half, or close the note, and do something plainly friendly that is not a debate: water, a window, a minute of quiet. Ending is the skill.

**What you might print.** Six slips, large type, one motion each, with the affirmative foothold and the negative foothold underneath. A small card that reads, in ordinary type, "I do not hold this position." You can put it on the table and turn it face up when the timer ends, as a visual cue that the voice has to change. No score sheet. The string ribbon, if you use one, has a home in a pocket and a duty to be returned.

**Ending.** The round ends when both abandonment lines have been spoken and both glad-list topics have been named and left closed. If you play a second motion, it is a new round with a new coin. It is not a chance to answer the first debate more cuttingly. When you are finished for the night, the last thing said in a debate voice should already be behind you. The last thing said in the room can be ordinary. "Tea?" is a perfect closing argument.

### Six motions

These motions are original examples, written so you can play without inventing a single one. Footholds are optional handles. You may ignore them and build your own false evidence.

**1. This house believes soup is a beverage.**
Affirmative foothold: define a beverage as any liquid a person can drink from a mug when a spoon has left the room, and cite a fictional survey in which spoons reported feeling unemployed.
Negative foothold: define soup as a food that requires a shoreline, and warn that beverage status will encourage cereal to file the same petition.

**2. This house believes socks deserve opinions.**
Affirmative foothold: define an opinion as a consistent preference, and submit the testimony of a left sock that has refused a sandal since April, in an April that does not need to be yours.
Negative foothold: define opinion as something that can be revised in conversation, and warn that consulting socks will delay every departure until winter.

**3. This house believes the moon is showing off.**
Affirmative foothold: define showing off as appearing at parties uninvited and looking better than the lamps, and enter into evidence a fictional guest list kept by the tide.
Negative foothold: define the moon as a rock with a schedule, and warn that flattery will make it late.

**4. This house believes spoons are the only honest utensil.**
Affirmative foothold: define honesty as the willingness to hold soup without stabbing it, and quote the minutes of a fork who confessed to drama.
Negative foothold: define honesty as fitness for purpose, and warn that a spoon-only kitchen will be helpless before a steak, a steak that remains theoretical.

**5. This house believes Tuesday is a fictional day kept for administrative reasons.**
Affirmative foothold: define Tuesday as a rumor spread by calendars, and cite a survey of spoons who have never met one.
Negative foothold: define Tuesday as the day that keeps Monday from running directly into Wednesday, and warn that abolishing it will create a crowd at the middle of the week.

**6. This house believes houseplants should be consulted before guests are invited.**
Affirmative foothold: define consultation as a decent pause in which the plant is told the guest's name, and present the fictional complaint of a fern that was surprised by a saxophone.
Negative foothold: define hospitality as a human decision, and warn that plant vetoes will shrink the social circle to people the fern already likes.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 12 minutes.** One motion. Coin, 30 seconds of notes, 70 seconds a side, no rebuttal, abandonment, glad list. Skip applause if you want the room quiet. One round is a full use of the rules.

**Standard, 25 minutes.** Two motions, with a new coin each time. Include the 20-second rebuttals if you are having fun, and cut them if the bit is getting sharp. Applaud or nod. Abandon both positions. Two glad-list topics per person is plenty. Do not let the second topic become the first real argument of the night.

**Extended, 50 minutes.** Three motions from the printed six, then a break in which you both invent one new motion that passes the emptiness test. Read the new one aloud and give either person a veto before the coin. If it survives, debate it under the same timer and end it with the same abandonment sentence. Extended play includes a deliberate return to ordinary voice between rounds. Sip water if you want it, speak as civilians for a minute, then put the costume on again. The game itself stays seated.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Depth, in a game about nothing, means better fake structure, not a hidden real topic. In a deeper round, each speech must contain a definition, a piece of fake evidence, and a warning, in that order. The constraint makes the comedy more formal and makes it harder to smuggle in a genuine irritant. If you cannot fill the three beats without using your real week, pass the speech and say, "I have only a real example, so I yield."

You may also switch sides halfway through a longer evening and argue the reverse. Switching teaches the costume as a costume. It is not training you to win against each other in the life you actually live. This book does not claim that absurd debate reduces conflict or improves persuasion at home. When you want real disagreement handled with care, use The Gentle Disagreement, on a day when you have both agreed to talk about something true.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Written debate.** Exchange two paragraphs. Read them aloud in the formal voice, or read them silently and then speak only the abandonment line. The glad list still happens out loud or in text.

**Quiet house.** No applause, no gavel, no raised voice. The exaggeration lives in word choice. "I tremble for the republic of cutlery" can be whispered.

**Extra motions for another night.** This house believes clouds are loafing and ought to file a schedule. This house believes the alphabet should be rearranged by deliciousness. Use the same foothold pattern: a definition, fake evidence, a grave warning. Test each motion against the emptiness rule before it enters the hat.

**Ribbon retired.** If the ribbon starts to feel like a prize with status, leave it in a drawer. The game is funnier without rank.

Replay when you want the music of argument and you do not want a winner. Retire any motion that picks up a real charge. Paper can hold a grudge. Fresh slips are cheap.

The Ridiculous Role Reversal is the nearby chapter if you would rather exaggerate each other's manner than a spoon. Keep the two games distinct. One corrects a portrait of a person. This one abandons a portrait of nothing.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you.

They draw the moon. Vale flips tails and must oppose. Rowan, affirmative, 70 seconds, grave: "Showing off is the art of arriving uninvited and outshining the lamps. The moon has done this nightly, according to a guest list kept by the tide, which I have not brought because the tide asked for it back. If we fail to censure it, the lamps will unionize."

Vale, negative: "The moon is a rock with a timetable. Flattery will make it late, and lateness in a rock is how you get ships confused and poets unbearable. I move that we leave it alone."

They nod, because the apartment is small. Both say, in kitchen voices, "I do not hold this position." Rowan adds, "I am glad the card was not about how we load the dishwasher." Vale says, "I am glad it was not about my brother." They do not discuss dishwashers or brothers. Vale asks about tea. The moon, outside, continues its uninvited shift. In the fictional room, nobody takes it personally.

A second fictional beat, to show a stop. They once drew a slip Rowan had doodled that said, "This house believes people who hesitate at menus are a threat to supper." Vale said, "Too close." Rowan tore it in half before the coin left the table. They drew the spoons instead. The tear was the successful move.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Make one fully ordinary remark each, so your ears can hear the difference. If the debate voice is still clinging to you, say the abandonment line once more, without an audience voice, and then talk about something with no sides at all.

If a glad-list topic is knocking, you have choices. You can leave it. You can agree to a real conversation later, with the rules of a real conversation. You can say, "I named that topic so it would stay off the card, and I still want it off the card." All three are complete.

Nothing in the debate is a position you may quote against each other tomorrow. The honorable opposition has been dissolved.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the motions you actually debated. If you tore one up, you may note that you tore it up, without pasting the grievance back onto the page. Private notes stay private unless you choose to share them.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Which motion was the most fun to defend or oppose, and what did I enjoy about the seriousness?
- Which real topic was I glad stayed off the card?
partner_b:
- What was it like to argue a position a coin handed me, and how did it feel to put that position down?
- When the ordinary voices came back, what did I want the rest of the evening to be?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Formal debate, dinner-table absurdity, and parlor motions ("this house believes") are the tradition this game borrows. The six motions are original. No research finding is claimed. Absurd debate is not offered here as conflict coaching, as a way to reduce real arguments, or as practice for persuading a partner. Rowan and Vale are fictional.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 12 minutes · Standard 25 minutes · Extended 50 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Keep your names, change the world, and get your alternates through a meeting, a spark, and a fixable mess.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
End on one trait carried back from a shared plot. Keep the names you already call each other. Change the job, the gravity, and the century. In one sentence you will choose a world. In about 10 minutes you will find out how these versions meet, what they find attractive, and what small disaster they repair together. Then you will come back to the room and name that trait in the person who is actually here.

Without the plot, this is only a costume. Without the return, it is only collaborative fiction. 039, The Romantic Time Machine, ends on the quality that survives a different meeting, and it keeps your real selves in the costume. This chapter wants the mishap, and then one trait brought home. The misadventure should be funny or tender. It should be solvable. It is not a coded retelling of a real injury, and it is not a chance to build a better spouse.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Plotting is a low-stakes way to watch which traits you already trust. When the cake collapses, the map is upside down, or the ticket has vanished, the repair inside the story can borrow something true: calm hands, a memory for steps, humor when the plan frays, the willingness to ask a clear question. You feel that trait in costume first, then you name it in ordinary life, where it already lives.

Attraction, in the story, is specific. Not "they are perfect." A way of apologizing to a tray of buns. Letters that lean forward. A voice on a radio that works only at dusk. Specific attraction is more interesting than a halo, and it gives you language you can bring home if you want it.

Entry 039, The Romantic Time Machine, keeps your real selves and asks what would still draw you if you met under other circumstances. This chapter changes the versions and wants a plot, including a mishap. Entry 104, The Two-Person Civilization, invents a society's principles and then stresses them. This chapter is a couple's caper, not a constitution. Entry 041 tells true stories with one beautiful fiction beside them. Here, the whole scene is invented, and the truth arrives only at the end, as a trait you recognize.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need a timer and a willingness to trade sentences. Paper is optional. Oral telling and alternating written paragraphs are equal. Cameras can be off. Low light is welcome. Long-distance is a natural fit. No props are required, and no one has to act the disaster out. Language can be plain. Mythic diction is not the price of admission.

Either of you may reject a world. "Another world" is a complete sentence. Draw again. If you reject three, take the undersea library and make the plot very small. Do not cast a real third person as a villain. If the story needs a stranger, invent one and give them a gentle exit.

Romance in the story is fictional. It is not a request to reenact a meeting, a kiss, or anything else. Either of you can steer a beat toward tenderness and comedy and away from sex. If a beat starts to accuse the real partner ("and then, like always, you forgot the tickets"), stop and rewind the sentence until the fault belongs to the fictional situation. A lost ticket is a situation. A character indictment is a different conversation, and it does not belong in the caper.

Use the first names you use for each other. If you would rather not put those names into a story, initials are enough. Add a role each. The role is a job in the world, not a personality transplant.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Choose the world, one sentence.** Read the menu and pick one, or write a sentence of your own at the same scale. The world should be describable before anyone falls in love or breaks anything.

1. An undersea library where the books are sealed in glass and the librarians negotiate with fish.
2. A failing bakery during a festival, with one working oven and a line around the block.
3. A small research outpost on a windy plateau where the radio works only at dusk.
4. A night train whose dining car serves only breakfast.
5. A lighthouse supply shop that also rents umbrellas during storms.
6. A map room in a city that moves its streets on Thursdays.

Reject any world whose joke depends on oppression, cruelty, or a real harm. Reject any world that requires combat. The menu above is built to avoid those plots. If your own sentence drifts there, thank it and take the bakery.

**Assign roles.** Keep your names. Add a job that could exist in the sentence. Oven-minder. Window-letterer. Dusk-radio technician. Breakfast conductor. Umbrella clerk. Thursday cartographer. Say the full title once, in the name you use: "I am ____, window-letterer." Then keep using your names. The illustration later in this chapter is fictional. It is not the role you play.

**Three beats, about 10 minutes, trading sentences.** Set a timer. You are aiming to arrive at all three beats, not to finish a novel.

1. How these versions meet.
2. What attracts them. Each of you should say what your own alternate notices. Attraction can be competence, humor, a moral choice, a voice, a kindness. It does not have to be a body, and it does not have to be mutual in the same way.
3. A misadventure they get through together, with a repair inside the fiction.

If the story stalls, use this handoff, which is enough to finish:

- One of you says how you meet.
- The other says what they notice.
- The first breaks something small.
- The second gets you out, using a trait the real partner actually has.

**Misadventures that stay the right size.** Pick one if you are staring at the timer.

- A lost ticket, found in a book that was shelved by color.
- A collapsed cake, rebuilt into something shorter and honest.
- A map read upside down until someone starts again from the title.
- A radio that works only when someone hums the first note.
- Two invitations for the same hour, solved by combining them into one peculiar event.
- An order written in butter, legible only when the page is tilted toward the oven light.

The repair should borrow a real trait: patience with instructions, memory for names, calm hands, humor under mild chaos, a good eye for the next step, the ability to ask a stranger one clear question. Name the trait lightly inside the story. You will name it again, plainly, at the end.

**The return, required.** When the timer ends, even if the cake is only half rebuilt, stop the fiction. Each of you tells the other, "One trait your alternate shares with you, the person in this room, is ___." If the story made an alternate into an improved partner, correct it in this sentence. The trait should be one the real person already has, not one you wish they would develop. If you cannot find a shared trait, say so, and name a detail you liked in the fiction that you are willing to leave in the fiction.

**Fatigue cut inside the rules.** Hit the three beats in 5 minutes: one sentence per beat from each of you, then the return. The short version of the whole chapter is built on this cut.

**What you might print.** A half-page with the six worlds, the handoff lines, and the return sentence with a blank. No map to follow, no objects to gather, no costume. If you write the story, alternating paragraphs on one page is enough. Date it if you want it kept.

**Ending.** The game ends when both return sentences have been spoken. Close by repeating the two traits in ordinary language, without the job titles. "Calm hands. Reads the instructions." Those phrases, or whatever yours are, are the souvenir. The undersea library can close.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 15 minutes.** Pick a world with almost no debate. Use the 5-minute, one-sentence-per-beat version, including the handoff if you stall. Speak both return lines. This still has a meeting, a spark, a mishap, and a way back. It is the right length when language feels heavy.

**Standard, 35 minutes.** A minute or two on the world and the roles, about 10 minutes of traded sentences, then the return, then a few minutes to say which beat you liked telling. If a beat was thin, you may add three sentences to it before the return, not after. The return stays last.

**Extended, 60 minutes.** Play a full caper. After the return, take a break, choose a second world, and play a shorter caper of about 8 minutes. The second misadventure must use a different real trait, so you are not telling the same compliment in a new hat. End by choosing which of the two stories, if either, is worth writing down in a page. Writing it down is optional. The traits are not.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A deeper round keeps the three beats and adds a constraint: the misadventure is solved without a special skill the alternate just acquired. The repair has to use something the real person could do this week. That constraint prevents the story from handing your partner a fantasy upgrade.

You may also retell the attraction beat more slowly. Each of you adds two concrete details. What did they notice first? What did they respect? Leave the details in the fiction unless you want to offer one of them as a real compliment, in which case offer it in your own voice after the return, where it can be accepted or declined.

Do not deepen the plot by adding a villain who resembles a real person, a sexual scene you expect to reenact, or a conflict from your actual history with the serial numbers filed off. If that material shows up, say "that belongs to us, not to them," and give the alternates their lost ticket back.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Paragraph pass.** Set a 3-minute timer three times, once per beat. Each of you writes a short paragraph during the timer. Read the meeting, then the attraction, then the mishap. The return is spoken.

**Single-sentence world from a hat.** Write three original worlds on slips, draw one, and allow one rejection. A good original world is still one sentence and still free of a real wound.

**Low-plot evening.** If invention feels like work, use the handoff exactly, then sit with the return. A complete game can be four sentences and two traits.

**Replay.** New world, same names, different trait. Over time you may collect a small list of traits you have been willing to call true. That list is a nicer artifact than a single perfect story. If a world stops being fun, retire it. The bakery will not be offended. It was already failing.

The Romantic Time Machine is the chapter for real selves in an altered meeting. The Two-Person Civilization is the chapter for laws and pressure. Use this one when you want a caper and a way home.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you. The traits in the example were chosen so the tone is obvious. They are not a hint about your household.

World: a failing bakery during a festival, one working oven, a line around the block.

"I am Rowan, oven-minder." "I am Vale, window-letterer."

Meeting. Vale is hired at noon because the regular letterer has gone to a quieter festival. Rowan is already apologizing to a tray of buns that rose with too much ambition.

Attraction. Vale's alternate notices that Rowan apologizes to the buns as if they had feelings worth respecting. Rowan's alternate notices that Vale's letters lean slightly forward, as if the words were eager to be read from the street.

Misadventure. The festival cake collapses into a sweet landslide. They have been reading the butter-smeared recipe from the bottom. Vale turns the card and starts from the top. In this illustration, that move is Vale's habit of reading the steps when everyone else has begun to improvise. Rowan rebuilds the cake with calm hands into something shorter and honest. They sell it as a festival pavilion. The line around the block decides that pavilions are a known dessert.

Return. Vale says, "One trait your alternate shares with you, the person in this room, is calm hands." Rowan says, "One trait your alternate shares with you is that you read the instructions when the rest of us are already guessing." They drop the bakery titles. Calm hands. Reads the instructions. The fictional oven cools.

A stall, also fictional, from another evening: they chose the night train and went silent after the meeting. They used the handoff. Vale said they met when the dining car ran out of forks at dawn. Rowan said they noticed that Vale asked the cook one clear question instead of a speech. Vale broke the plot by losing both tickets in a teapot. Rowan got them out by remembering the car numbers, a memory-for-detail trait Rowan actually has in the illustration. The story took 4 minutes. It still counted.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Say the two traits once more if they pleased you, and leave the world in the world. If one trait felt like pressure ("you are the person who always fixes things"), revise it before you sleep. "Calm hands when a cake falls" is kinder and truer than "responsible for every disaster."

If you want to keep the story, write a half page while it is fresh. If you want to keep only the traits, write those and let the fish and the festival go.

The caper is not evidence of destiny, compatibility, or an unresolved fight. It is a story you built, plus two qualities you were willing to recognize. Recognition can be thanked. It does not have to be repaid in plot.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
The shared page can hold the world sentence, the three beats in miniature, and the two traits. Private pages are optional to share. A doodle of a collapsed cake is a legitimate memento. Date it if it stays.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- How did our alternates meet, and what did mine find attractive in yours?
- Which trait in the story belongs to the actual person beside me?
partner_b:
- What misadventure did we repair, and which real trait did the repair borrow?
- What did I enjoy about this version of myself that I also recognize in ordinary life?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Collaborative make-believe, bakers and outposts and night trains included, is a folk form of play. This chapter uses that form for a three-beat caper and a return to a real trait. No research finding is claimed. Shared storytelling is not offered as narrative therapy, a compatibility test, or proof of destiny. Rowan and Vale are fictional, and their bakery is fictional too.

experiences.title: Truth, Dare, or Discover

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: On your turn, choose a truth, a funny dare, or a tiny discovery, and count a pass as a finished move.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Truth or dare usually pretends there are two brave doors and a coward's exit. This game has three doors with the same dignity. On your turn you choose Truth, Dare, or Discover. Truth is a short question you may answer or pass. Dare is a funny, reversible, seated bit from a printed deck that never humiliates you. Discover is a joint micro-exploration, so you can stay in the game without performing bravery or handing over a disclosure.

The choice of mode is the mechanism. Pressure to pick the "spicy" option ends the game you came to play. A pass returns the turn with no penalty. A declined dare is complete. Discover is not a consolation prize.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Some evenings want a secret. Some want a performance. Some want a shared glance at the room you are already in: a meal you both remember, a 10-second skill, the texture of a sleeve. A game that offers only confession and stunts teaches people to equate intimacy with exposure. Adding Discover keeps curiosity available when exposure is the wrong tool.

The dare deck in this chapter is optional in a stronger sense than most party games allow. You can play an entire night on Truth and Discover and still be playing Truth, Dare, or Discover. You chose. The third pile can sit untouched and be proud of itself.

Playful affection, if you want it at all, comes from a menu you both accept before the first turn. A hand squeeze, a short compliment, a 10-second hug, sitting closer for one turn. Any item can be declined in the moment, with no replacement penalty. Sexual dares are outside the default rules. If you want a sexual version someday, that requires a separate, explicit agreement in your own words, and it can be withdrawn. This chapter does not print that deck. A yes to a truth is not a yes to a dare, and a dare is not consent to sex or to a harder dare.

Entry 013, Confession Without Consequence, is one chosen disclosure, received with curiosity, with no dare attached. Entry 081, The Forbidden Question Box, is a pile of rarely asked questions and a free pass. This chapter is a three-mode party structure. All three can exist in a life. They do different jobs.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit. Put three piles where you can both reach them, or simply agree to read from the lists below and cross off what you use. On a call, number the items and have the chooser say a number, or send the card in text. Speech and text are equal. If the night is bright and loud in the wrong way, keep Discover at "name a texture you like," and keep dares at whisper volume.

Agree, or explicitly decline, the affection menu. Write the accepted items on one card. An empty card is a valid menu. If the card is empty, dare 12 becomes an automatic complete turn should it appear, and you move on. Read the menu aloud so both of you hear the same limits.

Who starts: flip a coin, or let the person who most recently laughed go first. Then alternate. The person whose turn it is announces the mode before drawing. They choose Truth, Dare, or Discover. Their partner does not assign the mode. After hearing the card, the chooser may pass. A passed card is set aside. It is not inherited by the partner. Passing does not cost a turn, a point, or a kiss, because this game has no points and no forfeits.

Leave alcohol out of the rules. Leave audiences out. Nothing in the deck asks you to post, perform in public, involve an ex-partner, endure pain, or mock a body. If a card feels humiliating in your particular life, treat it as declined. Declined is complete.

Long-distance favors truths and discovers. Dares stay inside the call: a silly face, a sung line, a written toast. No errands, no "go to the store," no dark-room searching, no balance feats. Every printed dare includes a seated, low-pain alternative that does not require you to get up.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**A turn.**

1. Announce the mode.
2. Draw one card from that pile only, or pick a number your partner reads aloud if you would rather be surprised within the mode you chose. You may change mode before the card is read. After it is read, your options are do it, use the seated alternative, or pass.
3. If you pass, say "pass." The turn ends. Your partner does not answer the card for you.
4. If it is a Discover, both of you take part. It still counts as the chooser's turn. The partner's next turn remains theirs.
5. Stop when you reach the turn limit for the version you chose, or earlier if someone is done. Ending early is a clean finish.

There is no escalation. The decks do not get harder, hotter, or more revealing as the night goes on. Shuffle. There is no spicy tier hiding at the bottom.

**Affection, only from the menu.** Dare 12 points at the menu. Any other dare stays nonsexual and non-affectionate unless you both, in the moment, want to add a menu item, and either of you can still decline it. A declined hug is a completed moment. You do not owe a substitute hug, a joke, or an explanation.

**What you might print.** Three piles of 12 cards, about three by five inches, 14-point type. Truth cards are questions. Dare cards print the dare and the seated alternative on the same face. Discover cards print a joint action of 1 minute or less. One extra card titled Affection menu, mostly blank. No score column. No "level two." A pass token, if you want something physical, can be a paper clip you move back to the center after each pass, so it never accumulates into shame.

**Ending.** The game ends at the turn limit or at the first "let's stop." The last move, if you want a shared close, is one Discover you both choose from the pile, or a simple goodnight if you are tired. Do not finish on a dare. Do not add a final truth that "proves" anything. Trust is not measured by which door you used.

### Truth

Answer in a few sentences, or pass. These questions are original to this book.

1. What is a compliment you remember because you almost waved it off?
2. What small competence are you proud of that rarely gets mentioned?
3. What did you believe as a child about adulthood that turned out charmingly wrong?
4. What preference of yours has changed in the last year?
5. When, in an ordinary week, do you feel most like yourself?
6. What kindness do you hope you repeat without announcing it?
7. What sound, taste, or smell steadies you?
8. What rule do you keep for yourself that nobody else assigned?
9. What are you looking forward to that would sound minor if you said it at a party?
10. What story about you do people tell slightly wrong?
11. What do you want more of in the next month that is not a purchase?
12. What do you like about our life that you have not said aloud this week?

### Dare

Funny, reversible, and optional. The seated alternative is part of the card, not a lesser version you must apologize for using.

1. Speak in a whisper for 2 minutes. Seated alternative: the same whisper, or write the whispers and pass the note.
2. Invent a ridiculous toast to the nearest piece of furniture and deliver it from your chair. Seated alternative: write the toast and let either of you read it.
3. Swap seats. Seated alternative: swap cushions, or swap which side of the table your cup is on. On a call, lean to the other side of the frame, or rename your chair aloud. If changing seats would hurt, the alternative is the dare.
4. Narrate the next minute as a nature documentary, hushed and admiring. Seated alternative: write three documentary sentences about the room.
5. Give a sports-announcer call of pouring a glass of water. Seated alternative: type the call in three lines and send it.
6. Invent a kind, ridiculous title for your partner based on a real kindness, and use it once. "Patron of the Second Cup" is the altitude. Seated alternative: write the title on a card. A title that mocks a body, a mood, or a flaw is a declined dare, and declined is complete.
7. Hum an original tune of six notes. Seated alternative: tap the rhythm on the table or on your own knee.
8. Describe a mug, a book, or a pair of shoes in the room as if a museum had acquired it, kindly and in under 30 seconds. Seated alternative: describe a sound you can hear right now in the same museum voice.
9. Give a sincere weather report about the mood of the room. Seated alternative: write the forecast in two sentences.
10. Applaud an ordinary object for 10 seconds. Seated alternative: a quiet nod and one sentence of praise aimed at the object.
11. Tell the plot of today in exactly four words, then translate them into one ordinary sentence. Seated alternative: write the four words and the translation.
12. Offer one item from the affection menu you both already accepted. If the menu is empty or you decline, the turn is complete. Seated alternative: a compliment already on the menu, spoken from where you sit. No substitute is required if you pass.

### Discover

A Discover is something you do together, in the seats you already occupy. It is not a trail, a list of objects to collect, or a set of errands.

1. Recall a shared meal. Each of you names one detail.
2. Teach a 10-second skill: a word in another language, the way you fold a sleeve, a knot demonstrated in the air with no need to stand.
3. Describe a texture you can touch without getting up, without naming the object. The other person guesses. If guessing is tiresome, skip the guess and both name a texture you like.
4. Name a texture you like. That can be the whole discover.
5. Each name a song you both already know. Hum one line if you want. Silence after the titles still counts.
6. From where you sit, name the warmest color you can both see, and each say why it appeals, in one sentence.
7. Teach your current tea or coffee order as if your partner might order it for you tomorrow. They repeat it back. Nobody has to leave and buy it.
8. Build a two-sentence story about a polite dragon who is bad at queues. One sentence each.
9. Notice how you each hold a cup or a pen. Name one difference without ranking it.
10. Each say, in one sentence, the last time you laughed at the same thing. If neither of you can recall it, invent a laugh you would like to share later. You do not go looking through photos unless you both feel like it, and even then it is optional reminiscing, not a search with a list.
11. Name a tool you can already see without getting up, and describe its least dignified use. If nothing is in view, name a tool you used today and let it stay offstage.
12. Each offer a word you like the sound of. Put both words in one shared sentence.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, 20 minutes.** Four turns each. Modes are free, including four Discovers in a row. Use the whisper dare only if you want it. Close with a goodnight or with Discover 4, a texture you like.

**Standard, 40 minutes.** Six turns each. The affection menu is settled before turn one. Passes count as turns taken, so a person who passes twice has still played. End on a Discover you choose together, or end in the middle of the six if the room is full.

**Extended, 70 minutes.** Eight turns each, with a pause around the middle for water and a check: "Do we still want the dare pile?" If the answer is no, the remaining turns are Truth and Discover only. That check is allowed to change the evening. After the last turn, do one extra Discover and stop. Do not open a second, secret deck.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A deeper round stays inside Truth, and it changes the listening, not the stakes. After an answer, the listener may ask one curious question. They may not attach a dare to the answer. They may not say "prove it." If the truth was small, let it be small. "I feel most like myself on the walk between the bus and the door" does not need a childhood excavation.

You may also play a Discover-only round in which each card is done slowly, at 2 minutes instead of 30 seconds. Slowness is a form of attention. It is a poor form of courage contest, so do not keep score of who chose the "harder" mode. There is no harder mode.

If what you want is a single disclosure with a careful listener, use Confession Without Consequence. If what you want is a box of questions you both filled in advance, use The Forbidden Question Box. Come back to these three piles when the choosing itself is the part you like.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**Two-pile night.** Remove Dare from the table at the start and say so. The chapter still works. Put the pile back on another evening if you miss the toast to the furniture.

**Text-only.** Send mode, card, and response in a thread. Discover 8, the dragon, is surprisingly good in writing. Dare 3's call alternative is the lean or the renamed chair.

**Receiver's choice of card, chooser's choice of mode.** If you want more surprise, the partner can pick the number inside the mode you named. They still cannot move you from Discover to Dare. That border is the game.

**Replay.** Retire any card that landed wrong. Write a replacement in the same mode, with a seated alternative if it is a dare. Replacements that humiliate, that require an audience, or that turn Discover into a list of stops do not enter the pile. A good replacement dare can be done in a chair, undone by sitting back, and laughed about without a flinch.

The Secret Mission Exchange, entry 048, is the multi-day cousin if you want assigned kindness rather than a parlor round. It is not a dare that escaped into the week.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you.

Their affection menu contains one item: a compliment of 10 words or fewer. The hug line is blank. They say the blank aloud so it is a decision.

Vale's first turn: "Discover." They draw the shared meal. Vale remembers orange slices on a wet park bench. Rowan remembers that the sandwiches were cut badly and eaten anyway. The turn ends. Nobody upgrades it into a confession.

Rowan's first turn: "Dare." The card is the furniture toast. Rowan stays seated and addresses a lamp. "To this lamp, which has seen us lose our keys and has never filed a report." Vale uses the quiet nod from dare 10 on a later turn, not as a punishment, as a choice. When dare 12 appears, Rowan offers a nine-word compliment about Vale's patience with a tangled charger. Vale accepts it and does not repay it. Repayment was never in the rules.

Near the end, Vale draws a truth about a childhood theory of adulthood, laughs, and says "pass." Rowan does not take the question. They play one more Discover, the polite dragon, and stop. In the fictional room the dragon is still bad at queues, and both of them are still in the game they chose, which includes the pass.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Name the mode you were glad existed. If it was Discover, that is a fine report. If a truth is still glowing and you want it held carefully, say whether it can be referred to later. Some truths are for the minute they were spoken.

If a dare is still funny, quote it once, kindly. If it stung, retire the card before you leave the chairs. Sting is not the point of this deck, and a card that stings has failed its job.

Nothing you did tonight is a standing permission. The menu expires when the evening ends, or when you close the call. Next time, you write it again.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Note the modes you chose and any card you retired. You do not have to transcribe a truth in full. A phrase is enough, and a blank is enough. Private pages are optional to share.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Which mode did I choose most, and what did that choice make easy?
- Which card do I want to remember, and did I pass on anything I am glad I passed?
partner_b:
- When did Discover suit me, and what did we actually notice?
- What did we put on the affection menu, what did I decline, and what should stay off the menu next time?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Truth or dare is a folk party game. This chapter adds Discover and tightens the dare rules. The questions, dares, and discovers above are original. No research finding is claimed, and no disclosure study is attached to a dare. The game does not measure trust or courage. Rowan and Vale are fictional.

experiences.title: The Secret Mission Exchange

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Trade three small missions for the week, thoughtful, funny, and affectionate, and treat a pass as a finished report.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
A mission, in this chapter, is a small action you hand to someone you like. You each write three: one thoughtful, one funny, one affectionate. You exchange them sealed. Over several days the receiver carries a mission out, shrinks it, or declines it. Then you sit down and compare notes, not scores.

Privacy means the assignment lives between the two of you. It does not mean one of you is watched. A declined mission is a successful use of the rules. The funny mission is playful. It is not a prank. Nothing in the default set is sexual, expensive, or owed to an audience.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Being given a specific kindness can feel different from being generally appreciated. A note on the tea tin, a radio-bulletin version of an ordinary errand, a sentence about a quality someone noticed: these are concrete. They also land on a real week, with a real body, a real budget, and a real desire to be left alone sometimes. The shrink and the pass are how the receiver stays the author of their days. The giver learns what it was like to offer care, including care that was returned unopened.

This is an action you assign. Entry 099, The Invisible Postcards, is a different instrument. Over several days you secretly collect short notes about moments your partner already helped, impressed, or delighted you, then you exchange the notes. You are gathering observations, not handing over tasks. Entry 032, The Everyday Devotion Experiment, is a stretch of days in which each of you chooses your own affectionate acts. Nobody assigns them. The Secret Mission Exchange is the one where a mission crosses the pair and the receiver may complete it, shrink it, or pass. A couple can use all three in a season. They do not replace one another.

The mischief is light. You are not building a trail of clues, a race, or a checklist of places and objects. There is no hidden monitoring, no location check, no reading of message logs to see whether the mission "really" happened. At the reunion you talk about what it was like to be given care. Performance quality is not the subject.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Pick the length. Short is two days and one mission each, any tone. Standard is four days and three missions each. Extended is seven days, the three missions, and one optional encore that the receiver may request. All three lengths are multi-day. The reunion is the seated part: about 20, 30, or 45 minutes.

You need paper, a pen, and a way to seal the exchange: an envelope, a folded note, a delayed message you do not read until the hour you agreed. Agree the hour you will open, or agree that each person opens on their own schedule. Agree the reunion time now, while you are still in the same conversation. A mission without a reunion turns into homework.

Each mission has to fit the receiver's week, budget, body, and privacy. Use the fit test before you seal anything. Every answer should be yes.

- Can this happen inside the week they are already having?
- Can they do it without spending money you have not handed them, in cash or as the object itself?
- Can they do it without driving, staying up late, or lifting, unless they have already told you that particular effort is easy?
- Can they do it without an audience, a post, or an unbriefed third person?
- Is there a smaller version written on the card?
- Is the funny one free of embarrassment, mess, and "got you"?
- Would you be willing to receive this exact mission yourself?

If any answer is no, rewrite. Sensory limits belong on the card when you know them: "no strong scent," "daytime only," "text rather than a call." When you do not know, write the mission so it can be done in daylight, in quiet, without a surprise of smell or noise.

No sexual mission in the default set. No mission that outs your partner. No prank. No list of stops to visit in order. A pass, later, will be reported as a pass, not as a failed grade. Tell each other that out loud before you write, so the pass exists before anyone is tempted to be heroic.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Day 0, about 25 minutes, together and then private.** Sit long enough to agree the calendar. Then write apart so the missions stay sealed.

Each person produces three cards, or one card with three short blocks.

Tone: thoughtful, funny, or affectionate.
The mission, in one or two sentences.
The limits you already know.
A smaller version, already authorized.
What you hope it feels like, in one line. Hope is not a grade.

At least one of the three may be written as "receive this" rather than "perform this," for pain, fatigue, or a week that is already full. "Receive a note and do nothing else." "Be brought tea, and you do not get up." "Hear one compliment, and you are not required to deflect it or repay it." A receive-this mission is still a mission. It counts as thoughtful or affectionate, whichever it truly is.

If you go blank, adapt from the sample bank below. The bank is a set of examples, not an assignment you must use. Check the fit test even when the line looks charming. A charming mission that ignores a bad knee is a badly written card.

Seal and exchange. Do not explain your intentions yet. Do not add a verbal footnote that turns the funny card into a warning. If it needs a warning, it needs a rewrite.

**The days in between.** The receiver opens on the agreed schedule, all at once or one a day. For each mission they choose:

- Did: they carried it out, at its written size or close to it.
- Shrank: they used the smaller version, or a smaller version they invented. A note on the tea tin becomes a text. A 30-second voice bulletin becomes two sentences. Shrinking is success.
- Passed: they returned it, in a sentence, whenever they like before the reunion. "I am passing the proclamation." A pass does not require a reason. A reason is a gift, not a fee.

They may tell the giver in the moment, or save the report for the reunion. The giver does not prompt, ping, or investigate. No asking a friend whether the note appeared. No treating silence as a clue to be followed. Silence until the reunion is an allowed pace.

The giver, during these days, does their own receiving. You are both on missions. There is no handler and no agent in the field.

**Sample bank.** Original examples. Rewrite the details so they fit a real week.

Thoughtful:

- Leave a note on the tea tin, or on the place they first stand in the morning, naming a quality you noticed this week. Smaller: send the sentence by text in daylight.
- Set out the thing they reach for first, then leave. Smaller: name the thing in a message so they can set it out themselves.
- Send one sentence about a difficulty you know they are carrying, with no advice attached. Smaller: "I remember this is a heavy week," and nothing more.
- Receive-this: a glass of water and the show they rewatch, with you out of the room if they want solitude.

Funny:

- Retell an ordinary errand as a radio bulletin in a voice message under 30 seconds. Smaller: two sentences in text, still in bulletin voice.
- Rename three leftovers, or three ordinary objects, as if they were on a grand hotel menu. Smaller: rename one.
- Issue a one-sentence proclamation that the dishes, or the inbox, have been pardoned for the evening. Smaller: pardon one mug.
- Narrate making toast, or pouring water, as breaking news. Smaller: a headline only.

Affectionate:

- A handwritten sentence about a quality you noticed, left where they will find it in daylight. Smaller: the same sentence aloud, once, easy to nod at and keep moving.
- Offer a 10-second hug once, easy to decline. Smaller, and fully sufficient: a hand squeeze, or no touch at all, replaced by the sentence "I am glad you are here." Declining the hug completes the affectionate mission.
- Sit nearby for 10 minutes while they do something ordinary, without improving it. Smaller: 3 minutes, or a message that says you are thinking of them at an agreed hour without requiring a reply.
- A voice note that says only "I like how you ___," with a true detail. Smaller: the same words in writing.

Long-distance, still not a trail:

- A mailed note that will arrive when it arrives. The mission is the sending, and the receiver may pass before it arrives by saying so.
- A parallel action: both make a warm drink at an agreed hour and, if you want, describe the mug. Skip photos if location feels exposed. A description is enough.
- A voice message the receiver plays when they choose.

**A tiny log, not a chart of virtue.** For each mission, the receiver may jot:

Date opened | tone | did, shrank, or passed | one line about being given it

The line is about the experience of being offered care. "The pardon made me laugh." "The hug was too much on Tuesday, and the sentence was right." "I passed the bulletin because my voice was gone." None of these lines is a grade. You do not assign points, streaks, or a winner. Incomplete is not a category you need. Passed and shrank already cover it.

**Reunion.** Receiver speaks first, one mission at a time.

1. Did, shrank, or passed.
2. What it was like to be given that card.
3. Anything they want retired next time.

Then the giver speaks.

1. What they hoped the mission would feel like.
2. What the response taught them.
3. If it was a pass, a thank-you for the pass. No makeup mission unless the receiver asks for one.

Go through all the cards this way. If a mission involved touch, a pass or a flinch still ends in thanks, not in a second attempt that evening. Touch in this chapter is never the price of the game. The default affectionate mission can always be words.

**Ending.** Each of you names one mission you would like again, or says "none this round." The game ends when every mission has been reported as did, shrank, or passed. You do not leave one card in a mysterious unfinished state so the mischief can linger. Lingering, here, would feel like surveillance. Close the envelopes. Keep a card only if both of you like it as a memento.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, two days, 20-minute reunion.** On day 0, each of you writes one mission. Agree the tone in advance if you want both to be funny, or let each giver choose. Open on day 1. Reunion on day 2, even if the mission was passed in the first hour. Report it anyway. A two-day pass is a complete short game.

**Standard, four days, 30-minute reunion.** Three missions each, sealed on day 0. The receiver opens at their pace across the next few days. Reunion on day 4 or on the morning of day 5 if the week slipped, which it may. Slipping the reunion by a day is still the standard game. Skipping the reunion is the thing to avoid. If you must delay, set the new time before you hang up.

**Extended, seven days, 45-minute reunion.** The same three missions, with more air around them. Midweek, either of you may send a one-line check that is not a status demand: "Still a good week for these?" The other person may say "yes," "shrink everything," or "pause until reunion." On the last day, the receiver may request one encore, built from a mission they actually liked, at the same size or smaller. The giver may also pass on creating an encore. No encore is required to complete the week. The reunion includes the encore only if it happened.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Depth is specificity, not difficulty. In a deeper round, the thoughtful mission must refer to something true of this month, not a generic romance. "You have been carrying the Tuesday appointment" beats "you are amazing." The funny mission must be shareable in the reunion without a wince. The affectionate mission must include its smaller version on the same card, so a tired day is already provided for.

You may add, on each card, "A version that is receive-only." That gives the receiver two legal sizes plus a pass. More options make refusal easier to say, which makes acceptance mean more.

Do not deepen the week by making the missions grander, more public, or more like tests of devotion. Grandeur is how a kind note becomes a production. If what you want is to notice what your partner already does, The Invisible Postcards is the fitting chapter. If what you want is to choose your own acts without receiving an assignment, The Everyday Devotion Experiment is the fitting one. Play this chapter when the gift is the assignment, and the freedom inside it is the right to shrink or return it.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
**One tone.** A funny-only week, or an affectionate-only week, if three tones feel like too many costumes. Say so on day 0. The fit test remains.

**Parallel distance.** You never see the execution. You hear about it at the reunion. This variation suits pairs who like a reveal and pairs who do not want to be observed.

**Receiver drafts the limit line.** Before day 0 ends, each of you writes limits the other must respect: bedtime, scent, budget, no surprise guests, no voice notes after 8. The giver writes inside those limits. This is often kinder than guessing.

**Replay.** Once in a season is plenty for many pairs. When you play again, read the retired lines first. A mission that delighted in April may be noise in November. Let November win. Keep one card that aged well, if you have one, and rewrite the other two from scratch.

Entry 047, Truth, Dare, or Discover, is a same-evening game with a pass inside the hour. This one spreads the pass across days. Use both if you like both clocks.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you.

On a Sunday they seal three missions each and agree to a Thursday reunion. Vale's thoughtful card for Rowan says: "Receive a note on the tea tin that names a quality from this week. You do not have to perform anything. Smaller: I will text the sentence if the tin is a bad place. Daytime. No scent." The hope line says, "I hope it feels like being seen on an ordinary morning."

Rowan opens it Tuesday, reads a sentence about the way Rowan talks to a worried neighbor, and leaves the note on the counter because the tin is empty. Shrank, slightly, by moving the paper. The log line: "It was good to be caught being decent when I thought nobody was scoring decency." They will say at reunion that they do not want a score. Vale will agree, and will be glad the sentence landed.

Vale's funny card: "Send a radio bulletin, under 30 seconds, about your walk to the mailbox." Rowan passes on Wednesday. "Voice is tired. Passing the bulletin." Vale does not send a follow-up. At reunion Vale says, "Thank you for the pass," and means it. The fictional pass is not a crack in the week.

Rowan's affectionate card for Vale: "A 10-second hug on a day you choose, easy to decline. Smaller: the sentence 'I like how you read instructions when I am already guessing,' spoken once." Vale takes the sentence on Thursday morning and declines the hug because the day is hot and touch is too much. The decline completes the mission. Rowan does not offer a second hug at the reunion to "finish." It is already finished.

They do not check each other's phones to confirm the bulletin was never recorded. There is nothing to confirm. The report was the game.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Thank each other for one thing: a mission that fit, a shrink that showed good sense, or a pass that kept the week honest. If you want a repeat, name the tone, not a permanent program. "Another funny one next month" is enough. A weekly quota would turn care into a chart, and this chapter is not a chart.

If a mission uncovered a preference you did not know, write it where you will see it before the next exchange. "No voice notes after 8." "Tea-tin notes are welcome." Preferences are the real souvenir.

A mission is not consent to touch, to spend money, or to be watched. The reunion closes the file.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Keep a line per mission in the log below if you want a record of the days, not a productivity tally. The private prompts ask about giving and receiving from two angles. Sharing a private page is optional.

Log, as many rows as you used:

Date opened | tone | did, shrank, or passed | what it was like to be given it

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- What was it like to receive a mission I did not choose, including any I shrank or passed?
- Which mission I assigned came closest to the care I meant, and what did the response teach me?
partner_b:
- What did I learn about giving an assignment, rather than only choosing an act for myself?
- Which mission I received felt like being known, and which did I change so it would fit the week?
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Friend groups sometimes draw names for small acts of care. This chapter narrows that custom to a pair, with three tones and an explicit decline. See G2012 only as a boundary. That paper linked feeling appreciative and feeling appreciated with responsiveness, commitment, and relationship maintenance, and it noted that appreciation can show up in behavior. It did not test assigned missions. A scripted task sits outside its claim. Nothing in this chapter is evidence that a relationship has improved. Rowan and Vale are fictional.

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One real fork, an ordinary day on the other side, and the desire that never quite left.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Name one real fork. A training you did not start. A move you priced and then did not make. A timing that closed while you were looking at it. The choice got made. The other road still has an ordinary day on it.

This hour is for one of those forks. A real one, from a life this person might have entered. You each pick one. You describe an ordinary day over there, the desire that still has a pulse over here, and one thing in the present you would not trade away. The listener's work is small and specific. Hear the desire, and say it back in a sentence.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
People edit a history until it leads neatly to now. Roads that stayed open for a while, then closed, fall out of the story because they complicate the plot. They still shape taste. Someone who almost became a field biologist may care about weather in a way the résumé does not explain. Someone who almost stayed in a city may go quiet when a certain train line comes up.

The mechanism is narrow. You are letting one alternate become imaginable, then noticing which desire survived the decision. A desire can be heard without being obeyed. Hearing it is different from agreeing to chase it, and different from congratulating the speaker for staying. The partner is not the prosecutor, and the speaker is not being recruited back onto the old path.

Wondering about a road not taken is an old kitchen-table habit. This chapter gives that habit a shape. It is a conversation or a letter, and it stops at one fork each. It is not a grief protocol, not career counseling, and not a clinical life review. If the fork that wants to be told is a death, an illness, or another loss, set it down. Choose a milder fork, or pass. Nobody here is required to mourn.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can hear each other, or agree to exchange letters. Phones facedown. If you are tired, the short version is the honest one.

A usable fork was imaginable from the speaker's own life: a city, a vocation, a timing, a course of training. "If I had been born someone else" is a different game. The person on the other side of the fork should still be recognizable as the person speaking.

Three agreements, said once, before anyone performs a past:

You may pass, pause, or trade the fork for a milder one.
The historical choice is not on trial. Skip the speech about how it all worked out, and skip the speech about how it did not.
If what you are about to describe is a decision you have already made that changes the other person's life, say that in plain language and pause. An imagined day is a poor hiding place for a plan to leave.

Paper or a notes app. A timer, if you want the day to stay ordinary instead of becoming a film.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Take 5 minutes of quiet. Each person writes four lines. You can say them later instead of reading them. The writing is there so the third line does not get swallowed by the first.

The fork. One sentence. Name the choice and the year as well as memory allows.

One ordinary day on the other side. Breakfast, the first tool, the commute, the sound of the place at 4 p.m. Keep the heroics out. If the day only works as a montage of triumph, the desire will be harder to see.

The desire that still lives in this life. Say it as a want. "I still want work that ends with an object in my hands." You do not owe an explanation of whether the want is practical.

One thing from the present life you would not trade away. A person, a skill, a street, a joke, a kind of morning. If the only available feeling is a grievance, choose a different fork.

The speaker goes first, about 4 minutes. Read the lines or tell them. The listener does not answer with a parallel story yet.

Then the listener reflects the desire in one sentence. A clean shape sounds like this: "What I hear still wanting a place is work that ends with an object in your hands." Stop. You may ask one question, and the question belongs to the desire. "Where does that want show up on a normal Tuesday?" is fair. A question that asks the speaker to ratify the old choice is a verdict, and this hour has no verdicts.

If the speaker cannot find the desire, they may say, "The day is vivid and the want is blurry." That finishes the turn. The listener repeats the blur. They do not install a more satisfying dream.

Switch. One fork each. A stack of almost-lives turns the hour into a catalog, and the desire disappears into the list.

Close with a sorting word from the speaker, said out loud so the imagining does not silently become a plan.

Keep. The story was good to tell, and it can stay a story.
Borrow. Some piece of the other day might fit inside this life. You are not deciding that tonight.
Leave. The fork was worth naming, and you are setting it back down.

Imagining a path is not agreeing to pursue it.

One hard case, handled in the open. Sometimes a person names their partner, or a child, as the reason a life was lost. If that sentence arrives, pause. The listener does not defend their existence, and does not agree to play the cost. The speaker either adds, with care, the thing they would not trade, or they pass and pick another fork later. Grief about a closed road can sit in the same life as love for the people in the room. This exercise has room for the grief when it is not being used as a blade.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One fork in the room, or one each if you are both already clear. Skip the written day. Say the fork, the desire, and the thing you would not trade. The listener gives the one-sentence reflection. A single fork is a finished session.

**40 minutes.** 5 minutes to write the four lines. Each person speaks for about 4 minutes and receives the reflection and, if they want it, one question. End with keep, borrow, or leave. This is the version that lets the ordinary day do its work.

**75 minutes.** Write the other day as a short letter, a page at most, and trade the letters before you speak. Read in silence. Then the same reflection, plus a little time to say which detail felt like the speaker and which detail felt like costume. Still one fork each. The extra minutes are for accuracy.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, if you both want another round, choose a fork of a different kind. A vocation the first time, a city or a timing the next. Same four lines. Leave the second round out of this sitting unless you are genuinely fresh. Tired people reach for the most dramatic road, which is rarely the truest one.

You can ask the speaker for one sensory detail from the other day that still appeals, and one detail that would have grated by week three. That question keeps the alternate from becoming a shrine.

A further question, only if the speaker invites it: "Is any small piece of that desire already present, in a form I might be walking past?" The listener may offer an observation. They do not assign a project.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By letter or voice note, the exercise travels. The reply is still one sentence about the desire, sent after the letter is read, not a debate in the margins.

If speech is tiring, stay on the page. If writing is tiring, tell the four lines and let the listener jot the desire so the sentence stays accurate. No map, photograph, or walk is required. The motif for this chapter is a second road drawn faintly beside the lived one. A private sketch of your own fork is optional, and it stays private unless you show it.

Replay when a new fork becomes visible, or when an old one changes temperature. The same town, described years apart, is often a different desire wearing the same place name. Date the page so the later version has something to meet.

003, The Five Defining Moments, is for experiences that did happen. 004, Before I Was Me, looks at younger selves that are still in the room. 053, If Nobody Were Watching, starts in the present and asks what you would pursue, express, or abandon if the usual audiences stepped outside. Different tools. Leave them different.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan writes: "In 2011 I was offered a two-year boat-repair apprenticeship in a yard I already knew. I took a salaried coordinator job because the apprenticeship paid almost nothing and the lease was real."

The ordinary day is up before light, coffee from a thermos, a skiff that needs a seam worked, hands cold until ten, lunch on the dock steps, the particular pleasure of a joint that fits. There is no regatta and no speech about the sea.

The desire: "I still want a kind of competence you can see. I want to fix a physical thing and have it hold."

Would not trade: "Sunday breakfast in our kitchen, and a sick day I can take without asking a boss."

Vale says: "What I hear still wanting a place is competence you can see. Work that leaves a thing repaired." Vale does not add that the city job was wise. Rowan says, "borrow," and means a maybe, not a career change announced before dessert.

Vale's fork is smaller. "I left a linguistics program after a year. I still sometimes want a life organized around sentences other people have not domesticated." The ordinary day is a library carrel, a bad sandwich, and an argument about a suffix. The thing Vale would not trade is a neighbor who knows nothing about suffixes and shows up with soup. Rowan reflects the want for undomesticated sentences and asks nothing else. Vale says, "keep."

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Sit for a minute before you tidy the evening into a lesson.

What did you hear about a desire, separate from the question of whether the old choice was right?
Did the ordinary day make the alternate life more human, or did it swell into a poster?
Where did you want to defend a choice, yours or your partner's?
Did either of you use the story to float a real decision? If yes, name it now, outside the exercise.

You do not owe each other a plan. You can keep the sentence about the desire, and you can keep it accurate.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write what you are willing to reread in a year.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The fork I chose to describe, and the desire that is still attached to it
- One thing in this life I would not trade, and why it held
partner_b:
- The ordinary day I pictured on the other side of my fork
- What I hoped my partner heard, and what I was glad they did not try to settle
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from a common habit of wondering about a road not taken, given a structure: one real fork, an imagined ordinary day, and the dream still attached. No empirical claim is made. The whitelist has no study of counterfactual life review as a couple exercise, and none is invented here. Imagining a path is not a commitment to take it. A fork that is mostly trauma may be declined.
