prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One shared day each, reconstructed in order, including the part you would not sand away.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Rebuild one shared day, in order, and say why it is worth reliving. If you could enter one shared day again, which date would you pick? Not as a do-over of a mistake. As a day you would walk back into, knowing what it cost and what it gave. The reason may be joy, ease, courage, or a sweetness that had strain running through it. Ordinary Tuesdays qualify. A day that looks romantic to nobody outside the room still qualifies.

Each of you picks one day you were both in, even if you lived it in different interiors. You reconstruct it in order, and you say why it is worth reliving. 073 compares two beginnings. 077 is the long arc. This tool stays inside a single date. A highlight reel of many days drops the premise. So does a plan to reenact the day as a test of whether you can still be those people. Reliving here is imaginative. Honoring the day may mean refusing to repeat the part that was hard.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Peak memories get polished until the middle of the day disappears. The middle is often the reason: a burnt piece of toast, a stairwell, a paragraph read aloud, 10 minutes with no errand. Asking only "what was your favorite day?" invites a winner. This chapter asks for a slow reconstruction and an explicit why, and it allows two winners, or one day seen from two chairs.

When someone shares a good event, a curious, specific response is the pattern that has been associated with higher relationship quality. See G2004 in the notes. Those studies did not test day-reconstruction. The listener's two questions of detail are borrowed from that interested shape. They are not evidence this hour has been tested.

In an oral-history study of married parents, the manner of telling was associated with later stability in that sample. See B1992. Reconstructing one day was not the study, and no percentage from it belongs here. You are not predicting your future by picking a good Tuesday. You are making a record while the details are still close enough to save.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
About 40 minutes. The day can be a quiet one at home. Travel, walking, crowds, and late nights are not required. Describe sensory details in more than one channel, so the day does not depend on a sight or a sound either of you lacks. A letter, then a conversation, works across distance.

Separately, each person picks one day both of you were in. Write before you talk, so the second day is not recruited to match the first. If you pick the same date, you will compare interiors and stay inside that date. If you pick different dates, each day gets a full telling. There is no required winner.

A day that includes later loss can be chosen. It can also be declined. Your partner does not push for the "real" best day. Skip any day whose retelling would expose someone who is not part of the exercise.

"I would relive it" is not a request that your partner become that year's person again. Say, before you finish, what you would not need to repeat in order to honor the day. The leak, the stairs, the fear, the errand. Honoring can be a bowl of noodles on a future floor. It does not have to be the four flights.

You may pass, choose a milder day, or stop after one telling.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Choose and reconstruct, about 10 minutes, apart.** Each person picks one day and writes five moves.

How it started. The first true thing, not the most cinematic. Weather, a clock, a chore, a door.

One middle detail the other person might have missed. This is the keeper. A look, a private minute, a sentence, an object in the wrong place.

The turn that makes the day worth reliving. It may be small. If the turn only works as a montage of triumph, you may be remembering a poster. Come back to the hour that actually happened.

How it ended. Include tiredness, a leak, a bus, an early sleep. Endings that are merely "and it was perfect" have usually been sanded.

What you would not need to repeat in order to honor it. Name the part. Leaving it out of the reconstruction entirely is a different choice, and sometimes the right one. If the strain belongs in the account, keep it in the account and still name what you are not asking life to restage.

**Tell without interruption.** One person reads or speaks the five moves. The listener holds their own day. When the telling ends, the listener asks two questions of detail. "Where was the book?" "Were you already afraid of the stairs, or only after the second landing?" Then the listener reflects why they think the day mattered, in a sentence or two. The teller confirms or corrects that reflection. "You heard rest. It was rest, and it was also the joke about the name in the book." Correction is part of the record. Prosecution is not. This reconstruction is not a case against the person who failed to enjoy the day at the time.

Switch. If the days differ, the second day gets the same full telling. If they match, stay inside that date and lay the two middles side by side, the way 073 lays two beginnings side by side. Same rain, different 10 minutes at the sink. Both interiors stay.

**Close.** Say what each day is doing in the story, especially if the pages name more than one. "Yours is the day we were kind while exhausted. Mine is the day nothing was required of us." There is no vote. If you want a journal line, write the date, the place, the missed middle detail, and the why, in both voices when the day is shared.

Then stop. The rest of the calendar can remain unchosen.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One day in the room. Start, the missed middle, the why, and what you would not repeat. The listener asks one question and reflects the why. A single day finishes the session. The second day can be next week's letter.

**40 minutes.** Both reconstructions, or two interiors of one date, with two detail questions and a corrected reflection. This is the version that lets the middle of the day do its work.

**70 minutes.** Write the day as a letter of about a page, trade letters, and read in silence. Then the questions and the reflection. Add, if you want, one sentence each about what the other's day is doing in the story. The extra time is for the letter's ordinary hours, which are easy to skip when you are talking. It is not a plan to restage either day next weekend.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On another day, take only the missed middle detail and give it a paragraph. Often that paragraph is the whole reason, and the famous part of the day was scenery.

You can also ask, once, "What in that day is already available on an ordinary week, without the stairs or the rain?" Answer with one concrete thing or with "nothing, and the memory is enough." Memory is allowed to be a memory. It does not have to become a project.

If a newer day joins the days worth reliving, add it on a dated page. The older day stays. A life can have more than one.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Home days, sick days, and days that ended at nine in the evening are valid. Describe sound, temperature, and the position of objects so the account is not only visual. If speech is tiring, the letter is the telling. If writing is tiring, tell the five moves and let the listener jot the why so the reflection stays accurate.

The motif is one calendar day circled, with both sun and rain. You might circle a date in an old calendar if you still have one. The circle is optional. The five moves are the day.

077, The Relationship Timeline, is the long arc, challenges and turns included. 090, The Future Memory, describes a happy future scene as if it had already happened, and then considers how to move toward it. This chapter stays in a day that already occurred. 073 compares beginnings. If you happen to pick the same day, you borrow that side-by-side method and you stay inside the date.

Replay when a newer day belongs on the list, or when a retelling has sanded off the strain you meant to keep. Date the attempt. Old reconstructions stay.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan's day is a Sunday in the apartment. It started with rain and a slice of toast that burned because the timer was a rumor. The middle detail Vale might have missed: Rowan stood at the sink for about 10 minutes with no errand in mind, and the absence felt like wealth. The turn: Vale read a paragraph from a library book and mispronounced a name on purpose so Rowan would correct it. The day ended with both of them asleep by nine, which is part of why it is worth reliving. What Rowan would not repeat: the leak under the window. "Honor the day with bad toast if you want. Leave the bucket out of it."

Vale asks two questions. "Which book?" "Were you happy at the sink, or only unloaded?" Rowan says, "A novel with a long name. Unloaded. Happiness is too shiny for it." Vale reflects: "I think it mattered because nothing was required, and the joke was small enough to live in the room." Rowan says, "Yes. And because you made the joke without an audience. Correct the shiny part. Keep the rest."

Vale's day is different. A mattress up four flights, noodles from a takeout container on the floor, a neighbor's dolly after the second landing. The middle detail: Rowan sang three wrong notes and stopped, embarrassed, and Vale does not want that embarrassment lost, because it was unguarded. The why: they were tired and kind in the same hour. What Vale would not repeat: the stairs. "I would relive the noodles and the wrong notes. I am not asking you to be a person who carries mattresses."

Rowan asks where the container sat, and whether the kindness was quiet or performed. Vale says, "On the floor by the plant. Quiet. You passed the napkin without a speech." Rowan reflects: "It mattered because the work was real and neither of us used it to audition." Vale says, "That is right. Add that I was scared of the turn on the third landing. Do not sand that into a caper."

They do not vote. Rowan says Rowan's day is the one where nothing was required. Vale says Vale's day is the one where effort and kindness shared an hour. Both days stay. Neither becomes a reenactment scheduled for next month.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Leave the days on the table for a minute before you rank them. You do not have to rank them at all.

What middle detail had gone missing from the usual telling?
What did your partner think the day meant, and where did you correct it?
What are you explicitly not asking life, or each other, to repeat?
If you chose different days, what is each one doing in the story?

A day worth reliving can include a leak and a wrong note. The worth was never the leak.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, and the place. Mood and initials are optional. Note whether you finished or paused.

Each private page can hold a day you did not read aloud. Sharing it is optional. The shared page says what the chosen days are doing in the story. There is no required winner.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The shared day you would relive: the place, and why it mattered, while the details are still close.
- A middle detail your partner may have missed, and what you would not need to repeat in order to honor the day.
partner_b:
- Your day, which may be a different day, reconstructed around what you do not want to lose.
- How your day started and how it ended, including a strain you are keeping in the account.
shared:
- If the pages name more than one day, what each day is doing in the story. There is no required winner.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Has a newer day joined the days worth reliving?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Reimagined from the folk question "What was your favorite day?" The slow reconstruction of one day, plus an explicit why, is the mechanism. Reliving here is imaginative. It is not a claim that the day can or should be repeated, and it is not a tested intervention.

See G2004. Telling someone about a good event was associated with positive affect and well-being beyond the event itself. Perceived active-constructive responses were associated with higher relationship quality. Passive or destructive responses were not the helpful pattern. The listener's detail questions are a design borrowed from that interested pattern. G2004 did not test day-reconstruction.

See B1992. In a selected sample of married parents, the manner of telling in an Oral History Interview conducted for the study was associated with later marital stability over about three years. Fondness, we-ness, negativity, chaos, and disappointment ran in the directions stated in the abstract. Sample limits are in the notes to 073. This chapter was not that interview. No divorce-prediction percentage belongs here.

Ordinary Tuesdays qualify. Do not use the reconstruction to prosecute what the other person failed to enjoy at the time.

experiences.title: The Forbidden Question Box

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Rare questions go in privately, chance draws them, and a pass finishes the turn.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text: Twenty-four slips, a private cut to five, a draw, and a pass. The questions that feel slightly impolite, slightly obvious, or slightly too alive for a weeknight are still in the room. They get a job only if chance draws them, and either of you may pass. The pass is the whole turn. No reason, no substitute dare, no speech about openness.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A host with a clever list can turn curiosity into an interview. The person who did not write the list spends the evening on someone else's timing. A box you both fill, then refuse to curate in the moment, asks something neither of you selected with eye contact. That is a different feeling from being praised, and a different feeling from being quizzed.

Rarity is the point. Invasion is a different sport. A question you are rarely asked can be about the first hour of a free Saturday. It can be about which compliment you trust least. Willingness to answer every slip is a poor way to measure love. The interesting information is often which question got air, which one went back, and whether a pass could sit in the room without a trial.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can both reach the bowl. Phones face down. If you are on a call, each of you needs a private list and a way to roll a number, described under variations.

Before anyone writes, name topics that are off the table tonight if either of you wants them off: sex, family trauma, ex-partners, money, faith, or anything else you choose. A nod is enough. A question that asks someone to disclose harm, an illness, or a third person's secret is a misfit for a random draw. If one appears, pass it and tear it up.

Two writing manners. Avoid a question you already know your partner will not want. And both of you supply slips. A bowl filled by one person is an interview. Rebuild it.

A pass is a finished turn. Ending the session early is a finished session. An answer is not a promise to act on what was said, and it is not consent to touch or to sex if a question wanders near either.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
### Build the box

Use the 24 slips at the end of this section, or blank paper if you want every question to be original. Cut the printed slips apart. Shuffle them face down. Deal 12 to each person.

Take your 12 somewhere the other person is not reading over your shoulder. Set aside any slip that assumes a body, a family form, or a sexual life you do not share. You do not owe a category name. From what remains, keep five. If fewer than five remain, write originals until you have five. You may also rewrite a kept slip in your own words, or swap one for a question you write from scratch. Questions you are rarely asked belong in the box. So do questions you rarely dare to ask. Pocket or tear up the rest without showing them.

Fold each kept slip so the wording is inside. Put an initial on the outside, small, so a drawn slip can be offered back to its author. Drop the five folds into the bowl. Do not comment on what you think the other person discarded.

If you would rather skip the printed bank, each of you writes five original questions under the same privacy rules and folds them the same way. The bank is there so the evening can start without invention. Originals are welcome. They are not a higher grade of honesty.

### A turn

Flip a coin. The winner draws first. After that, you alternate. A session holds at most four draws. Passes count. An early "close the box" counts as the end, even if draws remain.

The person who draws opens the slip. They may read it silently, or ask to hear it aloud.

They then choose one of three endings.

**Answer.** Speak as long as you want. When you are done, say "that's the answer." That sentence closes the turn. The listener may ask one question only if you invite it. After the close, the listener says "thank you" or stays quiet. A follow-up that corners a finished answer is outside the game.

**Pass.** Say "pass," or set the slip down and tap it once if you want a gesture instead of a speech. The listener says "Passed." The turn is complete. Leave it alone: no groan, no bargain, no translation of what the pass "really means," no dare to replace it. Tear up the passed slip. It does not return to the bowl.

**Offer back.** If the initial on the outside is yours, this option does not apply. You answer your own slip, or you pass. If the initial is your partner's, you may say, "This one is yours. Do you want it?" The author may answer, pass, or return the slip unread to be torn up. Their choice ends the turn. Offering a slip back is an invitation, not a penalty.

Every answered, passed, or returned draw counts as one of the four. Stop at four even if the bowl is full and the mood is good. Unread slips are torn up, or handed back face down to the person whose initial is on the outside, to be destroyed without a reading. Peeking "just to know what we almost asked" reopens a door the cap exists to keep shut.

A phone timer may mark 5 minutes as a check-in during an answer. At the chime, the speaker says whether they are done. The chime is not a buzzer and not a permission to interrupt.

Alcohol is a drink, if you even want one. It is not the price of a slip.

### The slips

Print and cut on the borders. One question per slip. Wording faces inward once folded.

```cards
Slip 01 | What do you edit out when you tell the story of your week?
Slip 02 | Which compliment do you trust least?
Slip 03 | What pleasure do you postpone until you feel you have earned it?
Slip 04 | What have you changed your mind about and not announced?
Slip 05 | What harmless hill are you still willing to die on?
Slip 06 | What do you reread, rewatch, or replay when you want to feel like yourself?
Slip 07 | What small luxury feels like too much to want out loud?
Slip 08 | Which of your habits is a preference, and which is a truce with the calendar?
Slip 09 | What are you proud of that rarely makes it into the story?
Slip 10 | What kind of quiet do you actually want at the end of a day?
Slip 11 | What do you know how to do that almost never comes up?
Slip 12 | When a Saturday is actually free, what do you want the first hour to contain?
Slip 13 | Which of your tastes have you talked yourself out of?
Slip 14 | What would you like asked about your days that nobody asks?
Slip 15 | Where does your ambition get shy?
Slip 16 | What do you do with a day that went well, before you raise the bar?
Slip 17 | What rule of yours is newer than you let on?
Slip 18 | What food do you want praised for, as if you invented it?
Slip 19 | When you say you are flexible, what are you hoping will stay where it is?
Slip 20 | What do you protect by being the person with the plan?
Slip 21 | Which story about your past do you tell in the short version, and what non-secret detail does that version skip?
Slip 22 | What are you tired of being good at?
Slip 23 | What belief about money, time, or rest have you updated without making a speech?
Slip 24 | What do you hope I have already noticed, without a hint?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** Each of you keeps three slips. Two draws, same three endings, same silence around a pass. Two draws are a whole session.

**40 minutes.** Five slips each. Four draws at most. This is the version the bowl was built for: enough chance to surprise you, a ceiling so the night cannot turn into a deposition.

**70 minutes.** Still four draws. The extra time is for writing original questions in place of the bank, for answers that want a quiet minute before they start, and for tearing up the unread slips without a recap. If four feels like too many, stop earlier. The cap is a ceiling. A second bowl belongs to another day.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, the listener may ask for one follow-up on a question that was answered. The speaker may decline. A decline completes that conversation. Passed slips stay passed. You do not reopen them by calling the new talk "just a follow-up."

You can also each bring one question you wish someone had asked you years ago, fold it, and play a two-draw box under the same rules. Old wishes can be tender. The pass still works.

If a drawn question was really a complaint about your partner wearing a question mark, say so after the session, in ordinary language, and retire that move. The box is a poor costume for a grievance you already know how to name.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Two colors of paper can replace initials. Color A is one person's slips, color B the other's. Offer-back still works.

Large print is the same game. If reading a fold aloud is easier, the listener reads it when asked and then returns to listening.

Apart, number your five private slips. Use a die, rerolling six, or any shared way of picking a number from one to five. A coin decides whose list is live. The person who did not write the slip answers, passes, or asks the author to take it. Unpicked numbers stay unread. Four draws remain the ceiling.

Replay with a new set of questions. A slip someone passed last time is not owed this time. Date the session so a later box can show whether the rarely asked questions moved.

The motif is a closed box and a hand setting one slip aside, unopened. A doodle of that is optional. The aside slip is the pass, and it stays unread.

005, The Things Nobody Thinks to Ask, is a direct interview of unusual questions. 047, Truth, Dare, or Discover, is where dares live, and a declined dare over there is its own complete turn. 087, The Question Behind the Question, keeps walking down from an answer. This box stops when the speaker stops.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They have already named money as off the table. Rowan draws Slip 02, which happens to be in Vale's handwriting: "Which compliment do you trust least?" Rowan says the easygoing one, because Rowan edits a week until it looks smooth, and the compliment praises the edit. Rowan says "that's the answer." Vale says thank you and does not ask whether Rowan is, in fact, easygoing.

Vale draws a slip about what a free Saturday's first hour should contain, feels the room tilt toward a real negotiation about chores, and says "pass." Rowan says "Passed." The slip is torn. Nobody translates it.

Rowan's next draw is Rowan's own slip, about a skill that never comes up. Rowan answers: a knack for getting a jammed window to sit square, learned from a neighbor, useless in conversation and oddly precious. Vale offers one invited question, "Do you want that known, or was the answer enough?" Rowan says the answer was enough.

They stop at three draws because Vale says "close the box." The unread folds go back by initial and are torn over the sink. The session is complete.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay at the table for a minute before you turn the evening into a verdict about who is braver.

Which question are you glad got air?
Which pass, if there was one, still feels like it belongs to the person who passed?
Did either of you want to groan, explain, or sneak a leftover slip?
Is there a topic you want named as off the table before the next box?

You can be glad you played and glad the cap arrived. Unread questions can stay unread.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, the place, and whether you closed the box early or played to the cap. Initials and mood are optional. Passing is a complete entry. Paraphrase a question on the page if the exact wording should stay unwritten.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A question you put in the box, and whether you hoped it would be drawn. Paraphrase it if the exact wording should stay unwritten.
- One topic you kept out of the box on purpose, named only as a topic, or left blank.
partner_b:
- A question you drew or passed, and what the pass, or the answer, protected.
- What you said or did when your partner passed, if they passed.
shared: The question you are glad got air, and the one you put back.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit: Are the rarely asked questions different now, and can you still pass without explaining?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from question jars and other folk games of the "ask me something you never ask" kind. Those forms are folk games, not validated protocols. The twist kept here is the three mechanics together: questions contributed in private, drawn by chance, and declined with a free pass. See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. L1998 did not test a question box. See A1997. In Study 1, a roughly 45-minute escalating self-disclosure procedure among strangers produced greater post-interaction closeness than a small-talk comparison. Studies 2 and 3 did not find closeness differences for attitude matching, expected liking, or making closeness an explicit goal. That procedure is a different activity. Its question list is not in this box, and the participants were not a study of long-term couples. A pass completes the turn.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 40 minutes · Extended 70 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Dilemmas with two real values in the same room, and no answer key.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Some conversations about right and wrong are over before they start, because one path has a halo and the other has a villain. The interesting ones are stingier. Two values you actually hold are pulling apart, each path charges a real cost, and a tidy verdict would be a kind of fib.

The Moral Gray Area is three of those scenes, taken one at a time. You name the collision. You name what each path spends. You may land in different places. The closing sentence is "what I want you to know about how I decide." The evening has no answer key.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
People who love each other can still spend values in a different order. One of you may spend loyalty more readily. The other may spend candor first, or a quiet evening that stays intact. Slogans hide the order. A scene with two live costs makes the order visible for a few minutes.

Disagreement is a finished outcome. A shared landing is also a finished outcome. What the hour is for is the sight of how the other person decides when the right answer has left the building. Hearing that is different from winning the point, and different from being graded as the more ethical one in the kitchen.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Read this page together, or send the scenes ahead of time if one of you thinks better with the text in hand. Sit, or talk by phone. You need scrap paper so the first speech does not have to invent the values from scratch.

Retire a scene that sits on a current wound: a bereavement, infertility, immigration, a real betrayal, or anything else that is already sore. Say "retire." You do not have to name which nerve it touched. Draw another card.

If a scene is close enough to a real argument that you are already talking about last Thursday, set the card down and have the real conversation, or have it another day. A hypothetical is a poor coat for an accusation.

You do not have to disclose a past moral injury to play. Passing a scene is a full turn. Passing the whole sitting is a full sitting.

Nobody here is assumed to share a religion, a political stance, or a duty to family. If a card uses a parent, a sibling, or a shared fund you do not have, swap in a person and a promise that fit, or retire the card.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Shuffle the eight scene cards. Draw one. A coin decides who opens the first scene. Alternate the opening after that. Either of you may veto before any values are discussed. A veto retires the card with no debate. Draw the next. Play three scenes that survive the veto. If the deck runs thin, use Your Scene, the blank card, under the same veto.

### How one scene moves

1. Read the card aloud. Both of you should be looking at the words.
2. Take 2 quiet minutes. Each of you writes at least two values that collide, and the cost of each path. Keep the pen moving. Speeches wait.
3. The opener speaks for up to 3 minutes: the values, the costs, where you land if you land, and the edge you are leaving unresolved. "I do not land" is a landing.
4. The listener reflects one sentence: "The collision I heard was ___ and ___." Stop. A grade is not a reflection. "The right choice is" is not a reflection.
5. The other person gives their own account, up to 3 minutes. It may differ. Difference is the scene working.
6. The first speaker reflects that account in the same one-sentence shape.
7. Each of you says, "What I want you to know about how I decide is ___."
8. If you landed apart, say "We landed differently." That sentence ends the scene. There is no rebuttal round.

Cross-examination is the failure the timer is there to interrupt. If you hear yourself building a case against your partner's values, return to your own scrap. You each get one uninterrupted account. The second speech is yours. It is not a reply brief.

A scene you can solve by pointing at the obvious saint is the wrong scene. Retire it and draw again. Safety belongs outside this deck. If someone in a scene is in physical danger, you are in a different conversation, and the card goes away.

### The fourth scene, if you want it

After three, you may stop. That is a complete chapter. If you want a scene of your own, one of you writes two sentences on the blank card: a situation, and two real pulls. Leave the hero and the villain out. Read it once. Either of you may veto before discussion. A veto ends that round. Replace it by drawing any remaining bank card, or by stopping. Skipping the blank card is a complete way to finish. The bank is enough to play the whole chapter without inventing a dilemma.

### The scenes

Cut these apart. Play from the text, not from memory.

```cards
The lease | A manager told you, in confidence, that a colleague will lose their job next month. The colleague is about to sign a lease they can afford only if the job continues. Warning them breaks the confidence and may be traced to you. Staying quiet keeps your word to the manager and lets the colleague walk into the lease. The colleague has not asked you anything. Nobody is in physical danger. The job is ordinary work, not a moral crusade.
The public promise | You promised, in front of other people, to back a friend's request. Later you see that keeping your word would solve a real money problem for them by breaking a different promise you made in public, about how a shared fund may be used. The fund is not yours alone. The friend is not in danger. Both promises were spoken where other people heard them.
Three nights | A piece of work would fund a dream you have named for years. It would also take you out three nights a week for a year. The money is enough to matter. The absence is real. The dream is specific. Yes funds the dream and spends the evenings. No keeps the evenings and leaves the dream unfunded. The other person in your home is allowed to be unhappy either way. There is no villain in the house.
The recommendation | Someone you like asks you to recommend them. They are kind, and they miss deadlines in a way other people have to absorb. A letter that names both the kindness and the missed deadlines may cost them the chance. A letter that names only the kindness hands a problem to strangers who will have to work with them. You can also decline to write. You are not their boss.
The month on the couch | An old friend asks to stay for a month. They need the couch. They are good company, and they have a habit of small remarks about your partner that never quite become a fight. Yes is practical help for someone you have loved a long time. No keeps the weather of the home. A week, or help finding another room, are also on the table, and each of those spends something too.
The celebration | A relative who has been cruel to your partner, in ways your partner has already told you, will be at a gathering. They are a guest, not the guest of honor. A parent you love has asked you, plainly, to be there, and does not know the history. Going keeps a family tie and puts your partner in a hard room, or leaves them home while you go. Staying away protects them and costs the parent a presence they asked for. Telling the parent would expose a story that is your partner's. If a parent and a relative do not fit, use a community you cannot neatly leave and a person you love.
The updated vote | You told a neighbor you would stand with them on a building decision. New information has changed your mind. The neighbor still plans to speak as if you are allied. Changing your stance in public makes you look slippery. Keeping the promise means arguing for a position you no longer hold. The issue is a real inconvenience for the street. It is not a danger to anyone's safety.
The incomplete refund | A product failed in a way that matches the refund policy. You also caused part of the failure. You can describe the defect that happened and leave your part out. The clerk is a stranger following a script. The money matters. A complete account may mean no refund. You are deciding how complete a true story has to be when the audience is a policy.
Your scene | Write two sentences. Name a situation and two real pulls. Leave out the hero and the villain. Read it once. Either person may veto before any discussion. If you skip this card, draw another scene or stop. The chapter is complete without it.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One scene that survives a veto. Write for 2 minutes. Each of you speaks, each of you reflects the collision, each of you says the deciding sentence. Then stop, including if you landed apart. One scene is a finished session.

**45 minutes.** Three scenes, vetoes included, about 10 minutes each. Use the 2 quiet minutes and the 3-minute speeches. Skip Your Scene unless you still have appetite after the third. Appetite is optional.

**75 minutes.** The same three, with the text sent ahead if that helps, plus Your Scene or a fourth card from whatever remains. The extra minutes are for the costs, which are easy to skip when you are trying to look consistent. Still no rebuttal round. Still no verdict the room must share.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
After a scene, if you both want 1 more minute, each of you names the value you spend most reluctantly, and the value you spend more quickly than you advertise. Keep it to the scene you just played. A general theory of your soul can wait.

On another night you may look at a card you retired and ask only this: was the retirement about the topic, or about the timing? You still do not have to play the card.

If the same collision keeps appearing in real life, you have learned something about the week. The card is not a ruling you must obey when the real version shows up. It is a record of how you were thinking when the stakes were still made of paper.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By phone, one person reads the card slowly twice, then you both go quiet and write. The reflection sentence matters more on a call, because tone arrives late.

If a scene feels too large, replace it with a smaller everyday cousin you both recognize: a white lie about being busy, a group chat that wants a side, a favor that bumps a plan you already announced. Write it on Your Scene. The veto remains. Smaller is often grayer, because the halo has less room.

Low energy: one scene, spoken without the scrap paper, with the reflection sentence still required. The sentence is doing the work of keeping the listener off the judge's bench.

Replay when a real version of a dilemma shows up, or when you want to see whether a value changed order. Date the page. Old landings stay. A new landing does not erase them.

The motif is a balance scale allowed to stay uneven. If you sketch one, leave the pans at different heights. Even pans would be a different chapter.

085, What Would You Do If…?, asks what you would do at an unexpected practical fork, including the regret you could live with. 086, The Unpopular Opinion Club, is for an opinion you actually hold. 101, The Borrowed Brain Experiment, asks you to answer as your partner and then compare. Tonight you answer as yourself, and a scene may stay unresolved.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They draw Three nights. Rowan writes "the dream I have already named" against "evenings that are when we actually talk." The cost of yes, for Rowan, is a year of arriving home with the best part of the day already spent. The cost of no is watching the dream become a story Rowan tells about restraint. Rowan would take the work, and leave this unresolved: whether the dream will still feel like theirs if the evenings are the price.

Vale hears the collision as the named dream against the ordinary week. Vale would decline the work, and names the cost honestly: a mean little story in which Vale is the person who made the dream wait. Vale says, "What I want you to know about how I decide is that I will spend a dream before I will spend the week, and I know that can look small."

Rowan says, "What I want you to know about how I decide is that an unnamed evening feels cheap until I imagine a year of them." They say, "We landed differently." Vale does not open a second round about whose cost is nobler. The card goes back in the deck. Nothing has been scheduled.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
A few questions, none of which need a moral.

Where did you feel the pull to win?
Which cost surprised you because your partner was willing to pay it?
Which scene did you retire, and are you glad it stayed retired?
Did anyone use a card to prosecute a real choice? If yes, name that, outside the game, in one plain sentence.

You can understand each other's ethics better and still order the values differently. Take that home. Leave the verdict.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, and the place. Note a mood if you want one. The personal pages can hold a landing you would rather not debate again. They do not have to be shown. The shared page is for what you are willing to keep together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A dilemma in which values competed, where you landed, and the edge you left unresolved.
- The cost of the path you did not take, in one sentence, or a blank if you never landed.
partner_b:
- Your values in that dilemma, or in another one. You do not have to land in the same place.
- What I want you to know about how I decide, in the sentence I actually said, or a note that I did not say one.
shared: What you understand about each other's ethics that a slogan would miss.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit: Did a real version of the dilemma show up, and what did you do?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from a long dinner-table and philosophical habit of posing dilemmas. Famous thought experiments are a different literature, and this chapter does not reproduce them. No empirical claim is made. No whitelist source was claimed for this activity, and none is invented here. The chapter is a structured conversation. It is not a character test, not an ethics course, and not a ruling. Disagreement is a finished outcome. Scenes that turn anyone's body into a prop, or that put a person in physical danger in order to make a puzzle, are outside the deck on purpose.

experiences.title: The Secret Nobody Would Guess

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One true fact that complicates an assumption, volunteered, with nobody guessing first.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
People who know you well carry a portrait that mostly works. It gets you the right coffee and the right kind of joke. It also goes stale in patches. A taste, a private opinion, a competence, a small fear, a pleasure that does not match the public manners: any of these can be true and still missing from the portrait, because nobody had a reason to update it.

The Secret Nobody Would Guess is one volunteered truth each, chosen because it complicates a real assumption. The whole disclosure is true. Nobody guesses beforehand. The listener gets three questions, then says which assumption moved.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A surprise with nothing attached is trivia. Twelve olives, once, at a party, challenge no portrait unless the portrait was "this person refuses olives," and even then the evening is thin. The mechanism here is narrower. You name the assumption you think is operating, you offer a fact that makes it worse as a picture, and your partner reflects the assumption back. Being accurately updated feels different from being admired for having a hidden layer.

Shock is a poor score. Some true things land quietly. The listener does not owe amazement, a speech, or a hunt for the bigger secret behind the one you chose. Privacy remains legitimate. A partner who keeps a fact off the table is allowed to finish the evening that way.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
A coin decides who volunteers first. Shuffle the lens slips. Each of you will draw one, privately, and you may set the first aside and draw a second. The second one sticks, unless you switch to the Lighter Truth slip, which is always available. You may also ignore the draw and choose a lens with your eyes open. Chance is a helper. Volunteering is the door.

Two gates, asked privately, before you speak. Both answers need to be yes.

Is this mine to tell?
Can I stand this being remembered later?

If either answer is no, pick a lighter truth or pass. A pass sounds like this: "I am not volunteering one tonight." That sentence is a full turn. The listener does not ask what the heavier truth was.

Trauma, sexual history, health, and other people's lives are often a poor fit. A lighter truth still completes the chapter. You are the only one who can open the door. The listener does not fish.

Say this once, out loud, before anyone draws: there is no guessing round. If a guess escapes anyway, drop it. It does not count as one of the three questions, and it does not get developed.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
### The speaker

Take a minute with the lens. Write the three lines if that keeps you honest. Then say them.

1. "The assumption I think is in the room is ___."
2. The fact, experience, or thought, in a few sentences. All of it true.
3. "What that complicates is ___."

If you cannot find an assumption, you are holding trivia. Set it down and take a different lens, or pass. A true detail with no portrait attached can be charming at dinner. It is the wrong shape for this chapter.

Keep it to one truth. A pile of secrets turns the update into a performance. One complication is enough for the portrait to change.

### The listener

Ask up to three questions. Spend them on the fact and on the assumption. Useful shapes: when it started, what it changes on an ordinary day, and whether the speaker wants the detail stored or only the correction to the assumption. A question that hunts a larger secret is outside the three. The speaker may say "that is outside the fact." The question is spent. You do not replace it.

Then one reflection: "The assumption that moved is ___." You may be slightly wrong. The speaker may correct you once. After the correction, the turn ends.

A complete response can be as small as "I have that now." Amazement is optional. Treating shock as success pushes the speaker toward the most disruptive fact they can stand, which is a different assignment.

### Both of you

One truth each, speaker then listener, then you switch roles. The second truth should be that person's own, not a sequel, a correction, or a matching confession. If the second person passes, the chapter is still complete.

When you are done, the speaker may add one storage instruction: "Keep the assumption. Let the detail fade." The listener follows that. Curiosity can survive without a filing cabinet.

### The lenses

Cut these apart. A lens is a place to look, not the secret itself.

```cards
Lens 01 | A food, drink, or comfort that does not match the person people think you are.
Lens 02 | A skill you are quietly good at that rarely comes up.
Lens 03 | A skill people assume you have, which you do not.
Lens 04 | A low-stakes opinion you hold and almost never say.
Lens 05 | An ordinary, specific fear. Leave harm, illness, and other people's secrets on the other side of the gate.
Lens 06 | A pleasure you like that your public manners would not advertise.
Lens 07 | A chapter of work or school that people tell wrong, corrected with one true detail that is yours to tell.
Lens 08 | A way you spend a free hour that would surprise someone who knows your calendar.
Lens 09 | A belief about luck, money, or fairness that you do not perform in public.
Lens 10 | Something you keep, or refuse to keep, that contradicts your reputation.
Lens 11 | A kind of weather, place, or time of day that changes you in a way the portrait misses.
Lens 12 | A short version of a story you tell, plus one true detail the short version edits out. If that detail belongs to someone else, or is a harm, choose another lens.
Lighter Truth | A small true thing that still complicates an assumption. Lighter completes the chapter.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One truth in the room, or one each if both are already clear. Skip the second draw. One question, then the assumption sentence. A single volunteered truth finishes the session. A pass finishes it too.

**30 minutes.** Each of you uses one lens. The speaker has about 3 minutes. The listener has three questions and one reflection. Then you switch. This is the version that lets the assumption get named twice: once by the speaker, once by the listener, corrected if needed.

**50 minutes.** The standard round, with notes written first and read if speaking is harder than paper. Add a second truth only if both of you invite it, and only at the lighter end. The extra time is for accurate reflection, not for a stack of revelations. If the second invitation does not come, stop after one each.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On another day, the listener may ask, "Has that assumption stayed down?" The speaker may answer with a yes, a no, or a pass. They may add how the fact feels now, if they want that layer. They do not owe a larger disclosure because the first one went well.

You can also trade the reflection in writing. The listener sends one sentence, "The assumption that moved is ___," and stops. Writing slows the hunt for a bigger secret, which is useful if either of you gets curious in a way that overreaches.

If the truth you volunteered was actually a criticism of your partner, say that plainly and choose again. A surprise at someone else's expense is a different conversation, and this chapter will not launder it.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Written notes are a full version. So is a voice memo listened to all the way through before the three questions. Long distance works on a call with the lenses read aloud.

If the surprise is sensory, describe what it means, not only the stimulus. A partner with a different sensory life can follow the assumption even when they cannot share the sensation.

No photograph, search, costume, or proof is required. The speaker's word is the whole evidence. Asking for proof turns a volunteered fact into a cross-examination.

Replay when a portrait has gone stale again. The same person can have a new unguessed fact without owing you the old one in more detail. Date the page. Notice, later, whether the surprise joined what you know or stayed a surprise.

The motif is a pocket turned out, with one marble in it. One. A pocketful would be a different game.

013, Confession Without Consequence, offers a chosen embarrassment for curious listening, and harmful behavior stays harmful under that listening. 041, Two Truths and a Beautiful Lie, is built so a fiction can be detected. 107, The Memory Smuggler, hides one invented detail inside a true memory. Here nothing is planted. The disclosure is true all the way through, and guessing waits outside.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They say the no-guessing rule out loud. Rowan draws Lens 06 and checks the gates. Both yes. Rowan says the assumption in the room is that Rowan's private taste matches the serious books on the shared shelf. The fact is that Rowan reads romance novels on the train and turns the cover toward the window. What that complicates is the idea that the shelf is the whole reader.

Vale asks when it started, what Rowan wants from those books, and whether the covers should stay unteased. Rowan answers. Vale says, "The assumption that moved is that your private reading is an extension of your public taste." Rowan corrects one word: "extension" is wrong, "alibi" is closer. Vale stops. Nobody performs amazement. Rowan asks that the titles stay off the shared page and the assumption stay on it.

Vale draws Lens 05 and chooses a lighter truth than the first fear that came to mind. The assumption is that Vale is "not a beach person" in some general aesthetic way. The fact is a plain fear of deep water, specific, old, and managed by staying where Vale can stand. Vale can stand this being remembered. It is Vale's to tell. Rowan asks one question, "What do you want me to do with beach invitations?" Vale says, "Believe the reason." Rowan reflects the assumption. The romantic titles and the deep water do not get compared. Two updates. No pile.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Sit with the portrait for a minute before you improve it further.

Which assumption actually moved?
Did the listener's three questions stay with the fact?
Where did you want a bigger secret, and did you leave that want unfed?
What should be stored, and what should be allowed to fade?

You can know each other well and still be carrying one stale patch. One patch updated is the chapter. The rest of the portrait can stay.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, and the place. Store only what you choose. A page that says you talked, and then stays nearly blank, is a complete page.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A surprising fact, experience, or thought you volunteered, written only as far as you want it stored.
- The assumption it challenged. You can name the assumption and leave the fact off the page.
partner_b:
- Yours, different from the first, including the freedom to write that you talked and the page stays nearly blank.
- The assumption that moved, as you heard it, whether or not you write the fact.
shared: Which assumption fell over.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit: Does the surprise still surprise, or has it joined what you know about each other?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the ordinary "you would never guess this about me" exchange, aimed here at a partner who already holds assumptions. It is a volunteering ritual, not a confession rite and not a validated protocol. See L1998. In diary studies, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. A fact in this chapter may be emotional or simply factual. L1998 did not test this ritual. Responsiveness is the listener's job in the design. It is not a measured outcome of the chapter. Withholding a secret remains a legitimate choice. Surprising, in this room, is a complication of an assumption. It is a poor synonym for the thing you are most ashamed of.

experiences.title: The Dark Side of Me

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One unflattering tendency, a recent small example, owned by the person who has it.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The title sounds like a cape. The exercise is closer to a recent Tuesday. You each look at one less flattering tendency you can already see in yourself: jealousy, vanity, resentment, control, scorekeeping, withdrawal, or a cousin of those. You keep it specific. You keep it yours. You use a small recent example, the kind that still fits in one scene, and you say what you think the tendency buys you.

Your partner's job is to show they heard you. They may say how it lands. They do not prosecute an older file, and they do not rush to erase the thing you are trying to see. This is self-awareness at a size you can survive. It is a poor arena for a roast, a diagnosis, or a contest over who is worse.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
An unflattering habit described by its owner, at the size of one example, can be looked at. The same habit described by a partner, or inflated to a lifetime, becomes a case. Cases produce defense. Defense is how a tendency keeps its job.

The mechanism is ownership plus proportion. You say what you do, what you think it protects or purchases, the effect you are willing to name, and one thing you are not asking your partner to manage. Hearing yourself say the purchase price is different from being accused of it. Hearing your partner repeat it back, without a pardon and without a prosecution, is different from being reassured that you are fine.

Self-awareness includes scale. A glass left in the sink can reveal scorekeeping. It cannot support a theory of your entire character. Proportion is part of honesty.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Lay the cards face up. Each of you will choose one you can discuss without drowning. You may decline any card. A declined card leaves the table, and the decline is a full turn. You may choose another, or you may say, "Nothing from this menu tonight." If both of you say that, the session is complete.

Bring a tendency you can look at, tonight, at the size of a recent example. If what you are actually looking at is coercion, sexual pressure, or monitoring of a partner's movements and messages, stop this game. Say the plain thing in a direct conversation. When there is danger, outside help belongs in that plan. Jealousy and control, on this menu, mean the smaller social kinds: a hot feeling about attention, a grip on plans and clocks. Possessiveness is not treated here as proof of love, and it is not a style to admire.

Either of you may refuse a tendency you do not want in the air. Stop if either of you is flooded. "Pause" ends the scene. No eye contact is required. Letters are a full version.

The listener is in the example sometimes. The listener is not cast as the cause, and is not assigned the repair. Harmful behavior remains harmful after it has been described. Receptive listening is the style of this hour. It is not a pardon.

You do not owe a childhood, a diagnosis, or the worst night of your life. Clinical nicknames stay off the table. Ordinary words are the whole vocabulary.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Choose who goes first by a coin, or by who is already clear. One tendency each. A second tendency in the same night slides toward a contest. Leave it for another sitting unless both of you, after the first round, explicitly want one more. Default is one.

### The four beats

The speaker uses a recent small example. They speak in the first person. If the sentence trying to get out is "you make me this way," they pause and return to what they themselves do.

1. **What I do.** The example, plainly, with the tedious details left in if they keep it small.
2. **What it buys.** What you think the tendency protects or purchases for you. Status, safety, a private sense of fairness, an image, a way to avoid surprise.
3. **The effect I am willing to name.** One effect, at the size of the example. You choose the size. Your partner does not enlarge it.
4. **What I am not handing you.** One thing you are not asking your partner to manage. A chart, a vow, a new way of praising you, a promise to stop teasing, the job of noticing the tendency before you do. If you do want a specific response, it belongs in the optional sentence at the end, and it is a request, not a sentence they must serve.

Then stop. The speaker does not add a worse example to prove sincerity.

### The listener

1. Reflect what you heard in two sentences at most. Stay with the four beats.
2. You may say how it lands, in one sentence, without opening an older incident.
3. If they are trying to see clearly, leave the eraser in the drawer. "You are not really like that" can be kind, and it can also steal the look they just took. You may say what you appreciate. Appreciation can sit beside the tendency. It does not have to delete it.
4. Do not expand the confession, diagnose, score who is worse, or begin your own turn inside theirs.
5. If you are flooded, say "pause."

Matching them with a worse story of your own is a later turn, about you, if you still want a turn. It is not comfort, and it is not a duet.

### The optional sentence

When both turns are done, each speaker may say: "When this shows up, a useful response from me is ___. A useful response from you is ___."

Either blank may stay blank. A blank is information. It means you are not outsourcing the watch, or you do not yet know what help would actually help.

If you have no watch-for yet, say that. "I do not have a signal yet" completes the session. Reform is not the exit ticket. A clearer look is.

### The menu

Choose with the cards in view. Read the steer before you commit. If a card's example would have to be the worst one you own, choose a different card or pass.

```cards
Jealousy | A recent small moment when you wanted attention, ease, or status someone else had, and what you did with that want. Keep possessiveness at that size. If the pattern is surveillance or a threat, leave the game.
Vanity | A recent moment when you needed the flattering version of yourself to be the one on record.
Resentment | One recent item on a tally you have not said out loud. Leave the archive in the drawer.
Control | A recent time you steered a plan, a tone, or a clock so you would not have to be surprised. Monitoring a phone, a body, or a person's whereabouts is outside this card.
Scorekeeping | A recent count of who did the last chore, kindness, or repair, and the satisfaction or the sting inside the count.
Withdrawal | A recent time you left the conversation without leaving the building: silence, a screen, a delay.
Envy | Wanting a life, a skill, or a freedom that is not yours to take, as it showed up once lately.
Image management | A time you were agreeable so the picture of you would stay pleasant, separate from whether you agreed.
Stubbornness | A recent moment when you already saw the other point and kept arguing.
Competitiveness | A recent time you needed to win against someone you love, over something that did not need a winner.
Dismissal | One joke or shrug that made another person's feeling smaller.
Martyrdom | An extra thing you did, and the part of you that needed it noticed.
Suspicion | A motive you drafted for someone before you asked them. One recent draft.
Your own words | Name a cousin of these in ordinary language. No clinical nickname. One recent example, or pass.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One tendency in the room. Three sentences that cover the example, what it buys, and one signal you hope to catch sooner. The listener reflects once. The other person may pass. A pass completes their half. This is the short path: one tendency, one example, one hoped-for signal.

**40 minutes.** Both of you, one card each, all four beats, a real reflection, and the optional sentence with permission for blanks. This is the version that lets the purchase price get said out loud, which is usually the part people skip in favor of apology or accusation.

**70 minutes.** Write the four beats as a short letter first. Exchange them. Read in silence. Then speak, and let the listener's reflection meet the letter rather than a performance. Still one tendency each unless you both ask for a second. The extra time is for accuracy and for stopping if someone is flooded. Letters travel. Eye contact remains optional.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, each of you may report one sighting of your own tendency, in a single sentence, without a trial. You report yourself. A sighting of your partner is not your report. If you want to talk about something they did, that is a different conversation, asked for in plain language, outside this chapter's shape.

You can also revisit only the optional sentence and fill a blank you left empty, or confirm that the blank should stay blank. Changed blanks are worth dating. A useful response that has become a new chore is worth retiring.

If the tendency has changed costume, say what the new costume looks like, still with one example. Costumes are how these habits stay employed. Naming the new outfit is the deeper round. A full confession of origin is not required, and it is not the prize.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By letter or by call, use the same four beats and the same limit on the listener. Apart, read the letter twice before you answer. The first reading is for your own pulse. The second is for the reflection.

Low energy: one card, one example, reflection, stop. Skip the optional sentence rather than inventing a request you do not mean.

If speech is tiring, stay on the page and let the listener write the two-sentence reflection underneath, then read it aloud or hand it back. If writing is tiring, speak the beats and let the listener jot the "what it buys" line so the wording stays yours.

Replay when you can look at the same tendency a size smaller, or when a new one is the honest choice. Date both. The later page can show whether you caught it sooner. It can also show that you did not. Both are records.

The motif is a shadow given a face and drawn without scorn. If you sketch anything, keep the face specific and the pencil ordinary. Scorn is a different instrument.

009, The Uncomfortable Truth, is one uncomfortable fact with its own shape. 013, Confession Without Consequence, is a chosen embarrassment, and the listening there still leaves harmful behavior harmful. 088, The Thing I’m Still Figuring Out, is an unresolved question you are in the middle of. Tonight is a tendency you can already describe.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan chooses Scorekeeping and stays with one glass. Last week Rowan noticed a private count of who starts the dishes, and a small hot satisfaction when Vale left a glass by the sink. What it buys, Rowan says, is a sense of fairness Rowan can hold without having to ask for anything. The effect Rowan is willing to name: the kitchen went colder than a glass requires. What Rowan is not handing Vale: a chore chart, or a new duty to praise the dishes.

Vale reflects, "You count, it buys you a private fairness, and the room gets colder than the glass." Vale does not say Rowan is not really like that. Vale does not import a fight from March. Vale adds one landing sentence: "I felt the cold, and I did not know there was a count." Then Vale stops.

Vale chooses Vanity. At a dinner last month, Vale told a story that kept Vale looking calm, and edited out having been rude to a barista that afternoon. What it buys is the seat of the person who has it together. The effect Vale will name: the story was prettier than the afternoon, and the barista remained outside the plot. Vale is not asking Rowan to stop teasing, and is not asking Rowan to advertise Vale's goodness to repair it.

Rowan reflects the sanded story and the edited barista. Rowan does not offer a second example of Vale's vanity. Rowan does not absolve it. Rowan fills one blank, "a useful response from me is to say the count out loud before the kitchen changes temperature," and leaves the response from Vale blank. Vale leaves both blanks blank and says so. The blanks stand. Nobody is crowned more honest.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay with the size you chose.

What did the tendency turn out to be buying?
Did the listener keep the example at that size?
Where did you want to erase it, enlarge it, or match it with a worse one?
Which blank are you glad stayed blank?

You can see a tendency clearly and still like the person who has it, including when that person is you. Clarity is the evening. A renovation schedule is a different project, started only if you want one.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, and the place. Write only what you mean to own. This page is a record of your own look at yourself. It is a poor place for one person to diagnose the other.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A less flattering tendency you examined — jealousy, vanity, resentment, control, or another — and what you already know about how it behaves. Write only what you mean to own.
- The effect you were willing to name, and one thing you are not asking your partner to manage.
partner_b:
- Your tendency, examined by you. This page is not a diagnosis of one person written by the other.
- A useful response from you, a useful response from your partner, or a blank you are keeping blank.
shared: What you will watch with honesty, and what you will not save up to use later as a weapon.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit: Have you caught the tendency sooner, or has it changed its costume?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the broad tradition of moral inventories and character examinations. No particular school's map of the psyche is adopted here, and none was used as a source. No empirical claim is made. No whitelist ID is claimed, and none is invented. The activity is a bounded conversation: one owned tendency, one recent example, four beats, a listener who reflects and stops. It is the wrong container for coercion, sexual pressure, or monitoring of a partner's movements and messages. Those need a direct conversation and, when there is danger, outside help. Describing a tendency does not pardon harm. Possessiveness is not offered as romance. A traumatic origin is not required. The cruelest available sentence is not the goal. Proportion is part of the exercise.
