experiences.title: What Would You Do If…?

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One money fork, one loyalty fork, one life-changing chance, answered in your own voice.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
"What would you do if" is an old way couples and friends poke at a future. Left loose, it becomes a test: did you give the loving answer, the ambitious answer, the answer that matches mine? Tightened a little, it becomes something more useful. An unexpected fork, answered in your own voice, with the first pull still visible and the regret you could actually live with named out loud.

What Would You Do If…? plays three forks. One is money. One is loyalty or a moral tug of ordinary size. One is a life-changing chance. Chance picks the order. You each answer for yourself. Your partner reflects the tradeoff. The room does not score the match.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
You can know someone's favorite breakfast and still not know which regret they would sign. Money, loyalty, and a door that would rearrange a year are three places that knowledge hides, because the real forks arrive already tangled in logistics. A card lets the first pull show up before the reasonable speech smooths it over.

The product is the approach: first pull, value underneath, regret you could live with, and what you would want to talk about before acting. Matching answers are a pleasant accident when they happen. Different answers are a successful round. A hypothetical spoken here stays hypothetical. It is a way of thinking aloud. It does not spend the savings, accept the job, or take a side in a family fight.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Separate the cards into three piles: Money, Loyalty, Opportunity. Keep the two warm-up cards in a fourth pile, face down, out of the main draw. Shuffle each main pile. Then write the three pile names on slips, shuffle those slips, and play the piles in that order. Use a coin only to decide who speaks first on the opening fork. After that, alternate who opens. Neither of you chooses the pile order to suit a point you hope to make.

Show each fork in writing. Take 2 quiet minutes before anyone speaks. If a card mirrors a current crisis, a real debt, a real job search, a real rupture, say "retire" and draw the next card in that pile. You do not have to reveal the crisis. This chapter does not collect confessions by dressing them as hypotheticals.

If a card assumes a shared bank account, a sibling, a marriage, or a promise structure you do not have, swap the people and the money for a version that fits your actual life, or retire it. The chapter does not assume monogamy, marriage, or joint finances. Relationship forks stay inside the agreements you already have. A card is not a proposal to rewrite them.

Passing a fork is a full turn. The other person may still answer it, or you may draw a replacement for both of you. Either way, nobody owes a performance of decisiveness.

If the first real fork is too charged and the evening needs a sillier on-ramp, play one warm-up card, laugh, and then return to the premise. The warm-up is a doorway. It does not replace the three stakes.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
### One fork

Read the card aloud. Both of you can see it. Write for 2 minutes if you like. Then the opener answers all four beats, about 3 minutes.

1. **The first pull.** What you would want to do before you talk yourself into looking reasonable.
2. **The value underneath.** The thing the pull is protecting or chasing.
3. **The regret you could live with.** Name it as a regret, not as a flaw in your partner.
4. **Before acting.** What you would want to talk about with your partner, or with someone else, before you moved. "I would decide this alone" is an allowed answer. Say so, and say why that fork stays personal.

The listener reflects the tradeoff in one sentence: "You would spend ___ in order to keep ___." They do not announce the right answer. They do not translate the answer into a promise. A useful check, said lightly, is "The card did not just decide this." Then the other person answers the same fork with their own four beats, which may diverge. The first speaker reflects that tradeoff in the same sentence shape.

If you differ, say "Different is a result." If you lean the same way, say "We leaned the same way." Neither sentence scores the relationship. There is no bonus for agreement.

One foul to retire on contact: a fork built so that only one answer counts as love. If you feel the card, or your partner's follow-up, arranging that trap, name it and draw a different card. Rapid-fire dilemmas that never reach the value are the other foul. If you are three forks in and nobody has said a regret, slow down and finish the beats on the one in front of you. Drop the rest if you must.

Leave "what my partner would do" out of this sitting. That round has its own chapter. Here you answer only as yourself. Guessing your partner is a different instrument, and it turns their turn into a grade of your imagination.

### The forks

Cut the cards. Keep the pile name with the card so a retired draw can be replaced from the same pile.

```cards
Money · the object | A sudden debt in your name could be cleared by selling something the other person loves and uses. You could also keep the object and live a tighter year. Answer for yourself. If a real debt is already in the room, retire this card. The card does not sell anything.
Money · the quiet sum | You receive a sum that would loosen a daily money worry. A letter from the giver asks you not to tell the rest of the family the amount. Your partner would be living beside that secret if you accept the condition. You might tell them, tell everyone, decline the gift, or negotiate the condition. If this describes a real inheritance you have been hiding, retire the card.
Money · the cushion | A friend asks for a loan that would empty the cushion you count on. If your money is separate, use a cushion that is yours. You can say no, say yes, or offer a smaller amount that still changes the next few months. The friend is not in danger. Saying no is a complete answer.
Money · the ugly bonus | You are offered a legal bonus for work you find pointless, large enough to fund a year of something you care about. Taking it funds that thing. Leaving it keeps a story you tell about what you will not do for money. Poverty is not a virtue in this card, and ambition is not a vice. Both paths spend something.
Loyalty · the unwitnessed fight | Someone close to you, a sibling or a friend, asks you to take their side in a fight you did not witness. The other person in the fight also matters to you. You can take a side, refuse, or ask for time. You do not have new facts. Loyalty and honesty are both pulling, and so is the wish to stay out of a story you only half know.
Loyalty · the small lie | You learn that a friend lied to your partner about something small that will keep mattering if it continues. It is not a danger, and it is not an affair. You might tell your partner, ask the friend to fix it, or wait. If a real lie is what you are actually trying to announce, retire the card and speak plainly another way.
Loyalty · the favor | Someone with influence offers a legal favor that would help a person you love. You do not respect the someone. Doing the favor spends a standard you like having. Refusing spends a real convenience for the person you love. The favor is not sexual, not illegal, and not a threat.
Loyalty · the same night | Two people you love have asked for you on the same night. One asked first and is in a hard week. One is celebrating and would feel the absence. You can be in one room. You can also tell both the truth about the clash and disappoint them more evenly. Nobody is in danger. The hard week is ordinary hardship, not an emergency.
Opportunity · the other city | A one-year offer in another city would advance a craft you care about and interrupt the life you are living now. The offer, in this card, is still a hypothetical. It is not a job you have already accepted. Yes advances the craft and relocates the year. No keeps the current life and lets that particular door close.
Opportunity · your name on it | A six-month project would put work into the world with your name on it. It would also make you the person who is often gone. The work might matter. The absence would be definite. You can take it, refuse it, or try to reshape it, knowing the reshape might fail.
Opportunity · the delayed plan | A training you have wanted has one open seat. Taking it would spend savings you and your partner, or you alone, had named for a shared plan. The plan could wait. Waiting might become canceling. You can also let the seat go. If there is no shared plan, use a plan that is yours and still costly to delay.
Opportunity · the decent job | Someone you respect asks you to join a venture that fits what you are good at. It might fail within a year. Joining means leaving work that is dull, decent, and predictable. The dull job is allowed to be a real loss. The venture is allowed to be a real want. Neither is the moral winner by default.
Warm-up · breakfast or the chair | For a year you may keep either a perfect ordinary breakfast or a perfect chair. The other is gone. This card is a warm-up. Play it to loosen a heavy start, then return to a money, loyalty, or opportunity card.
Warm-up · the late train | Your train is late. You can reach only one of two low-stakes plans: a casual dinner you can reschedule, or a shop that closes in an hour where you meant to pick up a gift. Warm-up only. Then go back to the premise.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One card from any main pile. Both of you answer the four beats. Each of you reflects the other's tradeoff. Say whether you differed. Stop. One fork is a finished session. If that fork has to be retired, a replacement from the same pile still fits in the short version. A warm-up alone does not finish the chapter. It only opens the door.

**45 minutes.** Three cards, one from each pile, in the shuffled order. About 10 minutes a fork, including the quiet 2 minutes. Replace retired cards from the same pile until each pile has had one real hearing, or until you choose to stop because the evening has done enough. Stopping is allowed. A stack of untouched regrets is not a prize.

**75 minutes.** One warm-up, then the three main forks, with the text in front of you the whole time. Use the extra minutes on the regret and on the "before acting" beat, which are the ones people rush. You may replace one fork that mirrored a live crisis and still finish three. You may not add a fourth round of guessing each other's answers.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Pick the fork where your regrets differed, if one did. Each of you says what you would want from the other in the hour before a real decision of that kind. Keep it concrete: a night to think, a look at the numbers together, a conversation with a friend, solitude. This is still not a promise to decide that way when a real fork arrives. It is a sketch of the hour before.

If your regrets matched, skip the victory lap and ask a smaller question: which beat was hardest to say, the first pull or the regret? The hard beat is usually the interesting one.

A real version, if it ever shows up, gets to be real. You can remind each other what you thought you would do. You also get to be different from the person on the card. The revisit page is for that surprise. The card is not a contract you broke.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
On a call, read the card twice before the quiet. The reflection sentence does the work of proving you heard the tradeoff rather than the speech you expected.

Low energy: one fork, four beats spoken without paper, reflection, done. If thinking on the spot is the hard part, trade written beats and read them aloud with no extra debate.

Long distance is the same piles, photographed or copied, drawn by a shared number. Show the fork in writing even if you are tired. A fork only heard once is easy to warp into the argument you were already having.

Budget is paper. Mobility is a chair or a bed or a walk slow enough for the four beats. No physical challenge is attached. A game result here is talk. It is not consent to touch, to a move, or to a sale.

Replay when a real fork has come and gone, or when you want new cards because the old ones became too easy. Date the answers. "Then versus now" is often a change in which regret you are willing to hold, which is more interesting than a change in your slogan.

The motif is three doors under a single handwritten "if." If you draw it, leave the doors shut. The chapter opens them one at a time, on purpose.

042, Would You Rather: Unhinged Edition, is the deliberately ridiculous fork. 082, The Moral Gray Area, stays inside competing values and can end without a landing. 101, The Borrowed Brain Experiment, is the round where you answer as your partner. These cards stay at recognizable adult stakes, and the voice that answers is your own.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Chance puts Money first. They draw the object. Rowan feels the first pull as "sell it and clear the debt," the value as relief from a weight that would otherwise run the next year, and the livable regret as the loss of a thing Vale loves and uses. Before acting, Rowan would want one conversation about what replaces the daily use, and a night between the talk and any listing. Rowan says the card did not just sell the object.

Vale's first pull is to keep it and take the tighter year. The value is that some objects are how a life feels inhabited. The livable regret is the stress of the tighter year, named as stress, not as Rowan being careless. Before acting, Vale would want the numbers on one page and no decision in the same sitting.

Rowan reflects, "You would spend a tighter year in order to keep the thing in use." Vale reflects, "You would spend the object in order to get the weight off the year." They say, "Different is a result." Nobody updates a budget. The card goes back in the pile. They are a little more readable to each other, and the object, which in their real kitchen is a heavy pan, stays where it is.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Before you turn answers into forecasts, ask:

Where did the first pull differ from the answer you think you should admire?
Which regret sounded livable in your mouth and expensive in your partner's?
Did any card try to announce a real decision? If it did, take that decision out of the game and speak it as itself.
Where would you decide together, and where did "I would decide this alone" show up?

You can be glad you know the approach and still meet the real fork differently. Leave room for that. The cards are paper.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session, the version, the place, and which piles you actually played. A hypothetical on this page stays a hypothetical. Write the choice you argued for yourself. Leave your partner's choice on their page.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The dilemma you took on — money, morality, a relationship, or a life-changing chance — and the choice you argued.
- The regret you could live with. This page does not bind you to act.
partner_b:
- Your choice on another horn of that dilemma, or on a different dilemma, so both lines of thought are in the record.
- What you would want to talk about before acting, and where the decision stays yours.
shared: Where you would decide together, and where the decision stays personal.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit: Did a real version arrive, and were you who you thought you would be?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from ordinary "what would you do" talk among friends and couples. The structure is three unexpected forks, in an order neither person controls, answered as oneself: first pull, value, livable regret, and the talk before acting. No empirical claim is made. No whitelist ID is claimed, and none is invented. A hypothetical answer is not a binding promise. The chapter does not moralize poverty or ambition, does not assume shared finances, marriage, or monogamy, and does not treat different answers as a failed match. Guessing a partner's choice belongs to 101, The Borrowed Brain Experiment, and stays out of this sitting.

materials: the fork cards below, kept in three piles

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 45 minutes · Extended 75 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One view you usually sand down, met with two questions and a single honest reply.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You can love someone and still edit yourself down to the opinions that keep dinner easy. The holiday you tolerate. The show you pretend to finish. The civic take you sand until it could belong to anyone in the room.

The Unpopular Opinion Club is for one view you usually swallow, in this relationship or in polite company. You say it at full size, including why it matters. The other person asks two curious questions and may offer a different view in one short turn. Then the stack stops. Understanding is the skill. Heat is how this hour goes cheap.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
An underexpressed opinion is a piece of a person, the way a preferred street is a piece of a person. When it only leaks out as a joke, a sigh, or a flare three weeks later, the listener has to guess which part was the view and which part was the weather.

Curious disagreement has a small shape. You learn the value the speaker is protecting. You state your own view once, in your own words, and you leave it there. Matching is optional. Constant sparring is optional too. Plenty of couples do well with a wide patch of easy agreement and a few places where they stay different on purpose.

Classrooms and comment sections love an unpopular opinion because the reward is temperature. This club reverses the reward. The person who can say, "I don't share that, and I can see the value you named," has done the thing. No study in this book's sources tests the club. It is a craft conversation with a stop rule.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can hear each other, or agree to do it in writing if rapid talk is punishing. Phones down.

Before anyone writes, either of you may name protected ground: body, identity, family, faith, or trauma. A view that demeans those stays outside the club. If it needs air, it needs a different conversation and an explicit yes. Passing, pausing, and trading a sharp opinion for a milder one are ordinary moves. Say that once, then begin.

Pick a view you often soften. Useful scale: a holiday ritual you dislike, a doubt about a shared goal, a taste the other person adores, a civic opinion you rarely air at home. Leave the hot take you chose because it will get a rise. Leave a grievance about your partner's behavior. That belongs in a direct request, where they can answer as themselves.

A sand timer is welcome if both of you treat it as a courtesy, a way to keep a turn from becoming a speech. It is a buzzer in nobody's hands.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Take 5 minutes of quiet. Each person writes the opinion in one or two sentences, then one sentence on why it matters to them. The writing keeps the view from changing shape once the other face is in the room. You can speak from notes. You can also hand the card across and read it yourself. The author reads. The listener does not perform the other person's opinion.

Speaker first, about 3 minutes. Read it. Stop talking.

The listener asks two curious questions, one at a time, and waits for the answer before the second. Fair questions reach for the value, the history, or the cost of saying it plain. Any two of these:

What does this protect?
When did you start keeping it small?
What would it change for you if I understood it and still disagreed?

A question with a rebuttal hiding in it is a third speech. Save it.

After the two answers, the listener may state a different view in one short turn. Four sentences is plenty. Then the stack stops. No sequel, no friend quoted as a chorus, no eye-roll treated as a contribution. If you have no different view, say what you understand. That completes the turn as cleanly as a disagreement does.

Switch. One opinion each. A second round in the same sitting turns the club into a tournament, and the curiosity thins out.

Close with one sentence from each listener, said to the person who spoke: "One thing I understand about your view that I did not understand an hour ago." You may still disagree in the sentence after that. The understanding is the souvenir. Agreement is a bonus, and it is not required for the club to have worked.

One misfire, handled in the open. Sometimes an "opinion" is a complaint about the person listening, wearing a philosophy hat. If that becomes obvious, pause. Name it. Thank them for the misfire if you can do it without a joke at their expense. Move the content to a direct request on another day. If the disagreement is real, current, and still manageable, 059 is the room with repair in view. This club is the wrong furniture for that work.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One opinion, fully hosted. The speaker reads. Two questions. One short different view, or one sentence of understanding if you share the view. The closing line. The other person brings an opinion next time. A single hosted opinion is a finished session.

**35 minutes.** Both of you write, both of you speak, with 1 quiet minute between turns so the second opinion is not a reply in disguise. End with the two understanding sentences. This is the version that lets the stop rule do its job.

**55 minutes.** Exchange the written opinions before anyone speaks, so a person who needs time can read the view cold. Then the same two questions and one short reply. Still one opinion each. The extra minutes are for accuracy. They are not a license for an essay.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On another day, choose a smaller opinion on purpose. The grand civic take is easy to perform. The view about how you like to leave a party, or about a shared hobby that has become homework, is often the one familiarity has been editing in real time.

You can agree that the different view will be spoken in ordinary language, without a slogan either of you borrowed for armor. If you cannot say your objection without a paragraph you found somewhere else, you do not yet have your own sentence. Wait, and bring the sentence when it is yours.

A further pass, only if you both want it: each person names one opinion they are glad the other holds, even though it is inconvenient. That is a different muscle. It keeps the club from becoming a museum of friction only.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By text, the order stays the same. Send the opinion. Wait. Two questions, in two messages if you need the pause. One reply. The understanding sentence. Long distance is a natural fit, and so is a week when one of you is too tired for voices.

If speech is tiring, stay on the page and read only what you want heard. If writing is tiring, say the two sentences and let the listener copy them so the wording remains yours. No podium, no scoring, no standing. The motif is two chairs and a small flag that never quite becomes a banner: `assets/chapters/086/motif.svg`.

007, The Opinion I Changed, looks backward at a conviction that already moved. 045, The Great Debate of Absolutely Nothing, assigns absurd sides and asks you to abandon them when the game ends. 059, The Gentle Disagreement, takes a real, manageable conflict and looks for a next step you can both try. This club is a view you still hold, said at full size, met once.

Replay when a new opinion starts leaking out sideways, or when an old one has changed temperature. Date the page. An opinion that becomes more sayable, or that you revise, is news worth keeping beside the first card.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan reads: "I think our group chat has become a second job. I dread the part where everyone performs being fine. I would rather hear one true sentence a week than forty cheerful ones a day."

Vale asks when it started feeling like work. Rowan says it was the month the jokes got faster than the check-ins. Vale asks what a quiet week in that chat would look like. Rowan says a photo, a real answer, and permission to be absent without a story.

Vale's one different view: "I like knowing the gossip before Sunday. When I am tired, the noise is how I feel included. I can see the performance exhausting you. I don't need you to love the chat in order for me to stay in it." Vale stops. The understanding sentence comes after Rowan's nod: "You want the chat to be a place you can leave without owing a performance."

Vale's opinion is smaller and closer to the kitchen. "I think we should stop hosting the big December dinner. I like our people. I don't like spending a month as a restaurant that doesn't charge."

Rowan asks what the dinner costs besides money, and what Vale is afraid will be lost if it ends. Vale says the cost is the two weekends of shopping and the feeling of being reviewed. The fear is that Vale's brother will take it as a rejection.

Rowan answers once. "I love that dinner because it is the one day my own brother sits in a good chair and stays through dessert. I understand that you are tired of being the venue, and that the brother in your sentence is a real stake, not an excuse." The stack stops there. They do not decide the dinner's fate. They decide they both heard the stake.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
What do you understand now that an hour ago was only a mood?
Where did you want a second rebuttal, and what did you do with that want?
Did either opinion turn out to be a request wearing a costume?
Is there anything you want to ask for, on a later day, in plain language?

You can leave the opinion exactly where it is. Being able to say it, and being met without a pile-on, is a complete result.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write what you are willing to reread.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- An underexpressed opinion you shared, and what you needed the disagreement around it to feel like.
- The two questions you were glad to be asked, or the one you rewrote.
partner_b:
- An opinion of yours, and how you stayed curious when you did not share the other one.
- One thing you understand about their view that you did not understand an hour ago.
shared:
- A disagreement that stayed friendly, and an opinion you understand better even if you still differ.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Has the opinion become more sayable, or have you revised it?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from salon disagreement and from "unpopular opinion" formats common in classrooms and online. Those formats often reward heat. This chapter rewards understanding the view and stating your own once. It is a conversation design. No empirical claim is made, and no statistic about conflict is attached. Opinions that demean a person's body, identity, family, faith, or trauma stay outside the club. A grievance about a partner's behavior belongs in a direct request. 059 holds the practitioner neighborhood of repair for a manageable disagreement, and this club does not borrow a clinical script.

experiences.title: The Question Behind the Question

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Start with an ordinary answer, then follow it down a few honest steps.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Start from an ordinary sentence. Lunch. How the day went. Fine. Busy. The sandwich was fine too. Sometimes that sentence is the whole report. Sometimes it is sitting on a want, a memory, or a line almost said to a stranger at noon.

The Question Behind the Question asks one follow-up at a time, aimed at meaning. After each answer, you reflect what you heard and check whether it is close. The person who lived the day remains the authority on what it means. You are making room. You are not installing a theory.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Daily talk runs on facts because facts are fast. Where you were, what you ate, whether the meeting ended. Intimacy, in the diary research that sits near this chapter, tracked both people's disclosure, and perceived partner responsiveness sat partway between that disclosure and the feeling of intimacy. In Study 2, emotional disclosure predicted intimacy more strongly than factual disclosure. A ladder is one way to leave the door open for the emotional part. It is not the procedure those diaries tested, and four questions are not a dose.

The mechanism is successive. A single plunge, "But what does it really mean?", skips the speaker's pace and often smuggles the listener's theory in with the question. A reflection that checks itself, "Is that close?", gives the speaker the last word on their own afternoon. Poorly timed depth is pressure. Well timed, it is curiosity with a handrail.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Choose a time when neither of you is too depleted for questions. If you are, the kindest version of this chapter is to skip it and eat the sandwich in peace.

Print or copy the four directions below so the asker is not inventing cleverness under pressure. Agree that the speaker can stop the ladder, rewrite a question, or park a meaning. "Park it" means the topic is named and set down, and it is not homework.

No eye contact is required. A written ladder, passed back and forth, suits overload and long distance. Pauses are part of the pace. The maximum is four follow-ups. Four is a ceiling, not a quota. Two good questions beat four nosy ones.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Person A starts with something ordinary and true. How the day went. What they had for lunch. What they are looking forward to this week. One or two sentences. Keep it mundane on purpose. If you begin at the deepest thing you know, you have skipped the chapter's trick, which is to discover whether the ordinary answer has a basement.

Person B asks one follow-up. Then waits. Useful directions, in any order, and you will not need all of them:

What was good about it, or what did it cost?
What did it remind you of?
What did you want in that moment, and what did you not say?
What do you hope I understand, now that you've said this much?

After the answer, Person B reflects a little of the content and a little of the feeling, in one or two sentences, and asks, "Is that close?" Person A corrects the reflection or lets it stand. The correction is the point of the check. A listener who argues with the correction has stepped off the ladder.

Then, if Person A wants to continue, one more question. Same pattern: ask, listen, reflect, check. Stop at four even if the room feels electric. Stop earlier if the speaker says stop, or if the answers start repeating, or if you notice yourself steering toward a theory you brought in from the hallway.

The last word on meaning belongs to the speaker. They may say, "That's the layer I want," or "The rest stays spoken," or "I don't know yet, and that is the answer." You do not convert a mood into a verdict about the relationship. You do not fix the problem that appeared, unless they ask for an idea and you still have the sense to ask whether an idea is welcome.

Switch. Person B offers an ordinary answer of their own. It should be a different afternoon, a different lunch, a different looking-forward. Using your turn to analyze their turn is a second interview in a costume.

If grief, work trouble, or desire shows up, it can be told at the depth the speaker chooses. It can also be parked. Depth is theirs to set.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**12 minutes.** One ladder only, with a ceiling of three questions. Reflect and check after each. The other person can be the speaker on another day. Say so out loud so the short version does not feel like a skipped turn. One completed ladder is a finished session.

**25 minutes.** Both of you take a turn. Ordinary answer, up to four follow-ups, reflection after each, a clean stop. Leave 1 minute between turns. This is the version that keeps the authority where it belongs, on both sides.

**45 minutes.** Write the ladder. The asker writes the question, the speaker writes the answer, the asker writes the reflection, the speaker marks it close or corrects it. Useful when talk outruns thought, and useful across distance if you exchange the page before a call and use the call only to hear the last layer aloud. Still four questions at most. Still the speaker's meaning.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Once you trust the check, you can begin from a slightly richer ordinary thing: a message you answered too quickly, a purchase you made without thinking, a plan you are looking forward to and also dreading. The directions stay the same. The richer start is a choice you make together, after a plainer ladder has gone well.

You can also replay a ladder a week later and see whether you reach the same layer in fewer steps, and whether you still want to. Speed is not the prize. Sometimes the second visit wants to stay at lunch.

A question you may add, only with a yes: "Is there a practical piece in this, or is company the whole request?" That keeps help from arriving uninvited. If the answer is company, your next sentence can be quiet.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By voice note, the speaker sends the ordinary answer, the asker sends one question, and you proceed in pairs of messages. The reflection still ends with a check.

If the printed directions feel stiff, paraphrase them. Keep the aim: meaning, memory, the unsaid, and what you hope the other person understands. Leave copyrighted lists of "powerful questions" where you found them. These four directions are enough.

010, The Fear Beneath the Fear, starts with fear and looks under it. 020, The Listening Experiment, gives a longer uninterrupted turn. 097, The Emotional Archaeologists, takes one strong reaction and refuses to invent a cause. This chapter starts at an ordinary answer and does not require a powerful feeling. The motif is a short flight of stairs under a plain door: `assets/chapters/087/motif.svg`.

Replay on a walk, a call, or a tired evening when "How was your day?" deserves a real chance. Date the deepest layer you are willing to write. The rest can stay in the air.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan says, "Lunch was a cheese sandwich at my desk. I ate it in about 4 minutes."

Vale asks what it cost. Rowan says it cost the break they had promised themselves, and the sandwich was fine, which almost made it worse. Vale reflects: "You got food, and you missed the pause you wanted. The fineness of the sandwich rubbed that in." Rowan says, "Close. The pause was the point, not the food."

Vale asks what the desk reminded them of. Rowan is quiet, then says it reminded them of a year when meals were something you survived between tasks, and they have been proud of leaving that year. "I don't like catching myself back in it."

Vale reflects the catch, and the pride. Rowan says the reflection is close, and stops the ladder. "That's the layer. I don't want a new lunch plan tonight."

Vale says, "Understood. Company, then." They do not produce a schedule.

Vale's ordinary answer is, "I'm looking forward to Saturday, and I also hope nobody adds a plan to it." Rowan asks what kind of Saturday they want. Vale describes a hardware store, a bad coffee, and coming home with one screw that solves a rattle. Rowan asks what they hope Rowan understands. Vale says, "That a small errand can be the treat. If you join, join the errand, not a project." Rowan reflects that, checks, and is told it is close. They stop at two questions because the meaning has already arrived.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Where did the ordinary answer open, and where did you try to pry?
Did the reflection land, or did the speaker have to correct you?
Did either of you start solving a life in the middle of a sandwich?
What layer, if any, are you willing to remember later?

You owe each other the check, and the right to park the rest. A corrected reflection is a successful turn.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together. The deepest layer goes on the shared page only if you both want it written once.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The ordinary answer you started from, and the deeper question it led you to.
- Where you stopped the ladder, and whether that stop was the depth you wanted.
partner_b:
- The follow-up you asked that opened another layer, and what you heard when you did not stop at the first reply.
- A reflection you offered, and whether they said it was close.
shared:
- The deepest layer you are willing to write down once.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Can you reach that layer in fewer steps, and do you still want to?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. The ladder is a way of making room for a more emotional disclosure. L1998 did not test a scripted series of follow-up questions, and it does not show that any number of questions produces intimacy. See R1988 for the process model that work tested: disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood. R1988 is a framework. This chapter is a consent-based conversation. It is a clinical interview in no one's office.

experiences.title: The Thing I’m Still Figuring Out

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Name a question you cannot honestly answer tonight, and keep each other company beside it.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Some questions are still in the middle of you. Whether the work you are good at is the work you want. How much solitude you need before closeness feels like a choice. What you think about faith, or children, or the kind of body you are trying to live in. You can love your life and still have a sentence you cannot finish.

The Thing I’m Still Figuring Out is that sentence, said out loud, and then left unfinished on purpose. The listener's success is company. Advice that ties the bow ends the chapter early. Uncertainty is allowed to be adult.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Couples get practiced at reporting decisions. They are less practiced at sitting next to a decision that has not arrived. The unfinished question then shows up as irritability, as a fake certainty, or as a quiz the other person did not know they were taking.

Company is a specific offer. Silence. A curious question. A story from the listener's own unknown. The simple act of being believed when you say you do not know. Perceived partner responsiveness, in the diary research nearby, was a partial mediator between disclosure and intimacy. That finding is a neighbor to this hour. It is not a test of leaving a question open, and this chapter claims no such test.

The mechanism is restraint. You tell the truth about the blank. The other person does not research you into a conclusion before you have finished the sentence. Two people can be fond of each other and still refuse to turn a personal unknown into a referendum on the relationship.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit, or trade letters. If you dislike open loops, you may set a date to look at the question again. The date is a revisit. It is not a deadline for an answer.

The speaker chooses a question they can hold in this company tonight. Sexuality, gender, faith, leaving, staying, or having children can be offered. They can also be too charged for a casual night. Pick a question you can stand beside without recruiting your partner into a plan.

If the unknown includes safety or a crisis, step out of the exercise and respond as a partner. Outside help is the right move when you need it. This page is for questions that can wait for company, not for emergencies that need a professional.

Passing and pausing are ordinary. So is choosing a smaller unknown because the large one is real and not for tonight. The two questions do not have to be equally dramatic. A person who is mostly content can still be figuring out how they want their Tuesdays.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Each person completes one sentence, in writing if that helps: "I am still figuring out ___." The blank is a question you cannot honestly answer tonight, about yourself, your life, intimacy, identity, or the relationship. If you can answer it, pick another blank. The chapter loses its nerve the moment the question is already a thesis.

The speaker may add three short pieces, any of which can be skipped.

What makes this alive right now.
What you have already tried, including thinking, avoiding, and asking other people.
What kind of company helps: silence, curiosity, a story from the listener's own unknown, or simply being believed.

Then stop. The listener's first response is not advice. One fair question is, "What makes this alive right now?" Ask it only if the speaker did not already answer it, or if they invite you to ask. Reassurance that cancels the question is a miss. "You'll definitely be fine" shuts the door you just watched them open. "I believe you that this is unfinished" leaves the door as it is.

If the speaker asked for a story from your own unknown, tell a short one and hand the room back. If they asked for silence, practice silence long enough that it counts, at least 1 minute, without filling it with a framework they did not choose. Clinical labels and spiritual systems stay off the table unless the speaker brought those words themselves.

Switch. The second question is not a reply to the first, and it is not a contest about whose unknown weighs more. If you notice the contest starting, name it and drop it.

After both turns, write the two questions in the journal as open items. Solving them is not the assignment. Review weeks later is optional. At the review, you ask what is clearer and what is still honestly unfinished. A question that closed on its own can be celebrated without pretending you closed it on schedule.

One boundary. The listener does not recruit the question into a plan for the household, the body, or the future. If a plan is wanted, the speaker will say so, and you can choose another day to make one. Tonight the question stays the speaker's.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** Both sentences, spoken. The listener offers the kind of company that was requested, or silence if none was named. No advice. Write the two open items in a line each. A short sitting can be complete.

**35 minutes.** Write the sentence and the three optional pieces. Each person has about 8 minutes. The listener asks at most the one fair question, then gives the company that was requested. End by reading the two open items aloud so they stay questions.

**60 minutes.** Letters. Each person writes the sentence and whatever of the three pieces they want, a page at most, and you read them in the same room or before a call. The reply is company, still not a solution. The extra time is for the part where nobody rushes the blank into a moral.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
If the first question was about work, a later sitting can be about intimacy, or the reverse. Same sentence stem. Leave the second category out of a tired night. People reach for the most dramatic unknown when they are spent, and drama is a poor substitute for the question that is actually alive.

You can ask, on a later day, "Do you want me to remember this question, or do you want the freedom to change it without reporting to me?" Both answers are respectful. Remembering can become surveillance if the speaker wanted privacy after the telling.

People who need a next step can choose a private experiment that does not require the question to resolve: one conversation with a friend, one hour of trying the thing, one week of not trying it. The partner witnesses the experiment if invited. They do not grade it.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Long distance suits this chapter because the pace is slow. Send the sentence. Ask for the kind of company you want in the same message, so the other person does not improvise a rescue.

If metaphor feels slippery, use the plain stem and stop. If speech is tiring, trade the pages and sit together without a discussion afterward. No ritual object is required. The motif is an open ring, a line that does not close: `assets/chapters/088/motif.svg`.

051, The Unfinished Version of Me, is about qualities still being developed, a self in progress that you can describe. 056, The Questions Without Answers, is for questions that may have no human answer at all. 087, The Question Behind the Question, climbs down from an ordinary fact. This chapter is a personal unknown that still belongs to the speaker, and it is allowed to stay unknown.

Replay when the question changes shape, or when you promised yourselves a revisit and the date has arrived. Bring the old wording. Notice what moved, and refuse to fake a conclusion for the sake of the page.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan writes, "I am still figuring out whether I want work that other people can point to." What makes it alive is a colleague's promotion, which Rowan is glad about and also unsettled by. What they have tried: a class, a sketchbook, a month of telling themselves that usefulness should be enough. The company they want is curiosity, and a ban on career plans.

The promotion is already on the page, so Vale does not ask for it again. Vale says, "I believe you that the question is open. I am not going to turn it into a five-year sketch." They sit with it. Vale does not mention salaries.

Vale's sentence is quieter. "I am still figuring out how many evenings I want to spend being useful to other people, including you, before I disappear inside the usefulness." The company they want is being believed, plus one story from Rowan's own unknown if Rowan has one that is actually unknown.

Rowan says, "I believe you. Here is mine, still open: I don't know how much of my drawing is a hobby I love and how much is a dare I have not taken. I am not offering that as a lesson." Vale says that is the right size. They write both sentences in the journal as open items. Nobody assigns a task.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Did the question stay a question?
What kind of company actually helped, and what kind arrived uninvited?
Did either of you compete, reassure the unknown away, or make a plan nobody requested?
What is still unfinished, on purpose?

You can love someone through a blank. The blank does not have to be your project.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. An open question can be written as a title only. Detail that stayed spoken can stay spoken.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- An unresolved question about yourself, your life, intimacy, or identity that you are in the middle of.
- What kind of company helped, if any: silence, curiosity, a story, or being believed.
partner_b:
- Yours. The page does not require a solution.
- What you offered instead of advice, and whether that matched the request.
shared:
- How you keep each other company while a question stays unfinished.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What is clearer, and what is still honestly unfinished?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the ordinary human habit of unfinished questions, the kind that show up in friendship and in late conversation. No tradition was used as a manual. No empirical claim is made for the practice of leaving a question open. See L1998 only as a neighbor: in diary studies, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator, and in Study 2 emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. That is not a test of this chapter. Uncertainty here is not immaturity, and the listener's job is company. If the unknown is a crisis or a safety matter, leave the exercise and get the right help.

experiences.title: The Relationship We Would Invent

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Name the scripts you inherited, then draft a few agreements you can picture this month.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Every relationship arrives with a suitcase it did not pack. Who apologizes first. How a holiday is supposed to look. Whether an evening alone needs a defense. What counts as a date. The suitcase comes from families, religions, movies, apps, and old relationships, and a lot of it is useful. Some of it is only heavy.

The Relationship We Would Invent is a draft you make on purpose. First you set the borrowed assumptions where you can see them, and where you may decline them. Then you write a few living agreements in plain behavior. Then you try one tiny ritual for two weeks. Starting from scratch includes the freedom to keep a familiar form because you want it, including a form one of you needs for culture, disability, or simple love of the old way.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Unnamed defaults feel like nature. When they clash, people argue as if the other person invented selfishness, when both of you may be reciting a script with the label worn off. Putting the script on a card does not make it a villain. It makes it a choice. Chosen is a different feeling from inherited, even when the behavior stays the same.

This is a craft conversation about the relationship you are already in. You design for the channel you actually have: the kitchen, the call, the week with low money and low energy. A beautiful agreement that only works on vacation is a poster.

104, The Two-Person Civilization, builds a fictional society, with founding principles and random events that press on them. That game can rhyme with a real life, and it stays inside the fiction. Here the agreements have to be something both of you can picture this month, in your real week. 095, A Promise I Actually Want to Keep, is a later kind of sentence, small and followable, said by the person who will do it. Tonight's draft is revisable on purpose. It is a design, and it can be retired without a moral.

No study is claimed for inventing a relationship this way. Two people talking carefully is the method.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Give yourselves a protected stretch. Phones elsewhere. If you are designing across distance, use the channel you actually share, and write where both of you can see the words.

Either person may mark a topic "not tonight": sex, money, children, family contact, or public identity. Those can be named as parked. They are not smuggled into a greeting ritual.

Agreements that police a body, a phone, or a friendship are out. So is a utopia document. You are drafting four behaviors and one small ritual, not a constitution for a better species.

A partner who wants to keep a family ritual, a religious practice, or an access need says so early. Retaining it, with both of you clear, counts as designing. Discarding is one freedom. Keeping is another.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Three rounds. Write as you go, on one page, so the borrowed cards stay visible beside the new lines.

Round 1, about 15 minutes. Each person names two assumptions they imported. Sources you might recognize: family, religion, culture, an app, an old relationship, a friend group that seemed to have it figured out. Examples of scale: who apologizes first, how holidays run, whether solitude needs an excuse, what a date is required to include. Put each one on a borrowed card, in a sentence a stranger could follow. Read them aloud. The listener's job is to understand the import, not to prosecute the family that handed it over. You may decline a card, keep it, or mark it "examine." Decline means it is not your default anymore. It does not mean the person who grew up with it was doing relationship wrong.

Round 2, about 25 minutes. Draft four living agreements in plain language.

How you greet each other after time apart.
How you repair a small miss.
How you celebrate.
How you protect solitude.

Each agreement is a behavior both of you can picture this month. "We honor each other's autonomy" is a value, and it is not yet an agreement. Translate it. "When one of us closes the office door, the other waits for the door to open, unless the building is actually on fire" is an agreement. If you cannot picture it during illness, low money, and low energy, write a smaller version underneath. At least one of the four should survive a hard week. Long-distance couples write for the call, the voice note, or the letter they really use.

Read the four. Either of you may refuse a line. A refusal is recorded in a few words, so the draft does not quietly reinstall the refused idea. Abstract warmth does not overrule a no.

Round 3, about 10 minutes. Choose one ritual to try for two weeks. Keep it tiny. Tea poured on Sunday. A three-line note after a night apart. A 10-minute walk that becomes standing at a window if walking is too much. Set a review date. The review asks what you lived by, and what looked better on the page than in the week. The ritual does not receive a forever stamp tonight.

Stop. Further ideas go in a margin labeled "later." A draft that becomes a second job has left the chapter.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**25 minutes.** One borrowed assumption each, one agreement you can picture this week, and one tiny ritual with a review date. Name the assumption out loud so "from scratch" still has something to push against. A thin draft is a finished session if the borrowed card is real.

**55 minutes.** The three rounds as written: two borrowed cards each, four agreements, one ritual, a review date. This is the version that keeps the defaults visible beside the choices.

**75 minutes.** Read the cards and the agreements back on another pass, slowly, and test each agreement against a hard week: sick, broke, traveling, or just finished with people. Revise the line that fails the test. Still four agreements. The extra time is for honesty, not for a fifth category.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later sitting, take one card you marked "examine" and live with the question for a week before you draft again. Some imports only show their shape on a Tuesday. A holiday rule, for example, can look sweet in the abstract and expensive in December.

You can also design a ritual that belongs to one person and is witnessed by the other. Solitude, prayer, a game, a nap with the door shut. Shared life includes unshared practices. The agreement is how the witness behaves, which is often "do not turn it into a group project."

If a cultural or religious form matters to one of you, describe what it gives, in concrete terms, before anyone proposes a replacement. Replacements are optional. Understanding is the first draft.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Speech or writing both work. If one of you thinks better on paper, write the cards first and talk second. No purchases. The motif is a simple floor plan with one old postcard pinned in the margin, still visible: `assets/chapters/089/motif.svg`.

032, The Everyday Devotion Experiment, tries a small act of care in the life you already have. 095 is where a sentence becomes a promise the speaker wants to keep, with a cue and a follow-through. 104 is the civilization game, event cards included, played as fiction. Come back to this chapter when a default starts running the week again, or when the two-week ritual is ready for its review. Date the page. A line you drop is part of the record, not a failure of imagination.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan's borrowed cards: "In my family, the person who is less upset apologizes first." And: "A proper date involves leaving the house and spending money."

Vale's: "Solitude needs a reason, or it looks like withdrawal." And: "Holidays mean the largest available table, even if the cook is miserable."

They decline the apology rule. Rowan says it trained them to perform calm in order to be the one who repairs. They keep a rewritten date card, on purpose: a date can be a walk or a desk picnic, and a paid outing is a treat, not a test. Vale's solitude card is marked "examine." The holiday card is declined for this household. Vale still wants one loud meal a year with their people, hosted by someone who likes hosting, which might be a restaurant or a sibling.

The four agreements, in language they can picture:

After time apart, they say one true thing about the day before they open mail or a feed.
A small miss gets a specific sentence within a day: what happened, and one repair that is actually available. Grand apologies can wait.
A celebration can be a cake from the shop and a song sung badly. Achievement is named out loud.
Solitude: a closed door means the person inside is not available for logistics. A text that says "door" counts when they are apart. Emergencies are named as emergencies.

The two-week ritual: on Sunday, one of them boils water and the other brings two mugs. If someone is ill, the ritual shrinks to a message that says the kettle is imaginary and the greeting is real. Review in fourteen days. They do not add a clause about phones, sex, or families. Those are marked "not tonight," on the same page, so the silence is visible.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which borrowed card surprised you by still running?
Which agreement can you picture on a tired Wednesday?
What did you keep on purpose, and what did you decline?
Did the ritual stay small enough to survive a bad week?

The draft is allowed to be modest. A relationship you would invent can look a lot like care you already know how to do, chosen with your eyes open.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Keep the borrowed cards on the page with the agreements, so the defaults remain visible.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A ritual, expectation, or rule you would design from scratch, and a borrowed assumption you would drop.
- The tiny ritual you are willing to try for two weeks, including its low-energy version.
partner_b:
- One you would design that is not the same, and an assumption you want examined before either of you adopts it.
- An agreement you refused or parked, and why it can wait.
shared:
- What you are actually choosing, marked as chosen.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What you lived by, and what looked better on the page than in the week.
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the ordinary fact that couples inherit rituals and expectations, then sometimes design agreements on purpose. That design is a common therapeutic and secular habit. It is not a validated protocol, and no empirical claim is made. Traditional and cultural forms are available to keep on purpose. The draft assumes nothing about marriage, monogamy, shared finances, or children. Agreements are revisable. They are a craft conversation between these two people.
