metadata.duration_summary: Short 25 minutes · Standard 55 minutes · Extended 75 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Tell one happy scene as if it has already happened, then look at the bridge back to this month.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Wishes live in the future tense, which is a polite tense. "Someday we might." The verb stays hypothetical, and the scene stays foggy enough that nobody has to want it on a real Thursday. A memory is ruder, and kinder. It has a place, a line someone said, a smell, a feeling you can almost date.

The Future Memory asks for one happy scene that has not happened, written as if it already has. You read it the way you would read a diary page. Then you write a shorter page that tells the truth about the bridge: what is already true, what would have to be built, what you could do this month, and what is weather. Weather cannot be forced. The other person's desire is often weather.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A foggy wish is hard to join and hard to decline. A scene with a coat, a sentence, and a feeling can be loved, revised, or set beside a different scene without anyone pretending it was only a mood. The past tense is the mechanism. It makes you choose details. Details are where a fantasy stops spending the other person as a prop and starts describing a day.

Imagining is not causing. A scene can be vivid and still depend on money, health, timing, and a yes you do not control. The practical page exists so the memory does not get promoted into a plan by tone of voice alone. Happiness in the scene can be quiet. A rented kitchen, a train, a nap, a joke that landed. Cinematic romance is one option among quieter ones.

098, The One-Hundred-Year Interview, puts you both in a long-life frame, welcomes contradictory decades, and later asks each person for three invented memories they would like to make real. 031, A Love Letter From the Future, is a letter. This chapter is one scene and one bridge. 095 is where a sentence becomes a promise. A future memory is earlier than a promise, and it can stay a story.

Schacter, Addis, and Buckner argue that imagining the future depends on much of the same neural machinery as remembering. See S2007. Their constructive episodic simulation hypothesis says future simulation recombines details from the past, and the review says that hypothesis has support. The same review says further work still has to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments. That argument is about how a future scene is built. It does not show that the scene will happen, and it does not validate this chapter. The past tense here is a writing device. Label the page fiction-as-memory so a later reader knows it is not a diary of record.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit, or exchange pages before a call so the call is for listening. Dictation is welcome if writing is hard.

Choose a scene that does not require an unstated physical ability. If the scene includes dancing, travel, sex, children, relocation, or a proposal, mark it as one possible future. It is a desire on paper until the other person wants the same scene. You may keep a scene private and offer only the practical step you control.

Skip any scene whose hidden sentence is a complaint. "In the memory, you finally..." spends the partner as a corrected version of themselves. Write a day you would be glad to have lived, including the people as they actually are, with room for them to want something else.

If the two scenes conflict, they stay side by side. Nobody edits their hope into the other's paragraph.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Each person writes one page, about 10 minutes. Four ingredients, all in the past tense, about a happy time that has not happened.

A place.
A line of dialogue, something one of you said.
A sensory detail: wool, rain, sugar, the sound of a station.
A feeling, named plainly.

Read it aloud as a memory. The listener does not interrupt to fact-check the future. When the reading ends, the listener may say one sentence of what they heard, the way you would if a friend told you about a day. "I hear a wet Thursday and a cake you bought anyway." They do not grade the dream. They do not annex it.

Then a second, shorter page, a few minutes. Four lines.

One condition already true.
One condition that would have to be built.
One step available this month.
One element that is weather and cannot be forced.

Read the practical page in a different voice if you can, a plainer one. The memory was allowed to glow. The bridge is allowed to be ordinary. If the step this month is "look at a timetable," it counts. If the weather is "you would have to want this too," say that without a sulk.

If you want a shared project, it comes after both scenes exist, and only where they overlap by a real yes. One of you may love a scene and still decline to build it. The decliner can name a piece they would join, or they can leave the scene as the other person's private hope. Private hopes are allowed to stay single-author.

Label both pages fiction-as-memory. A later rereading should be able to tell a wish from a diary.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One scene each, spoken in the past tense, with the four practical lines said aloud and unwritten if you are short on paper. The listener offers one hearing sentence. A spoken pair of scenes is a finished session.

**35 minutes.** Write the memory page and the practical page. Read both. Leave the scenes side by side if they differ. Choose a shared step only if you both want one. This is the version that keeps the tense and the bridge in the same hour.

**55 minutes.** Exchange the pages before you speak, and read them in silence first. Then each listener says what felt like the speaker, and what detail they are not ready to treat as a plan. Still one scene each. The extra time is for the difference between a day you can almost remember and a day you are willing to build.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A second scene, on another day, can be a different scale. If the first was a trip, the second can be a Tuesday at home. Quiet futures are easy to skip, and they are often the ones with a real step attached.

You can ask the speaker, only with a yes, which detail is load-bearing. The cake. The empty afternoon. The particular city. Load-bearing details tell you what a smaller version could keep. A smaller version is still the memory's cousin. It is not a consolation prize you announce without them.

If a scene keeps returning in conversation as a complaint about the present, set the page down and have the direct conversation. The past tense is a poor place to hide a grievance.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Long distance: send the memory ahead, and use the call for listening and for the practical page, which you can write while you talk. Dictate into a phone if a pen is the obstacle.

Scenes that need a body to do something difficult are marked possible, and a seated or home version is welcome beside them. The motif is a photo frame with the date left blank: `assets/chapters/090/motif.svg`.

Replay when a season changes and the old scene no longer fits, or when a piece of it has become a memory of something that happened. Bring both pages. Notice which line moved from fiction into the diary, and which line is still weather.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan reads, past tense. "We took a Thursday train to the city we can reach without a plane. It rained. In the museum cafe, Vale said the cake was overpriced and then bought it anyway. I remember the wool of their coat against my wrist on the platform, and the feeling was uncomplicated pleasure, the kind that does not need a lesson afterward."

Vale says, "I hear rain, a train, and a cake you were glad to share. I also hear my coat doing some of the work."

Rowan's practical page: already true, they both like trains and neither needs the trip to be a production. To build, a free Thursday and the fare. This month, look at one timetable and a free museum hour. Weather: Vale has to want the day, and the rain is none of their business.

Vale's scene is different, and Rowan does not edit it. "We spent a whole Sunday in the apartment. The project bench stayed covered. Rowan read on the floor. I fixed the rattle in the cabinet with one screw, badly, and we laughed at the extra screw I still had in my hand. I was proud and unhurried."

Vale's bridge: already true, the rattle is real and the floor is available. To build, a Sunday with no guests. This month, pick a Sunday and put a note on the bench that says covered. Weather: Rowan may want to go out, and a covered bench cannot be a law.

They do not merge the train and the Sunday into a compromise city picnic. Rowan says the train can wait. Vale says the Sunday is the one they are willing to try. The first step is the note on the bench. Both pages are labeled fiction-as-memory, including the Sunday, until it happens.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which detail made the scene feel like a memory, and which detail was costume?
What is already true?
What is weather, including the other person's want?
Did you use the scene to scold the present? If you did, say so in the present tense, outside the story.

You can keep a future memory as a story you like. Liking it is a complete outcome. Building it is a second decision, made with a yes.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Mark the scene as fiction-as-memory so it is not later mistaken for a record of an event.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. A private scene can stay on the personal page. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A happy future scene, written as if it had already happened.
- One condition already true, one step this month, and one element that is weather.
partner_b:
- Yours, a scene of your own hoping. It is not a correction of the first scene.
- The practical step you control, if you want one on the page.
shared:
- One scene you are willing to try to make, and the first practical step if you want one.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Has any piece of that future memory become a memory of something that happened?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Reimagined from visualization and "act as if" exercises that circulate in sports and self-help. Those habits are not a validated couple protocol.

See S2007. Schacter, Addis, and Buckner argue that imagining the future depends on much of the same neural machinery as remembering. Their constructive episodic simulation hypothesis says future simulation recombines details from the past, and the review says that hypothesis has support. The same review says further work still has to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments. S2007 does not show that imagining makes an event happen, that people cannot tell memory from imagination, or that neuroscience validates this chapter. No clinical case from that review is used here. The past tense is a writing device. Label the page fiction-as-memory. A partner's body, money, family, or yes is weather unless they offer it. This chapter is one scene and one bridge.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 35 minutes · Extended 55 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Name the presences you want to grow, then try one shared and one that is yours alone.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
A lot of couple talk is a list of removals. Less snapping. Less phone. Less of that joke. Removals matter, and they are a different conversation. This one starts from appetite. More walks. More of the stupid joke that is actually funny. More quiet in the same room. More of a kindness you already know how to do on your good days.

What We Want More Of asks each of you for five presences, then a rewrite of any line that is secretly an accusation. Together you pick one shared increase and one individual increase, for a short, stated period. The individual one does not need the other person's labor. Rest and maintenance count. A good life is allowed to want more of what already works, and it is also allowed to stay at enough.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Complaints are easy to hear as indictments, even when the wish inside them is simple. Starting from appetite keeps the wish in its own clothes. "More of the slow kissing in the kitchen, before anyone decides anything else" can be received, questioned, or declined as a wish. "You never touch me" cannot be tried on a Thursday. It can only be defended.

Specific wishes are easier to meet with curiosity. There is research nearby about telling someone a good event, and about responses that build on the telling. That work is about sharing news that already happened. It is not a test of scheduling more of a behavior, and this list is not that study. The reminder, for us, is only that a concrete good thing can be heard. The hearing in this chapter is manners you choose. It is not a research protocol.

063, The Appreciation Behind the Complaint, starts from an irritation and looks for the wish under it. This chapter starts before the complaint, at the appetite itself. 106, The Intimacy Negotiators, has its own way of weighing wants. Leave your five items here. They are not points in that other game.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Include items you can do at home, at low cost, and on low-energy days. Travel, restaurants, and late nights can appear. They cannot be the whole list. Sensory limits and pain shape what "more" can mean. A wish that costs the other person's body, sleep, or other relationships can be said, and it can be declined. More of something never overrides a limit.

You may keep one item private. Sex, time, money, and family are information, not entitlements. If a line is really about an ongoing harm, park it for a direct conversation. This chapter does not repair a wound by asking for extra dessert.

Passing is allowed. So is a list of three honest items when five would be padding.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
10 minutes of writing. Each person lists five "more of" items that name a presence. Shared walks. A kind of joke. A sexual or affectionate pattern, if you want that on the page. Quiet in the same room. Time with friends. Making something. A weekday ritual. Letters, overlapping calls, a shared watch-list if you live apart. Maintenance: more of going to bed before you are ruined. More of an ordinary Tuesday that does not improve itself into an event.

Read the list to yourself before you read it aloud. Any item that is secretly "less of your flaw" gets rewritten until the positive action is visible. "Less of you being distracted" might become "more of 10 minutes with the phone in the other room, if you want that too." If you cannot rewrite it without blaming, park it. Parked lines are for a direct request outside this chapter. They do not get smuggled back in with prettier verbs.

Share the lists. Each person asks one curious question, aimed at texture. "When you say more walks, do you mean talking walks or quiet ones?" "Is the drawing hour something you want witnessed, or protected?" One question. Then stop interviewing.

Together, choose one shared increase and one individual increase to try for a short, stated period. Two weeks is a humane default. The shared increase is something you will both invite, and either of you can still decline a given day. The individual increase belongs to one person. The other may cheer, stay out of the way, or join if asked. They are not assigned the labor.

Write the two chosen increases, the period, and a date to notice what happened. The notice is a description. It is not an audit of compliance. "We walked once, and the second week it became standing at the window in coats" is a successful review. A quota is how appetite turns into debt.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** Three items each. Rewrite anything that blames. Pick one increase, shared or individual, and a date to notice it. Say the parked lines only if you need to mark that they are parked. A short list with one real try is a finished session.

**35 minutes.** Five items, the rewrite, one question each, one shared increase, one individual increase, a period, and a noticing date. This is the version that protects the wish that does not require a partner.

**55 minutes.** After the choices, each person describes the smallest version of their increase on a bad day, and the version that would be too much. Write those beside the items. The extra minutes keep "more" from meaning "unlimited." Still no scores.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
A month later, tell each other what increased, including the increases that happened sideways. Sometimes the walk did not happen and the joke did. Keep the appetite that is still hungry, and retire the one that turned out to be a mood from a single afternoon.

You can sort the list, on a second pass, into "together," "beside each other," and "mine alone." Beside each other is a respectable category: reading in the same room, working at the same table, napping within earshot. It is easy to forget, and it is often what people mean by more closeness when they are tired of plans.

If "more sex" or "more talk" appears, give it texture before it leaves the page. Which hour, which pace, which kind of talk, which kind of touch, and what a no looks like in the middle. A textured wish can still be declined. An untextured wish is a fog the other person cannot consent to.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Across distance, more of letters, a standing call, or a show you watch in the same hour counts. The individual increase might be a local class the other person will never see. Witnessing it can be a photo or a sentence, if the dreamer wants a witness.

The motif is a cup with more in it, sitting on an ordinary table: `assets/chapters/091/motif.svg`. No rising chart. Enough is a legal result.

032, The Everyday Devotion Experiment, picks a practice of care and lives with it. 063 begins at the complaint. Come back when the period ends, or when a new appetite shows up and you want it named before it becomes a grievance. Date the noticing. What increased, and what you still want, can both be true.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan's first draft includes "more help with the week" and "more sex." The help line, read twice, is a complaint about Vale's chores. Rowan parks it for a direct request on Sunday and does not pretend the park is a wish. The sex line gets texture: "More of the slow kissing in the kitchen, before anyone decides whether the night goes further. Either of us can stop at the kissing."

The rest of Rowan's list: more of reading in the same room, more of the ridiculous voice Vale uses for the cat, more of a drawing hour that does not need an audience, more of leaving a party while they still like the party.

Vale's list: more of soup on cold Sundays, more of overlapping phone-free breakfast, more of seeing friends without turning it into a reunion, more of being asked before plans land on the calendar, more of naps.

Vale asks whether the kitchen kissing is a hope or a standing expectation. Rowan says hope, and a no is a complete sentence. Rowan asks whether the naps are social. Vale says the naps are alone, and company means not being teased for them.

Shared increase, for two weeks: reading in the same room on two evenings, which can shrink to 15 minutes. Individual increase: Rowan draws for half an hour on Wednesday, door shut, and Vale does not turn it into a critique session. Noticing date, the Sunday after next. They agree the chore conversation will happen, and that it will not wear this list as a costume.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which line was an appetite, and which line was a flaw in a nicer shirt?
What did you each ask, and what did you learn about texture?
Which increase needs nobody's permission but your own?
Where did a wish bump into a limit, and was the limit treated as real?

You can want more of a life that is already good. You can also hear a more, love the person who said it, and keep your no.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write the two chosen increases and the date you will notice them.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. One private list item can stay off the shared page. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- An experience or action you want more of, named as an appetite rather than as a problem to solve.
- The shared increase or the individual one you are trying, and for how long.
partner_b:
- What you want more of, from your own appetite, which may not match.
- An item you rewrote until the presence was visible, or one you parked.
shared:
- The overlap you will actually invite in, and the individual wishes you will protect.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What increased, and what you still want more of.
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: See G2004. Telling someone about a good event was associated with greater positive affect and well-being beyond the event itself. Perceived active-constructive responses were associated with higher relationship quality; passive or destructive responses were not the helpful pattern. G2004 does not study a list of behaviors to increase, and it is not evidence that this chapter changes a relationship. The wish here is specific so it can be heard. How you hear it is this book's manners, not a definition borrowed from that paper. A rising line is not required. Rest and maintenance count as more of. Wishes are information, and limits still hold.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 35 minutes · Extended 55 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Name one ambition that stays yours, then accept, decline, or rewrite the help.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Some ambitions have your name on them, and the relationship is the neighborhood, not the project. A craft. A trip that is yours. A change of work. A friendship you want to tend. A way of living in your body. A thing you want to make that does not need a co-author. The loving mistake is to improve it until the dreamer cannot find their own hands on it.

The Dream Exchange is one ambition, said in the dreamer's words, and a conversation about support that the dreamer can accept, decline, or rewrite. One clean exchange is enough. A second dream can wait for another day. Ownership includes the right to want something your partner does not share.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Couples are good at "we" projects and clumsy at "yours." Help arrives as a schedule, a purchase, a better idea, a mood when the offer is declined. The dream shrinks to fit the helper's enthusiasm. Or it stalls because asking feels like assigning the other person a second job.

Support has a menu, and the menu is not a ladder of sacrifice. Witness. Practical help. An introduction. Money, only if it is truly available and truly offered. Cheer. Protected time. "I need to think." The dreamer chooses. A declined offer is information about the dream, and sometimes about capacity. It is not a verdict on the relationship.

No goal-setting paper is claimed for this exchange. Mentorship and counseling talk about individual aims beside shared ones. That talk is not a protocol you are reproducing. The mechanism here is narrower: the ambition stays the dreamer's, and the help stays negotiable.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Ambitions may be small, local, and compatible with pain, caregiving, and limited money. A modest dream is a whole dream. It does not have to warm up for a grander one.

Either of you may say the dream is not ready to be helped. Either of you may refuse to fund, relocate, or set down your own ambition to carry the other person's. Dreams that involve a third person's body, money, or consent stay incomplete until that person is actually asked, outside this hour.

If a dream is about leaving a harmful situation, or about danger, leave the exercise and respond as a partner. This page is for ambitions that can be talked about. It is not a playful frame for a crisis.

Passing is allowed. So is telling the dream and asking only to be believed, with no offer yet.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Each person takes a few quiet minutes and writes one ambition in a sentence or two. Say whether the relationship stars in it. Many good dreams do not. Then write what support has felt like in the past, including support that was too much. Too much is part of the information. A partner who bought every tool and built the schedule may have been generous and still have taken the work away.

Choose who goes first. The dreamer reads their own words. The listener does not improve the dream, audition a better version, or explain how they would do it if it were theirs. Those are résumé moves. They end the chapter.

The listener offers from the menu, out loud, and offers one thing, or at most two. Name which:

Witness. I will listen to updates at a pace you set.
Practical help. I will do a specific task you name.
An introduction. I will connect you with a person, if you want the connection.
Money. Only if you can actually offer it, and only as an offer.
Cheer. I will be glad in your direction without managing the steps.
Protected time. I will guard a particular hour, as well as I can.
I need to think. A real answer, and a date when you will come back to it.

The dreamer accepts, declines, or rewrites the offer before the conversation moves on. A rewrite sounds like, "I want the Saturday morning, and I don't want the tools." The listener agrees to the rewritten offer or says they need to think. Sulking at a no is a second offer the dreamer did not ask for. If you feel it, say "I notice I wanted to be useful in a bigger way" and stop there.

Then switch. The second ambition is not a correction of the first, and it is not a bid to be equally impressive. One of you may have a public aim and the other a private one. Both are in bounds.

Write, in the dreamer's words, the dream, the offer, and the response. Ownership stays visible because the wording stays theirs. If you only finish one exchange cleanly, stop. A rushed second dream is how help gets sloppy.

A dream that is actually a demand on the other person's life needs to be named as a request, on another day, where they can answer it as themselves. "I want us to move" is a household question. "I want to learn the buses in a city I love, and I am not asking you to move" can live here.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One dream in the room. The dreamer names the ambition and the help they do not want. The listener offers one menu item. Accept, decline, or rewrite. The other dream waits. A single clean exchange is a finished session.

**40 minutes.** Both dreams, including the sentence about support that was too much. One or two offers each. Write the dream, the offer, and the response before you leave the table. This is the version that keeps the record from sliding into the helper's summary.

**60 minutes.** Add a short history: one time support fit, in any relationship, not only this one. Then the same menu. The extra minutes are for recognizing your own pattern as a helper and as a dreamer. Still one ambition each. Still no project-management system.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, the dreamer can report what moved, and whether the support fit. The report is a description. It is not a performance review of the helper. If the help was too much after all, say so while the rewrite is still cheap.

You can also name the help you want from people who are not your partner: a teacher, a friend, a class. Some dreams need a witness who is not in love with you. That is a respectful discovery, and it can spare the relationship a job it was never shaped for.

If both dreams pull at the same scarce hour, put the collision on the table as logistics. Protected time for one person may be the other's only quiet evening. The menu includes "I need to think" for that reason. A solved calendar is pleasant. A stolen one is how resentment learns the dream's name.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Across distance, presence may be calls and logistics. The menu still applies. Cheer can be a voice note on the day of the attempt. Practical help can be looking up a form. Witness can be one question a month: "Do you want to say how it's going?"

The motif is two hands, one holding a small object, the other open and unhurried: `assets/chapters/092/motif.svg`.

053, If Nobody Were Watching, asks what you would pursue if the usual audiences stepped outside. 055, What I Want to Experience Before I Die, is a personal list of experiences, and it can hold many. 093, The Relationship Bucket List, is a shared collection. This chapter is one owned ambition plus the help around it. Come back when the ambition changes shape, or when the support needs a rewrite. Date the offer so a later you can see whether it fit.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Vale says, "I want to learn to repair bikes well enough to keep mine alive. Support that was too much, in another year, was someone buying a stand, a full tool roll, and a Saturday plan before I had touched a tire. I felt managed. The help I don't want is a curriculum."

Rowan offers protected time: "I can keep Sunday morning clear of errands, and I can leave the kitchen if you want the table. I will not buy tools unless you hand me a list." Vale rewrites it. "The clear morning, yes. The kitchen can stay shared. I'll work in the entry where the light is mean and honest." Rowan agrees to the rewrite.

Rowan's ambition is a night class in drawing, already local, already cheap. "I want the class. I don't want a critique at home, and I don't want money. Too much support would be framing everything I bring back."

Vale offers cheer, and one practical piece: "I'll be glad on the nights you go, and I'll heat the soup. I won't ask to see the pages." Rowan accepts both, and adds, "If I do show you a page, the response I want is that you looked, not that you improved it." They write the two dreams in the speakers' verbs. Nobody opens a shared spreadsheet.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Whose words are on the page, the dreamer's or the helper's?
What help was declined, and did the decline get to stand?
Where did you want to be more useful than you were invited to be?
What, if anything, will you do this month that the dreamer actually accepted?

You can love a person and leave their ambition in their hands. That is one of the steadier forms of support.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write the dream in the dreamer's words, then the offer and the response.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- An ambition that is yours, and the kind of support that would respect your ownership of it.
- The offer you accepted, declined, or rewrote.
partner_b:
- Your ambition, and the help you do not want, so the support stays clean.
- Where you will cheer, assist, or stay out of the way.
shared:
- How you will cheer, assist, or stay out of the way, named dream by dream.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What moved in the ambition, and did the support fit?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the ordinary pairing of a personal ambition with help that can be accepted or refused. No goal-setting study is claimed, and no effect size is borrowed from other chapters. The ambition stays the dreamer's. A declined offer is a complete response. Dreams that spend a third person's body, money, or consent wait until that person is asked. A dream of leaving harm is a partner conversation, and it leaves this exercise.

experiences.title: The Relationship Bucket List

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A short shared menu of adventures, traditions, achievements, and goals that are ridiculous on purpose.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Bucket lists have a way of becoming travel brochures with a moral attached. See the fjord or admit you wasted your one wild life. Meanwhile the good shared plots are often smaller, funnier, and more repeatable: a soup, a terrible contest, a shelf you finish, a breakfast the birthday person does not cook.

The Relationship Bucket List is a joint collection with range. Adventures, traditions, achievements, and goals that are delightfully ridiculous. Twelve items or fewer. At least two of them should be unserious on purpose, and at least two should be ordinary enough to do on a tired week. Nothing on the list is overdue. Retiring a line is part of keeping it honest.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A shared menu gives you something to point at when a free Saturday shows up and habit would spend it on errands. The range matters. A list of status milestones is a résumé. One partner's private hopes copied onto a joint page is a donation the other person did not make. Ridiculous items keep the list from becoming a character test. Ordinary items keep it from becoming a brochure.

Novelty can be one reason an item appeals. See A2000. Correlational work linked shared exciting activities with relationship satisfaction, with boredom as a mediator. In laboratory experiments, about seven minutes of a novel and arousing joint task increased experienced relationship quality more than a mundane task. That was short-term experienced quality, not a permanent change. A bucket list is not that experiment. An item here can be exciting, and it can also be soup. The paper does not show that finishing a list changes a relationship's long-term course.

The mechanism is curation. You choose a few futures you would be glad to meet, you mark what they ask of money and energy in words, and you leave the rest of your life unlisted.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Include items you can do at home, in daylight, seated, at low pain, and at low sensory load. Adventure includes a new recipe, a local bench, and a game. Flights are allowed. They are not the definition of adventure.

If you live apart, put at least one item on the list that you can do in separate places, and one that wants you in the same place. Geography should not be punished by a list that only works in one kitchen.

Either of you may veto an item off the shared page. A tradition one person experiences as harm is not a bonding challenge. Cultural and religious traditions belong here when both of you want them.

Items that involve sex, other people, or someone's body do not pre-consent anything. The list is a menu of maybes. The real yes happens later, in the actual hour, and it can be withdrawn. No deadline on this page functions as an exam. You are not late for your own life.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Aim for 12 lines or fewer, written where you can both see them. Take turns adding one item at a time, so the page does not become a single handwriting. Each item gets a kind, said in a word: adventure, tradition, achievement, or ridiculous. If you cannot tell, it is probably two items, or it is a mood. Split it or let it go.

Constraints, checked before you call the list done:

At least two ridiculous goals, unserious on purpose, and kind. Humiliation is not ridiculous. Ridiculous is a pet-photo contest entered with a houseplant, or learning the chorus of a song you both mock, in the car, badly.

At least two ordinary, repeatable items. Soup. A bench. A game you already own. A phone call with no agenda.

A mix across the four kinds. If you finish with twelve adventures, you have a tour, and the premise asked for a collection.

A cost band in words: free, modest, or save-for. Numbers can stay private. "Save-for" means the item waits for money you actually have a plan to gather. It does not mean a confession of accounts.

Optional, and useful: star one item for the next season. Leave the rest as a menu. The star is a preference, not a vow. If the season eats the star, the item returns to the menu or retires. Unfinished is not failure.

Read the list once for labor. If every hard item spends one person's energy, add or replace until the effort can move. A list that is one partner's vacation and the other's staffing plan needs a rewrite before it is called shared.

Close by reading the ridiculous items aloud. If nobody laughs, they are not ridiculous yet, or they are jokes at someone's expense. Fix them or cut them. Then read one ordinary item, so the hour ends on something you could do without a suitcase.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**20 minutes.** Six items. One ridiculous, one ordinary and repeatable, and a mix of the kinds you can reach in the time. One cost band each. Star one or star none. A short menu is a finished list. You can add later because the page has room.

**50 minutes.** Up to 12, with the full constraints: two ridiculous, two ordinary, all four kinds represented if you can do it without padding. Vetoes exercised in the room. One optional star. This is the version that keeps the collection from collapsing into a single genre.

**70 minutes.** After the list, write a smallest version of the starred item, doable on a low-energy week, and a note on what would make you retire it. The extra minutes are for honesty about bodies, money, and boredom. Still no deadlines that scold.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Keep the page alive. Add a line for the pleasure of adding it. Drop a line when it no longer belongs to both of you. A dropped trip is not a dropped relationship. Write the date beside the retirement so the list has a memory.

Once a season, look only at the star, or at the absence of a star. You can live through a season with a menu and no featured item. Maintenance is allowed to be the adventure.

If an item keeps getting starred and never approached, ask one curious question: is it a wish, a fantasy you like having on paper, or a task you are using to feel behind? All three can stay. Only the wish needs a plan, and the plan can be tiny.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
The list can live on paper, in a shared note, or as a voice memo you both can find. Handwriting is pleasant. Searchability is also pleasant. Choose the form you will actually reopen.

The motif is a jar of mixed tickets, some of them absurd: `assets/chapters/093/motif.svg`. No branded challenge, and no published list copied in to look worldly.

055, What I Want to Experience Before I Die, is one person's list, and it can hold hopes that never become joint. 066, The Twenty-Dollar Adventure, is one outing with a small budget, done rather than collected. 092, The Dream Exchange, is a single ambition that stays owned by the dreamer, with help that can be declined. This page is the shared menu. Come back when you do something, when you drop something, or when a ridiculous idea arrives and deserves a line. Nothing on it is overdue.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They write twelve lines and then cut to nine, because three of them were the same trip in different clothes.

Ridiculous: enter a pet-photo contest with the snake plant. Learn, badly, the dance from a video they both pretend not to know, in the kitchen, once.

Ordinary and repeatable: soup on the first cold Sunday. A 10-minute card game after dishes, which can be played seated, and can be skipped without a speech.

Adventure: sit on a local bench they have never sat on, and bring tea from home. Achievement: finish the half-built shelf, using the brackets they already own.

Tradition: a birthday breakfast the birthday person does not cook. They check. Both want it. Vale vetoes a sunrise hike that spends a bad knee and a religion of early mornings Vale does not have. Rowan wanted the hike as scenery. It leaves the shared page and may live, if anywhere, on Rowan's private list.

Cost bands: the contest, the dance, the soup, the cards, and the bench are free. The shelf is modest, mostly time. One save-for item remains, a night in a motel by a lake they both like, with no itinerary attached.

They star the bench for this season. The smallest version is the bench nearest the bus stop, 15 minutes, coats on. They laugh at the snake plant until the laugh is real. The list is allowed to stay unfinished for years.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which item is ridiculous, and which item is only expensive?
Where did the labor pile up on one person?
What did you veto, and did the veto get to be dull and final?
What, if anything, is starred, and what is its smallest version?

A relationship with a short menu and no fjord is allowed to be full. The list is a toy you keep, not a test you pass.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Copy the list onto the shared page with room under it. Mark kind and cost band in words.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. A hope that stays individual can stay off the joint list. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- An adventure, a tradition, an achievement, or a ridiculous goal you want on the shared list.
- The cost band in words, and whether it is starred for this season.
partner_b:
- One you want added that is not already there, including one that is unserious on purpose.
- An item you vetoed off the shared page, or one you are glad stayed.
shared:
- The list as it stands, with room to grow. Nothing on it is overdue.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What you did, what you dropped, and what you added for the pleasure of adding it.
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Bucket lists are a popular form, often individual and often commercial. This chapter is a joint menu with ridiculous and ordinary items beside achievements. It is not a validated planning protocol, and it copies no published list.

See A2000. Correlational work linked shared exciting activities with relationship satisfaction, with boredom as a mediator. In laboratory experiments, about seven minutes of a novel and arousing joint task increased experienced relationship quality more than a mundane task. That was short-term experienced quality, not a permanent change. A bucket list is not that experiment. Novelty can be one reason an item appeals. Completing the list is not shown to change a relationship's long-term course. The list does not pre-consent sex, other people, or anyone's body. Retiring an item is part of the practice.

experiences.title: The Annual Reintroduction

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Once a year, if you can, tell each other who you have become and what you want now.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
People keep changing in ordinary ways, and couples often meet the change late, in a mood, because nobody scheduled a day to be reintroduced. A new sleep. A value that shifted half an inch. A wish to retire a ritual that used to be the point. A need that is the same as last year, which is also news, because you checked.

The Annual Reintroduction is an invitation to do that checking on purpose, about once a year, in a week you can actually protect. Needs, interests, values, and wishes are all in the room. If you miss the week, the next calm week counts. There is no penalty, no performance review, and no prize for displaying growth. "I want the same things, and I checked" is a complete answer.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Anniversaries, birthdays, and the turn of a year already give people an excuse to talk. Those occasions often fill up with guests, gifts, and the story of how you began. The reintroduction uses the calendar for a different job: to notice who is here now. A yearly page gives last year's portrait a chance to be wrong.

The ritual is repeatable because the point is change, including the change that did not happen. A one-time recap of a book, or a date that assumes nobody moved, is a different hour. 001, The Stranger Across From Me, pretends you have just met, for an evening. 096, The Next Chapter, is a landing after a season of experiences, where you design a few practices. This chapter is the invitation you can keep on a calendar of your own, including in a year when you are tired of designing anything.

No study is claimed for annual talks. They do not come with a promise about staying together. They are a craft: five questions, one shared revision, a page you can set beside next year's.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Tie it to a week you can protect. The week does not have to be a New Year, a wedding anniversary, or anyone's holiday. A borrowed room, a kitchen table, a video call, or a hospital dayroom will do. A walk is welcome only if walking is welcome. The seated form is the default.

Send the prompts ahead if either of you thinks better with warning. No gift is required. A lavish setting is how this ritual becomes easy to postpone. Illness, grief, or a tired mouth may mean you answer three of the five. That is a full reintroduction.

Changes in desire, faith, family role, or the wish to stay are welcome as topics, and they are declinable if the speaker is not ready. The listener does not cross-examine a change. New agreements about sex, money, or where you live can be noted, then given a separate sober conversation. The annual date does not have to close them. Either of you may pause, or bring a support person if that is what makes the hour possible.

Passing a prompt is ordinary. Saving every grievance for this day will swamp it. If a grievance is live, give it a nearer conversation, and let this one stay a reintroduction.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Each person answers all five, or the three they can manage. Speak, or write and then read your own words. Leave room between you so the second set of answers is not a revision of the first.

What is new in your body, your work, or your daily life?
What do you want more of?
What do you want retired?
What do you still want known?
Which value has shifted, even slightly?

"Nothing new, and I looked" belongs in every blank it truthfully fits. Identical answers copied from last year out of politeness are the failure mode. If the answer is the same because it is still true, say that you checked. The checking is the ritual.

Then one shared revision, chosen together. A ritual to keep. A ritual to drop. Or a wish to carry forward. One. A stack of revisions turns the hour into a summit. If you cannot agree, write both wishes down and pick a later day. Disagreement is allowed to remain unfinished when the tea is gone.

Write a single journal page and date it for next year's comparison. Include the year, the place, and the answers you are willing to reread. Next year, set the pages side by side and ask what would have surprised the people who wrote the old one.

If you keep a chapters-of-us recap in the companion to this book, it can be written beside this sitting, or in a year you skip the reintroduction. The recap is a story of the year. This chapter is a meeting between two changing people. They can share a weekend. They do not have to.

Close with one sentence each: who you understand the other person to be this year, said lightly enough that they can correct you. The correction is part of the reintroduction. You are not drafting their biography.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**25 minutes.** Three prompts each, chosen by the speaker, plus one shared revision if you have it. Say which prompts you left, so the skip is visible and unpunished. A shorter return still counts as the annual invitation. Put the date on the page anyway.

**50 minutes.** All five, both people, then one shared revision and the dated page. This is the version to protect if you can. Send the prompts ahead so the hour is for saying, not for inventing under a clock.

**70 minutes.** Read last year's page first, slowly, and mark one surprise before you answer this year's five. If this is the first year, skip the reading and use the extra time for quieter pauses between answers. Still one shared revision. Still no review of each other's character.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
The prompts can be answered in writing the week before, and the meeting can be the reading. Some people are more accurate on paper. The listener's job in the room is to receive, ask one curious question if invited, and survive the correction.

You might notice a value that shifted in opposite directions. One of you wants more public life. The other wants a smaller room. Write both. The annual hour does not have to reconcile them. It has to make them visible before the year spends itself on the louder one.

A further kindness: each person names one interest the other has taken up that they want to keep understanding. A show, a friend, a tool, a god, a sport, a joke. Curiosity is welcome here. Interrogation is how an invitation becomes an audit, and this chapter declines that job.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Long distance is a natural fit. Same prompts, cameras on or off, pages exchanged the day before so the call can be unhurried. If one of you is linguistically tired, answer in the language that is easiest and let the other ask for a gloss only where it matters.

The motif is a doorway with two chalk marks, last year's and this year's: `assets/chapters/094/motif.svg`. The marks are allowed to match.

077, The Relationship Timeline, looks along the story you have already lived. 001 borrows a stranger's curiosity for an evening. 096 designs what you want to carry after a season of trying things. Replay this one yearly, or in the next calm week if the year got away. The people who wrote last year's page are allowed to be surprised.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan, at the kitchen table, no gift in sight: "New in my body: I am sleeping earlier, and I am less willing to pretend that midnight is a personality. More of: mornings, and friends in small numbers. Retire: the Sunday planning meeting. It became a trial. Still want known: I get quiet when work is good, not only when it is bad. Value: I care more about being a reliable friend than about being impressive. I checked. That last one moved."

Vale answers, given the same room. "Body: the knee is a fact this year, not a plot twist. More of: soup, and being asked before plans land. Retire: nothing structural. I want the Wednesday call, and I checked. Still want known: my quiet is often contentment. Shifted value: I want our home to be easy to leave for other people, and easy to come back to. Last year I was more interested in being hard to find."

They do not cross-examine the knee or the midnight. Rowan asks one question, invited: "Easy to leave, meaning guests, or meaning us going out?" Vale says both, in small doses.

Shared revision: keep the Wednesday call. Drop the Sunday meeting. They write one page, dated, and leave a blank line for next year. Vale says, "If we miss the week, we take the next calm one. I will not build a case about it." Rowan agrees. The invitation stands.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
What changed, and what did you check and find steady?
Which prompt did you skip, and was the skip a kindness?
Did the listener try to close a change before the speaker was finished?
What one ritual stays, drops, or gets carried, and what waits for a separate conversation?

You can be proud of a year that looks similar on paper. The work was the reintroduction, not the plot twist.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. This page is meant to sit beside next year's. A chapters-of-us recap may live next to it, or in a year you skip this sitting.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- What has changed in your needs, interests, values, or wishes since last year, or since you began if this is the first time.
- A ritual to keep, a ritual to drop, or a wish to carry, in one line.
partner_b:
- Your changes, in your words, given the same room.
- Which of the five prompts you answered, and which you left for another week.
shared:
- Who you are this year, as two people and as a pair.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Set last year's page beside this one. What would have surprised the people who wrote it?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Reimagined from the calendar excuses couples already have, turned into an explicit reintroduction. No empirical claim is made. An annual conversation is not presented as protection against parting. The date need not be a New Year, an anniversary, or a holiday. "I want the same things, and I checked" is a valid return. Missed weeks move to the next calm week. Topics that touch sex, money, or living arrangements can be noted and then given their own conversation. This is an invitation you can decline in a given year.

experiences.title: A Promise I Actually Want to Keep

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One to three promises you would still want if nobody applauded, each with a follow-through you control.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Promises get big when they are performing. Forever. Always. The feeling you will arrange to have on demand. Then a Thursday arrives, the phone stays on the table, and the vow has no handle. You can want a promise that is smaller than a vow and still mean it. The test is private: would you want to keep this if nobody clapped, and if your partner never used it as a receipt?

A Promise I Actually Want to Keep is a few of those, one to three, each made by the person who will do it. Realistic. Specific. Possible inside a month. Attached to a follow-through they control. The partner does not enlarge it. At the review, a promise can be kept, rewritten, or retired. A miss gets named. Shame is not the method.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A relationship collects floating intentions. "We should talk more." "I'll be better about the mornings." Floating intentions are easy to love and hard to do, because they never say when, or what the hands will actually do. A cue and a small action give the week something to recognize.

Gollwitzer distinguishes a goal intention, "I intend to reach x," from an implementation intention, "When situation x arises, I will perform response y." See G1999. The review describes a research program in which those if-then plans supported goal attainment in the domains studied. In that review, goal intentions had modest effects. They were not useless. That program is not a study of promises between partners. It does not show that a sentence you make in this chapter will be kept. The if-then line below is optional scaffolding. It is not a tested couple treatment, and it is not a reason to trust a vow you do not actually want.

The mechanism in this room is consent and scale. Few promises. Each one wanted by the speaker. Each one small enough to meet on a low-energy week. Meaning lives in ordinary care as easily as in grand language.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You will each offer promises you control. You cannot promise the other person's feelings, friends, body, or time. You can promise what you will do with your own.

No one may demand a promise in exchange for affection or safety. Promises about sex are welcome only as commitments the speaker wants, and they never bind the other person's body. Either of you may refuse to witness a promise that pressures you. If witnessing it would corner you, say so, and the sentence goes back to the speaker to revise or drop.

Gates, applied before a promise is spoken as final:

It matters to the relationship, or to how you show up in it.
You control it.
It can be done within a month.
It is specific.

A promise of a feeling fails the gates. "I will always desire you" is a wish, and it belongs in a different conversation if you want to talk about desire. This page is for actions.

Write where both of you can see the wording, in the speaker's own verbs. If you want a signature, use a letter page and sign only what you just said. The signature is a private emphasis. It is not a legal document and not a wedding liturgy.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Take 10 minutes alone. Each person drafts one to three promises they would still want to keep if the other person never thanked them. Read each draft against the gates. Cut anything grand, anything that polices a partner's other relationships, and anything you are offering in order to be seen as good.

Optional second sentence, if you want the cue: "When [situation], I will [response]." An example of the shape, not a script you must adopt: "When we sit down on Thursday, I will put my phone in the other room until the tea is finished." The first sentence can be the promise in plain speech. The second sentence is the if-then plan. You may keep only the first. In the G1999 review, goal intentions had modest effects. They were not useless. Choose the shape you will actually recognize on the day.

Read your promises aloud. The partner's job is to witness, ask one clarifying question if the action is fuzzy, and stop. They do not add "and also the dishes," and they do not trade their affection for a larger version. If they want a promise of their own, it belongs in their turn, chosen by them. Symmetry is optional. One person may make one promise and the other may make three, or one, or none tonight.

Set a review date inside the month, or just past it. Put the date on the same page as the words. At the review, the outcomes are kept, rewritten, or retired. A broken promise is named in one or two sentences: what the cue was, what happened, what you will change in the wording or release. Then you rewrite or retire. You do not hold court on character.

Across distance, promises about calls, letters, and logistics are the natural set. "When your morning is my evening, I will send the one-line note before I open the other app." The act still has to be possible on a tired week. If the only version requires a heroic day, shrink it until a hard week can carry it.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One promise each, already specific, with or without the if-then sentence, plus a review date. Witness, and do not enlarge. A pair of small promises is a finished session. More can wait.

**30 minutes.** Draft with the gates. Up to three each. Read them. One clarifying question allowed, aimed at the action, not at the speaker's worth. Write the cue, the act, and the review date in the speaker's verbs. This is the version that keeps the list short on purpose.

**50 minutes.** Include a first look at an old promise you are still carrying from somewhere else, and decide whether it belongs in this set, rewritten, or released. The extra time is for retiring sentences you never wanted. Still no more than three live promises each when you stand up.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
At the review, describe the keeping in ordinary detail. "The phone was in the other room for three Thursdays, and on the fourth I answered a work text and then put it back" is a useful record. It gives you something to rewrite. A perfect record is not the entrance fee for the next promise.

You can also notice promises you are keeping without having written them down. Naming one of those can be enough for a season. The chapter does not require you to manufacture new virtue. It asks you to be picky about the sentences you attach your name to.

If a promise keeps breaking at the same cue, the cue may be fantasy. Change the situation you are waiting for. "When we have a free Sunday" may never arrive. "When the kettle boils on Thursday" arrives. Shrink until the world you live in can host the act.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Non-physical promises belong beside any that involve errands or outings. A promise to let a sentence finish. A promise to say you are leaving the room before you disappear into a task. A promise to ask before you add a guest. These travel into sick weeks and small apartments.

The motif is a small knot tied on purpose, easy to retie: `assets/chapters/095/motif.svg`.

012, The Permission Slip, is about what you are allowed to want or to stop, a permission rather than a pledge. 060, The Repair Shop, looks backward at a misstep and how you mend it. 090, The Future Memory, is a happy scene told as if it happened, plus a bridge. A scene is earlier than a promise. Come back when the review date arrives. What you kept, what you amended, and what you released all belong on the page.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan drafts two and cuts one. The cut line was "I will be more affectionate," which fails the gates by being a feeling and a fog. The line that stays: "When we sit down on Thursday, I will put my phone in the other room until the tea is finished." Rowan wants this even if Vale never mentions it. It can be done in a month. The phone is Rowan's.

Vale asks one question: "If the tea is the 5-minute kind, does the phone stay away for 5 minutes?" Rowan says yes. Vale does not add the dishes, the inbox, or a speech about presence.

Vale's promise is different, and unpaired. "When I notice I am about to joke over your sentence, I will let the sentence finish." Vale does not promise to stop being funny. The cue is the moment of noticing. The act is the pause. A second promise: "When I say I will look at the shared bill, I will open it the same day, even if I only look for 2 minutes." Both are Vale's to keep. Neither requires Rowan to be impressive.

They write the sentences where both can see them, in the speakers' verbs. Review in three weeks, on a Sunday they already have. They agree that a miss will be named and rewritten, and that nobody will be prosecuted for character. Rowan signs the Thursday line on a letter page because the ritual of the signature pleases them. Vale does not sign, and the unsigned promises count the same.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which promise would you keep if it stayed unwitnessed?
Where did a draft fail the gates, and did you cut it?
Did either of you try to enlarge the other's sentence?
When will you look again, and what will you do with a miss?

A small promise kept, or honestly rewritten, is the whole achievement. Forever can remain a private hope. This page is for Thursdays.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write the promise, the cue if you used one, and the review date.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you both recognize. A letter page is optional if you want a signature line.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A promise you are willing to make: realistic, specific, and yours to keep.
- The cue and the small action, if you want that second sentence, and the review date.
partner_b:
- A promise you choose on your own. It does not need a matching vow for the sake of symmetry.
- What you will do if you miss it: name it, rewrite it, or retire it.
shared:
- The few promises you both recognize, and the check-in you actually want.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- What you kept, what you amended, and what you released.
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Promises, vows, and New Year resolutions are old folk forms. This chapter is a reimagined promise ritual. It is not an established clinical protocol, and it borrows no wedding liturgy.

See G1999. Gollwitzer distinguishes goal intentions ("I intend to reach x") from implementation intentions ("When situation x arises, I will perform response y"). The review describes a research program in which those if-then plans supported goal attainment in the domains studied. In that review, goal intentions had modest effects. They were not useless. G1999 is not a study of promises between partners, and it is not proof that a promise in this book will be kept. The if-then line is optional scaffolding. It is not a tested couple treatment. A missed promise is material for a rewrite or a retirement. It is not evidence about character. No promise here binds the other person's body, and none is owed in exchange for affection or safety.
