metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 30 minutes · Extended 50 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Look back only at what you actually did, then choose a very small way to go on.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
After a season of talking, playing, and telling the truth in pieces, it is tempting to design a second life: every good idea, every skipped chapter, a calendar that would impress a stranger. The season you lived was smaller than that, and more specific. You learned a few things. You liked a few practices. You are done pretending to want some of the rest.

The Next Chapter is a landing. You reflect on discoveries you actually made, then you choose at most two recurring practices and one dated future experience. Each practice needs a smallest version for a hard week. Further ideas go in a margin labeled "not now." You may also choose no new practice, and keep one old kindness. That is a complete next chapter. It may be quiet.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Endings in workbooks often become goal avalanches. The avalanche feels like seriousness, and then it becomes guilt, which is a poor material for a life. A landing works when it is short enough to remember without the book in your hand.

The look-back is limited to experiences you truly did. A discovery about a chapter you meant to get to is a discovery about intention, and it can sit in the margin. What you carry forward should have already survived contact with your actual week: your energy, your distance, your humor, your limits.

This hour can install 094, The Annual Reintroduction, if you want a repeating invitation on the calendar. It does not replace that yearly meeting, and it does not assign the original games that follow this part as homework. Closeness does not require finishing every experience in a book. The next chapter is yours. No finding here claims the book's arc is an evidence-based program.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You do not have to reread anything first. If your memory of earlier hours is fuzzy, use whatever you still carry. A clear sentence you can say without notes is enough. A foggy sense that "the listening one mattered" can be enough if you can say what you do differently when you remember it.

Discoveries that were vulnerable belong to the person who made them. Reuse one only with their yes. The dated experience is a plan you both want. It is not a surprise that spends someone's body, money, or stamina.

If what you actually need to renegotiate is safety, monogamy, or where you live, flag it for a dedicated conversation. This landing is the wrong pocket for a stealth rewrite of the terms of your life.

Passing is allowed. So is the sentence, "No new practice. We are keeping one old kindness." Name the kindness so it is real.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Set a margin on the page and write "not now" at the top of it. Anything that arrives as a good idea and is not one of the few choices goes there without debate. The margin is a gift to your future restless selves. It is not a debt.

Each person, in turn, names four things, and any of them can be "nothing new under this heading."

One discovery about yourself, from something you actually did.
One discovery about the other, offered gently, and corrected if they say you missed them.
One practice worth keeping.
One practice worth dropping, including a practice of saving every hard topic for a summit, if that is what you are done with.

Keep each item to a few sentences. A discovery is not a verdict on the relationship's health. "I learned I like ordinary questions more than grand ones" is a discovery. "We are finally doing this right" is a poster. Leave the poster in the margin or off the page.

Then choose together, and stop when you have chosen:

At most two recurring practices.
One dated future experience, or none.
The smallest version of each practice on a hard week: in bed, on a call, or inside 10 minutes.
When you will notice how it is going. One date, not a surveillance schedule.

Write them on a single page: what, how often, the smallest version, and the noticing date. Read the page aloud. If it sounds like a second job, cut it in the room. Two practices that survive a hard week will outlast twelve that require a personality transplant.

Examples of scale, not assignments: a monthly page in the shape of a future memory, whose smallest version is a voice note. A bench from a shared list, on a Saturday you already have off. The two-question cap from a disagreement, used once the next time opinions heat up. A Wednesday call you already know how to keep. If 094 appeals, the practice can be "the reintroduction in a week we can protect, and the next calm week if we miss it." That is an invitation you are choosing, not a compulsory audit.

Close by naming what you are done pretending to want. One thing each is plenty. A trip, a ritual, a kind of talk, a fantasy of being people who journal every night. Saying it aloud keeps it from sneaking back in as guilt.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**20 minutes.** One discovery each, one practice you are keeping, and its hard-week version. The dated experience can wait. "No new practice" is available in this version and counts as done. Put the not-now margin on the page even if it holds a single line.

**40 minutes.** The four headings each, then at most two practices, one optional dated experience, smallest versions, and a noticing date. Include the thing you are done pretending to want. This is the landing to use if you have had a real season and want it distilled.

**60 minutes.** Begin by listing, briefly, the experiences you actually did, titles or phrases only, so the discoveries have to come from that list. Then the same small design. The extra minutes are for accuracy about the past, not for a larger future. Still two practices at most. Still a margin.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On the noticing date, ask three questions and then leave it. Are we doing the smallest version? Has the practice become a resentment? Does the dated experience still belong to both of us? Revise in a few lines. Do not open the margin and promote everything.

You can keep a practice that looks like almost nothing. Tea without phones. A question behind an ordinary answer, once a week, with permission to stop at lunch. Company for an unfinished question, with advice staying outside until invited. Small is not a rehearsal for large. Small is often the whole intimacy.

If the season was thin, because of illness, work, grief, or a book that stayed mostly closed, the next chapter can be one kindness you already perform and want to keep seeing. You do not owe the unread chapters a penance.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Across distance, name practices that survive screens and travel. A letter. A call with a start time and an end. A photo of the ordinary day, sent without a caption requirement. The smallest version should be possible in a bad time zone.

The motif is a page with two written lines and a wide margin: `assets/chapters/096/motif.svg`. The margin is part of the design.

073, The First Chapter, is for the beginning of the story you already share. 091, What We Want More Of, starts from appetite and chooses increases for a short period. 094 is the yearly invitation to be reintroduced, if you want it on the calendar. Come back to this landing when a season ends, or when the practices have quietly become either beloved or fake. Life may hand you a different chapter than the one you designed. The page can say so.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They list what they actually did: an unpopular opinion apiece, a ladder that started at a cheese sandwich, two unfinished questions left open, a draft of how they greet each other, one future memory about rain and cake, a short "more of" list, a bike-repair dream, a bucket list starring a bench. They do not inventory the hours they skipped.

Rowan's discovery about themself: "I like being asked ordinary questions, and I hate being handed a plan in the same minute." Discovery about Vale, offered and accepted: "You want company beside an unfinished question, and advice later, if ever." Practice to keep: the two-question cap when an opinion shows up. Practice to drop: the Sunday meeting that turned into a trial.

Vale's discovery about themself: "I disappear into usefulness, and I want that noticed without a rescue." Discovery about Rowan: "Your quiet is sometimes a good work week." Practice to keep: reading in the same room, which can be 15 minutes. Practice to drop: pretending they want a passport trip this year.

Together they choose two practices. Once a week, the shared reading, smallest version 15 minutes or a call where they both read a page and say one line. Once a month, a future-memory page, smallest version a voice note in the past tense plus one practical step. Dated experience: the local bench, two Saturdays from now, tea from home, 15 minutes, coats allowed. Noticing date, the Sunday after the bench.

In the margin, labeled not now: the motel by the lake, a night class critique, a resolution spreadsheet, the rest of the unread book. Rowan says, "I am done pretending I want a journal practice that happens nightly." Vale says, "I am done pretending the December dinner is a moral duty." They write that on the page. The next chapter fits on one sheet.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Which discoveries came from hours you actually lived?
What did you drop, and did you drop it cleanly?
Do the practices have a hard-week version you believe?
What went to "not now," and can it stay there without a guilt tax?

You can leave a season with two lines and a margin. The margin is how the next chapter stays yours.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. One page: the practices, the smallest versions, the dated experience if you chose one, and the noticing date. The margin is allowed to be long.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. Vulnerable discoveries stay off the shared page unless the speaker wants them written. The shared notes are the part you write together.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A discovery from this season that you want carried forward.
- The smallest version of a practice on a hard week.
partner_b:
- A practice, or a future experience, you want designed in from your side of the planning.
- What belongs in the margin labeled not now.
shared:
- The next chapter as you mean it, including what you are done pretending to want.
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Are you in that chapter, or did life hand you a different one?
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Retreats and workbooks often end with goal setting. That custom is not a validated protocol, and this landing claims no clinical standing for the book. The look-back stays with experiences actually done. At most two recurring practices and one dated experience, each with a smallest version. "No new practice; we are keeping one old kindness" is a complete result. 094 may be chosen here as a yearly invitation. It is not installed by default, and the chapters after this one are not assigned. A next chapter may be quiet.

experiences.title: The Emotional Archaeologists

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One strong feeling, examined in layers, while the explorer keeps the right to change the cause.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Start from a strong feeling whose first cause may change. Annoyance at the dishes. Pride at the news. Jealousy at a glance. The caption glued to it may be right. It may also be the sentence that was fastest, the one that kept the moment from having to be looked at twice.

This hour is a dig with two roles and one feeling. The explorer chooses the reaction and says, in a single sentence, what they assume caused it. The archaeologist asks a short sequence of questions, reflects the words they actually heard, and withholds the clever theory. Partway through, the first cause may stop fitting. The explorer is the person who gets to notice that. The archaeologist does not diagnose a better one and hand it over.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
The same heat, the same flush, the same slump, and the household already has a story ready. Official stories save time. They also hide the layer that was skipped because it was awkward, tender, or simply slower. The explorer is allowed to leave with a different cause than the one they walked in with.

The mechanism is narrow. Hearing your own account reflected, without an upgrade, lets you test whether the cause still holds. Being explained feels like help and often functions as a lid. Being accurately repeated feels different. You get to say "close," or "no, the heat was earlier than that," or "the cause I walked in with is the wrong object."

A need may show up under the feeling: company, fairness, a witness, a limit, a little glory that wants to be seen. Treat that need as a hypothesis. The explorer may keep it, revise it, or set it down. It is not a work order for the partner, and it is not a find the archaeologist gets to name.

This shape was formulated for this project. Nothing here claims a discovery, a treatment, or a guarantee that one sitting will reach a buried truth. Sometimes the first cause survives the dig. That is a finished result.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can hear each other. Phones facedown. Paper or a notes app, so the opening sentence can be compared with the closing one. A timer helps the dig stay a dig.

Choose who explores first. One reaction only: joy, jealousy, embarrassment, pride, sadness, or a close cousin. Recent enough to remember, small enough to hold tonight. If the feeling that wants the floor is panic, or if the hour is a crisis or anything involving abuse, leave the roles. Respond as a partner. This frame has no business managing danger.

Jealousy and anger are allowed as self-observation. They are a poor courtroom. If what you actually need is a direct complaint about something the other person did, say that in ordinary language, or schedule it. Do not bury a case inside a dig and hope the questions will prosecute it.

Three agreements, said once:

You may pass, pause, or trade the reaction for a milder one.
A stop word ends the dig immediately. Pick a word that will not appear by accident. "Shelf" works. So does "red pen."
The explorer speaks the last sentence, which may keep, revise, or abandon the original cause. The archaeologist does not announce the revision.

No lying down, dimmed lights, or touch is required. Long pauses count as answers in progress.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Take 3 minutes. The explorer writes one sentence: the reaction, and the cause they are walking in with. Read it aloud. The archaeologist copies it, or lets the explorer keep the paper in view. That sentence is the ground level. You will want it later, when memory tries to pretend you began somewhere wiser.

Agree the stop word again, out loud.

The archaeologist asks one question at a time, in roughly this order, and may skip a layer the explorer does not want:

1. What happened just before?
2. What did your body do?
3. What meaning arrived first?
4. What else might be true?
5. What might the feeling be protecting, or wanting?

After each answer, reflect words, not a theory. Use the explorer's nouns. Then ask, "Is that close?"

A clean reflection sounds like this: "Hot face, plates that were already stacked, and a meaning that you were too much at the table. Is that close?"

If the explorer says no, repeat their correction and stop improving it. If they say "partly," ask which half. If they go quiet, wait. Offer the stop word rather than a better question.

Leave these moves unused. They end the dig even when they sound kind:

A diagnostic label.
"So you're really just..."
A summary cleverer than the sentence the explorer just said.
A dig into a feeling they only mentioned as an example.
A turn that starts gathering evidence about the partner.

When the explorer notices the cause moving, let them be the one to say so. You will hear it in ordinary language. "That isn't the dishes." "The pride is real, and the audience I wanted was smaller than the one I named." The archaeologist's next line is still a reflection, plus "Is that close?" The archaeologist does not unveil the true feeling.

The last minute belongs to the explorer. They look at the opening sentence and say one of three things, in their own words:

Keep. The cause I walked in with still holds.
Revise. Here is the cause I would write now. The first one was a guess, and I am marking it as a guess.
Abandon. I do not have a replacement, and I am done looking tonight.

If a need showed up, they may add it as a hypothesis: "Under this I think I wanted a witness. I might be wrong." The archaeologist thanks them and does not assign the need to anyone. Close there. A second feeling is a different day, unless you are both genuinely fresh and the first dig already ended with a thank-you.

15 minutes and one layer is a complete short path. Stopping at "what my body did" can be the whole session.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**15 minutes.** One reaction. Write the opening cause. Ask only the first question that has any life in it, reflect it, and ask "Is that close?" The explorer says keep, revise, or abandon. One layer is a finished dig.

**40 minutes.** The full sequence, still one reaction. Pauses included. The closing sentence gets a full minute, and the opening sentence stays visible so a revision is a revision, not a foggy memory of having always known.

**50 minutes.** The explorer writes the five answers first, slowly, in silence. Then they read, and the archaeologist reflects only what was read, with "Is that close?" after each layer they choose to keep. Use this when speech is costly, when you are in different rooms, or when a voiced theory would be too tempting. The extra time is for pace. It is not an invitation to excavate a second site.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, bring the hypothesis back beside a fresh example of a similar reaction. Ask only whether it still fits. A hypothesis that fails is useful. Write the failure down. Do not promote it into a personality.

You can add one question, only if the explorer invites it: "Where does this show up on an ordinary Tuesday, in a smaller size?" That keeps the dig from living only in dramatic weather. The archaeologist may notice a pattern. They offer it as a sighting, one sentence, and the explorer decides whether it belongs in the closing line.

Leave the partner's motive out of the deeper pass. If the explorer wants to know why the other person did something, that is a different conversation, with both people allowed to answer for themselves.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By letter, the explorer writes the five layers and the closing sentence. The reply is a reflection and "Is that close?" sent after the letter is read. No theory in the margin.

If writing is tiring, say the opening cause and let the archaeologist jot the exact words. If speech is tiring, stay on the page and trade the paper. The motif for this chapter is a cut bank of earth, one stratum labeled in the explorer's hand. A private sketch is optional.

Replay when a familiar reaction returns and the old caption feels automatic. Date both sentences, the first cause and the last, so a later dig has something to meet. The same heat, a year on, is often a different object wearing the same name.

010, The Fear Beneath the Fear, stays with successive layers under a fear. This dig can start from joy, pride, jealousy, embarrassment, or sadness, and the assumed cause is allowed to move while you watch. 087, The Question Behind the Question, starts from an ordinary answer and follows it. 020, The Listening Experiment, gives one person a longer uninterrupted turn and a reflection at the end. Different tools. Leave them different.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan chooses embarrassment from a dinner last week and writes: "I got quiet because the story about my old boss ran too long, and I was ashamed of talking so much."

Vale asks what happened just before. Rowan says the question was ordinary. Vale had asked how the reorganization was going. Rowan started talking, then heard their own voice speed up. The body layer: face hot, hands stacking plates that were already stacked. The first meaning: "I am too much at this table."

Vale reflects: "Hot face, plates that were already stacked, and a meaning that you were too much. Is that close?"

Rowan says, "Close. The too-much sentence is old. What else might be true is that I wanted you to want the next part, and I got scared you were being polite."

Vale does not say that this is really about work, or about a parent, or about anxiety. Vale asks what the feeling might be wanting. Rowan says, "A sign you actually wanted the rest. I didn't check. I supplied the shame instead."

Rowan's last sentence: "The cause I walked in with was half right about the shame and wrong about the source. I was embarrassed that I wanted interest and didn't ask. I'm keeping that revision, and I'm marking the first cause as a guess. I am not asking you to prove interest on a schedule."

Vale says, "Thank you for the dig," and stops.

Vale's own turn, on another night, is pride after a small public thanks at work. The opening cause is "I was proud because someone noticed." Midway, Vale hears themselves say that the pride got sharp when they imagined Rowan hearing a shorter version and thinking it was nothing. Vale revises: the pride was real, and under it was a wish to be believed at home without performing the whole story. Vale names that as a hypothesis. Rowan, now the archaeologist, repeats the hypothesis and does not accept a job.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Sit for a minute before you tidy the dig into a lesson.

What was the opening cause, in the sentence you actually wrote?
Did it keep, move, or get set down, and who was the person who said so?
Where did the archaeologist want to offer a better theory?
If a need appeared, did it stay a hypothesis, or did it turn into an assignment?
Do you want this reaction left alone for a while?

You do not owe each other a cleaner emotion. You can keep the two sentences, the first and the last, and you can keep them accurate.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional. Write what you are willing to reread.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together. If you were the archaeologist, your page is still about your own reaction when you take a turn. It does not excavate the other person.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- A strong reaction you investigated, layer by layer, and the need under it if you found one. Mark a guess as a guess.
- Stop before you invent a motive. If the first cause moved, say what it moved to, in your words.
partner_b:
- Your reaction, your layers, your pace. This page does not excavate the other person.
- What you kept, revised, or left alone about your own first cause.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- The need you think was underneath, written as a hypothesis you are allowed to revise
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- Did the hypothesis hold the next time a similar reaction appeared?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Formulated for this project: one chosen reaction, layer-by-layer questions, and a rule that the explorer, not the archaeologist, announces any change in the assumed cause. That is a provenance note. It is not a claim of worldwide novelty, and it is not a validated method. See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator, and in Study 2 emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. See R1988 for the model behind that finding: disclosure, response, and the feeling of being understood. Both support a listener who reflects. Neither tested this dig, and neither shows that a buried need can be reliably excavated in one sitting. The need stays a hypothesis the explorer may decline. If the hour meets abuse, panic, or a crisis, leave the roles and respond as a partner.

materials: a stop word you both know

metadata.duration_summary: Short 15 minutes · Standard 40 minutes · Extended 50 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A long fictional life, contradictory decades, and three invented memories you would actually like to make.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Sit down as if the long life has already happened. You are both about 100. If that number feels cruel, call it a long life from now. The decades ahead are fiction, and the fiction is allowed to disagree with itself. One of you remembers a night class. The other remembers that the night class never existed and that the real story of those years was trains, a bad suitcase, and a joke that took a decade to land.

Then the costume comes partway off. Each of you names up to three invented memories you would genuinely like to make real. Fewer than three is a complete answer. The interview is the play. The three memories are the appetite hiding inside the play.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Couples often talk about the future as a single plan that has to survive both people's vetoes in the same 10 minutes. That is a useful way to book a trip. It is a cramped way to find out what either of you still wants. A century of obvious fiction gives the wants somewhere to sprawl. Contradictions can sit on the same porch without a vote.

The mechanism is the costume, then the cut back to now. You build those decades out of scraps already in reach: a town, a skill, a kind of Tuesday, a mistake you are willing to claim in advance. The theatrical frame should stay obviously fictional. You are not remembering. You are inventing in the past tense, which is a pleasure, and then you are choosing which inventions still tug once the scarf is off.

This was formulated for this project. Interviews with a future self are an old coaching habit. They are not this chapter. Nothing here extends a life, repairs a regret, or requires the two of you to share one canonical century.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit as if on a porch, even if the porch is a kitchen. A scarf is optional and slightly ridiculous, which helps. Nothing is also correct. Speak a little more slowly if you want the theater. Skip the creaky-voice impression. Old age is not the joke, and illness or death at a partner's expense is out of bounds.

Set the year as 100 years from the older partner's birth, or skip the arithmetic and say, "We are both about 100." If disability, illness, or grief makes the number unkind, use "a long life from now" and keep every other rule.

Phones facedown. Paper for the future-memory page. A timer, so one person does not narrate both lives.

Three agreements:

You may pass, pause, or leave the interview without naming three memories.
During the interview, neither of you corrects the other's fiction. Afterward you may say which story you loved. You may not prosecute it.
An invented memory that spends the other person's body, fertility, faith, or home needs a plain conversation before it lands on the "make real" page. Wanting it in costume is allowed. Listing it as a plan is a different act.

The future is a poor place to indict the present. If a centenarian story is mostly a complaint about the person sitting here, set the decade down and choose a kinder fiction, or tell the complaint in your own age, outside the game.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
One of you interviews. The other answers as the centenarian. About 8 minutes, then you switch. Use these questions, or any three of them. They were written for this chapter:

What adventure still makes you laugh?
What mistake taught you a skill you were glad to have?
What ordinary Tuesday would you repeat?
What did you stop pretending?
What did we get wrong about each other, and later understand?

Answer in scenes. A town, a tool, a meal, a sentence someone said. If you catch yourself delivering a moral, return to the Tuesday. Contradictory versions of the same decade stay in play. One centenarian may have learned to sail. The other may have no memory of a boat and a vivid memory of a roof garden that mostly died. Both centuries are affectionate. Neither is the official one.

The interviewer may ask one follow-up that asks for a picture: "What did the Tuesday smell like?" or "Who was in the room when you stopped pretending?" A follow-up that asks the centenarian to justify the present relationship is a verdict. This porch has no verdicts.

When both interviews are done, take the scarf off, or simply sit up. Each person names up to three invented memories they would genuinely like to make real someday. Say them as wants, from the age you are now. A memory you enjoyed inventing and do not want to attempt is a good story. Leave it on the porch.

For each want that survives, one block on the future-memory page:

The scene, in two sentences, still a little cinematic if it must be.
A step available without heroics, from the life you actually have. One afternoon, one invitation, one class that already exists, one tool already in the house.
A piece that remains fantasy unless the other person wants it. Name that piece so it does not sneak into the step.

The page is practical and optional. It is not a promise sheet. A step can be declined later. A fantasy piece can stay loved and undone. If you cannot find a step without heroics, the memory stays fiction, and that is an honest outcome.

Read the pages to each other only as far as you want them heard. One of you may have three. The other may have one. You do not average them into a joint destiny.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**30 minutes.** Each person answers two interview questions, about 5 minutes each. Then each names one invented memory and, if they want, one step. Fewer than three is complete. Use this when you are tired or when the number 100 needs to stay light.

**50 minutes.** Both interviews, with room for one contradiction to be enjoyed rather than sanded down. Then the three-memory naming, spoken. Write the page only for the wants that still have a pulse after they are said out loud.

**60 minutes.** The standard interview, plus a quiet 10 minutes to fill the future-memory page before you read any of it. The extra time is for separating the scene, the step, and the piece that must stay fantasy. Still no shared canonical century. Still no correction of the other person's decades.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, pick one step that was small enough to attempt and tell the truth about whether you did it. A step that shrank, or that turned out to belong only to the costume, goes back on the porch without a speech about follow-through.

You can replay a single decade you both described, side by side, and read the two versions aloud. The pleasure is the mismatch. Ask, "What did your version protect?" only if the speaker wants that question. Some mismatches are just style. A person who tells adventures and a person who tells Tuesdays can love each other without merging genres.

If a want keeps returning across replays, it may be ready for a real conversation about time and money. Have that conversation in the present tense, with the costume off. The centenarian does not get to sign for both of you.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By call, one person reads the questions and both answer. The future-memory page can be a shared note you fill after you hang up. By letter, write one decade and one want. The reply names a detail that felt like the writer, and does not edit their century.

If the age frame is wrong for your bodies or your grief, drop it and keep the questions, the contradictions, and the three wants. The control that matters is the return to the age you are.

No makeup, no props required. The motif is two chairs and a long shadow, with three small marks for the memories you might try. A doodle in the margin is optional.

Replay on a birthday, or when a plan has gone stale and you want appetite before logistics. Date the page. A want that was a boat at 40 may be a lake afternoon at 50, and both entries deserve to exist.

090, The Future Memory, builds one happy scene in the past tense and then asks how you might make it. Here the span is decades, contradiction is welcome, and the twist is up to three chosen inventions. 095, A Promise I Actually Want to Keep, is for commitments you mean to hold. This page can feed that chapter later. It does not do the promising. 049, The Life Not Taken, looks backward at a real fork. This interview looks forward through obvious fiction.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They say they are both about 100. Rowan claims that at 72 they opened a tiny night class in reading maps, and that Vale fell asleep in the front row on purpose, as a review. Vale's version of the same decade has no class. It has trains, a suitcase that broke in a station, and a roof garden that failed with commitment. Vale says the suitcase fight became their best story. Rowan does not correct the missing classroom. Vale does not sink the boat Rowan adds, 5 minutes later, for a summer they also did not live.

Scarves off. Rowan names three invented memories worth trying to make real. A week in a coastal town with no agenda. A clumsy class taught once, to people who already like them. A kitchen table that feeds neighbors once a season. The steps are smaller than the costume: one long weekend this year, phones in a drawer in the mornings; one evening offered to a friend who asked, not a school; two people invited, not six. The cottage they do not own stays fantasy. So does the loyal front row.

Vale names two, and stops. Learning the names of the birds on their actual street, which can start on the next walk. And a birthday where nobody performs, which can start by telling Rowan that a restaurant speech would miss. A third picture, fixing a boat together, stays on the fantasy side because it spends a weekend and a chunk of money Vale has not asked for. Vale says so. Rowan does not recruit the boat back onto the page.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Before you turn a good story into a calendar, check the cut.

Which invented decade did you want to protect from correction, and what was the pleasure in it?
Which of your three, or fewer, still feels like a want once you are the age you are?
Which step is available without heroics, and which piece must stay fiction unless you both want it?
Did either century smuggle a complaint about the present? If yes, say the complaint in plain language, or drop it.
Are you willing to let the other person's incompatible future stand?

You do not owe each other a shared old age. You can keep one step, and you can keep it small.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together. Fewer than three aspirations is a finished page.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Speaking as the centenarian you imagined, one invented memory, and the real aspiration inside it.
- A second invented memory only if you want it on paper. Fewer than three is complete.
partner_b:
- Your invented memory, and the aspiration you still want once the costume comes off.
- Anything in that memory that has to stay fantasy unless the other person wants it.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- Up to three aspirations you are willing to aim at from the age you are now. Fewer than three is complete.
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- Which aspiration has left a footprint in real life?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: No research citation is claimed for this activity. Future-self letters and interviews circulate in coaching. They were not the source of this chapter, and they are not its protocol. The decades you describe are fiction on purpose. The frame should stay obviously fictional. Formulated for this project. That is a provenance note, not a claim of worldwide novelty, and not a claim that imagining a century makes it happen, lengthens a life, or repairs regret. Two incompatible centuries can both be affectionate. The future-memory page is optional. It is not 095's promise sheet, and a piece the other person does not want remains fantasy.

experiences.title: The Invisible Postcards

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Keep a few tiny true notes in secret, then hand them over after the week has had time to swallow them.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
Somebody closed a door softly while you were on the phone. Somebody passed the salt and looked up. Somebody said a name the way its owner says it, at a counter where you had already flattened it. These are terrible candidates for a speech. By Thursday the person who did them could easily fail to pick them out of the week.

For a few agreed days, each of you keeps a private stack of very small postcards about moments the other helped, impressed, delighted, or attracted you. You both know the notes are being kept. You do not know the wording. At the end you trade the stacks. The sharpest cards are often the ones the recipient cannot remember. Forgetting is a feature of the form. A moment too small to file can still be a moment someone kept.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
The salt works, so the salt disappears. For a few agreed days you keep a private note about a moment the other person will not see until the exchange. A gratitude practice usually stays private, or it gets said while the act is still obvious and slightly embarrassing to praise. This ritual waits. The delay is the mechanism. A note written the same day holds a detail the week will eat. Read later, it shows a kind of attention the recipient was not performing for.

Feeling appreciative and feeling appreciated have been tied, across several methods, to responsiveness, commitment, and the ordinary work of looking after a bond, and appreciation can show up in behavior. See G2012 in the notes. That is a finding about appreciation in intimate life. It is not a test of secret cards, and it does not show that a stack of paper changes a couple. The ritual was formulated for this project. A short stack of true tiny notes completes it. The recipient does not have to feel the moment at the size the writer felt it.

[074](074), The Moments You Didn’t Know Mattered, is one sitting about past gestures whose impact outran what the other person realized. These postcards look forward across a few coming days, and their pride is how little they had to be.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Agree the span before the first note: three, five, or seven days, and the hour you will exchange. Secret means the wording stays unseen. The practice itself is agreed in advance. A surprise stack, sprung on someone who never knew notes were being kept, is a different event. Leave it alone.

Each of you needs a few copies of `journal/templates/postcard.md`, or blank cards you can hide. An envelope, a drawer, or a locked note the other person will not tidy into the open. A pen. If handwriting is the wrong tool, a voice memo in a locked folder, transcribed on exchange day, is a full postcard. Large print is a full postcard. If you are apart, date-stamped messages scheduled to arrive on the exchange hour are a full postcard. A call, a text that landed well, a small digital kindness: those count. Watching a location, reading someone's messages to harvest a note, or logging their ordinary freedom is outside the ritual. If that is the impulse, stop the collection.

Say these once, out loud:

You write when something actually happens. You do not perform extra goodness in order to be postcarded, and you do not announce that a note was just earned.
A short stack is a finished collection. Different lengths are allowed. Nobody is scored.
Either of you may withhold a card that, on a private reread, feels like pressure, a request, or a future exhibit in an argument.
Keep notes about attraction or sex only if you both opted in before day one. Skip anything that exposes a third person.
"I don't remember that" is a welcome sentence. The writer adds one concrete detail if it helps the picture, and then stops. There is no lesson in having forgotten.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**Day zero, about 10 minutes.** Pick the span and the exchange. Each person takes blank sheets and puts them where the other will not read them. If you share a desk, use two envelopes with your own initials in two different places, or two locked notes. Tell each other the hiding is allowed.

**During the days.** When the other person helps, impresses, delights, or attracts you, write the card the same day. One to four lines is the right size. Include what happened, where, and the effect on you. Tiny is the point.

Passed the salt and looked up.
Closed the door softly.
Remembered the neighbor's dog and used its name.
Laughed at their own joke in the kitchen in a way that made you want to stay in the room.

A card is a note about a moment you saw. A request ("keep doing this or I'll keep score") belongs in a different conversation, on a day you are both awake to it. If a day offers nothing true, leave the day blank. Blank days are unmarked, and they are allowed. If you are apart, write about the contact you actually had. The window has to fit how often you see or speak.

**How to use the postcard template.** Print or copy `journal/templates/postcard.md`, one sheet per moment. Baselines on the printed sheet are at least 0.32 inch apart, and each prompt gets at least eight handwriting lines. A cut-down paper postcard still uses that gap, so it may hold only the first eight lines. Do not tighten the lines to imitate a shop postcard. Add a second sheet rather than crowding the words.

Fill the header. Day in the collection. The date you noticed it. Optional initials, from and to. The exchange date you agreed. Before that date, the sheet stays with the writer.

Under "The moment," write what they did, in the place it happened, small enough that they might not file it.

Under "What I hope you know about it," write the effect. Help, delight, a flicker of attraction, the feeling of being backed. If the hope is simply "I saw this," that is a complete note.

The sheet is a note about a moment, kept until the exchange, then traded. It is a record of attention. It is not a tally of who noticed more. After the exchange, a caption for a card you decide to keep can live on `journal/templates/memento-caption.md`: what it is, the date, where the object lives, and a local filename if you photographed it. Digital files stay in `journal/private/mementos/` on your own machine. This project does not upload them. A joint note about the reading uses the shared page in this chapter.

If you are using a blank card instead of the full sheet, keep the template's three facts even when the paper is smaller:

Front: "You didn't know I kept this."
Inside: when, what you did, what it did to me.
Back: "Remembering this is optional."

The full sheet, with its eight-line spacing, remains the journal copy if the pocket card is too small to hold the lines honestly.

**The exchange.** Sit together, or open the scheduled messages at the agreed hour and stay on the call. Trade stacks. Read in each other's presence or side by side. Aloud or in silence, both are legal. The reader may say "I don't remember that." The writer may add the blue table, the elbow, the pharmacist's pronunciation, and then stop. No ranking of whose stack is longer. A card you want to save for a later fight has expired. Leave it in the envelope, or destroy it.

If a card, on the second reading, feels like pressure, the writer may take it back before it is discussed. Taken back is a finished card.

**Keepsake.** If you both want to keep them, date an envelope and put it with the journal, or photograph the cards and store the photo where you both can reach it. If you disagree, the writer keeps their own outgoing cards, and the recipient keeps only the ones they ask to hold. Destroying a card is allowed. The moment was already given.

Close by naming one card you are glad exists, or by letting the stacks sit without a speech. Either close is complete.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**3 days, then 20 minutes.** Two to four true notes if they happen, fewer if they do not. Read, allow the forgotten ones, and put the stack in an envelope or let it go. A short stack completes the ritual. This is the right length when your days together are few. One evening of notes cannot produce the forgotten-moment effect, so the short version is still a span of days.

**5 days, then 30 minutes.** The standard span. Write the same day, on the template or the three-label card. Leave a little silence after the first note the recipient cannot place. Decide together whether the envelope stays.

**7 days, then 45 minutes.** Same rules, longer weather. On the last evening before the exchange, reread your own stack alone and pull any card that has turned into a request. You may say, for one card each, what you hope the other knows. Still no quota.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later collection, if you both opted in, try one card that is only about attraction or delight, and keep it as small as the salt. "You laughed at your own joke and I wanted to stay in the room" is the size. A scene you would not want a stranger to find in the envelope stays off the card, or lives in a voice memo you delete after you have said it at the exchange.

You can also choose, on day zero, to let one card be the moment you almost dismissed as too small to count, and to read that card first. The form likes that card.

A third pass can split the lanes, said out loud so nobody is graded on the lane they were not given: one of you watches for help, the other for delight. Drop the lanes the moment they feel like homework.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Low energy: one true card across three days is a complete collection. A voice memo counts. Large print counts.

Long-distance: schedule the send for the exchange hour. A week of rare contact can produce two true notes about calls. That is the week.

Budget: scrap paper and an envelope. The template is a copying guide.

The ritual asks for attention and a delayed reading. You stay in the life you already have. No route around the house, no objects to find, no scoreboard.

Replay with a new span and a new dated envelope. The old envelope stays closed unless you both want it open. Read an old card as a memory of being seen. Leave it out of any argument about who does more.

[026](026), The Appreciation Avalanche, is one sitting of increasingly specific praise. [032](032), The Everyday Devotion Experiment, is several days of small acts offered on purpose. [078](078), The Unspoken Thank-You, writes the thanks that never arrived for something already past. This chapter's notes stay unseen until a date you both know.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Across five days Rowan writes four cards. One of them: "Tuesday, the laundromat. You moved my sweater off the folding table before the damp jeans landed on it. I was arguing with a form on my phone. I felt looked after in a way I did not have to thank in the moment, because I did not notice until I reached for the sweater and it was dry."

Vale, at the exchange: "I don't remember that."

Rowan: "It was the blue table, and you did it with your elbow because your hands were full." Then Rowan stops. Vale keeps the card.

Vale's shortest card says: "Thursday, you pronounced the pharmacist's name the way she says it, after I had already flattened it. She smiled. I wanted to stand closer to you." Rowan remembers the pharmacy and not the name. That is the ritual working.

Vale almost includes a fifth card: "Please keep taking the late calls so I can sleep." On the private reread it is a request. Vale leaves it in the drawer. The exchange is the other cards. Rowan does not learn the number Vale withheld, and does not ask.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
What did you write that the week would have erased?
Which card met a blank look, and was the blank a pleasure, a sting, or both?
Did any card try to become a job description, and did you pull it?
What, if anything, do you want to keep noticing without turning it into a quota?

You do not owe each other a matching number of cards, or a matching size of feeling.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the exchange, the span you played, and the place you read. Until the exchange, the private prompts stay blank on purpose. The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them.

Printed prompts want at least eight handwriting lines, baselines at least 0.32 inch apart. Use one postcard sheet per moment, and the partner page if you want the prompts at full size. Add sheets rather than tightening the lines.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Until the exchange, leave this prompt blank. Afterward, which postcard you wrote still feels true, in a sentence or two?
- The smallest moment you kept, and whether you were glad it was small.
partner_b:
- Which postcard you received that you want to keep, and which one you wrote that you hope landed as you meant it?
- If one received card had already left your memory, what you want this page to hold about being handed it. A title is enough.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- The exchange itself: when you read, what you laughed about, and what you are saving.
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- After the collection ended, did you keep noticing the small moments anyway?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Original formulation for this project: a multi-day secret collection of small notes, exchanged once, with forgetting treated as part of the form. That is a provenance note. It is not a claim of worldwide novelty, and it is not a research protocol.

See G2012. Gordon, Impett, Kogan, Oveis, and Keltner (2012) tied feeling appreciative and feeling appreciated to responsiveness, commitment, and relationship maintenance, and observed that appreciation can show in behavior. The studies did not test postcards, secrecy, delay, or this ritual. Do not read them as proof that a stack of cards changes a couple.

Gratitude journals are a common practice, usually private or shared at once. This chapter delays the sharing on purpose. Another project's postcard name, submission rules, and card designs are not used here.

A card is not a quota and not an exhibit for a fight. The recipient does not have to match the writer's feeling. Sexual or explicit notes stay opt-in. Anything that exposes a third person stays off the card.

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A short inner forecast, plus an optional line about tomorrow that the weatherperson keeps.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
"How was your day?" is a kind question that often wants a verdict. Fine. Long. Don't ask. A forecast is ruder and more accurate. You name the sky you are actually under, including the ridiculous sky, and the other person is allowed to look at it without becoming the meteorological service.

The weatherperson may add one optional line: what could help tomorrow. That line stays in their hands. They can arrange the help themselves. They can make an explicit request. They do not hand the other person the climate and call it love.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Days get summarized into a word, and the word invites a manager. Fine gets a nod. Bad gets a fix. A forecast asks for a description: condition, direction, region. Description gives the listener something to stand next to. It does not appoint them.

The mechanism is the split between weather and labor. "Tomorrow would go better if I stepped outside once. I can do that myself" is a complete kindness to the future, and it leaves the partner unemployed by the metaphor. "Company in the kitchen would help, and I will ask if I want it" keeps the request voluntary and specific. A partner can be company. A partner cannot be the sky.

This ritual was formulated for this project. Mood metaphors are common in classrooms and in other people's kitchens. They are not a treatment, and naming a feeling is not claimed to change a brain or a forecast. Wit is optional. A plain sentence is the same ritual.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You can do this at the sink, on a walk, or in two lines of text. No one has to forecast every day. "No forecast tonight" is a complete answer. Then talk the way you already talk.

Pick one region so the sky stays local: work, body, the relationship, or the private interior. A forecast of every system on earth is a speech. One region is a report.

Three agreements:

The listener may ask where it is heaviest, or whether it is passing. Advice waits until it is requested.
Tomorrow's help is spoken by the weatherperson. It is not assigned to the partner by default.
A forecast that is really a coded complaint deserves a plain sentence instead. You can still name the relationship as the region. Say your weather. If you want a change from the other person, call it a request, out loud, and let them answer as a person.

If the report is despair, panic, or danger, treat it as a real signal. Step out of the metaphor. Stay with them, and bring in outside help when safety is in question. A poem is the wrong tool for an emergency.

Skip thunderclap theater if loud weather play is too much. The ritual fits fatigue because it is short.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
The weatherperson gives three beats, and a fourth only if they want it.

Region. One word or one phrase.
Condition, and the direction of change. Clearing, steady, incoming, stuck, a break and then more.
Optional: what could help tomorrow, and who will carry it. Use one of these shapes. "A help I can arrange is ___." "A help I am actually requesting is ___." "I am requesting nothing."

Then stop. The listener does not hand over an umbrella in the form of a plan.

Two sample forecasts, written for this chapter. Use them as patterns, not as scripts you have to earn.

Playful: "Region, work. Late fog, a small break of sun after lunch, chance of existential drizzle tonight. Tomorrow would go better if I stepped outside once. I can do that myself."

Serious: "Region, body. Steady rain since the appointment. I don't want ideas. Company in the kitchen would help, and I will ask if I want it."

A request, when there is one, is specific enough to accept or decline. "I am asking you to sit in the kitchen while I heat soup. You don't have to talk." That is different from "You should fix my rain." The first can be declined, and the decline is not a weather failure. The second was never a fair job.

Listener questions that stay inside the ritual:

Where is it heaviest right now?
Is it passing, or is it the kind that sits?
Do you want a question, or is the report finished?

Questions that sneak a fix, such as "Have you tried," wait for a yes.

If you dislike metaphor, use the same beats in plain language, and treat that path as equal:

Right now I am ___.
It may last ___.
A help I can arrange is ___.
A help I am actually requesting is ___ / none.

Both of you may report. The two forecasts do not have to merge. Two weather systems can share a coast. A combined outlook is optional and usually unnecessary on a weeknight.

If you keep a log, the columns are date, region, forecast, help I will arrange for myself, and anything I am explicitly asking. The asking column is often blank. The log is a memory, not a compliance chart. Missing days are none of the log's business.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**5 minutes.** One person, one region, condition and direction. The tomorrow line only if it is already obvious. The listener asks at most one question, or none. "No forecast" counts as played.

**10 minutes.** Both people report their own sky. Each may add the help line, including "nothing requested." The listener reflects the condition in a few words if that helps, and does not problem-solve. This is the version that replaces "How was your day?" on an ordinary evening.

**15 minutes.** Both forecasts, plus the log line written down, plus one optional combined outlook only if you both want it. Use the extra minutes when the weather is real and you want the request, if any, to be unmistakable. Still one region each. A second region is another day, or a sentence you add because it will not stay quiet, not a tour of the whole climate.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Once a week, if you like the ritual, read the log backward and notice only this: which help you arranged for yourself, and which explicit request was actually answered, declined, or never made. Skip the scoring. A kind forecast is one you can reread without wincing at your own drama or at a job you quietly gave away.

You can name a micro-climate inside a good day. Sun with a pocket of hail is a legal report. Performing cheer is optional and usually detectable. If the true condition is mixed, say mixed.

A further question, only when the weatherperson invites it: "Is any of this mine to know overnight, or can it stay yours?" Some reports are for company. Some are for the record of having said them. The difference is theirs to draw.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By text, two lines: region and condition, then the help line or "no request." The reply can be "Heard" plus, if wanted, the listener's own forecast. Advice by message is still advice.

If speech is tiring, point at a picture of a sky, then add one sentence of the plain-language path. If metaphor is tiring, stay with the four blanks and skip the rain entirely. The motif is a small square of sky with an empty line under tomorrow. You do not have to draw it.

Replay whenever "How was your day?" has gone numb, or whenever you notice you have been fixing each other out of habit. You can also use it in the morning, as a departure forecast, with the same rule: tomorrow's help is not a task dropped on the way out the door.

020, The Listening Experiment, is a longer turn and a reflection after uninterrupted speech. This report stays brief, and solving is off the job description. 088, The Thing I’m Still Figuring Out, is for an unresolved question you are willing to share. 091, What We Want More Of, looks at appetite over time. A weather report is a snapshot. It can mention a want. It does not negotiate the whole menu.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan, at the counter: "Region, work. Late fog, a break of sun after lunch, chance of existential drizzle tonight. Tomorrow would go better if I stepped outside once. I can do that myself. I am not asking you to be the outdoors."

Vale asks, "Is the fog passing?" Rowan says, "Mostly. The drizzle is a meeting I keep rewriting." Vale nods and does not offer a script for the meeting.

Vale's own report does not match the metaphor and does not have to. "Region, body. Steady rain since the appointment. Right now I am wrung out. It may last through tomorrow morning. A help I can arrange is going to bed when the dishes are done, even if the dishes are mediocre. A help I am actually requesting is none. Company in the kitchen would help, and I will ask if I want it. Tonight the request line is blank."

Rowan says, "Heard." They do not write a combined outlook. Two systems, one coast. In the log, Rowan's asking column is blank. Vale's is blank. The blank is the point.

On another night Vale does make a request. "I am asking you to sit in the room while I answer that message. You don't have to draft it." Rowan can say yes or not tonight. The rain stays Vale's.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
This debrief can be 1 minute, or it can be silence.

Did the report describe weather, or did it assign a job?
Was tomorrow's help arranged by the person who owns it, requested outright, or left blank on purpose?
Did the listener try to clear the sky?
If you are keeping a log, is the asking column honest, including the blanks?
Do you want this ritual tomorrow, or is "no forecast" the true forecast?

You do not owe each other better weather. You can owe a clear request when you actually have one, and you can survive the evening without one.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session if you write it down. Note the version and whether you finished or waved it off. Mood is optional. A blank day in a log is allowed.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The shared notes are the part you write together, and only if you want a combined page at all.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- Today's inner weather: the front, the pressure, and, if you want it, what might help tomorrow.
- The help you will arrange for yourself, and anything you are explicitly asking. Often the second line is none.
partner_b:
- Your forecast, drawn from your own sky. The two forecasts do not have to merge.
- A help you can arrange, and a help you are actually requesting, or none.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- Write a combined outlook only if you want one. Two weather systems can share a coast.
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- What the next day actually brought, and whether the forecast was kind.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: No research citation is claimed. Mood metaphors and emotional check-ins are common. They are not a validated protocol for couples, and this chapter does not claim that naming a feeling changes the brain or the weather. Formulated for this project. That is a provenance note, not a claim of worldwide novelty, and not a mood treatment. The optional line about what could help tomorrow stays with the weatherperson. The partner is company only by request. A forecast of despair, panic, or danger is a real signal, not a figure of speech. The log is not a compliance chart.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 5 minutes · Standard 10 minutes · Extended 15 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Guess the reason your partner would move, and let a lucky yes stay worthless if the reason is wrong.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The wallet is the activity: why this person would return it, keep it, or walk it to a desk. The answer moves through a value, a fear or a hope, and some practical wall. This experiment asks you to borrow that movement.

A scenario is read. Each of you writes the choice you believe the other would make, and three beats of why. Then the person whose mind it is explains the choice they would actually make, and the reasons. A matched yes with a wrong reason scores below a missed yes with a grasped reason. The yes itself is worth zero. Differences are information. They are not a failed evening.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Stored trivia and borrowed reasoning are different skills. This hour scores the reasons, if you score at all, and the yes itself is worth zero. Being accurately imagined in your reasons feels different from being correctly labeled yes or no. A lucky label can still be a stranger wearing your answer.

The partner is the authority on their own mind. A score, if you use one, glorifies the reasons you could name. It does not measure love, and it does not measure empathic accuracy. No study is claimed for this game. If the points start to sting, drop them and keep the conversation.

[043](043), The Newlywed Game, Without the Wedding, asks you to match facts and preferences you have stored. [085](085), What Would You Do If…?, asks what you yourself would do. This chapter stays on the borrowed reason.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Sit where you can both write before either of you speaks. A call works if the writing stays private until the reveal. Phones facedown unless one of them is the paper. Either person may reject a scenario before any reasoning is written. After three rejects, write a replacement together in four lines: who asks, what is at stake, what it costs your partner, and what it costs someone else. Leave sex, fidelity, and humiliation of a body or a culture out of the deck. A guessed betrayal or a guessed sexual refusal is a poor joke. Do not deal one.

Replace any scenario that assumes a job, a sibling, a car, money, or a household you do not have. A night class can become a friend's project. A car can become a bike or a tool. A parent can become an older relative who still visits. The funny ones have to stay funny for the person inside them.

Agreements, said once:

You are answering as your partner, with the facts on the card. You may add a constraint you know is true ("you don't drive at night") and you name it as one of the three beats.
The person being imagined may correct the reason. They may not be outvoted about their own values.
A warm miss costs nothing. You ask, "What value did I miss?" and you write the answer down.
You do not bring a miss into tomorrow as a grievance.
Passing a scenario is a complete turn.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Play three scenarios in a night: one realistic, one funny, one morally gray. Cap the night there so the debrief stays kind. Draw by number, from a hat or from a die you both trust, and veto before writing. If the clock dies after two, save the gray one for another night. A finished night can be two. The bank will wait. If you are tired at the start, play the funny one and stop.

**The turn.**

1. Read the scenario aloud. Confirm you both accept it.
2. For 2 minutes, in silence, each of you writes the other's answer. Do this before anyone speaks, or the second writer will cheat by accident.
3. On the slip: the choice you think they would make. Then three beats: a value, a fear or a hope, and a practical constraint. If one beat is "none that I can name," write none.
4. Reveal one borrower at a time. Read the slip. Then the person whose mind it is gives their actual choice and their actual reasoning. They say which beat was a real value, which was a real constraint, and which belonged to a stranger.
5. If you are scoring, mark the slip. Then switch borrowers on the same scenario.
6. Each person writes one line: the value they missed, in the other's words if those words were offered. That line is the point of the turn.

**Scoring, optional and light.** The choice itself scores zero, whether you matched it or missed it. Naming a real value of theirs, a value they recognize as theirs in this situation, scores 2. A constraint you understood scores 1. A wrong value cannot be rescued by a lucky yes. Adjacent counts as the 2 only if they say "that's mine." If they hesitate, it is a miss. Ask what value you missed, write it down, and subtract nothing. There is no prize for the higher total. If the total makes either of you smaller, throw it away before you leave the table.

| Round | Value (2 or 0) | Constraint (1 or 0) | Choice, recorded and not scored | Value I missed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 |  |  |  |  |
| 2 |  |  |  |  |
| 3 |  |  |  |  |

**A blank you can copy.**

Scenario number and title.
The choice I think you would make.
Value.
Fear or hope.
Practical constraint.

After the reveal: your actual choice, your reasoning, the beat I had, the beat that was a stranger.

**How to draw.** Realistic uses R1 through R8. Funny uses F1 through F8. Gray uses G1 through G8. One of each is a standard night. Retire a number after you play it. A later night starts where the hat left off.

### Realistic

**R1. Overtime, and a friend in crisis.** Your partner is asked to stay late on the one night a friend has asked them to come over because the friend is in a real crisis, not a vague bad mood. The work is genuine. The friend is someone they love. Leaving work has a cost. Staying has a cost. What do they do in the next hour, and why?

**R2. Housekeeping, in front of them.** A parent, or an older relative who still has opinions, criticizes your partner's housekeeping in front of them and in front of you. The criticism is about a messy room, not about a moral failing, and it lands anyway. What do they do in the next 10 minutes?

**R3. The car for a week.** A neighbor asks to borrow the car for a week. The neighbor has been decent. The car is needed for ordinary life. There is no villain in the ask. If you have no car, use a bike, a camera, or the one good pot. What do they do?

**R4. The wallet.** They find a wallet with cash and an ID, on a sidewalk or a shop floor, with no owner in sight. What do they do before the day ends?

**R5. The restaurant already won.** The group chat has agreed on a restaurant your partner dislikes. Everyone else has said yes. Objecting now makes them the problem. Going means an evening of food they do not want. What do they do?

**R6. The sudden toast.** They are asked, with two hours' notice, to give a toast for someone they like and do not know how to praise in public. Refusing is allowed and a little ugly. Accepting means standing up. What do they do?

**R7. The airport.** A friend asks for a ride from the airport at an hour that wrecks their sleep before a hard day. The friend could take a cab. The friend asked them. What do they do?

**R8. The gift from the avoided person.** A package arrives with their name on it, clearly a gift from someone they have been gently avoiding. You are the one who sees it first. What do they want done with it, and what do they do when they find out it is in the house?

### Funny

**F1. The solemn dessert.** A solemn host serves, with visible pride, a dessert your partner hates. The table is watching the first bite. What do they do?

**F2. The free tattoo.** They are offered a free tattoo of your face, today, by an artist who is genuinely good. It is a joke that could become permanent if they nod. What do they do?

**F3. The hated song.** Their most disliked song comes on, and everyone else starts dancing as if the song were a civic duty. What do they do with their body and their face?

**F4. The incorrect expert.** A stranger explains your partner's own job to them, incorrectly, with great confidence, for 9 minutes. Escape is possible and slightly rude. What do they do?

**F5. The vegetable prize.** They win a contest. The prize is a year of the vegetable they cook badly and pretend to enjoy when other people serve it. Public refusal is available. So is a cupboard full of the vegetable. What do they do?

**F6. The microphone.** At a party they are handed a microphone and the room expects a character they did not agree to play. The character is silly, not cruel. What do they do?

**F7. The houseplant threat.** Their phone autocorrects a tender text into something that sounds like a threat against a houseplant. The recipient has already replied, "Are you okay?" What do they send next?

**F8. The accidental sculpture.** In a museum they have been leaning, for several minutes, on what they thought was a bench. A guard arrives to explain that it is a sculpture. What do they do in the first 30 seconds?

### Morally gray

**G1. The small secret.** A sibling, or a close friend if there is no sibling, asks them to keep a non-dangerous secret from you. The person is taking a night class, failing it, and does not want advice or an announcement. The class harms no one. Your partner knows you would rather not be left out of something true. What do they do?

**G2. The refund.** A refund is available only if they give a reason that is not quite true. The product disappointed them for a true reason the form does not list. The false reason is mild. The amount matters to the week and would not ruin a person they know. What do they do?

**G3. The skipped event.** A friend wants them to skip your event to help someone else. The someone else is in a real bind. Your event is one you have been looking forward to, and you would feel the absence. What do they do?

**G4. The shortchange.** They see a stranger shortchanged by a large amount. The stranger has not noticed. The line behind them is long, and speaking up will make a scene. What do they do?

**G5. The taken credit.** In a meeting, a coworker presents an idea that was your partner's, and the room praises the coworker. Correcting the record embarrasses everyone. Letting it go costs them the credit. What do they do before the meeting ends?

**G6. The hallway fifty.** They find a fifty that clearly fell from a neighbor's pocket. The neighbor is proud, short on money, and would hate to be seen as careless. Returning it in public and sliding it under the door are different acts. What do they do?

**G7. The grieving untruth.** A relative on the phone asks them to agree with a claim they think is false. The relative is grieving, and the claim is how the relative is making sense of the week. The claim is untrue and not dangerous. What do they say on that call?

**G8. The early table.** At a community sale they can have early access because they know the organizer. The advantage is small, legal, and slightly sneaky. Using it means a nicer thing in the house and a worse story if anyone asks how they got it. What do they do?

Close the night by reading the missed-value lines aloud, or by putting them in the journal and saying nothing clever. Thank the person who corrected you. Stop at three scenarios even if the bank is tempting. The gray one does not need a verdict. You were practicing the borrow, not sentencing anyone.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**20 minutes.** One scenario, both of you writing. Skip the score. Read the missed value and stop. The funny list is the kindest single draw. One scenario is a finished session.

**40 minutes.** One realistic, one funny, one gray, in that order, unless you are too tired for gray and you say so. Both people write every time. Optional scoring. Timer on, so the third scenario still happens as a conversation and not as a rush. If you pass 40 minutes after two, save the gray card.

**70 minutes.** The same three, with a slower reveal. After each actual answer, the borrower may try one second borrow: rewrite the three beats now that they have heard the correction, and read the new slip. The second borrow is practice. It does not erase the first score, and it does not have to be scored at all. Still cap the night at three scenarios.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later night, take one scenario you both found slippery and ask only the constraint question: "What practical fact about your life did I leave out?" Constraints are often where love of accuracy actually lives. The value can be shared and the wall can still be private.

You may invent one scenario from your real week with the names removed, if both of you agree it is cold enough to play. A live fight is not a card. If either of you feels the heat, the card goes back in the drawer and you talk as yourselves, outside the game, or you do not talk about it tonight.

A deeper gray card, only if you both want it, can be one you write about loyalty to a friend and loyalty to each other where nobody is in danger and nobody is being lied to about sex. Keep G1's scale. Small, non-dangerous, and still uncomfortable.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Low energy: one funny scenario, spoken instead of written, with the three beats still named. The writing rule bends. The silence-before-reveal rule stays, so jot a word on a scrap even if the rest is talk.

Long-distance: private notes, then a call for the reveal. The bank travels.

Accessibility: read the card aloud, allow extra time, skip any scenario that assumes a body, a job, or a family shape you do not have. Large print. No humiliation of a culture or a body, including in the funny list. F8 is about a bench that was art. If museums are a sore subject, draw again.

Replay until the bank thins, then write four new cards using the four-line replacement rule. Retire any card that produced a flinch you do not want to repeat. House rule worth keeping: the choice column stays unscored.

[082](082), The Moral Gray Area, is a conversation about dilemmas with no obvious right answer. The gray list here is fuel for a borrow, and then a correction. Leave the chapters different.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

They draw R4, the wallet. Rowan, writing as Vale, chooses "turn it in the same day," fears that Vale is managing a reputation and dreads being seen as a thief, and names the ID as a constraint because a lost-and-found exists.
