experiences.title: The Intimacy Negotiators

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Spend exactly 100 imaginary points so an evening can be built from overlap, limits included.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You each receive exactly 100 points and a blank evening. The points make appetite visible, including the zeros and the categories you would rather rename. They expire when you stand up. They are a toy for seeing what you feel like spending. They are not a bill, a debt, an entitlement, or consent.

The evening is the real object. You design one that both of you can picture, from wishes that survived the cross-outs, with every piece still free to be declined when the night actually arrives. A chart with no evening abandons the chapter. An evening that overrides a limit because a number was higher abandons it too.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A fixed sum forces a preference into the open. You cannot give every form of closeness a perfect score. That would teach you nothing. What you spend, what you leave at zero, and what you leave unspent are three different sentences. Being shown someone's spending is different from being praised, and different from being assigned their evening.

People sometimes want a chart like this to prove a single main way of loving, sorted into exactly five types, with matching as the thing that makes a relationship work. A review of that popular claim found little support for one primary language, for exactly five, or for matching as what predicts satisfaction. A range of affectionate behavior seems to matter instead. See I2024 in the notes. This sheet will not sort you into a type. A balanced chart is not healthier than a lopsided one. Two charts that fail to match are a conversation, not a diagnosis.

Wanted affectionate touch has its own literature, a review and a model, not a trial of point allocation. See J2017. Unwanted touch sits outside that claim. A high number beside any form of touch does not create a duty or a permission. A game result is not consent to touch or to sex. A change of mind after the chart is shared outranks the chart. A headache outranks the chart. A zero outranks a speech about the zero.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
You need two copies of `journal/templates/hundred-points.md`, or a careful handwritten twin with the same number of rows and the same spacing. Baselines are at least 0.32 inch apart. Both columns have eight rows. Leave a row blank if you want. Put a form on a private copy if you do not want it on the shared page. Either person may refuse the whole exercise. Refusal finishes the chapter.

Sit apart for the first pass, even if apart is two ends of the same table with the papers angled away. No commentary while the numbers are being placed. Phones down. The evening you design has to have a version that is low-pain, low-cost, and at home. Sex and adventure are ordinary things to cross out. Long-distance, the evening may be a call plus a solitary pleasure each person actually wants. No one has to disclose why a category is zero.

Say these once:

You have exactly 100 points. Every point goes on a form or sits in the remainder. Forms plus remainder equal 100. You do not exceed 100.
Integers. Zeros allowed. A zero describes this season or this evening. It is not a permanent identity.
Points never outvote a limit.
Crossing out is unilateral and sufficient. A reason is optional.
You will not average the charts. The larger number is not the winner.
Renaming a category in order to dissolve the other person's no is a foul. Restore the no.

[034](034), The Yes, No, Maybe Game, is a different list. A no recorded there still governs here. The chapters stay unmerged.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
**The default menu, which you may change.** Affection, romance, playfulness, meaningful conversation, sensuality, adventure, closeness, quiet, spontaneity, privacy. That is ten names for a sheet with eight rows. You choose what to write down. You may rename up to three. If you both want the distinction, split sensuality so sexual closeness has its own name, and drop a row you are leaving at zero or add a line at the same spacing. Privacy may be renamed solitude when you mean kindly separate time. Words you may ignore, from the sheet itself: a long talk, a walk, cooking, sitting quietly, playful nonsense, affectionate touch. Use them, replace them, or leave them off.

If you want a wholly different menu, agree the new names before you score, or let each person name their own eight and spend the comparison on what the words were doing. You are not required to share a vocabulary. You are required to hear a limit.

**Filling the sheet.** Alone, place the points. The sum line reads 100, or less if you left some unspent. Unspent is a choice. Write the remainder so the arithmetic is honest: the points you were given are still exactly 100.

Read your own chart aloud. The listener asks one curious question per category they do not understand, and then stops. The listener does not say what the other person should have scored.

**Circles and crosses.** On your own chart, circle up to three forms you would enjoy tonight. Cross out any that are off the table. A zero may be crossed out or simply left. Crossing out needs no explanation. A form you do not want named on the shared page can live on the private copy, and the cross-out can be spoken as "that one is off the table" without the name, if that is the privacy you need. If the designer of the evening cannot see the limit, say the limit in whatever words you can stand. A hidden no that gets planned over has not been honored.

**The menu.** Lay the charts side by side. Any form either person crossed out leaves the menu, even if the other person scored it high and circled it. What remains is available. Offers are volunteered. A circle is an invitation to consider. It is not a claim. From that menu, design one evening both of you can picture. Write the shape on the sheet, including rest, food, talk, or an early night. Name one thing you are willing to drop without argument.

If every circled form was crossed out by the other person, or every offer is declined, the result is parallel quiet or a rain check. That completes the chapter. Parallel quiet means you share a place, or a call, without turning the hour into a project. A rain check means you do not schedule the crossed-out forms as a debt.

**The evening rule, in one breath.** Use only forms nobody crossed out. Build from volunteered offers. Include a version that fits the rooms, the money, and the bodies you have tonight. Every piece can be declined in the moment. The points expire at the end of the conversation. Tomorrow's want can be different, and it does not owe this sheet an explanation.

**Worksheet logic, field by field.** The sheet is `journal/templates/hundred-points.md`, activity 106.

Date and attempt at the top.

Partner A, "my 100," eight rows: a form, then points. Then a sum, 100 or less if some were left unspent.

Partner B, the same eight rows, the same spacing, the same size of sum. Equal lines. Neither column is a correction of the other.

"The evening we actually want to try" is eight writing lines. Every piece optional. Write the shape, including rest, food, talk, or an early night.

The last line is what you are willing to drop without argument.

A private copy follows the same logic if a form should stay off the shared page. The shared evening still has to respect a cross-out that was spoken.

Close by reading the evening aloud once. Each person says "yes, with these pieces" or "rain check" or "parallel quiet." A yes to the shape is still not a yes to every gesture inside it when the hour comes.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**30 minutes.** Fill the sheets, read them, cross out, and write a one-sentence evening or an honest rain check. Skip the curious questions except where a word is genuinely opaque. A short page is a finished negotiation.

**45 minutes.** The full pass: private scoring, one question per unclear form, circles, crosses, and an evening written in enough detail that you could start it tonight. Include the thing you will drop without argument.

**60 minutes.** Add a second look after the evening is drafted. Each person may move up to 10 points on their own sheet, once, in light of what they heard, without erasing a zero they meant. Then check the evening again. A moved point does not reopen a cross-out. If the second look turns into lobbying, return to the first sheets and keep the first evening.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On another night, spend the 100 points on a different horizon: a month, or a season, rather than tonight. Keep the same rule. The number is information. The plan, if you make one, still cannot spend a no.

You may each add one form the default menu missed, in your own words, and give it points by taking them from somewhere else. The new form can be crossed out by the other person. Invention does not smuggle a demand.

If the overlap is rich and you are both glad, you may sketch a second evening and then choose one. Two sketches are play. Neither sketch is owed.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Low energy: the evening is soup, a shared silence, and an early night, if those forms survived. If they did not, parallel quiet is the variation, and it counts.

Low pain: stay horizontal, shorten the talk, drop anything that asks for stamina. Adventure and sexual closeness are easy to cross out, and a high score beside them stays on the paper.

Long-distance: design the call, its length, and one solitary pleasure each of you actually wants during the same evening. The solitary pleasure can be privacy or quiet. It can also be crossed out if separate time is the wrong gift tonight.

Budget: the home version is the default. If a form seems to require tickets, write the version that happens in the kitchen.

Replay when the season changes, or when a zero moves. Date the sheet. Old points expire. They are not a constitution. [025](025), What Loving Me Actually Looks Like, names behaviors that land as love. [040](040), The Intimacy Blueprint, maps conditions. This chapter spends a toy sum and then builds one evening inside the limits.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan spends exactly 100: affection 15, romance 10, playfulness 20, meaningful conversation 15, sensuality 0, adventure 0, closeness 10, quiet 30. Rowan renames closeness, on the sheet, to "being in the same room without a job."

Vale spends exactly 100: affection 10, romance 20, playfulness 15, meaningful conversation 5, sensuality 20, adventure 15, quiet 5, privacy 10. Vale renames privacy to "an hour with the door closed."

Rowan asks one question: "Door closed means the apartment, or a room?" Vale says, "A room. The apartment can stay alive." Vale does not tell Rowan to move the 30 on quiet. Rowan does not tell Vale that 15 on adventure is too many.

Rowan circles quiet, playfulness, and meaningful conversation, and crosses out adventure and sensuality. Vale circles romance, playfulness, and sensuality, and crosses out nothing. Sensuality and adventure leave the menu because Rowan crossed them out. Vale's 20 and Vale's 15 do not buy them back.

The evening they write: cook side by side, which they are both willing to call playfulness; 20 minutes of one real conversation; then Rowan reads in the room while Vale does a crossword, which Rowan calls quiet and Vale can live with. Vale offers to switch on the lamp Rowan likes. Rowan accepts the lamp and declines anything further. Early night. They are willing to drop the crossword without argument if the conversation runs long.

On another fictional night the circles fail to overlap. Vale has circled only sensuality and adventure, and Rowan has crossed both out. Neither person volunteers a remaining form. They call a rain check, sit in the same room with separate books, and the chapter is complete. The points are not collected later as a debt.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
What did your own zeros say that a speech would have padded?
Where did you want the larger number to win, and did you let the cross-out stand?
What did you design that both of you can picture, including the piece you can drop?
Did the evening ask for a body, a budget, or a bravery you do not have tonight? Rewrite that piece before you start.
What expires with the conversation, on purpose?

You do not owe each other the evening you designed. You can start it, change it, or let it become quiet.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the attempt. Note whether you designed an evening, called a rain check, or sat in parallel quiet. The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The hundred-points sheet is the working copy. These prompts are the record. Printed lines are at least eight per prompt, baselines at least 0.32 inch apart. A category, a zero, or a change of mind is a complete entry. Nothing on the page is a promise to act.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- How you spent your 100 points across forms of closeness you named, and what the totals were trying to say.
- A form you crossed out. The reason can stay off the page.
partner_b:
- How you spent yours, and which of the other forms you do not share.
- The piece of the evening you were willing to drop without argument.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- The evening you designed together. Every piece can be declined. The points are not a bill.
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- What you actually did with the evening, and whether you would spend the points differently.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Original formulation for this project: a private allocation of exactly 100 imaginary points, then an evening built only from overlap and volunteered offers, with points barred from acting as entitlements. That is a provenance note. It is not a claim of worldwide novelty, and it is not a test of desire.

See I2024. Impett, Park, and Muise (2024) review love-languages claims and find little support for one primary language, for exactly five languages, or for matching languages as what predicts satisfaction. A range of affectionate behavior appears beneficial. Cite that review against the popular sorting claim. Do not cite it as praise for matching. This worksheet is not five love languages.

See J2017. Jakubiak and Feeney (2017) offer a theoretical model and review of wanted affectionate touch and well-being. It is not a trial of point allocation. Unwanted touch sits outside the claim. A high score in a touch category creates neither a study, a duty, nor a permission.

Pie charts of needs are a practitioner habit. They are not a validated protocol here. The imaginary points expire at the end of the conversation. A no on [034](034) still governs. Averaging two charts into a compromise that erases a zero abandons the chapter.

experiences.title: The Memory Smuggler

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A true story with one invented detail, and that detail has to stand for a wish, a fear, or a chance you did not take.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
One true story, one symbolic seam, three guesses, then the real story and why the fiction appealed. 041, Two Truths and a Beautiful Lie, is three peer scenes and a whole fiction beside them. This chapter hides one stitch inside a day that otherwise happened.

Tell a story that is true, except for that one stitch. The listener hunts the stitch. A swapped color, a trick for its own sake, a whole invented evening: those are other games. Here the false detail has to matter to the teller. It stands in for a wish, a fear, or a possibility that did not happen. After the guess, the truth comes back, and the teller says why the fiction appealed.

The story is a suitcase with one object that does not belong. Finding the object is the play. Hearing what it was doing there is the point.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A true memory is easy to nod through when you have lived beside the person for years. One counterfeit detail wakes the listening up. The constraint makes the invention do work. If the detail is trivial, nobody would care. If it is the teller's own unfinished business, the guess becomes a way of handling something that was hard to say in a straight sentence.

The mechanism is the order. Fiction first, inside an otherwise true story. Then the true version, put back on the table in full. Then the kind of symbol: wish, fear, or unrealized possibility. Then why that fiction appealed. Until the truth is restored, the symbol is just another story you might both start living in. The listener does not grade the symbolism. The teller names it.

This was formulated for this project. It is not a claim of worldwide novelty. It does not improve memory, test honesty, or measure whether a partner is gullible. "Two truths and a lie" is a folk game. This is a cousin with a stricter suitcase.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Each person prepares one memory they are willing to have examined. The true version should already be safe to tell. If the only story you want to smuggle through is a crisis, choose another story, or step out of the game and talk as yourselves.

Fair-play rules:

Exactly one invented detail. Everything else is true as you believe it.
The invention belongs to your inner world. It is not a false motive pasted onto your partner.
The listener gets three guesses. Then you reveal, even if nobody has caught it.
You must be able to point at the detail without rewriting the story a second time.
After the reveal: the true version, the kind of symbol, and why the fiction appealed.

Some inventions are too costly to drop as a twist, even as symbols. Leave these out: infidelity, pregnancy, illness, hidden money, violence, or any harm. A packed bag by the door can stand for a feared outcome, and it belongs here only if both of you can hold that image. If you cannot, choose a smaller fear. A ticket you wish you had bought is plenty.

Either person may discard a prepared story. The listener may decline to guess and still hear the reveal. No reenactment. You are talking, or reading.

You may pass, pause, or trade a heavy symbol for a lighter one before you begin. Once the story is underway, the single-detail rule still holds. Adding a second fiction to make the first one kinder is a different story. Stop and choose a new memory instead.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
The teller takes a minute in silence to fix the true story and the one seam. Optional: write the invented detail on a slip and sit on it, so you do not accidentally smuggle two.

Tell the story in 3 or 4 minutes. Include ordinary freight: weather, a sentence someone said, what you did with your hands. Hide the seam in the plot, not in a color only one of you can picture. The symbol should be something a listener can suspect from how the events turn.

The listener listens for the load-bearing oddity. What changed the ending, the courage, the risk, the decision? They get three guesses, said as claims. "The word stay is the invention." "The coffee is the invention." "The laugh is the invention." The teller says only yes, no, or "not that," until the third guess is spent. Then the teller reveals, caught or not.

Three beats after the reveal, in this order:

The true version, told cleanly, with the seam removed.
Which kind of symbol it was: a wish, a fear, or an unrealized possibility.
Why the fiction appealed. One or two sentences. Often it appealed because it rehearsed a courage, or gave a fear a shape small enough to show, or let a decision feel finished.

The listener may say which guess they were proud of, and whether the symbol matched what they felt in the room. They do not score the metaphor. "I thought it was a wish, and you say it was a fear" is information, not a miss that needs repair.

Switch. One story each is the session. A third story turns the symbols into a stack.

A worked example, original to this chapter. True memory: a rainy train platform, years ago, leaving a city after a short job. You said goodbye to a friend and watched the doors close. Smuggled detail: you said "stay," they laughed, and they missed the train. Kind: unrealized possibility. True version restored: you said goodbye. The fiction appealed because it rehearsed a courage you still want in smaller rooms. You are not asking anyone, including your partner, to miss a train.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**20 minutes.** One story only, from whoever wants to tell. Three guesses, the reveal, the three beats. The other person may tell theirs on another night. One suitcase is a finished game.

**30 minutes.** One story each. Keep the telling under 4 minutes so the guesses have something to grip. Leave a minute after each reveal before you switch, so the true version actually lands.

**40 minutes.** Both stories, plus a slower second pass on one symbol: say the wish, fear, or possibility once more in ordinary language, with no scene around it. "I still want to be able to ask someone to stay in a conversation." The extra time is for that plain sentence. It is not a license to add details you withheld.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
If the plain sentence is more interesting than the story, stay with the sentence. Ask, only if the teller invites it, whether any inch of that wish or fear is available this month without heroics. An unrealized possibility can remain unrealized. Naming it was the work.

On a replay, choose a different kind of symbol from last time. If you smuggled a wish, smuggle a smaller fear, or the reverse. The repetition to avoid is the same confession in a series of costumes.

Do not use a later dinner to re-hide the detail and see if they catch it now. Once revealed, the seam stays revealed. The true story is the one you are keeping.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
The story can be read aloud from a page. Guesses can be written. Distance works: tell, three guesses in the chat, then the reveal. Skip a story that requires the listener to picture a sensation they cannot access. Put the symbol in the plot.

If speech is tiring, the slip of paper with the invented detail can be shown after the three guesses instead of described. The true version still has to be said or read.

The motif is a packed case with one object that does not match the rest. You do not have to draw the object, and you do not have to leave the fiction in the journal. The prompt allows the detail to stay hidden on the page. The wish, fear, or possibility can be named without the costume.

041, Two Truths and a Beautiful Lie, tells two true personal stories and one convincing fiction, and the fiction is an entire story. Here the story is true except for one load-bearing detail, and the detail is a symbol. 083, The Secret Nobody Would Guess, volunteers a surprising truth, and nothing is planted. 080, The Day Worth Reliving, reconstructs a shared day you would want back. A smuggled memory can be old and private. It does not have to be a day you shared.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan tells a rainy platform. They were leaving a city after a short job. A friend was there. Vale was not in this story, and Rowan does not put Vale on the platform. In the telling, Rowan says "stay," the friend laughs, the friend misses the train, and they drink bad coffee until the next one.

Vale's guesses: the brand of coffee, the laugh, the word "stay." The third guess hits. Rowan still does the three beats, because a catch is not the end. True version: Rowan said goodbye and watched the doors close. Kind: unrealized possibility. Why it appealed: it rehearsed a courage Rowan still wants in smaller rooms, including conversations in this kitchen. Rowan is not asking Vale to miss a train, or to play the friend.

Vale's story is quieter. A true, calm conversation about a weekend plan, at the table, with the tabs still open. Smuggled detail: Vale says the tickets were already bought. Rowan guesses the restaurant, the day of the week, then the tickets. Reveal: Vale had only looked. Kind: wish. The fiction appealed because a finished decision felt easier than an open tab. Vale says the wish in ordinary language: "I want us to pick the weekend instead of orbiting it." Rowan does not grade the metaphor, and does not go buy the tickets as a prize for listening. If they book something, that happens later, in a real conversation.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Put the true stories back in the room before you get up.

What was the one invented detail, if you want it spoken again?
Was it a wish, a fear, or an unrealized possibility?
Why did that fiction appeal, in a sentence you could say without the story?
Did the listener's guess match the symbol, and does the mismatch need anything besides being noted?
Is the true version the one you are both keeping?

You do not owe each other the smuggled ending. You owe the truth back, and you may keep the want in plainer words.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The invented detail may stay off the page. Write that one detail was smuggled, and name the wish, fear, or possibility, if that is the part you want to reread.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The true memory you told. Name the invented detail here only if you want it on paper. Otherwise write that one detail was smuggled, and the wish, fear, or possibility it carried.
- Why the fiction appealed, in a sentence you are willing to reread.
partner_b:
- As the listener, the detail you flagged, why you flagged it, and whether the symbol matched what was meant.
- The true story as you heard it once the invention was lifted out.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- The true story you are keeping, and the unrealized possibility you can name without pretending it happened
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- Has that smuggled wish become easier to say in ordinary language?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: No research citation is claimed. "Two truths and a lie" is a folk detection game, and detection games are not a validated intimacy protocol. Chapter 041 tells two true stories and one entire fiction. This chapter keeps one true memory and one invented detail, and that detail symbolizes a wish, a fear, or an unrealized possibility. Formulated for this project. That is a provenance note, not a claim of worldwide novelty, and not a claim about memory or honesty. The true version has to be told. Forbidden inventions, even as symbols: infidelity, pregnancy, illness, hidden money, violence, or any harm. The listener does not grade the symbolism.

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: A door the other person may not have known was there, and a key they cannot demand.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You can live with someone a long time and still be handed a title you have never heard. A shop they visit alone. A job they have not described. A Sunday feeling with two weathers in it. The title is a door. It may be a door you did not know existed. That is an offer, not a tease that has to be satisfied.

You may ask for a key. You may not demand one. The person who offered the door decides which key, if any, gets handed over, and how far the sentence goes. A key already given can be put back down mid-sentence. The other person does not finish it.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Shared life builds a map, and maps go out of date quietly. New rooms appear. Old rooms get renamed. The surprise of a title you have never heard is already a kind of news. News is not a debt. If every unknown door had to be opened because love was in the room, privacy would be a failure. It is a successful outcome of this hour.

The mechanism is revocable depth. The partner may ask. The sharer chooses the key, refuses the key, or ends the tour. Asking by name, Brass or Glass or nothing, gives the request a shape, so "tell me everything" has somewhere specific to land and somewhere specific to be declined. A listener who can tolerate a closed door stays interested. The rest is not owed.

This hour was formulated for this project. That is not a claim of worldwide novelty. Leave therapy, shadow work, and trauma-method language off it. A door offered once may be declined the next time. Love does not mean every door eventually opens.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Each person prepares up to four doors. The front of a card shows a title only. The back stays blank, or holds notes only the sharer will see. Themes you might use: a cherished memory, a fear, an unrealized ambition, a private desire, a paradox, or something hard to explain. Include at least one lighter door if the others are heavy. A stack of only the hardest rooms wears the evening out.

Titles can be new to your partner. That is the twist, and it is allowed to remain a title.

Optional physical cards. No dark room, and no locked physical space. The door is verbal. If symbolic play feels silly or wrong, use the word "topic" instead of "door" and "level" instead of "key." The control rule does not change.

Keys the sharer may offer or refuse:

Brass. The facts of what happened.
Glass. How it felt.
Iron. What it costs to say more.
Ribbon. What I hope you do with this, which can be "nothing."
Blank. The door exists, and the tour stops.

Three agreements:

The partner may request a key by name. Silence, and "not that key," are complete answers.
A demanded key ends the round. Wheedling after a refusal ends it too.
No one earns access by being a good partner. You do not unlock a room as payment for listening well.

Sexual doors require a prior willingness to have that kind of conversation at all. A key is not consent to touch or sex. Desires and fears can be named at Brass and stopped there. A Ribbon key is a hope, not a contract.

Ongoing danger, abuse, or a crisis is not game content. Those need a direct conversation, and outside help when someone is unsafe.

You may pass, pause, or put a card away before it is read. Stop on fatigue.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Trade stacks, or keep your own cards and read titles one at a time. The sharer reads a title. They may add, "This is a door you have not heard of," or they may let the newness be obvious. They do not apologize for the newness, and they do not promise a tour.

The partner may request one key by name. "Brass, if you're offering." "Glass?" "Ribbon, and I can hear 'nothing.'" The sharer answers with the key, with "not that key," or with silence. If they offer it, they speak only as far as that key goes.

Brass sounds like facts. "A shop on 4th. I go alone. About 20 minutes. I buy nothing."
Glass sounds like weather inside the facts. "I like the paper smell. I don't want to explain my week."
Iron sounds like the price of continuing. "Saying the next part would wreck the afternoon, so I am stopping."
Ribbon sounds like a hope with the contract taken out. "Enjoy knowing the shop exists. Don't suggest we go. That is a hope, not a rule."
Blank sounds like a title and a stop. "The door is real. The tour is over."

A key already offered can be set down mid-sentence. The partner does not supply the ending, the diagnosis, or the clever interpretation. Clinical language stays outside. If you hear yourself explaining what the room "really means," you have left the game. Return the sentence to its owner.

Then the next door, alternating, until you have each shown the titles you meant to show. You do not have to offer a key for every title. Two doors and one key, total, is a complete short path.

Debrief, short, and not a second attempt on a refused key:

Which door surprised you by existing?
Which closed door can you respect with no story attached?
Is there anything that needs a conversation outside the game?

The partner does not keep notes on a closed door. Journal titles only, unless the sharer wants a sentence kept. A blank key is not a puzzle to solve later.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**30 minutes.** Two doors each. One key offered somewhere in the round, or none, if that is the true offer. Read the debrief questions and stop. Use this when four doors would become a confession marathon.

**50 minutes.** Up to four doors each, titles first, keys by request. Time for at least one refusal to stand without a follow-up question. This is the version that lets a new door be news and lets an old door stay locked in the same evening.

**75 minutes.** The standard round, with a few extra minutes of quiet before the debrief so each person can decide what, if anything, belongs on paper. The extra time is for choice. It is not a second pass at a key that was refused. If you are tired at 50 minutes, the 50-minute version was the right one. Stop.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
On a later day, you may return to a door that was offered at Brass and ask whether Glass is available now. The answer can be no. A no this week does not cancel a yes from last month, and a yes last month does not create a standing ticket.

You can label a door more clearly without opening it. "The paradox about Sundays" can become "Sundays, still a paradox," and the tour can remain Blank. Better labeled is a real change.

If the debrief surfaced something that needs a conversation outside the game, schedule that conversation in ordinary language. Do not smuggle it back in as a bonus key.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
By video, each person holds their own cards, backs unseen. By voice, titles are spoken. Cards can be large print. Seated the whole time.

People who want no metaphor still use the list: topic, then the level they are willing to give, facts, feeling, cost, hope, or stop. Write the five level names on a card if the metal and ribbon are in the way.

The motif is a door and several keys, one of them blank, none of them in the other person's hand.

Replay when a new room becomes nameable, or when an old title needs a more careful lock. Date the titles you are willing to keep. A door that was open in one sitting may be declined in the next, and the journal should be allowed to show that without apology.

013, Confession Without Consequence, offers one chosen embarrassment, regret, insecurity, or harmless private truth for curious listening. The frame is receptive listening. It is not immunity for harmful behavior. This chapter is a tour of several possible rooms, with a pass on any door, and it can include a door the other person did not know was there. 011, What I Don’t Show the World, describes parts you hide and what would make them safer to reveal. 081, The Forbidden Question Box, lets either of you pass on a drawn question. Here the sharer controls the keys for the whole round, including doors they themselves opened.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Fictional. Rowan and Vale are an illustration, not a portrait of you.

Rowan lays down four titles: "The map store on 4th," "The version of my job I have not said out loud," "A fear with a boring name," "Something I want that I have not scheduled." Vale has never heard of the map store. That is the news.

Vale asks for Brass. Rowan gives facts. A shop, 20 minutes, alone, nothing purchased, the smell of paper. Vale asks for Glass. Rowan says, "Not that key." Vale asks for Ribbon. Rowan says, "Nothing. Enjoy knowing the shop exists. Don't suggest we go." The job door gets Blank. Vale does not guess the job. The fear gets Brass only: "I get sharp about being late, and the sharpness is embarrassment, not a verdict on you." Iron is refused. The unscheduled want stays a title.

Vale's door: "The paradox about Sundays." Vale offers Glass without a full Brass tour. "Sundays feel like a gift and like a clock. I don't want to explain the week that made them that way tonight." Rowan asks for Iron. "Not that key." Ribbon: "If you make a plan on Sunday morning, ask first. That is a hope, not a rule I am installing." A second Vale title is read and then given Blank. Rowan does not fish.

In the debrief, the map store is the door that surprised Vale by existing. The blank job title is the closed door Vale can respect with no story. Nothing needs a meeting outside the game. Rowan does not write Vale's closed title in a notebook. Vale writes "map store" only because Rowan said the title could be kept.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
The debrief above is the whole ending. If you want one more pass, use these, and then leave the keys alone:

Which title was news?
Which refusal are you willing to leave intact?
Did anyone start to earn a key by being good, patient, or hurt? If yes, put that key back.
Is a Ribbon hope being mistaken for a contract?
Do you need a conversation that is not a game?

You do not owe each other the house. A title, a refusal, and a thank-you are a complete visit.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Date the session. Note the version, the place, and whether you finished or paused. Initials and mood are optional.

The two personal pages are yours. Share them, keep them, or leave them blank. Unread is a complete way to use them. The key-holder decides the depth, including on the page. A lock that stays locked is a finished choice. Do not keep notes on a door the other person closed.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The door you offered, the key you were willing to give, and how far you wanted the exploration to go. All three stay in your control.
- A title you are willing to keep on paper. Leave the room behind the title blank if you want.
partner_b:
- The door you offered from your inner life, with the same control. A lock that stays locked is a finished choice.
- Which key you gave, which you refused, and the fact that a refusal needs no sequel.
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- Which doors you opened together, and which keys were declined with the decline left intact
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
- Is a given door more open, more carefully locked, or simply better labeled?
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text: Formulated for this project: imaginary doors, keys the sharer can offer or refuse, and the chance that a door exists which the other person did not know about. Nobody can demand a key. A demanded door ends the round. That is a provenance note, not a claim of worldwide novelty. See L1998. In diary studies, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. L1998 did not test key rituals or closed doors, and disclosure is not owed. Privacy is a successful outcome. Leave therapy, shadow work, and trauma-method language off this hour. Ongoing danger is not content for the game.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 30 minutes · Standard 50 minutes · Extended 75 minutes

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Set questions down a table so they grow more personal with distance, and leave the last card face down unless both of you choose to turn it.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
A long table wants a banquet and an audience. Disappoint it. Two chairs sit at the near end, turned a little toward each other, and the cards run the other way. The near questions are light enough to answer while a kettle boils. They grow more personal with distance. The last card lies face down.

Twelve questions sit in three stretches: near, middle, and far. You play them in order. Each person gets half the time on a card, and a follow-up waits for a spoken yes. Far 4 stays face down until both of you say yes. Either of you may leave the table at any card. Leaving ends the escalation, and the night still counts as finished. If either person says no to the last card, it stays down, and the evening is already complete.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
A shared dialect is intimate, and it retires questions. The retired one is often the question that would show a region praise does not reach. Being accurately imagined feels different from being told you are easy to know.

John Gottman's clinical writing uses love maps for a partner's inner world and bids for the reaches people make toward each other. A card is a bid in that picture (see GOTTMAN). Neither metaphor grades a pass or predicts your future.

See L1998 in the notes for diary studies of disclosure and perceived partner responsiveness. Those diaries did not test this table. In Study 1, a roughly 45-minute pair of escalating self-disclosure and relationship-building tasks produced greater post-interaction closeness than a small-talk comparison among people who had just met (see A1997). This table is a different procedure, and it does not use that question list. The study was not a recipe for couples falling in love. Arriving at the far end earns nothing.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Any table works. Distance is the order of the cards. Sit together at the near end with place cards or blank cards, a pen, and a timer you can both see. A phone may keep time if notifications are quiet. If you have lamps, set the brighter one near you and let another go lower toward the far end. Ordinary room light is complete. Darkness is not required. Raise the lamp if the ink is hard to read.

No guests. Use a room with a door when the house is busy. Do not send one person to sit at the far end alone. Eat first if you are hungry. A drink may stay. A served meal makes one of you staff, and that is a different evening.

Name closed subjects before you copy a card. They stay closed, clever rewording included. You may mention an absent person with care. You may not build a case they cannot answer. End the card if an answer turns into that case. A pass needs no substitute confession: no smaller story, no reason, and no replacement question.

Touch is not part of this session. A question answered is not consent to touch or sex, and neither is a laugh, a tear, or a long look. A request for a hand belongs to another night. No is a complete answer there.

Say which version you are playing. If either of you is too altered for a clean no, end before the first card. That night still counts. Writing is a full answer. Stay seated if movement hurts, and let the cards come to you. On a call, cameras stay optional. Each of you keeps the same order.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Copy the cards before you sit, or the short version disappears into handwriting. Use index cards, about 3 by 5 inches, or quarter-sheets, with the zone and number in the upper left and about half an inch of margin. They mark questions, not seats. Near cards sit closest to you, middle cards farther off, and Far 1 through Far 3 farther still, face up. Far 4 lies face down at the far place: the number on the back, the question on the front. Three stacks suit a short table. A desk counts.

These questions are printed, so Far 4 may already be known. Knowing the words is not a yes. For an unseen wording, use the substitute in Variations, and do not read that last question until both of you have said yes. There is no score. Share each card, answer or pass, then move. A tame card stays where it is. The ritual is that order, the question "Do we turn it?" and a spoken end.

**Near.** A detail is enough.

Near 1. What trivial rule of your own household, real or imagined, would you enforce with a straight face?

Near 2. What skill did you pick up because the alternative was waiting, and what do you use it for now?

Near 3. Which pleasure in your week is so ordinary you have stopped calling it a pleasure?

Near 4. When something small goes right, what do you do with the pleasure if you are unlikely to make a speech about it?

**Middle.** A live fact, still ordinary enough for a kitchen.

Middle 1. What are you getting better at when nobody is grading it, and do you want that skill to stay unofficial?

Middle 2. Which of your good habits has begun to boss the rest of your life around?

Middle 3. What do you shorten when you tell the story of a hard year, and what does the shorter story protect?

Middle 4. Where do you want me near you, and where does nearness start to crowd the thing you are doing?

**Far.** Ask these because either of you can stop. Far 1 is an impression you allowed, not a list of flaws. End it if it becomes a bill of complaints. Far 2 is not a standard for the listener to repeal tonight. Far 3 asks to be heard. Calming it was not offered. Far 4 is the face-down card.

Far 1. What have you let me misunderstand because the correction felt like more work than the misunderstanding?

Far 2. What standard are you using on yourself this season that you would argue me out of if I used it on you?

Far 3. What do you want me to know about a fear without also taking the job of calming it?

Far 4, placed face down. What do you want this bond to make room for that your competence does not need, and what do you want it to leave alone?

```cards
Near | What trivial rule of your own household, real or imagined, would you enforce with a straight face?
Near | What skill did you pick up because the alternative was waiting, and what do you use it for now?
Near | Which pleasure in your week is so ordinary you have stopped calling it a pleasure?
Near | When something small goes right, what do you do with the pleasure if you are unlikely to make a speech about it?
Middle | What are you getting better at when nobody is grading it, and do you want that skill to stay unofficial?
Middle | Which of your good habits has begun to boss the rest of your life around?
Middle | What do you shorten when you tell the story of a hard year, and what does the shorter story protect?
Middle | Where do you want me near you, and where does nearness start to crowd the thing you are doing?
Far | What have you let me misunderstand because the correction felt like more work than the misunderstanding?
Far | What standard are you using on yourself this season that you would argue me out of if I used it on you?
Far | What do you want me to know about a fear without also taking the job of calming it?
Far | What do you want this bond to make room for that your competence does not need, and what do you want it to leave alone?
```

Copy in that order, and leave the last line face down.

The person who did not copy answers first. If you both copied, or neither did, use a coin, then the earlier birthday in the calendar year, then whoever woke earlier. Alternate after every card. A pass does not change the rotation. The person who answers second reads the card once, and does not pick up Far 4 until both of you have said yes.

Each half of the clock belongs to one speaker. Times are below. Silence in a half belongs to the speaker. The listener does not advise, diagnose, or take the half over with a matching story. Four sentences can finish a near card.

One follow-up fits inside the speaker's half, and only after the word yes to "May I ask one follow-up?" It has to use a detail they actually said. Advice, or a story of your own, ends the privilege. When the half ends, finish the sentence. Spare time stays spare. You may add 5 minutes once, split evenly, if both of you agree.

"Pass" ends your half and needs no substitute confession. The other half still belongs to the other person. They do not answer for you. "That's enough of this one" closes the card for both of you, even mid-sentence. The fragment is not an opening.

"I'm leaving the table" ends the escalation before the first card, during a card, or between cards, even while the other person is speaking. They stop and do not owe the rest. The night is finished. Leftover cards, including Far 4, stay unread. Nobody plays them alone or charges a summary for the exit. If one of you says leave and the other hoped for a pause, the leave stands. "Pause" only freezes the row. Starting again needs a fresh yes from both of you at the next unplayed card, and it carries no yes for the far end.

You reach Far 4 only after each earlier card in your version has been answered, passed, or closed, in order. Leaving does not deliver you there. Ask, "Do we turn it?" Both of you have to say the word yes. Silence, a shrug, and "if you want" do not count. If either person says no, the card stays down, and the evening is already complete. Do not swap in another question, read the first line, or turn it later that night because the mood improved. Another day needs a new yes. The person who said no does not owe it.

If you disagree about keeping an unturned card, put a printed question away without discussing an answer. Tear up an unread substitute. If you both want to keep it, use an envelope, write the date on the outside, and write no hint.

Two yeses mean you turn the card and play it under the same rules. Hearing it counts, even if you then pass. You may not turn it and pretend the turn did not happen. There is no card after it. An answer at this end of the table is still not consent to touch or sex.

You are done when the cards in your version are finished and Far 4, if it was set, has been played or left down; or when either of you has left; or when either of you has refused Far 4; or when the clock ends. Finish the sentence you are in. Do not sprint the far cards. If you reach Far 4 with less than 10 minutes left, it stays down. Say, "The night is complete."

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
The short version takes about 45 minutes. Set Near 1 through Near 4 only, and say, "The far place is not set." Use about 5 minutes to lay the cards, 8 minutes for each card (4 minutes each), and about 8 minutes to sit before you get up. If the clock ends mid-sentence, finish the sentence. Do not promote a middle card into a leftover minute. Ending at the near end is a finished night.

The standard version takes about two hours. Play the four near cards, the four middle cards, and Far 1 through Far 3, then ask the question at Far 4. Setup is 10 minutes. Each near card is 6 minutes, 3 minutes each. Each middle card is 10 minutes, 5 minutes each. Each of Far 1 through Far 3 is 12 minutes, 6 minutes each. Far 4 gets 10 minutes, the decision included. If those 10 minutes are too small after you turn it, pass, or both agree in words to finish on the extended clock. One person's wish does not lengthen the night.

The extended version takes about three hours, with the same twelve cards and the same stops. Near cards stay at 6 minutes each. On every middle card, and on Far 1 through Far 3, write together for 4 minutes, then speak for 10 minutes on a middle card or 12 minutes on a far card, split evenly. Unread lines stay yours. Take a break of about 15 minutes between middle and far: tea or quiet, with the cards and touch left out of it. Leaving on the break finishes the night. If you turn Far 4, give it up to 20 minutes. Setup and landing are about 10 minutes each. If you skip the writing, end in the quiet instead of inventing a card.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
After a middle or far half, the listener may say, "The sentence I heard was," if the speaker wants the check. The speaker edits it, or says, "Leave it." Accuracy is the courtesy. The speaker may also mark a line "remember" or "tonight." A tonight-line stays off the shared page, and it does not come back later as ammunition. A private note can record a pass without the question.

A week later, replay one named card if both of you still want that card. Far 4 needs a new yes even if it stayed down last time. An old no is neither a ban nor a debt. Going deeper does not reopen a pass or a closed subject. If the speaker wants to replace a polite answer, they do it inside their own half. The listener does not dig.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Three stacks on a short table are a complete long table. So is this page, if you cover every line you are not playing, and keep the last far line covered until both of you say yes.

For an unseen Far 4, write one substitute before you sit: personal, answerable in a few minutes, with no request for touch or sex, and a question the writer will also answer. The other person may refuse it and keep the printed card face down. If you both write one, put them in an envelope, draw one unseen, and return the other unread. Tear up any card someone sees. If no unseen substitute is left, use the printed Far 4. Before you sit, also tear up a substitute that circles a closed subject or asks for a sexual disclosure.

On a call, one person holds Far 4 and reads it only after two spoken yeses. A bad connection is a pause. Do not finish a cut-off sentence for the other person.

Near and middle can be one night, and the far cards another. The first night is already complete. The second starts with a check, and either of you may cancel. Keep a heavy week on the short version. Morning is a fair hour. Do not save the far cards for a tired night. A tired yes is a poor yes.

New cards stay in register. Near can be answered beside a kettle. Middle asks a live fact. Far includes a limit on the listener's job, because stopping is what makes it askable. Tear up a trap. Retire a card that worked only by startling. Keep the order, the halves, the pass, the leaving, and the face-down rule. If you think on paper, write inside the shorter clock and speak two sentences. Stretching is not leaving. Say it when you mean it.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you. They are here so the rules have a shape.

They use a kitchen table and leave the ceiling light on. Rowan copies the cards, sets Far 4 face down, and admits the printed question is already known. Vale says, "Then we know the words. We still both have to say yes."

On Near 1, Vale's straight-faced rule is that leftover noodles belong to the cook, even when the cook is full. Rowan waits out an urge to spend that half on a counter-rule about forks, then offers a half-joke: shoes live by the door. They let the last minute finish.

On Middle 3, Vale says "Pass" when a shortened story about a hard year reaches a colleague who is already off the table. Rowan does not ask for another story. In Rowan's half, the shortened story of changing cities left out a good year of work and a bad habit of coming home already arguing. Vale asks, "May I ask one follow-up?" Rowan says yes. Vale asks what the arguing sounded like, then says, "The sentence I heard was: you liked the work, and the temper belonged to the trip home." Rowan edits it. "The temper belonged to being talked out. The trip was where it showed."

Rowan nearly leaves before Far 1. Vale says leaving would end the night and still count. Rowan stays for one correction: the bright question "Are you fine?" lands on days when quiet would be better. Vale does not defend it. The face-up far cards still get played. At Far 4, Vale asks, "Do we turn it?" Rowan says, "No." The card goes into a dated envelope with no hint. They wash up. They do not touch.

On another fictional night, Vale says, "I'm leaving the table," at Middle 2. The remaining cards stay unread. They make toast. That night is finished too.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
If you want words, take one sentence each: what you want kept. It is not another question. You can also wash the cups and say nothing.

If a card produced a practical decision, name it and give it a daylight hour, unless waiting would leave someone unsafe. If the night stirred you, choose quiet, a walk alone, or the same room, without touch. If Far 4 stayed down, leave it down. One accurate detail is enough to carry. The sentence they edited will outlast a portrait of who they really are.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write the date, the time, the place, which version you played, a mood if you want one, a one-line intention, and your initials if you want them. Mark the session done or paused. Partner A and Partner B are pages, not roles. Trade them if you like. Sharing either private page is optional. Keep yours aside if the shared book should hold only what you both choose. A pass can be noted without the question. A repeated sitting gets its own lines.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The card where I wanted to go farther, and the card where I was glad a stop existed
- What I now know about your privacy that I do not need to solve
partner_b:
- Where I passed, left, or kept the far card down, and what that choice was protecting
- A sentence of yours I can carry without making it my project
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: original-formulation. This session sits outside the 108 cataloged experiences. The long table, the card that stays face down unless both people agree, and the rule that leaving finishes the night are formulated for this book.

See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. Those diaries did not test this table.

See A1997. In Study 1, a roughly 45-minute pair of escalating self-disclosure and relationship-building tasks produced greater post-interaction closeness than a small-talk comparison. The participants were not a study of long-term couples falling in love. Studies 2 and 3 did not find closeness differences for attitude matching, expected liking, or making closeness an explicit goal. This table is a different procedure, and it does not use that question list.

See GOTTMAN. Love maps and bids come from John Gottman's clinical writing. They are practitioner metaphors for knowing a partner's inner world and for reaches toward connection. Neither is a test of this evening, and neither supplies a statistic this chapter may quote.

Related experiences: 001 The Stranger Across From Me, 013 Confession Without Consequence, and 056 The Questions Without Answers. The first is a timed stranger interview. The second is one harmless item under curious listening, with no immunity for harm. The third keeps a question unfinished on purpose.

metadata.duration_summary: Short 45 minutes · Standard 2 hours · Extended 3 hours

signatures.title: The Night With the Lights Low

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: One lamp, music you already own, and five slow stations where a want can be spoken and any touch can be declined.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The picture is a sitting room with nobody in it yet. One lamp. A record waiting, not playing. A throw over a chair, burgundy in the picture, any throw you actually own. Two glasses. A window that has already gone dark. You can hear a glass meet the table in a room like that. Heat can arrive when the lights change, and the door can still close.

You come in after a short list. Five stations follow: the light, music you already own, a slow pass through a few senses, a conversation that keeps a request from becoming a job, and one optional touch you named while the other lights were still on. A yes to one station is not a yes to the next. A low lamp, a finished song, a warm mood, or a candid sentence is not consent to touch or sex.

Stay dressed. Water is a complete drink. Ending after the first station still counts as the night. No bed is required. The chairs are enough.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Evenings at home often run bright and fast. Desire waits until you're tired, or it becomes a slope you're expected to finish. This night spends the time another way: one lamp, music you actually hear, sensations in sequence, and a want the other person can refuse. Familiarity files someone under "I already know how this goes." One lamp asks you to look again at a person you already like.

Wanted touch has a narrow neighbor in the research. J2017 is a review and a model. It argues that affectionate touch a person wants can relate to relational, psychological, and physical well-being, including stress-related pathways. Unwanted touch sits outside that claim. The paper is not a trial of this night. See the notes.

You may have met the claim that each person has one primary love language, that there are exactly five, and that matching them is what predicts satisfaction. The evidence does not support one primary language, exactly five languages, or matching as the predictor. See I2024. Station 4 will not sort either of you into a type. It asks you to point at one want.

One evening is the result on offer. You might like it. You might learn one true thing.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Use chairs or a sofa in a sitting room, or in a corner that can be one. If one of you needs a particular chair, the night comes to it. Nobody has to stand. If other people are home, close the door and agree on a low voice.

Set out one lamp you can see by, a throw, two glasses, and music you already own. A record is welcome. A playlist you already own is enough, cooking music included, chosen before it starts. The glasses can hold water, tea, or alcohol. Alcohol is optional. One glass can be wine and the other water. If either of you is past a clear no, pick another night.

Every physical step depends on a yes you both still mean, and either of you can decline it in the moment. While the lights are up, say the words once. "Stop" ends the station. "Not this sense" retires one sense and leaves the night going. "Pass" skips a prompt. "Pause" takes a moment. "Lights up" brings the room back and either pauses the night or ends it.

Write two lines on a card you can pocket. What is off the table: sex, a part of the body, undressing, alcohol, stories about other lovers, a kind of talk. Disagreement keeps the narrower list. "Maybe, if the mood changes" reopens a closed item, so choose off or on for the whole night. Then name the closer, or write none. A hand on a shoulder. Sitting under the same throw. Another contact of that same modest scale, through clothes, in words you both know. At station 5 you may shrink it. Anything larger needs another conversation and another yes.

The card can stay private. Retire senses that hurt or make someone ill. Scent stays out unless you both opt in. Phones can leave. If a real call might come, say which interruption still belongs to the night. Keep enough light to see a face, a glass, and the floor.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Give the standard night about 90 minutes. Keep a clock where one of you can see it, so the slowness stays chosen.

**Station 1. Arrival and the light. About 15 minutes.**

If the card is blank, write it now. The other lights stay on until both of you can say the list plainly. Read it aloud before any switch: sex if it is off, a part of the body, a story, a fight, alcohol, clothes coming off, whatever is true. Off stays off at every later station.

Then leave one lamp and turn the others off. The window can stay dark. If either of you needs more light to see or to feel steady, raise the lamp or bring one back, and say so. Sit. Pour what you chose. One sentence, or none.

Stop with "lights up," or end in the chair. Saying the list and leaving the lamps as they are is a finished arrival. So is a few quiet minutes with the record still waiting.

**Station 2. A record and listening. About 15 minutes.**

Start what you named, together: one piece, one side, or a short run you already own. That may be the record that has been waiting, or a playlist you left on pause.

Each of you names one specific thing you want the other to notice. The low note under the melody. The ice. Your hands on your own glass. An exhale at the first phrase. If you want a feeling noticed, point at the sound or gesture that carries it.

Listen, talking or quiet. Either of you may lift the needle, pause, or stop the player. A hard lyric, a wish for quiet, or boredom is enough, and the reason can stay private. Leave the music off unless the person who stopped it asks for another piece. Silence can finish the station.

Stop with the needle or with "not the music." Going on is a new yes.

**Station 3. A slow sensory pass. About 20 minutes.**

A yes to the sensory pass does not carry every sense. Offer the small things one at a time, slowly enough that a sip stays a sip.

Taste: a sip, or one bite you can both eat, allergies first. Water counts. Ask before the first sip or bite. A second bite is already a new question.

Scent: only if the card opted in, and only something you can clear. Otherwise say "no added scent." If you both opted in, ask before you bring it in. A yes on the card lets you offer it. That yes does not start the scent.

Temperature: the glass, air by the window, or a warm cup. Name which. Temperature needs its own yes before it starts. A yes to the sip is not that yes.

Fabric: the throw or a sleeve in one person's hands. Fabric needs its own yes before the cloth moves. Sharing the throw, if you named it, waits for station 5.

Each of you can stop a sense without stopping the night. "Not scent." "Not the cold." "Not wool." Whoever made the offer clears it. The next sense still needs its own yes, or you can end the pass and remain. A yes to one station is not a yes to the next. Stations 4 and 5 ask again.

One sentence of desire can be said and left there. "I like your mouth in this light." The reply may be "keep that," or "leave that part of me out," and the second one ends it. Arousal, named by the person who feels it, is a fact about that body. It doesn't move the clock, and it doesn't ask to be matched.

Stop with "not this sense," or "stop the pass."

**Station 4. A conversation about desire. About 25 minutes.**

This is talk. Each of you writes two lines, or speaks them if a pen will make you perform. The first is one want, concrete enough to picture. The second is, "You do not owe me this." Read yours. The listener answers once, and the ask is over.

- "Yes, inside what we already named for tonight."
- "I want that on another night. Tonight, no."
- "No."
- "I heard you. I am not taking that on."

A want can be sexual and still be only a sentence. "I want your hand at my waist, through my shirt, on a night we both choose." "I want more kissing in the kitchen, and I'm saying it while kissing is off the table." "I want to feel wanted with both of us dressed." Match the privacy you have.

Answer once. "Pause," a smaller prompt, and "pass" are ordinary. Let a no stay a no.

If you want more after the two lines, use two of these.

- What do you want that lives in pace, in this lamp, or in the hour?
- Where should my attention land: your mouth, your hands, your voice, a habit?
- What do you want less of, as a fact about your body or your time?
- Which no have you been hiding in a joke, a delay, or a convenient headache?
- Say "I want this." Then say "You owe me this" once, hear the seam, and keep only the first sentence.

Two prompts are a full station. Thank each other in one sentence that lets the answer stay as it was.

Stop with "pass," or "close the talk." You can close it and still choose station 5, or close it and skip the touch. A good sentence is not consent to touch or sex.

**Station 5. The closer you already named. About 10 minutes.**

Restate the form before anyone moves. A hand on a shoulder. The shared throw. The other modest contact on the card. Or none. You may shrink it, or trade it for none. Leave it at the size you named while the lights were still up.

None, or a decline now, means you stay as you are. Declining is ordinary. Warmth is welcome. A smaller form happens only if the person who declined offers it. Otherwise hands stay where they are.

If you both want the named form, do it and finish. A hand stays a hand. Under one throw you stay dressed, seated, and able to leave the cloth. Agree on the end first: a length on the clock, the close of music already playing, or the word stop. The person being touched sets pressure and place inside what you named. Either of you can be that person.

Stop when someone says so, when a hand goes back to its owner, or when the time is done. Touch for this chapter ends there. Anything further is a separate conversation that this chapter does not script.

Sit for a minute in the light you have. Bring the other lamps back when you want the house. What you took off the table stays off.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 30 minutes.** Station 1 in full, card and lamp included. One piece of music, one thing to notice, and the right to lift the needle. One sense, and a yes that covers only that sense. A second bite, if you chose taste, is a new question. One request, plus the line that it isn't owed, and one answer. Then the closer, which may be no. That is a whole night.

**Standard, about 90 minutes.** All five stations, with the times above as a guide you can bend. Use the stops. A yes still ends at the station where it was given.

**Extended, about three hours.** The same five stations, taken slowly. A second piece you already own, with a new notice and the same stop. Repeat only a sense that gets its own yes again. Two further prompts if you want them. Eat what's already home, leave for tea, and come back to the lamp. The extra hours are for staying. They don't add a station, and they don't move sex onto the table. Any different closeness, after the lights are up, starts as its own conversation and its own yes.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
If talk turns decorative, use the two written lines, or say them when a pen makes you ornate. A want with a limit can stay one sentence. "I want your mouth, and I want my shirt on." "I want your knee against mine, and I want to stay in this chair." The listener takes both halves. If you start sorting each other into types, come back to one want and one answer.

On other nights, a yes from this room doesn't travel. [The Attraction Interview](033) asks what caught you first and what catches you now. [The Sensory Date](036) gives each of you a channel to host. [The Slow Dance With No Music](038) is a sway with the player off. Each one asks again. Look at each other while looking is welcome, or watch the window. This chapter doesn't time your eyes.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
No player means a playlist, and pause stands in for the needle. Any throw stands in for burgundy. Water in both glasses is a full setup. A tired night uses the short version, materials already on the table, one of you reading the station names.

Pain or a crowded set of senses belongs on the card before the offer. Talk can carry the long version. Touch can be none every time. A mood doesn't overrule a current no.

Apart, call the night reduced: the same hour, a lamp each, music you can both start, the list, one notice, one request. Station 5 doesn't fit a screen. The sitting room, later, needs its own yes.

Replay from a new card. Change the music, the sense, or the named touch. Last time's yes expires when you sit down.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not the two of you.

The ceiling light is on while they write. Off the table: sex, Rowan's neck, stories about other lovers, and alcohol. Water in both glasses. The closer is the shared throw. A hand on a shoulder is written only as a smaller form the decliner may offer. Wool itches Vale, so the burgundy stays in the picture and cotton comes off the other chair.

Rowan asks Vale to notice a low note in an instrumental they already own. Vale asks Rowan to notice Vale's hands on Vale's own glass. A late chord crowds a memory Rowan wants left out. Rowan lifts the needle. Vale leaves it off. "Not the music." "Then we're done with the music."

Rowan offers one slice of pear. Vale says yes. They share it. Rowan says "not scent" before any peel, because fragrance becomes a headache, and Vale lets that sense go. A second slice is already a new question. Vale says yes, and they say aloud that the yes was about the pear. Rowan asks about the cold glass and waits. Vale says yes to the glass and no to air from the window. Rowan asks before any cloth moves. Vale says yes to cotton across Vale's lap only. Rowan says, "I like your hands in this light." Vale says, "Keep that."

Vale reads, "I want more kissing on ordinary Tuesdays, in the kitchen, with our clothes on," and, "You do not owe me this." Rowan says, "I heard you. I am not taking that on tonight." Vale would have liked a yes, and lets the no stand. The want stays information. Rowan reads, "I want your hand between my shoulder blades, over my shirt, on a night we both say yes in the same hour," and, "You do not owe me this." Vale says, "I want that another night. Tonight, no. I'm glad you said it."

Rowan restates the shared throw. Vale says, "No. The cotton on my lap was enough. I don't want us under it together." Rowan stays in the other chair and doesn't ask for the shoulder. Vale doesn't offer it. They finish the water, watch the window for a minute, and Vale turns the other lights on. Rowan says, "Your no was clear. Thank you." Vale says, "So was yours."

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Talk, or let the empty glasses be the close.

- What stayed off the table?
- Which sense stopped, and did the night continue?
- Did a no leave the request as a request?
- Did the closer happen, shrink by the decliner's offer, or stay declined?
- What might you ask another night, still as a request?

Two chairs and a lifted needle can end it. Bring the other lights up when you want the house.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Use this spread for the night you just had. Private pages are optional to share, and they need not be explicit. Skip any prompt. A blank line is a finished line. One word is enough for a yes or a no.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- What I took off the table, in a short phrase I am willing to reread
- One want I made as a request, and the answer I heard
partner_b:
- The specific thing I asked to have noticed, and the sense I stopped or kept
- My decision about the closer touch, including a decline, in words I would still use in the kitchen
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
See J2017. Jakubiak and Feeney offer a review and a theoretical model arguing that wanted affectionate touch can relate to relational, psychological, and physical well-being, including stress-related pathways. Unwanted touch is outside that claim. The paper is not a trial of this night, and it doesn't test the lamp, the music, the senses, or the conversation.

See I2024. Impett, Park, and Muise find little empirical support for one primary love language, for exactly five languages, and for matching as the predictor of satisfaction. This chapter cites that finding, and only that finding, so station 4 stays a conversation about a specific want. The review is not a test of these five stations.

The night is an original formulation for two adults who already like each other. No whitelist source tests it. Clinical sensate focus is a different procedure and isn't reproduced here. Desire may rise, fall, or stay where it was. The evening you agreed to, stops included, is the result on offer.
