signatures.title: The Case of the Missing Tuesday

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: An ordinary Tuesday went thin, and you reconstruct it from four objects that are already in the room.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
A Tuesday can vanish without anyone taking it. You both got to Wednesday. What's left is an empty square, a coat already on a chair, a receipt that never became a story, and the belief that nothing happened. Something usually did. It was too ordinary to file.

This is a parlor mystery for that kind of absence. Stay in one room, in two seats. You're both the detectives and the witnesses. There is no culprit, and there is no crime. The missing thing is the texture of a day. You solve it by talking. Each of you will point to one sentence the other wrote that you recognize as true, and one sentence you want corrected. The corrections are the solution. This book has no hidden answer for your Tuesday, and it won't invent your memories.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
You start from four objects already in the room and ask a thin Tuesday in both directions. One of the five sentences has to include "I don't know." Then each of you names one sentence you recognize and one you want corrected. Those corrections are the solution. A thin day never had to explain itself. Asking for it with the objects still in the room is a way to be specific about each other.

Praise says a memory was welcome. A correction says which sentence can live in both accounts. Diary studies found that intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator (see L1998). In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. Those diaries didn't test this hour. They're a reason to hear the mood in an answer.

A review argues that imagining a future uses much of the same machinery as remembering. The authors' hypothesis, which the review says has support, is that a future scene recombines details from the past, and the same review says further work still has to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments (see S2007). "That part is wrong" is this chapter's correction, not a result the review proved. This chapter hasn't been clinically tested.

Gottman's clinical writing calls a working picture of a partner's inner world a love map. An unmarked Tuesday is the kind of page that metaphor cares about. It isn't a score. If a small good thing turns up, say you're glad, and stop. The research limit is in the notes.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Play the standard version first. It takes about 70 minutes. Stay seated. Either of you may pause, pass, or stop. A pass ends that question. It doesn't end the case, and it doesn't demand a substitute confession.

Choose a Tuesday inside the last twelve months on which both of you were living, and which neither of you has asked to leave closed. You don't have to have shared the city. "I wasn't there" is a complete answer. Each of you may veto a day without explaining. Three vetoes, or a run of closed Tuesdays, means an older Tuesday or the fictional sample only.

Anything already off the table stays there: a third person, a body, an illness, a loss, a retired fight. "Pass" or "smaller" is the whole reply. "Smaller" narrows the ask to one visible detail, such as the cuff.

Every exhibit is already in this room. Name a substitute out loud.

- **Calendar.** One you can see from your seat, a phone calendar if that phone is already here, or a week drawn on paper you have. If Tuesday already has writing, copy the week, leave that square blank, cover the original, and say once what you covered. The blank copy is the exhibit.
- **Teapot.** The pot already here, or two cups, mugs, or glasses. "These two mugs are the teapot" is a legal naming. If the kettle is elsewhere, the exhibit stays cold.
- **Coat.** A coat or jacket already on a chair or a hook you can reach, or a layer one of you is wearing. Private pockets stay private. The coat is still an exhibit.
- **Receipt.** A receipt or ticket already in a wallet, bag, or pocket here. Turn medical totals and surprises face down. If you'd rather show nothing, label a blank card "receipt." "I don't know" still counts as the round.
- **Also.** Two seats, two sheets, something to write with, and a timer you can both see.

Photos stay out until the case is solved. Anything a camera tells you later is labeled later. A solved case isn't an agreement to touch or to continue into sex. That needs its own yes, separate from the game.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Finish the sentence you're in when the bell rings, then stop.

**Choose the day. About 4 minutes.** Name the Tuesday by date or by a marker you both accept. If either of you calls it closed, it's closed. If you're playing only the sample, go to Examples.

**Name the exhibits before any theory. About 4 minutes.** Lay out the blank Tuesday, the coat, the receipt or its card, and the teapot or its substitute. Say: "This is the calendar. Tuesday is unmarked. This is the coat. This is the receipt. This is the teapot." A substitute gets its real name and its role. An early theory goes on your paper, face down. It may feed the reconstruction. It stays unspoken during the rounds.

**Four rounds, about 11 minutes each.** Order: calendar, coat, receipt, teapot. One asks, the other answers, then you swap, so both of you answer every exhibit. Whoever has the more restless curiosity asks first on the calendar and on the receipt. The other person asks first on the coat and on the teapot. A coin already in the room can decide who asks first, if you'd rather not negotiate it.

Use one card from that exhibit, or a question of your own that the exhibit and memory could answer. One follow-up, and it stays on the answer. "Say more about the empty square" is a follow-up. The asker's own anecdote ends the question. The asker doesn't answer inside the turn. Silence belongs to the person asked.

A pass ends that question, not the night. The asker may offer one different card from the same exhibit. A second pass ends that answerer's turn. Swap anyway if the other direction hasn't happened. "Smaller" keeps the turn and shrinks the question. A blank receipt still gets the receipt cards, and "I don't know" is a full answer.

The cards are the questions. Cut them if you want a pile. Large print is welcome. Reading them from the page is enough.

```cards
Calendar | What else is written in that week, and which of those marks would have changed Tuesday if it had landed there instead?
Calendar | Who usually writes on this calendar, and what kind of event earns a mark rather than living in one person's head?
Calendar | This Tuesday square is empty. What would have had to happen before noon for one of you to write in it?
Coat | Where did this coat spend the middle of that Tuesday, as far as you actually know, and which part of the day are you tempted to fill in?
Coat | What on the cloth, or in the pockets you have agreed to empty here, belongs to that Tuesday, and what is left over from another day?
Coat | Who wears this when the weather turns, and do you know whether that same person had it on during the Tuesday you chose?
Receipt | Read every printed mark aloud, including the time, the items, and anything voided or crossed out. Which of those belongs to a stop on the way somewhere?
Receipt | If there is handwriting, whose hand is it, and does it record something that already happened or something that was still waiting?
Receipt | How many people does this paper feed, carry, or charge, and what does a single line fail to prove about who else was there?
Teapot | Was this pot used on that Tuesday, and if you think it was, what time of day can you actually support?
Teapot | How many people drank, and what would a clean cup mean if you are wrong about who was home?
Teapot | What, if anything, did you talk about while it steeped, and what subject was in the room and never said?
```

**Write, then read. About 8 minutes silent, then about 10 together.** Number a page from 1 to 5. Don't show it. Each sentence does one job, in this order.

1. Name the Tuesday by date or by the marker you both accepted.
2. Say where at least one exhibit was during part of that day.
3. Say one thing you believe the other person did that you didn't see.
4. Include the words "I don't know." This is the sentence that refuses an invention.
5. End on a sentence you'll let the other person correct.

The person who answered the first calendar question reads all five. If that turn was a pass, the other reads first. No interrupting. Then the four closing moves. The first reader names one sentence they recognize as true and reads it back. The writer confirms it or edits a word. A wrong recognition gets rejected, and the reader chooses again. If none is true, say so. The first reader then names one sentence to correct, in a sentence or two. The writer accepts, amends, or says "still open." The second reader does those same two moves. Stop, unless you both want one more correction.

The case is solved when those four moves are done. Corrections are the solution. "I wouldn't correct any of these" counts when the pages agree. There's no score. A score would pay you to invent. You're done when every agreed exhibit has been asked both ways, or passed, and the closing is finished. If you finish early, stop. Don't open a second Tuesday to fill the clock.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
The short version takes about 25 minutes. Choose the day or the sample. Name the calendar and one other exhibit honestly in the room. A blank card counts. Spend about 3 minutes choosing, 2 naming, 7 on each exhibit with both directions included, 3 writing, and 3 closing. Write three sentences: the day's name, what one exhibit can prove, and one line you'll let the other correct. Keep the four closing moves.

The standard version takes about 70 minutes. Play this first. All four exhibits, both directions, five sentences, the times named above.

The extended version takes about 120 minutes. Solve the standard case, then add the round called "what we still cannot know" (about 50 minutes). You may decline it. A solved standard case is a finished night. Spend about 10 minutes underlining any clause with neither an exhibit nor a witness. Spend about 20 minutes writing up to three lines each that the exhibits can't support. A line stays blank unless a real memory is offered and labeled "witness." Spend about 10 minutes on one optional witness memory each, closed with one recognition and one correction if a memory was offered. Spend the last 10 minutes on four joint lines: two sentences you both accept, one correction you both accept, and one blank you both keep. The blank belongs in the solution.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
If the day is sore, take a two-hour window and leave the rest unnamed. If it's so ordinary you freeze, keep the hour you can see. The person who remembers more reports what they saw and handled. "You always vanish on weekdays" is a theory. "I didn't see you between the door and the tea" is a report.

Repeat a correction once, and let the writer edit the repetition. If the pages match too neatly, each of you may add, "What I may have smoothed over is." Skip the line if you'd have to invent a quarrel. If speech sands an answer down, write it and read it. Another night, play the whole case on paper, same timer, same ban on theories during the rounds.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
On a call, name the exhibits you can see. No coat in reach means the blank-card rule. Cameras stay optional. A Tuesday from before you knew each other is legal if you're both curious, even when one page is mostly "I don't know."

Replay on a later thin day. Write one new question per exhibit, in the same shape as the cards. A question that worked by surprise will work less well twice. If the word Tuesday is the trouble, name another weekday and keep the rules. Stay seated. A garment in another room isn't an exhibit tonight. If reading the page is hard, one of you can read a card aloud and the other can answer on paper. There's no score and no forfeit.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They aren't you. Another pair can play this file before trusting the game with a real week.

### The fictional case file

One room, evening. The exhibits are already on the table and the chair. The coat pocket was emptied at the start. Nobody got up again.

**Calendar.** Monday: "Vale, dentist, 9:40." Tuesday: empty. Wednesday: "Rowan, library hold." Thursday: "late supper." Friday: "train, both." Saturday: empty. Sunday: "Jun, call." In the margin, outside every square: "rain?"

**Coat.** Charcoal, on a chair. The left cuff is dry, with a pale tide line. From the pocket: a transit slip printed "Tue 10 Mar" and no passenger name, a peppermint wrapper, and a library slip for *Kiln Street Atlas*, due Wednesday 11 March.

**Receipt.** Already on the table. Printed 10 Mar, 07:42: black tea, oat milk, ginger cake, an extra shot voided, cash, one order. On the back, Vale's hand: "ask Rowan about the blue folder."

**Teapot.** Empty, cool, copper on the lid, tag reading smoked black. The window cup has a tea ring. The other cup is clean. Under the pot, Rowan's hand: "9:10, not the morning."

Warm-up players use only this file and the cards. When the file is silent, say so. Don't give these two your own life. Ask both ways, write five sentences, and stop. Leave the key covered. The fictional close is past the notes, and your own Tuesday has no key.

Stop here if you are playing the sample.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay with the corrected sentence before you promote it into a theory of character. A thin Tuesday is a finding: the day never had to perform. If a closed subject got brushed, one sentence, then leave it. A later message that remembers the correction is plenty. A grand portrait will be less accurate than the line they already edited.

Solved isn't a yes to anything physical. If the evening turns that way, it needs its own yes. You can also stop, and let the day stay partly missing.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write the date, the time, the place, which version you played, a mood if you want one, a one-line intention, and initials if you want them. Mark it done or paused. Private pages are optional to share. Keep a personal note if the shared book should hold only what you both choose. If you played the sample, say so. A repeat gets its own lines.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The sentence you wrote that I recognized as true, and the words I used when I read it back
- The correction I offered you, and whether you accepted it, amended it, or left it open
partner_b:
- The question I passed, or the question I was glad you didn't push past
- A sentence in your reconstruction I could not have written myself, and what I did with it
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: original-formulation. Parlor mysteries are a folk form. This Tuesday, these exhibits, and these questions were written for this book. The chapter hasn't been clinically tested as a couple treatment. There's no culprit and no crime. Chapter 103 is a different puzzle, a ledger in packets. This case doesn't use that grid.

See L1998. In diary studies of daily interactions, intimacy tracked self-disclosure and partner disclosure, with perceived partner responsiveness as a partial mediator. In Study 2, emotional disclosure was a stronger predictor than factual disclosure. Those diaries didn't test a reconstruction of an ordinary weekday.

See S2007. Schacter, Addis, and Buckner argue that imagining the future depends on much of the same neural machinery as remembering. Their constructive episodic simulation hypothesis says future simulation recombines details from the past, and the review says that hypothesis has support. Further work still has to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments. This isn't proof the game improves memory, and it isn't a claim that people can't tell memory from imagination. The review didn't test a parlor evening.

See G2004. Telling someone about a good event was associated with greater positive affect and well-being beyond the event itself. Perceived active-constructive responses were associated with higher relationship quality. Passive or destructive responses weren't the helpful pattern. A glad sentence is enough. The studies didn't test this chapter.

See GOTTMAN. "Love maps" come from John Gottman's clinical writing, a practitioner picture of knowing a partner's inner world. The phrase isn't a test of this game, and it supplies no percentage this chapter may quote.

Related experiences: 043 The Newlywed Game, Without the Wedding, and 081 The Forbidden Question Box.


---

Stop here if you are playing the sample.

Your own Tuesday ends above. This book has no hidden answer for it. The corrections you make are the solution. Everything past the next heading solves only the fictional file, and only after both of you have written five sentences from the exhibits alone. If you haven't done that, stop.

### Cover this until the sample case is finished

Rowan and Vale, who are fictional, closed the sample this way.

Vale asks what earns a calendar mark. Rowan says they write only what the other person must remember, so Tuesday stayed empty, and "rain?" is a Sunday question, not a weather report. They swap. Rowan asks what would have forced a note before noon. Vale starts a closed work week, says "pass," and answers the neighboring-marks question instead: dentist, library hold, train, Jun. Then they play coat, receipt, and teapot from the cards.

Rowan's five sentences:

1. The Tuesday is 10 March, the empty square after Vale's dentist.
2. The coat was on Vale in the morning. The cuff met wet weather, and the transit slip is printed that day.
3. I didn't see the counter, and I believe Vale bought the tea and the ginger cake alone at 7:42.
4. I don't know whether the library slip means that anyone went for a book that day.
5. Correct this if it's wrong: we talked about the blue folder while the tea was pouring at 9:10, and both cups were used.

Vale's five sentences:

1. Tuesday 10 March stayed blank because we only write reminders the other person needs.
2. I wore the coat in the rain and kept the transit slip. The peppermint wrapper was already in the pocket from you.
3. I wrote the folder note because I hadn't asked yet, and the voided shot was me changing my mind at the counter.
4. I don't know what you did between the door and the evening, except that you were home when I left and home when the pot was on.
5. Correct this if I stole it: I made the smoked tea at 9:10, and you drank both cups.

Rowan reads first and recognizes Vale's third sentence, the note written because the question hadn't been asked. Rowan corrects the fifth: Rowan made the tea, wrote the scrap because Vale had asked whether the pot was left from breakfast, and drank the one cup. Vale's cup stayed clean. Vale accepts. Vale recognizes the solo purchase at 7:42, and corrects the folder talk and the two used cups. Rowan accepts. The library line stays "I don't know." The case is solved.

This key solves the fictional Tuesday only. It isn't a key to your lives. If you played your own day, stop. An exhibit supports a fact only as far as the object reaches. Witness means someone said it and the other accepted it, or left it uncorrected.

| Sample fact | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- |
| Tuesday 10 March, square left empty | Calendar. Receipt and transit slip carry the same date. None of them says the day mattered, or why the square is blank |
| They mark a square only when the other person needs the reminder | Witness: Rowan, echoed in Vale's first sentence, not corrected. The blank square doesn't prove the rule |
| Monday, Vale's dentist at 9:40. Wednesday, Rowan's library hold. Thursday, late supper. Friday, the train for both. Sunday, a call with Jun. Saturday empty | Calendar. Other days, not Tuesday |
| "rain?" outside every square | Calendar. Not proof of rain. Rowan witnessed a Sunday question |
| Dried tide line on the left cuff | Coat. Wet weather sometime. Not the day or the wearer |
| Vale wore the coat that morning and kept the slip | Witness: Vale's second sentence, accepted. The slip prints no name |
| Transit slip reading Tue 10 Mar, no passenger | Coat. A ride that day, not a named rider |
| Peppermint wrapper in the pocket | Coat. Not who ate it, or when |
| The wrapper was already Rowan's | Witness: Vale's second sentence, uncorrected |
| *Kiln Street Atlas*, due Wednesday 11 March | Coat, the library slip. A deadline, not a Tuesday visit. Rowan's "I don't know" stands |
| At 7:42: black tea, oat milk, ginger cake, a voided extra shot, cash, one order | Receipt. No printed buyer |
| Vale changed their mind about the extra shot | Witness: Vale's third sentence, which Rowan recognized. The void is on the receipt. The reason is not |
| Vale was alone at the counter | Witness: Rowan's third sentence, recognized by Vale. One order can't show who else was absent |
| Vale's hand wrote "ask Rowan about the blue folder" | Receipt. An intention still waiting, not a conversation already held |
| No folder talk at 9:10, and only one cup was used | Vale's correction of Rowan's fifth sentence, accepted. The pot never mentions a folder |
| Smoked black tea was brewed | Teapot tag. Not proof the brewing was Tuesday |
| Rowan wrote "9:10, not the morning" | Teapot scrap. Evening, and Rowan's hand. Not who heated the water |
| Rowan made the pot, drank once, and left Vale's cup clean | Rowan's correction of Vale's fifth sentence, accepted. The clean cup contradicts "both cups" |
| Rowan's midday unknown. Home when Vale left, and home at 9:10 | Witness: Vale's fourth sentence, left standing. No exhibit of the middle |

Rowan recognized the unasked folder note. Rowan corrected Vale's claim to have made the tea, and the claim that Rowan drank both cups. Vale recognized the solo purchase at 7:42. Vale corrected the folder conversation. Those corrections are the sample solution. On a real Tuesday, the only solution this book has is the one you correct yourselves.

signatures.title: The Branching Evening

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: From a night hall, choose a kitchen, a dark walk, or a quiet chair, and let every return be a way to finish.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The hall is the least celebrated room you own, which is why it can hold a decision. Kitchens tug toward hunger and hosting. Chairs tug toward staying put. The outer door tugs toward weather. Left alone, the nearest soft surface wins, along with a conversation you have already had three times this week.

This evening starts between the rooms. From the hall you may enter the kitchen, take the dark walk, sit in the quiet chair, or end the night. After a room, you come back to the same spot. Turning back is a complete choice. Saying "End the night" in the hall is a finished evening. Any room you never entered stays unentered, and it is not a debt.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
The first move is a choice you say in the hall: kitchen, dark walk, quiet chair, or end. You do know who wants the light off, who tells the day in the doorway, who is already halfway to the couch. The hall asks the smaller questions anyway: what you are hungry for once you drop the nice version, what a caring hand should stop doing, and what you will say while moving and then leave there.

A hall gives those questions a container with an exit. You name a room out loud, you do it, and you return to a place where stopping counts. A preference repeated in one sentence lands differently from a compliment. A sentence that stays on the walk stays off the agenda.

In laboratory experiments, about seven minutes of a novel and arousing joint task increased experienced relationship quality more than a mundane task (see A2000 in the notes). That is short-term experienced quality. This evening is a different procedure, and it does not inherit that result.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Choose the version at the hall mark. Short is one room, about 30 minutes. Standard is the hall plus two rooms, about 100 minutes. Extended leaves all three rooms open, about two and a half hours. Ending from the hall sooner is allowed in all three.

Take one minute for closed subjects, one sentence each. A pass needs no substitute confession. Stories about other people, bodies, money, and family stay optional. If a prompt lands on a closed subject, say "pass" or "smaller." Smaller means one tinier version, food only or the mug only, and a pass is still available after it. If the night is already a fight, take the short version or wait.

Phones may keep time if notifications are quiet. Mark the hall with a shoe or a book. Both of you there means you have returned. In a studio, the door is the hall, the counter is the kitchen, and the lamp seat is the chair.

When you want different rooms, each of you says one word. If the words match, go. On the first disagreement, one of you flips a coin and the other calls it in the air. A right call means the caller picks. A wrong call means the flipper picks. After that, the person who did not make the last accepted choice picks. "End the night" is a real pick. Either person may say "turn back" before both of you have entered the next room. Turn back spends nothing. You read the Hall card again, and you do not debate it.

A room begins only when both of you have crossed into it. Once you are inside, leaving early still spends the room. Say "hall," return, count it, and do not re-enter it tonight.

The walk's safety rule sits in that room: weather, a dark street, pain, or either person's no closes the block, and the hallway is a complete dark walk. Touch happens in one place, the quiet chair, and only as the hand named there. Nothing tonight is an agreement to sex. A yes to sitting is not a yes to the hand.

If speaking is hard, write and read aloud only what you want heard. If hearing is hard, face each other and use a visible timer. When a step needs a starter and the room has not named one, the person who did not choose that room goes first. If you chose it together, the later name in the alphabet goes first.

Print the four cards if you want them in hand: one choice point each, large type, a half sheet at most. Otherwise read only the card for the place where you are, and leave the next room's prompts unread until you enter. If a memory and a card disagree, the card wins.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Have the timer, a warm light, the lamp, and a snack within reach. Toast, a peeled orange, crackers, leftovers, tea, or water all count. No recipe, and no knife if a knife is a bad idea. You are finished when "End the night" is accepted at the mark, then go to Afterward. If you must stop sooner, say it where you are. The evening is still finished.

### The hall

1. Read the Hall card and speak one open sentence: "Kitchen." "Dark walk." "Quiet chair." or "End the night."
2. "End the night" stops the evening. Unvisited rooms stay unvisited.
3. For a room, both of you cross and start at step 1 of that room. "Turn back," said before both are in, returns you to this card.
4. Every time you come back from a room, say the count before anything else. "One room." "Two rooms." "Three rooms." Short ends at one. Standard ends at two. Extended may end at three, or earlier from this mark.
5. If the next room is already named, pass through in about a minute and do not vote again. Read the Hall card only if the sentence was "Hall," or if someone says "hall instead" before the next threshold. "Hall instead" replaces the named room. That replacement is a complete choice.

### The kitchen

Copper means a warm light you already own: a yellow shade, an under-cabinet bulb, a dimmed overhead. Colder lights can go off if the room stays safe.

1. Get a drink or a simple snack into both pairs of hands. Short version: whatever is already in reach, under 3 minutes. Standard and extended: up to 10 minutes, and still no project. Hands stay busy. Hosting speeches can wait.
2. Set 10 minutes. This timer runs in every version. Whoever did not pour, slice, or fetch reads. If you shared the work, the later name reads. The reader answers second on the first prompt. You swap for the second, and the person who has said less starts the third. If you cannot tell, the first starter takes the third too.
3. Appetite: "What are you hungry for tonight that you would admit if we dropped the nice version? Food counts. A kind of hour counts."
4. Care: "When someone looks after you in a small way, what should their hands do, and what should they stop doing?"
5. Ordinary preference: "Name one ordinary preference you have been folding away because it seemed too small to announce."
6. After each answer, the listener repeats it in one sentence. The speaker says "yes" or gives one correction. The listener does not upgrade the preference into a better one.
7. A pass replaces an answer. The timer keeps running. The listener asks nothing more. If the timer rings mid-sentence, finish the sentence and skip any unasked prompt. Unasked prompts are not a debt. If you finish early, eat until the bell, or both say "card" and go on.
8. Read the Kitchen card and speak one open sentence. The card says where that sentence takes you, always through the hall. Leaving early still spends the kitchen, and you still use the card.

### The dark walk

Teal is night air, a dim corridor, or a streetlight. Coats on for the block. Indoors, a coat is optional.

1. Before the outer door opens, say "Block" or "Hallway." Weather, a safety no, or a body that does not want the outside closes the block. The hallway is a complete dark walk.
2. The block ends at the first corner or where the sidewalk ends, whichever comes first, and then you walk back the way you came. If that point would cross a road you will not cross, stop at the corner before it. The hallway is the longest indoor corridor you can both use, down and back. No corridor means a loop from the mark to the farthest corner and back. That loop is the whole walk, parade past the bookcase included.
3. Start the timer as you move: 12 minutes in the short version and in the seated variation, 20 otherwise. If it rings away from home, turn at once. Back early, with a round still unspoken, you may repeat that same route once. No new destination. You may also stop.
4. Speak the rounds only while a foot, a wheel, or, in the seated variation, a hand is moving. If you stop to think, the round waits. "Curb," "slower," "I'm cold," and "hall" are always allowed, and they are not a round.
5. Notices, each of you: one sound, one light or color, one texture. "The exit sign is a tired green" qualifies. A mood, or a theory of the relationship, does not qualify.
6. Then one sentence you will say only while moving. Small is allowed. The listener says "heard" and asks nothing. "I have no extra sentence" counts. Once you stop for the night, only the speaker may reopen it, on another day.
7. If time remains, one question, still moving: "What have we been walking past on ordinary days that you want noticed once, with you?" The person who has not asked yet is the one who asks. If neither has, the person who did not choose the walk asks. Finish on the threshold if the door arrives, then stop. No second question. If the timer is close, drop this question first, then the sentence you say only while moving. One notice each still completes the walk.
8. Read the Dark walk card and speak one open sentence. "Hall" said mid-route also completes the walk. Shortest way back, then the card.

### The quiet chair

Gold is one small lamp. Other lights in that room go off if you can still sit safely. If the bulb is harsh, move it farther from your faces. Keep cloth off a shade that heats. Phone screens go face down.

1. Sit where a hand could be offered and where declining it is ordinary. If you already do not want the hand, say "chair only" now. Pain, numbness, disinterest, and a simple no all use that sentence. You will not be asked again.
2. The person who chose the room reads the only question. If you chose together, the later name reads. Then silence: 2 minutes, or 1 minute in the short version. "What pace do you want once the day is over, and where does my pace help it or crowd it?"
3. The person who did not choose the room answers first, about 5 minutes, or about 3 in the short version. Stopping sooner is a full answer. Then the other answers, same limit, with no biography dropped into the middle.
4. Each listener may say, "I heard that your pace wants ___." The speaker says "yes" or gives one edit.
5. Unless someone said "chair only," the person who answered second may turn one hand palm up on their own thigh. The other may lay a hand on that palm for three breaths, then lift it. That is the whole touch. Either person may decline in the moment by not offering, by not taking the palm, or by saying "not the hand" or "chair only." If both offer at once, leave both palms empty. One offer only. The first answerer may say "I will offer instead," and you swap once.
6. A declined touch does not cancel the chair and is not a failed evening. A yes to sitting is not a yes to touch. Do not add a massage, a kiss, a pull, or a second round. A wish named later in the hall is not an agreement.
7. If there was no hand, stay three breaths. Then read the Quiet chair card and speak one open sentence. Leaving early spends the chair. An unfinished question is finished.

### The cards

Cut these into four, or read one line at its place. Version lock: count the room you are leaving. After one room in the short version, after two in the standard, and after three in the extended, onward room names close. Only "Hall," then "End the night," remains. You may end from the hall earlier. The lock beats an adventurous mood.

```cards
Hall | Say one open sentence, then do only that. "Kitchen." Both start the kitchen at step 1. "Dark walk." Choose block or hallway here, then start the dark walk at step 1. "Quiet chair." Both start the quiet chair at step 1. "End the night." The evening is finished. Go to Afterward. Spent rooms stay closed. If you disagree, use the disagreement rule. Both enter, or say "turn back" and read this card again. On a return, say the count first. If the version lock has been reached, only "End the night" is open. Ending here finishes the evening.
Kitchen | When the 10-minute timer ends, or if you left early, say one sentence, then pass through the hall. "Dark walk." At the mark, choose block or hallway, then dark walk step 1. "Quiet chair." Quiet chair step 1. "Hall." Say the count and read the Hall card. "Hall instead," said before the next threshold, replaces a named room. If the version lock has been reached, only "Hall" is open.
Dark walk | Read this stopped at your door or at the end of the indoor route. Block and hallway are one room. Either spends it. "Kitchen." Return to the mark, then kitchen step 1. "Quiet chair." Return to the mark, then quiet chair step 1. "Hall." Say the count and read the Hall card. If the version lock has been reached, only "Hall" is open.
Quiet chair | Read this after the question and after the hand or the decline. A declined hand does not change the sentences. "Kitchen." Stand, return to the mark, kitchen step 1. "Dark walk." Stand, return, choose block or hallway, dark walk step 1. "Hall." Stand, return, say the count, read the Hall card. If the version lock has been reached, only "Hall" is open.
```

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 30 minutes.** One room. About 5 minutes in the hall, about 20 in the room, about 5 to return, say "One room," and end. The kitchen still uses its 10-minute timer, the walk its 12-minute cap, the chair its shorter silence. Other sentences on that room's card are closed. One threshold turn back lets you pick a different room. A second turn back ends the short evening, and that ending is finished.

**Standard, about 100 minutes.** The hall plus two rooms: about 10 minutes to open, 35 in the first room, 5 to cross and say "One room," 35 in the second, 15 to close on "Two rooms" and "End the night." The third room stays closed. Ending after one room is still a finished evening.

**Extended, about two and a half hours.** All three rooms may open. About 10 minutes to open, 40 in each room, 5 for each passage through the hall, and 10 to close: about 150 minutes. After the third room, end. Ending before it also finishes the evening. The unused room can wait.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
The sentence from the walk stays closed tonight. The speaker can bring it back on another day. After you end, you may each name the choice you almost made, one sentence, with no campaign attached. If the pace question opened a real knot, book another night. You may also decide whether "chair only" is the default next time. That decision waits for the next sitting.

On the extended version, after all three rooms, one napkin line is available if you both still want it: "What should stay in this kitchen without a discussion?" One item each, or a pass. Then stop.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
If the block and the hallway are both too far, take the seated dark walk at the mark. For 12 minutes, speak the walk rounds only while a hand moves along a sleeve, a wheel rim, or the seam of a chair. When the hand stops, the sentence waits. This uses the Dark walk card and spends the dark walk. It is a complete room.

In a hotel, the corridor is the hallway, the kettle is the kitchen, the desk chair is the quiet chair, and the inside of the door is the mark. A quiet-mouthed night uses only the appetite prompt, the walk's notices, and the chair question with "chair only" said at the start. You still end out loud. Thin talk creates no make-up conversation.

Replay with the same cards and a new walk sentence. Start in a room you skipped, or one you still think about. An old closed sentence, if you open it on purpose, belongs in the revisit lines. Retire a prompt that worked only because it startled. You may agree on one replacement chair question before you sit: one sentence, easy to decline, no follow-up. Daylight is allowed if you say so. The chair lamp still goes on.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They are not you. They play the extended version. This is the whole trail.

At the shoe, Rowan says "Dark walk." Vale says "Quiet chair." Vale flips, Rowan calls heads, the coin lands tails, and Vale picks. Both cross. Rowan, who did not choose the room, answers first: the first half hour at home should be quiet, and questions at the door crowd it. Vale wants about 10 minutes to put the day down, and hears silence at the keys as a shut door. Rowan reflects, "I heard that your pace wants a short report, then room." Vale says "yes." Vale reflects, "I heard that your pace wants an empty doorway." Rowan edits it: "Empty of questions. You can still say hello." Vale turns a palm up. Rowan says "chair only." Three breaths. The chair stands. Rowan says "Kitchen."

They pass the shoe. Warm light, toast, a spoon. Vale pours, so Rowan reads and Vale answers first: toast, and 10 minutes with no personality to solve. Rowan answers second: salt, and the missed walk. On care, Vale wants the glass set in reach and the drinking lecture stopped. Rowan wants the hovering stopped, and a hand at the neck only when asked. They repeat those sentences. Then the folded preferences: the heel of the bread, and the overhead off. The overhead goes off. The chair lamp comes in on loan. Rowan says "Dark walk."

Rain, and a street that looks wrong. Vale says "Hallway." Coats stay on the hook. The corridor is the whole walk. In motion they trade a radiator tick, a tired exit sign, a rough cuff, a neighbor's television, a dim stair light, and a cool handrail. Vale's closed sentence: "I was disappointed about the hand for a minute, and the minute is over." Rowan says "heard." Rowan says, "I still want the block on a dry night, and I don't want to settle it in this corridor." Vale says "heard." Vale asks what they have been walking past. Rowan names the bakery window that vanishes inside errand talk. At their door Vale says "Hall." At the shoe they say "Three rooms," then "End the night." The spoon gets washed. The minute and the bakery both stay where they were said.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Leave the lamp a minute if you like the room. The cups can wait. The count you already spoke is the summary. One practical check is enough, and skipping it is allowed: the door, the cold, whether "chair only" is the default next time, whether the walk's sentence is still closed.

A preference that is easy to keep may be kept this week. The heel of the bread. The overhead off. A glass set down without a lecture. Then the shoe goes back to being a shoe.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write the date, the time, the place, the version, a mood if you want one, a one-line intention, and initials if you want them. Mark it done or paused. Private pages are optional to share. Keep your own lines in a personal note if the shared book should hold only what you both choose. Name the rooms in the order you entered them, and note whether the walk was the block, the hallway, or seated.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The room I wanted from the hall, and the room we entered first
- A preference, a notice, or a pace I named, and the sentence I heard repeated back
partner_b:
- Where I said turn back, hall, or end, and what that choice gave the night
- The line I said only while moving, or the pass I used, and whether it stays private
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: original-formulation. The hall, the three rooms, the return, and the cards were made for this session. The prompts are not a published questionnaire.

See A2000. In laboratory experiments, about seven minutes of a novel and arousing joint task increased experienced relationship quality more than a mundane task. That is short-term experienced quality, not a permanent change. This evening is a different procedure, and it does not inherit that result.

Related experiences: 068 The Night of Random Decisions, 071 The Twelve-Hour Vacation, and 085 What Would You Do If…?

signatures.title: The Capsule We Open Later

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Seal a few pieces of this season at the table, write an opening date you can still change, and keep the key in the house.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
You can know someone well and still let a whole season flatten into "that year we were busy." Tonight you interrupt that flattening while the week still has a texture. You sit at a table, put a few pieces of this season into an envelope or a box, and write down a day when the two of you will open it together.

The date lives on paper. Both of you write it, and you can change it later by writing a new line together. The capsule stays in the house, on a shelf or in a drawer you can both name. The key stays with you. It means either of you may ask to open the capsule before the date. Opening early is allowed. It isn't a failure.

If one of you is away when the date arrives, the capsule waits. You open it alone only when the slip you wrote at sealing says that you may. You're making a meeting, and you're writing down the ways the meeting can move.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Seal a few pieces of this season, and clip the opening date outside the seal so either of you can rewrite it later. The kitchen joke, the hour the light hits the table, who is tired this month: later retelling keeps less of that. A page written tonight can hold a detail the smoother story would drop. The capsule is that page, plus a day you've agreed to read it beside the life you're actually having.

The date slip is an if-then plan. Gollwitzer calls that form an implementation intention: when situation x arises, perform response y (see G1999). "When this date arrives, we open the capsule together" is that plan. "We should open this sometime" is a goal intention. In the research program that review describes, if-then plans supported goal attainment in the domains studied. Goal intentions had modest effects. They weren't useless. A wish with no date can still be sincere. G1999 didn't study couples, and it didn't test this capsule. The slip names a day you can meet, move, or meet early. It doesn't make the opening go well.

You'll likely picture that day while you seal the envelope. Schacter, Addis, and Buckner argue that imagining a future event uses memory's constructive machinery (see S2007). Their constructive episodic simulation hypothesis says future simulation recombines details from the past, and the review says that hypothesis has support. The same review says further work was still needed, to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments. Use the picture to choose a date you can both actually meet. Imagining the evening doesn't make it happen, and the review doesn't show that this capsule works.

If a hard sentence needs an answer, say it tonight. A sealed page is a poor place for a line the other person hasn't heard. 031, A Love Letter From the Future, writes from a year you haven't lived. 090, The Future Memory, tells one happy scene as if it already happened. 096, The Next Chapter, chooses a small way to go on from what you did. This session stores pieces of the present and names a day to read them. A letter, if you add one, is from tonight.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
An envelope or a box is a complete capsule. A flap, a string, or a clasp will close it. Use a photograph you have the right to keep, or draw a stand-in. A key, if you want one, already lives in the house and goes back to its hook.

Sit where you can both see the date slip. A table works, and so does a call if you each write the same date while you're on the line. Stay seated if you need to. If a pen is tiring, dictate, and have the writer read the line back.

Say what stays out of the capsule. A pass needs no substitute confession. Other people's private lives, bodies, money, and any subject either of you has closed can stay out. Skip a sentence that would ambush the other person on the opening day.

The picture for this session shows a sealed capsule, a photograph, a folded letter, and a key, with the date drawn as marks on the lid. Those marks are a picture. Your date is a line on paper. Leave the lid, the envelope, and the box unmarked, so a later pen can change the day.

Choose one date you can both picture showing up for. Three weeks out, or a weekend you already know you'll share a city. Both of you write it on the slip, with the month clear enough for a stranger to read.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
Give the standard sealing about 90 minutes, and stop sooner once the capsule is closed. The opening is the later day on the slip, or the day you rewrite together. Blank is a complete choice for every item except the date.

```cards
Container | An envelope or a box. Anything you can close is a complete capsule.
Photograph or drawing | One picture from this season, or a drawing that stands in for a picture, or leave blank.
Caption line | What it is, the date, and who may see it, or leave blank.
Letter from one of you | A folded page, sealed if you want it sealed, or leave blank.
Letter from the other | A folded page, sealed if you want it sealed, or leave blank.
Shared note | A few sentences in both of your words about this season, or leave blank.
Opening date | The day you both write on a slip kept outside the seal, so you can change it later.
Key | A house key that stays in the house, a drawn key, or the sentence that either of you may ask to open early. Leave the object out if the sentence is enough.
Place | The shelf or drawer in the house you both can name.
If one of us is away | The capsule waits, unless a sentence you both write tonight says one of you may open it alone.
```

**Seal it.** Skip any optional piece.

1. Set the container down. "This is the capsule" is a fine start.
2. Both of you write the date, then the rules. "When this date arrives, we open the capsule together. Either of us may ask to open it earlier. Opening early is allowed. If one of us is away, the capsule waits." One blank line is for a different agreement you both want tonight, such as "A phone call counts as together." A rule invented the day someone is missing doesn't count. Clip the slip outside the seal so a later pen can change the date.
3. The shared note, if you want it: a scene, a fact that won't be obvious later, or a line you'd like to hear again. Each of you may add a sentence. Neither rewrites the other's words. Two paragraphs may sit side by side.
4. A photograph or a drawing, if you want one, and one caption line: what it is, today's date, and who may see it. `journal/templates/memento-caption.md` holds the longer version: where the object lives, a local filename, and the lines that you made it, that you have the right to keep a copy, and that you aren't granting anyone else the right to publish it. This book doesn't upload pictures. A drawing is a full stand-in.
5. A key, if you use one, returns to its hook in the house. It means either of you may ask to open early, and it stays out of the seal. The sentence on the slip is the same permission.
6. Name the shelf or drawer. Both of you can walk to it. The capsule stays indoors.
7. Seal what you're keeping. Leave the slip editable. You're done when you both know the date and the place.

On a standard evening, say aloud that there are no letters.

**Open it.** Sit together at a table, with the capsule, the slip, and the key if you use one. Read in this order.

1. The date slip. If you're early, say, "We're opening early, and that's allowed," then keep the same order.
2. The shared note. Either of you may read it aloud. The other may pass, read in silence, or leave it folded.
3. The picture, then the caption. Either of you may pass on talking about it.
4. The letters, writer first. They name keep private, read aloud, or share later. Private stays with the writer. Read-aloud can be withdrawn, and the listener may pass. After a pass, the person the letter is for may read it in silence, or it stays folded. Nobody owes a summary.

Then use `journal/templates/revisit-then-now.md`. Then is the sealing: what you played, what you put in, how it seemed that night. Now is this opening, before you measure it. After that, what changed, a new memory, and what you'd like next. "Almost nothing" counts. Finish another day, or log the date and leave the page.

If one of you is absent and the slip doesn't allow opening alone, put the capsule back. Waiting is the ritual. "We were here and we waited," written on the outside, records the wait. It isn't an opening. Together later, keep the date or write a new one beneath it and leave the old date readable.

You're done when each piece you're willing to open has been read or passed, and the comparison page is started or left for later.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
**Short, about 20 minutes.** One shared note and a date. Both of you write the date. Write that you open it together, that either of you may ask to open it earlier, and that if one of you is away the capsule waits. Opening early is allowed. Slide the note into an envelope, clip the slip to the outside, and name the drawer. That's a complete capsule. Picture, key, and letters can stay out.

**Standard, about 90 minutes.** The sealing evening above. Date and rules, shared note, a picture and caption if you want them, the key back on its hook, the place said aloud, the seal. Say what is inside so the opening isn't a surprise inventory.

**Extended.** The standard evening, plus a letter from each of you. A paragraph counts, and so does a full page. Use `journal/templates/letter-page.md` if you want the ruled surface: sixteen lines, another sixteen if you continue, and a mark for keep private, read aloud, or share later. Fold the letter. Seal it if you want it sealed. If only one of you writes, the capsule holds one letter. A blank is a complete choice.

All three versions open in the same order.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
Address a letter to the other person, to yourself on the opening day, or to both of you, and put that in the first line. Mark private, read aloud, or share later, even on scrap paper. Leave unwritten any confidence you'd rather say aloud and then let go.

The shared note can be plain: who cooked, what you're in the middle of, a sentence you might want to hear later. On a heavy week, one honest line is enough, and so is something small. A complaint the other person will hear for the first time at the opening stays out.

Close the old note before you write Now, and leave a crossed-out date visible if you moved it. What you'd like next might be another capsule, one revised sentence, or nothing.

To change the date, sit down together and both write the new day. The person home alone leaves the paper alone. Wanting it sooner is a reason to ask for the key and open together. Wanting it later is a reason to move the paper.

If the opening feels thin, let it be thin. If a letter stings, say so in a sentence and leave the rest folded. You can come back, or the writer can take the page back.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
Three weeks will still surprise you. Eighteen months asks more of the slip, because lives move. One date per capsule. Two horizons means two capsules in the same drawer, each with its own paper.

On a call, each of you writes the date while you're still on the line and reads it back. Seal only what both of you have heard. The capsule lives in one house. Opening on a call counts as together only when the slip says so. Otherwise you wait for a shared room, and you rewrite the date when you're both there.

The first capsule stays until its date, a rewritten date, or an early opening you both accept. Sealing another the same night is a new attempt, and it counts when you both mean to do it.

Large paper helps if reading is hard. If a read-aloud is costly, trade pages and stay quiet. You can seal the short version away from home, then bring the capsule back to your own drawer. A later year gets a fresh then-versus-now sheet. Keep the old pages, and put any correction on a new sheet, dated.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They aren't you. The two sentences in quotation marks were written for this example.

On a Thursday in October the capsule is an envelope from the bill drawer. They both write 14 March, the wait, and the early-open rule, and they leave the alone-opening line blank. The back-door key goes back on its hook. Vale draws the orange kettle and captions it for both of them. Rowan adds one line to the note about late dinners, invented for this example: "The radiator knocks twice before it gives heat, and we wait for the second knock before we start the dishes." Vale adds the drafty window and leaves that sentence alone. No letters. The envelope goes in the battery drawer, slip clipped to the front.

In December Vale picks the key up and puts it back. The almost-opening stays an almost. On 14 March, Vale is still away. Rowan leaves the envelope where it is. Home again, they write 4 April under the old date and both initial the change. March stays legible.

On 4 April they read the slip first, then the note. Vale passes on the weeks away and doesn't owe a substitute story. They laugh at the kettle's spout. Vale's sentence, also invented for this example, follows the radiator line: "It was replaced in January, and I hadn't noticed I missed the knock until this page." Then is the bill drawer and the wait. Now is a quieter kitchen and a moved date. They make tea. The empty envelope stays with the slip.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Stay with one line before you make a theory of the year. The knock, the moved date, a letter someone passed on, an early opening that stayed ordinary. Talk about that if you want to. You can also wash the cups.

The note and the slip can live in Our Story or stay in the envelope. A private letter stays with the writer. A digital picture stays on your machine under the filename on the caption. If the day was flat, write "flat" when that word is accurate. If you waited because one of you was away, record the wait when you're together again. The closed capsule is that session. The opening gets its own lines.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Use one session log for the stretch, from sealing through opening, with the date range in the date field. Mark short, standard, or extended, a mood if you want one, a one-line intention, and initials if you want them. Mark the sealing done or paused. When you open, add a short dated note in the shared pages. Blank days in between stay blank.

Private pages are optional to share. Keep a letter, a caption, or a partner page in your own stack if the shared book should hold only what you both choose. Letters use `journal/templates/letter-page.md`. Captions use `journal/templates/memento-caption.md`. The long comparison uses `journal/templates/revisit-then-now.md`. A repeat gets its own pages. The old ones stay.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The date I could actually meet, and what I put into the capsule or chose to leave out
- A sentence I sealed, or the sentence I kept unwritten on purpose
partner_b:
- What would make an early opening welcome for me, and what would make me want the capsule to wait
- The letter I wrote, sealed, or skipped, and whether I want it read aloud when we open it
shared:
- The date on the paper, where the capsule lives, and the sentence we wrote about opening early or waiting
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: original-formulation. Sealed notes for a later day are an ordinary habit. This one is made at a table: a paper date you may rewrite, a key that stays in the house, a wait unless you agreed otherwise while sealing, a reading order, the right to pass on reading aloud, and a then-versus-now page.

See S2007. Schacter, Addis, and Buckner argue that imagining a future event uses memory's constructive machinery: imagining the future depends on much of the same neural machinery as remembering. Their constructive episodic simulation hypothesis says future simulation recombines details from the past, and the review says that hypothesis has support. The same review says further work was still needed, to test whether future simulations recombine elements from different episodes or retrieve fragments. That argument doesn't show that a pictured opening will happen, doesn't prove recombination, and doesn't show that this capsule works.

See G1999. Gollwitzer distinguishes goal intentions ("I intend to reach x") from implementation intentions ("When situation x arises, I will perform response y"). The date slip is the second form. The review describes a research program in which those if-then plans supported goal attainment in the domains studied. In that review, goal intentions had modest effects. They weren't useless. G1999 isn't a study of promises between partners, isn't a couples trial, and isn't proof that a date in this book will be kept. The if-then line names the day. It isn't a tested couple treatment.

Related experiences: 031 A Love Letter From the Future, 090 The Future Memory, and 096 The Next Chapter.

signatures.title: The Long Toast

prose_blocks.heading: In short
prose_blocks.text: Raise one unmatched glass for a year you can actually remember, leave a fuzzy year honest, and set a hope on the blank card for a year that has not arrived.

prose_blocks.heading: The hook
prose_blocks.text:
The jam jar doesn't match the diner tumbler, and the tumbler doesn't match the good glass you're slightly afraid to break. Line them up anyway. Each one stands for a year, or for an era you'd rather name than number. Seven is as long as the row gets. One glass is raised at a time, for a year you want to honor. At the far end, past the last base, a blank card waits for a year that hasn't arrived.

Most toasts float. To us. To the next one. To whatever the room seems to need. This one has to land. You tell one scene you can still see. You name one thing the other person did that you actually remember. Then you stop. If the year has gone fuzzy, the glass holds water and a sentence that says so. The speaker doesn't invent a memory to fill a glass.

prose_blocks.heading: Why it might matter
prose_blocks.text:
Years collapse in the retelling. A long stretch becomes "the busy time," and the busy time becomes a shrug you both recognize. The shrug can be fond and still leave the year unnamed. A scene is harder to counterfeit. A particular act, such as quarters in a palm, a bowl left on a counter, or a person who stayed in the car, gives the other something they can recognize as theirs.

Feeling appreciated and feeling appreciative were tied to responsiveness and maintenance in that research, and this toast wasn't the procedure studied (see G2012 in the notes). A precise memory isn't a treatment, and a row of glasses won't maintain a life by itself. What the shape can do is keep a compliment from hovering at "you are wonderful," which may be true and still too large to hold.

The card at the far end does a different job. Each of you may write one hope there. A hope isn't a promise the other person must keep. Hearing it isn't agreeing to carry it. That gap is what makes the sentence writable. A year you leave unturned is still an honest year. In this ritual, a skip is a finished turn.

prose_blocks.heading: Before you begin
prose_blocks.text:
Stay indoors, at a table where a row of glasses can live through the evening. The two of you are the guest list. You need unmatched glasses, up to seven, blank cards, and a pen. Water is enough. Alcohol is optional and not required. If either of you wants water, pour water and let the drink question end. A mug counts. A jam jar counts. If the glasses already match, borrow one odd cup so the years don't look like a set.

Set them side by side, each on its own base. Earlier years go left and later years go right, unless you pick another order before anyone lifts a glass. The blank card stays at the far end, past the latest year. These cards name years and lean on the glasses. Place cards belong to a different session. One glass is raised at a time.

You can stop well before seven. Three eras inside one calendar year can be the whole row: the first month, the move, last month. A long life together still stops at seven. Park an eighth year on a scrap, off the table, for another night. Don't fatten a thin memory so the line looks finished.

Each of you may propose a year or an era. It joins the row only when you're both willing to see it there. "Not that one" is a complete answer. A year on the table isn't a promise to toast it. Either person may skip when the turn arrives, and a skip gets no substitute story. The other person doesn't supply one, doesn't ask for a harder try, and doesn't stretch their own toast across the quiet.

A year from before you were a pair belongs only if the speaker remembers a scene they saw, or a telling they can repeat without decorating it. A mood about the other person's past isn't a scene. Call it fuzzy, or skip it.

Before the first raise, leave out a third person's secret, any subject you've already closed, and anyone's body used as a joke. If the picture would embarrass them, choose another or leave the glass down. A joke you'd both tell is welcome.

You may say you love them in the toast, if you mean it, and then stop. The ritual asks for no touch. A toast isn't consent to touch or sex. Either of you may end the evening after any year.

Pour the water. Leave the far card blank until the row is underway.

prose_blocks.heading: The experience
prose_blocks.text:
In the standard version, give the choosing about 15 minutes. Write each year on a small card and lean the card against its glass. Read the names once, in order, before any story attaches itself. If a name is only a mood, "the good year," sharpen it until you could point at a stretch of time, or take that glass off the table.

The lines below are the printable set. Copy them by hand if you aren't printing. Seven year cards can be small, about the size of a business card, so they lean. The future card should take two handwritten lines, about 4 by 6 inches, and it lies flat at the far end. The numbers mark the order you move down the row. A later number isn't a harder year. Any year you chose may sit on any line. The fuzzy rule, the skip, and the stop apply to every glass. The cards repeat them in different words so a glance can catch a speech before it grows a second act.

```cards
Year ________ | Glass 1. Fill in a year or an era. One scene you can still see, one thing the other person did, then stop.
Year ________ | Glass 2. A different year. One room and one remembered act. Skip if you can't see it, with no substitute story.
Year ________ | Glass 3. If this year is fuzzy, let the glass hold water and say so in a sentence. Don't invent the rest.
Year ________ | Glass 4. Ordinary time counts. Name one thing they did. Stop before a speech about the whole year.
Year ________ | Glass 5. Name an action you remember, not a trait. Put the glass back when you finish.
Year ________ | Glass 6. If the scene would embarrass them, leave this glass unraised. A skip needs nothing in its place.
Year ________ | Glass 7. Last year in your row. Same shape. Don't add another glass to keep the evening going.
Year that has not arrived | Each of you may write one hope. It isn't a promise the other person must keep. Read it aloud only if you both agree.
```

Toss a coin for who leads the first glass. Each glass offers a turn to each of you before anyone moves on. The leader goes first. The other person may then raise that same glass for a different scene, skip, or call the year fuzzy. On the next glass, the lead swaps. A skip spends the turn. It doesn't add time, and it doesn't ask the other person to speak in the gap.

On a turn, raise the glass and toast, leave it down and skip, or leave it down and say the year is fuzzy. Each choice ends the turn. The glass can keep its water either way.

A toast uses this shape, and then it ends.

One concrete scene. A room, a sidewalk, a kitchen at a known hour, something you could point at. "We were happy" is a caption, and a caption isn't a scene. If you can't see a place, use the fuzzy rule.

One thing the other person did that you can actually remember. A verb you could show with your hands: they passed you quarters, they left a bowl, they sorted screws, they waited in the car. "You were supportive" doesn't qualify. Name the act. If you aren't sure it happened, don't promote the guess. If two winters have fused, say so, and keep the detail you can stand behind. The speaker doesn't invent a memory to fill a glass.

A stop. Set the glass back on its spot, or say "That's the toast," and stop. No lesson for them to absorb, and no second story that starts "and another time."

If a year is fuzzy, the glass holds water and one sentence. "This year is fuzzy for me." That sentence is the turn. Don't follow it with the version that seems likely. Your partner doesn't fill in the room unless you ask.

The listener keeps still while the glass is up. A correction, or a competing story from the same stretch of time, stays unsaid. After the stop, "I heard you" is enough, and so is quiet. If you remember the day differently, keep your version unless the speaker wants one sentence afterward.

Stop when you've both been offered every glass, or when 90 minutes have passed. An unraised glass isn't homework. Don't slide a scrap-paper year into the row because the talk feels generous.

Then the far card. Each of you may write one hope for the year that hasn't arrived, in a single sentence. If it gives the other person a job, rewrite it until it asks nothing, or leave the line blank. "I hope we get a week with no errands" can stay. "You'll arrange the week" can't. "I hope I ask first" is about your own conduct, and it's still a hope, not a voucher. In the standard sitting, turn the card face down. Don't read it aloud.

You're done when every glass has been offered, skipped, called fuzzy, or left because the clock ended it, and each of you has had a chance to write or to leave the line empty. Nothing is tallied. A longer memory isn't a lead. A skip isn't a loss. There's no winner.

prose_blocks.heading: Three ways to play
prose_blocks.text:
The short version takes about 35 minutes and uses three glasses. Choose them in about 5 minutes. Each glass gets about 8 minutes total. If you both speak, split that time: one scene, one act, a stop. A fuzzy sentence or a skip still closes the turn. Spend the last 6 minutes writing the hopes, and leave them unread. Spare quiet is part of this version. A fourth glass is a different night.

The standard version takes about 90 minutes, with up to seven glasses, under the procedure above. You may both speak to one year when the scenes differ. 8 minutes a glass is a fair guardrail. If you're both toasting every year, stop at 90 minutes even if a glass remains. That remainder is a finished standard evening. Write the far card and don't read it.

The extended version takes about three hours. Keep the cap at seven, and give both turns room, including the quiet after a stop. Eat first. A pause in the middle belongs here. Make tea, and don't spend the break ranking what you've heard. After the row, read the far card aloud only if you both agree. If either of you wants the lines left on the paper, they stay, and the evening still counts. Each person reads their own hope. The listener doesn't improve it. Glad, unsure, and too heavy to carry are all whole answers. A plan, if you ever make one, waits for a later day when you both still want it. If the row ends early, you're done. Stay at the table if you like. Don't pad a thin year to use up the clock.

prose_blocks.heading: Going deeper
prose_blocks.text:
If a toast starts to annex the night, write the scene and the act on the year card first. Read that, then stop. A second sentence can wait for the journal or be crossed out.

After the stop, the listener may repeat the deed in one sentence and let the speaker edit it. "The bowl was in the evening." Keep it that short. It isn't another toast, and either of you may skip the check.

A heavy year can stand in the row when you both want it there. The shape stays: one scene, one thing they did, a stop. You don't owe an explanation, a repair, or proof that you got through it. If what shows up is a grievance you can't tell without making them small, skip. The glass is for a thing you remember, at a size they can hear.

A hope may include fear. "I hope next year is quieter than this one." That still assigns nothing. If writing it would sour the night, leave the line blank. A private copy of your own hope can live on a separate slip in your own notes. The far card holds the lines you're willing to leave where the other person might see them.

prose_blocks.heading: Variations and replay
prose_blocks.text:
An anniversary, New Year's, or an unmarked Tuesday will all hold the row. When you play again, choose a new line of years. Repeat a year only when the scene is new. If all you have is last time's story, skip that glass.

On a call, each of you sets a row at home and counts aloud so the year matches. Lift toward the screen, or leave the glass down and let the words carry it. Write the hope off camera. Read it only in the extended version, and only if you both agree.

If lifting hurts, point at the glass and speak. If standing is the hard part, stay seated. A tray on a couch is a fine sideboard. Juice, tea, or water in a mug marks a year as honestly as anything else. If a stronger pour is making the stories longer and less exact, switch that glass to water.

When seven would feel like a performance, use three glasses. When you both want a single year, one glass is a fair short cousin. Say so in the session line. Don't borrow extra years for the look of a longer life. With thin walls or someone asleep nearby, use a kitchen voice or read a written toast softly. Either of you may pause after a glass and finish another night. A paused row is a real session.

prose_blocks.heading: Examples
prose_blocks.text:
Rowan and Vale are fictional. They aren't you. They're here so the rules have somewhere to stand.

They could overfill seven glasses and still have years left over. They set five. Vale keeps two proposals off the table with "Not that one." Rowan keeps off the year of a move that still snarls. Nobody smuggles those years back in as color for a safer toast. The row is the year they met, a winter of night shifts, a hardware-store spring, one heavier year they're both willing to see, and a recent quiet year.

Rowan raises the jam jar. "The laundromat on Pine, the broken change machine. You had quarters. You handed me two and didn't make a thing of it. That's the toast." Vale almost adds that the dryer ate a sock, then lets the turn end.

Vale lifts the diner tumbler. "The kitchen around 6 a.m., under that miserable light. You left a bowl on the counter and a note that said to eat before I tried to be a person. You were already asleep." Vale stops there, without asking the bowls to come back.

The hardware-store spring falls apart in Rowan's hands. "Drawers of screws, and then I'm in a different year. This one is fuzzy for me." The green tumbler goes back full of water. Vale knows the likely aisle and leaves it unnamed.

The heavier year reaches Vale. "I'm leaving this one." Rowan had a Wednesday and a vending-machine coffee ready, and keeps both. There's no substitute story. The glass stays, and they move on.

For the quiet year Rowan raises a chipped cup. "Last October, the Sunday we fixed the lamp and then forgot to be impressive. You sat on the floor and held the shade so it wouldn't roll under the couch. That's the toast." They laugh. The laugh isn't a score.

On the far card Vale writes, "I hope you stop starting projects," then crosses it out. The line that remains is, "I hope we get one week next year with no house projects." The first was a job. The second is a hope, and Rowan doesn't have to deliver the week. Rowan writes, "I hope I ask before I assume you want a plan." That binds Rowan alone, and it still isn't a promise Vale can collect later. They turn the card face down, drink the water, and return the glasses to the wrong shelves, where those glasses already lived.

prose_blocks.heading: Afterward
prose_blocks.text:
Leave the year cards up while you clear the glasses, if you like the row you chose. Keep what you want and recycle the rest. The far card can go into a book you'll both open, into a private note, or into the trash once you've each seen your own line. Pick one, and skip the second ceremony.

If you talk, talk about which toast was easy to stop and which skip you're glad you used. There's no best glass. The next day, a single message can repeat the act you heard, when that would feel like attention. A plan born from a hope waits for an ordinary day when you both still want it. If the evening touched a closed subject, name it in a sentence and set it down. Washing the glasses can be the whole close.

prose_blocks.heading: Our Story
prose_blocks.text:
Write the date, the time, the place, which version you played, a mood if you want one, a one-line intention, and your initials if you want them. Mark the session done or paused. Private pages are optional to share. Keep a line in your own note if you'd rather the shared pages hold only what you both choose to put there. A later sitting gets its own lines. Two revisits are a pattern, and you can keep going after that.

```journal
session: date, time, place, version played, mood if wanted, intention, initials if wanted, done or paused
partner_a:
- The scene I raised a glass for, and the thing you did that I could actually remember
- A year I skipped or called fuzzy, and what I refused to invent
partner_b:
- A toast of yours I can still picture, or the silence I managed not to fill with a better story
- The hope I wrote for the year that has not arrived, and whether I wanted it read aloud
shared:
- What actually happened
- The line or moment worth keeping
- What we discovered
- What we might do next, if anything
revisit:
- Attempt, date, and what changed
- Then versus now
```

prose_blocks.heading: Notes
prose_blocks.text:
Classification: original-formulation. Raising a glass to mark a moment is an old custom. The capped row of years, the refusal to invent a memory, the skip with no substitute story, and the hope that binds no one are the formulation used here.

See G2012. Feeling appreciated and feeling appreciative were tied to responsiveness and maintenance in that research. This toast was not the procedure studied.

Related experiences: 026 The Appreciation Avalanche, 075 Our Greatest Hits, and 094 The Annual Reintroduction.
