prose_blocks.heading: Why this book exists
prose_blocks.text:
Familiarity is a gift and a trick. The person across from you can be the one you know best and still be slightly out of date in your mind, edited down to the stories you both tell without thinking. This book is a way to interrupt that editing. It is a library of experiences for two adults who already like each other and want the liking to stay awake.

Closeness, here, is not a grade. It is the ordinary miracle of being more accurately known, and of knowing someone else without rushing to improve them. Some of that happens in a 10-minute question. Some of it happens when you cook a strange meal, walk with your eyes closed, or say the appreciative thing you usually swallow. None of these is homework. None of them is evidence that a relationship was failing until a book arrived.

You can be silly in these pages. You can be precise, romantic, philosophical, or candid about desire. The tone assumes you are competent. You do not need to be fixed, diagnosed, or walked through your own life as if you have never had a feeling before. You also do not need to perform vulnerability on command. An invitation is not a debt.

The activities come from three places, and the book says which is which. Some are established practices or folk games. Some are those practices rebuilt for a couple who will actually do them on a weeknight. Twelve, numbered 097 through 108, were formulated for this project. That is a description of origin, not a claim that no one on earth has ever had a neighboring idea. Where research is useful, it is cited narrowly. Where a chapter is simply a good game, it is allowed to be a good game.

Use the book out of order. Use it again in five years, when the answers have moved. The point of writing in it is not to prove progress. The point is that a shared life is mostly unrecorded, and a few pages, kept, become a memoir you could not have planned in advance.

prose_blocks.heading: How to use this book
prose_blocks.text:
Start with the time you actually have. The indexes are there so you can choose in a minute, not after a summit about which chapter would be optimal.

There are six time shelves:

- **5–10 minutes — Quick Connections.** A question, a forecast, a specific thank-you.
- **10–20 minutes — Little Discoveries.** One story, one game round, one small ritual.
- **20–45 minutes — Meaningful Sessions.** Enough time to go past the first answer.
- **45–90 minutes — Deep Dives.** Museums, maps, letters, a full game.
- **90 minutes–3 hours — Full Experiences.** An evening with a shape.
- **Multi-day — The Long Game.** Notes collected in secret, missions, a week of small devotion.

Time is not the same thing as effort. A 40-minute talk on the couch can be low energy. A 15-minute dance in the kitchen is not. Each chapter separates the two.

You can also choose by appetite: laugh, discover, be a little more seen, feel chosen, talk about desire, make something, go somewhere, think about a life. Emotional depth is descriptive, not a ranking of your courage. Light is a legitimate choice on a hard day. Intense is a choice, not a destination you are supposed to reach.

Skip freely. The parts are neighborhoods, not stages. Revisit anything. Answers change, and the second time is often the more interesting one.

If you want to be surprised, use Surprise Us only after you both set the limits: time, energy, depth, and whether touch is welcome tonight. The paper method is in Surprise Us. A choice that falls outside your limits is not a choice. Draw again.

Keep one copy that you write in, if you like writing in books. Keep a clean copy if you want to read without your own past answers leaning on you. The companion journal, Our Story, is for the overflow: repeats, years, tickets, and the long record.

prose_blocks.heading: Three kinds of ideas
prose_blocks.text:
Every chapter wears one of four labels. Three of them describe origin. The fourth, mixed, means the hour borrows from more than one.

**Established.** A practice or game with a recognizable public life: a folk game, a well-known exercise, a research procedure described honestly. We say where it comes from and what it does not prove.

**Reimagined.** A familiar impulse rebuilt so two specific people can play it with rules, examples, and a way to stop. Most of the book lives here. A new frame is not a discovery of science.

**Original formulation.** The twelve chapters 097–108 were written for this project. Their twists are deliberate. We do not claim that no one else has ever invented a neighboring game.

**Mixed.** Used when a chapter openly combines a research finding or a practitioner tradition with a design of our own. The notes at the end tell you which sentence is which.

Research in this book is a lamp, not a leash. A study of strangers in a lab does not become a promise about your Tuesday. A good ritual does not need a citation to be worth doing. What it must not do is borrow the authority of a paper it does not have.

You will not find the famous list of thirty-six questions reprinted here. The research behind that popular script is described, and then the chapters go on to ask questions built for this book. You will also not be told that 4 minutes of eye contact produces love. Looking at someone you care about can be intimate, strange, and funny. That is enough of a reason to try it, and a more accurate one.

front_matter.title: Using this as a living memoir

prose_blocks.heading: Using this as a living memoir
prose_blocks.text:
The book is a guide and a place to keep what happened. Each chapter ends with a first-session record and two private pages of equal size, one for each of you, plus a shared page. The private pages are yours. You may read them aloud, copy a sentence onto the shared page, or never show them. The book will not assume.

Write the date. Write where you were if the place will matter later. Note which version you played: the short one, the ordinary one, the long one. Mood is optional. Completion can mean “we did it,” “we stopped halfway and that was right,” or “we postponed.”

On the shared page, prefer a few sentences of what actually happened over a stack of scores. Keep a line worth remembering: a phrase, a correction, a joke that will be obscure in a year and precious because of that. Leave room for a ticket, a sketch, or a caption. If nothing needs to happen next, “nothing” is a valid plan.

Repeats are part of the design. The same chapter in a different year is a new document. Use the revisit sheet when a chapter matters enough to compare. There is no maximum number of returns. Our Story, the companion journal, holds the extras so you are not forced to buy another copy of the whole book just to write the fourth attempt.

Once a year, if you want, read backward. Not to judge the relationship. To see what you were curious about, what you laughed at, and what you could not yet say. Call that evening The Chapters of Us. It is an invitation, not a holiday you can fail.

Here is a fictional example, from no one you know. Rowan and Vale, after a short appreciation game: “Vale wrote that Rowan always warms the mugs. Rowan had filed this under ordinary and was surprised to see it treated as a story. We kept the sentence. We did not keep a score.”

Your pages stay blank until you write them. Nothing in the printed book is pretending to be your life.

front_matter.title: How to start, stop, and stay willing

prose_blocks.heading: How to start, stop, and stay willing
prose_blocks.text:
Read this once. The chapters will remind you briefly. They will not reprint a lecture every time.

Either of you may pass on a prompt, trade it, shorten the session, or stop. Passing is a complete answer. You do not owe a reason, though you may want to say whether you are done for the night or done with one question only.

Agree on the ceiling before you begin: time, energy, and how personal you want the hour to be. If one of you wants light and the other wants deep, play the lighter version. Depth is not a prize.

For anything involving touch, privacy, sex, or a story that could affect someone who is not in the room, consent is specific and current. Choosing a card is not permission to be touched. Yesterday’s yes is not tonight’s yes. Either person can change a touch to words, or a sexual idea to a conversation about the idea, without the evening becoming a failure.

“Confession Without Consequence” and any cousin of it set a style of listening. They do not erase real consequences. If something disclosed involves harm, safety, or a decision that needs a sober conversation, leave the game and have that conversation. Curiosity is not a gag order.

Disagreement is an allowed ending. So is laughter. So is discovering that an exercise is not for you. Mark it, skip it, and pick another. The indexes exist so you never have to force the next page.

prose_blocks.heading: Surprise Us
prose_blocks.text:
Surprise is only fun inside a boundary you both meant.

Before you draw, agree on four filters:

1. Time shelf: one of the six, or a pair of neighboring shelves.
2. Energy: low, medium, or high.
3. Depth ceiling: light, personal, deep, or intense. Anything above the ceiling is out.
4. Touch: welcome, or not tonight. Chapters that involve touch drop out when the answer is not tonight.

prose_blocks.heading: Paper method
prose_blocks.text: Use the ID index at the back, or write eligible IDs on slips. Shuffle. Draw one. If it misses a filter, put it back and draw again. Two vetoes each, for any reason, and then the third eligible draw stands. A veto is not a debate.

prose_blocks.heading: Dice method
prose_blocks.text:
Count the eligible IDs. If you have fewer than twenty, number the slips and use a twenty-sided die, rerolling empties. If you have more, split the list into two piles and flip a coin for the pile, then number within it.

The digital selector, when you use the file that ships with this project, must apply the same filters before it chooses. It does not get to be more daring than you were.

Do not use Surprise Us to corner someone into a chapter they already refused this month. Refusal expires when that person says it expires.
